Idempotency check — return cached response on retry. var cached = await db.Idempotency.FindAsync(req.IdempotencyKey); if (cached != null ) return Results .Ok( JsonSerializer .Deserialize< ChargeResponse >(cached.Response)); // 2. Guard rails.

if (req.Amount <= 0) return Results .BadRequest( "amount must be > 0" ); if (req.PayerAccount == req.PayeeAccount) return Results .BadRequest( "payer == payee" ); // 3. Fraud gate — non-blocking above the 100 ms budget. var risk = await _fraud.ScoreAsync(req, ctx.Connection.RemoteIpAddress); if (risk.Decision == RiskDecision .Decline) return Results .StatusCode(402); // 4. Atomic double-entry write + outbox in ONE transaction.

await using var tx = await db.Database.BeginTransactionAsync( IsolationLevel .Serializable); var txnId = $"tx_{ Ulid.NewUlid() }" ; db.Entries.AddRange( new LedgerEntry { TxnId = txnId, Account = req.PayerAccount, Direction = Dir .Debit, Amount = req.Amount, Currency = req.Currency, CreatedAt = DateTime .UtcNow }, new LedgerEntry { TxnId = txnId, Account = req.PayeeAccount, Direction = Dir .Credit, Amount = req.Amount, Currency = req.Currency, CreatedAt = DateTime .UtcNow } ); // Outbox: same transaction as ledger, so an event is published iff the ledger commits.

db.Outbox.Add( new OutboxEvent { EventId = Guid .NewGuid(), Type = "charge.succeeded" , Payload = JsonSerializer .Serialize( new { txnId, req.Amount, req.Currency }) }); var response = new ChargeResponse (txnId, "succeeded" , req.Amount); // Persist idempotency-key → response so retries return the same result byte-for-byte. db.Idempotency.Add( new IdempotencyRecord { Key = req.IdempotencyKey, Response = JsonSerializer .Serialize(response), ExpiresAt = DateTime .UtcNow.AddHours(24) }); await db.SaveChangesAsync(); await tx.CommitAsync(); return Results .Ok(response); }); Notes on why this is correct: (a) The idempotency check is the first thing — before validation, before fraud scoring — so

retries are as cheap as possible. (b) The ledger uses Serializable isolation, which is the only level that guarantees no lost updates on concurrent writes to the same account. (c) The outbox insert lives in the same DB transaction as the ledger, so events are published if-and-only-if the ledger commits (this is the Transactional Outbox pattern). (d) The response is serialized into the idempotency row, so a retry returns the exact same JSON, including the same txnId . Real production code adds: currency conversion, tenant isolation, fee splits (interchange, PSP fee, GST), and a "charge status machine" (requires_capture → captured → refunded → disputed).

⚖️ Trade-offs, bottlenecks & likely follow-ups Where it actually breaks Hot merchant accounts — a big-box retailer during Black Friday concentrates writes on one ledger partition. Fix: shard by merchant_id + hour and sum sub-balances asynchronously, or use per-shard append with a periodic roll-up. Slow issuer — one bank's auth endpoint goes to 5-second latency and takes down your whole checkout. Fix: circuit breakers with per-issuer budgets, retry with a backup route, degrade gracefully to "manual review." Reconciliation drift — bank fee changes silently and your ledger drifts by paise per transaction until someone notices at month-end.

Fix: daily reconciliation is non-negotiable; a tolerance of ₹0.00 with rollup diff alarms. Consistency & the CAP question Payments are one of the few domains where you cannot trade consistency for availability . If your ledger disagrees with itself across replicas, you have created or destroyed money. Design accordingly: primary ledger on a strongly-consistent store (Aurora with sync replicas, or DynamoDB with strongly-consistent reads); the fraud store, feature store, and analytics can be eventually consistent because a stale fraud feature is only slightly worse, but a stale balance is catastrophic. Interviewer follow-ups (with crisp answers) Q.

How do you guarantee exactly-once payment processing? A. You don't at the network level; TCP retransmits and app-level retries are unavoidable. Instead you guarantee it at the application layer with an idempotency key on every mutating call and an idempotency table that has a unique constraint on the key. First write wins; retries return the cached response. The ledger itself is idempotent by virtue of the same key being written inside the same transaction. Q. Why not just update a balance column? A. Because a balance is a derived quantity. Storing it as ground truth means a bug can silently corrupt it and you can never reconstruct the truth.

Append-only entries give you a self-auditing record, mathematical invariants (sum of DR = sum of CR), and the ability to reconstruct any historical balance for disputes or regulator queries. Balance snapshots are a performance optimisation, not the source of truth. Q. What's the difference between authorization and capture? A. Authorization is a real-time "yes, this cardholder has funds and this isn't obviously fraud" — it places a hold, no money moves. Capture is "please turn this hold into a real charge," which triggers the merchant getting paid in the next settlement batch. Some flows auto-capture (e-commerce), some delay it (hotels, marketplaces). Q.

Why do refunds go back the same way, not the other way? A. Because the card network only knows how to route money in one direction — merchant → cardholder. A refund is technically a "negative capture" traveling the same rails: acquirer → network → issuer, credited to the same card. If the card has expired, most networks now support account-level fallback, but if not, the issuer contacts the cardholder to arrange a manual credit. Q. How does UPI settle in real-time when cards can't? A. Cards inherit a batch-clearing legacy from the 1970s. UPI was designed in 2016 on top of RBI's IMPS rails, which are 24×7 real-time gross settlement.

So the settlement happens synchronously as part of the transaction, not overnight. This is why UPI's chargeback timelines and fraud model differ meaningfully from card networks. Q. What's a chargeback vs a refund? A. A refund is merchant-initiated ("I agree to give the money back"). A chargeback is cardholder-initiated through their issuer ("I dispute this charge as fraudulent or not-as-described"). Chargebacks bypass the merchant entirely; the network claws money back and only then invites the merchant to submit evidence. Losing rate is tracked (Visa allows up to 0.9%) — go over and you get fined or dropped. Q. How do you handle a network partition mid-transaction? A.

Every payment has a definite issuer response — approved, declined, or timeout. On timeout, the safe default is to reverse locally and mark the transaction "unknown; do not retry automatically." A reconciliation job the next day matches against issuer records to determine truth and posts a correcting entry. The point is: no state stays ambiguous past 24 hours; either the reconciliation confirms it or you create a compensating entry. 🗣️ Interview cheat sheet 30-second pitch: "A payment system moves money between a payer and a payee via a 4-party model — cardholder, merchant, acquirer, issuer — with a PSP fronting the API and a card network switching between banks.

The core primitives are idempotency keys so retries never double-charge, an append-only double-entry ledger so every balance is derivable and every batch sums to zero, and separation of authorization (real-time hold) from capture and settlement (nightly batch or real-time in UPI). Fraud sits inline under 100 ms; 3DS shifts chargeback liability; the outbox pattern makes downstream integrations reliable; and daily reconciliation with bank files closes the loop. Everything PCI-scoped is behind a tokenization vault so the rest of the system never touches raw card numbers." Numbers to quote UPI: 20 billion txns/month (Aug 2025), ~7,500 avg TPS, peak 10× that.

Auth latency budget: < 2 s end-to-end , fraud < 100 ms . Idempotency window: ≥ 24 hours . PCI DSS Level 1: > 6M card txns/year . Merchant payout: T+1 / T+2 for cards; near-real-time for UPI. Chargeback threshold: 0.9% (Visa) before penalties. 5 talking points that win the round Name the 4-party model + PSP + network explicitly on the whiteboard. Interviewers love it. Draw the outbox pattern — it separates "ledger is truth" from "webhooks are eventually consistent." Show a ledger table with DR + CR rows summing to zero. This is the single most senior-signal thing you can draw. Distinguish auth / capture / settlement — they run on different clocks and different rails.

Call out reconciliation as a first-class subsystem, not an afterthought. It's what makes the system self-healing. ❓ FAQ — your follow-up questions Questions asked about this topic No follow-up questions yet — ask one about this topic and it'll be logged here with a compact answer. 📚 Sources Stripe Docs — PaymentIntents API (lifecycle, idempotency, 3DS) UPI — Wikipedia (NPCI switch, PSP model, transaction volumes) Modern Treasury — Double-entry accounting for financial software NPCI — UPI Product Overview Stripe — Idempotent requests reference PCI Security Standards Council Generated by the design-research skill · researched via web search · open via localhost

System Design · Interview Prep Distributed Cache Millions of ops per second, sub-millisecond reads, and — when a node dies at 3 AM — only 1/N of the keys move, not the whole cluster. The design pattern behind Redis Cluster, Memcached at Facebook, and DynamoDB DAX. 🎯 Scenario 🧑‍🎓 Laymen 📋 Requirements 🏗️ Architecture 🎬 Animation 🔍 Deep-dive 🧮 DSA ☁️ AWS 💻 C# code ⚖️ Trade-offs 🗣️ Cheat sheet ❓ FAQ 📚 Sources 🎯 Real-world scenario What we're building & where it's used We're designing a distributed in-memory cache — the fast, forgetful layer that sits between the application and the database.

It's the class of system that powers Redis Cluster, Memcached (as used at Facebook, Twitter, Netflix, Reddit, Pinterest), Amazon ElastiCache, Amazon DynamoDB DAX, and TAO's cache tier at Meta . When a service needs to look up a user profile, a session, a feed page, or a hot product listing, the answer should come back in under 1 ms , not the 20–50 ms of a database round trip. A distributed cache lets us keep terabytes of hot data in RAM across dozens of nodes, spread the load evenly, survive individual node failures, and add or remove nodes at 2 AM without moving 99% of the keys.

Interviewers reach for this scenario because it forces you to defend the two hardest ideas in distributed systems in one conversation: partitioning (how do you split N keys across M servers?) and fault tolerance (what happens when one of those servers dies?) . The right answer — consistent hashing with virtual nodes, plus replication and gossip-based failure detection — is the same pattern that underpins Amazon Dynamo, Cassandra, Riak, Discord's chat routing, and Akamai's CDN. Nail it here and you can defend it everywhere.

🧑‍🎓 In laymen terms The whole thing, without any jargon Imagine a giant library that gets so busy that every question — "where's the biography section?" "what time do you close?" — takes three minutes for a librarian to answer because they have to walk to the archive every single time. So the library builds a whiteboard right at the front desk and writes down the most-asked answers. When someone asks a common question, the receptionist just glances at the whiteboard and answers in two seconds. That whiteboard is a cache . Now imagine the library grows to ten million visitors a day . One whiteboard isn't enough — even reading it becomes a queue.

So we buy twenty whiteboards, line them up along the wall, and split up the answers: whiteboard 1 holds anything about music, whiteboard 2 holds anything about history, whiteboard 3 holds cookbooks, and so on. Now twenty receptionists can answer twenty questions at the same time. This is partitioning — splitting the data so each server only handles its slice. Here's the tricky part. What if we simply said "take the question, count the letters, divide by 20, use the remainder to pick a whiteboard" ? It works — until one whiteboard breaks, or we buy a new one. Suddenly the formula changes to "divide by 19" or "divide by 21" , and almost every answer is now on the wrong whiteboard .

All the librarians spend the whole night rewriting everything. Chaos. The clever fix is to arrange the whiteboards in a circle around the room, and give each question a spot on that circle based on its name. When someone asks a question, they just walk clockwise from their spot until they hit a whiteboard — that one holds their answer. If a whiteboard breaks , only the questions that pointed to that whiteboard have to move; they simply walk one more step clockwise to the next one. If we add a whiteboard, it only takes over a little slice of the circle. This trick — the hash ring — means node changes only move a small fraction of the data, never the whole library. Two more tricks.

First, we write each answer on three whiteboards in a row, so if one dies mid-shift the next one already knows. That's replication . Second, the whiteboards constantly whisper to each other — "still here! still here!" — and if one goes silent for a few seconds, the others agree it's out and someone else takes over its slice. That's failure detection . Put it all together and you get the cache behind WhatsApp's contact lookups, Netflix's viewer sessions, Instagram's feed, and Uber's driver locations — all served from RAM in about a millisecond.

📋 Requirements & scale Requirements and back-of-the-envelope math Functional requirements GET(key) , PUT(key, value, ttl) , DELETE(key) — the classic three. Values up to a few MB (typically KB); millions of keys per node. TTL-based expiration + eviction policy (LRU, LFU, or TinyLFU). Add/remove nodes online without downtime. Optional: pub/sub, transactions, scripting, atomic counters (Redis-shaped) vs pure KV (Memcached-shaped). Non-functional requirements Latency : p99 GET < 1 ms within a datacenter, p999 < 5 ms. Throughput : 100K – 1M ops/sec per node; cluster scales linearly. Availability : 99.99% — survive single-node failures without losing recent writes (with replication).

Rebalancing cost : adding/removing a node moves ~1/N of keys, not all of them. Consistency : usually eventual (cache is by nature a best-effort projection of the database). Write QPS ~50 – 100 K writes/sec ~10:1 read:write ratio. Total dataset ~1 TB hot working set Common for a large web/service tier. Per-node RAM ~64 – 256 GB Modern cache instances: r7g.4xlarge / r6i.8xlarge. Nodes needed ~10 – 20 primaries + replicas 1 TB ÷ 64 GB usable per node. The two anchor facts to memorise for the interview: consistent hashing moves only K/N keys on a scale event (vs 100% for modulo), and virtual nodes are what make the distribution actually smooth — a single point per node gives you a bad, lumpy ring.

🏗️ High-level architecture How the pieces fit together The client library (or a proxy) holds the hash ring — a sorted structure mapping positions on a 2 32 or 2 64 ring to physical nodes, with each node placed at ~100–200 virtual positions. When the app calls GET(user:42) , the client hashes the key (MurmurHash3 / xxHash), walks the ring clockwise, and finds the first virtual node — that's the primary. The next N-1 unique physical nodes clockwise are the replicas. The client sends the request straight to the primary (one network hop). Writes go to the primary and are replicated to the followers either synchronously (strong-ish) or asynchronously (fast).

A background gossip protocol (Redis Cluster's approach) or a central configuration store like ZooKeeper (Memcached-mcrouter's approach) keeps everyone's view of "which nodes are alive" in agreement. When a node dies, gossip flags it "PFAIL → FAIL", the cluster elects one of its replicas as the new primary, and the ring position transparently switches over. When you add a node, it slots into the ring at 100–200 virtual positions and pulls in the small slice of keys that now belong to it — a bounded, background migration.

Partitioning — why modulo hashing fails The naïve approach is node = hash(key) % N . It's dead simple and O(1). It also utterly breaks the moment N changes: going from 10 nodes to 11 causes roughly 10/11 of all keys to relocate.

Every ounce of hot cache goes cold in one autoscale event. That's why every real distributed cache uses consistent hashing : nodes and keys both hash onto a large ring (typically 2 32 or 2 64 positions), and each key is owned by the first node clockwise. Adding or removing a node touches only the arc between the neighbour and the affected node — statistically K/N keys vs modulo's ~K. 2. Virtual nodes — smoothing the ring Placing a physical node at a single ring position gives you terrible variance: one node might own 30% of the keyspace, another 3%. The fix is to hash each physical node's identity multiple times (e.g.

hash("n2#0"), hash("n2#1"), ..., hash("n2#199") ) and place all those virtual positions on the ring. Two benefits: (1) load smooths out — with ~100–200 vnodes per physical, the largest node owns roughly 1.05× the average vs 2–3× without vnodes; (2) when a node dies, its arc is broken into ~200 pieces which get absorbed by many neighbours instead of doubling the load on a single unlucky one. 3. Replication — what happens when a node dies Each key is stored on the primary and the next N-1 unique physical nodes clockwise (walking past virtual duplicates). With N=3 you survive one full node loss without data loss and any single-node loss without unavailability.

Replication can be: Async (Redis default) — write acknowledged after primary; replicas catch up in ~ms. Small window of data loss on primary crash, but sub-ms writes. Sync — write acknowledged only after M replicas ack ( WAIT M timeout in Redis). Safe but slower. Quorum (Dynamo-style, N/W/R) — the client picks W (write quorum) and R (read quorum). If W + R > N you get read-your-writes; typical picks are N=3, W=R=2. On failure, gossip detects the dead node in ~5 s. One of its replicas is elected primary (via a mini-Raft or gossip vote), the ring's owner-of-that-slot flips to the new primary, and clients transparently retry through the client library.

Meanwhile the cluster spawns a hinted handoff or a fresh replica to restore N=3. 4. Rebalancing — the migration protocol When you add node N6, it registers on the ring at ~200 vnode positions. Each of those positions "steals" the arc between itself and the counter-clockwise neighbour. The cluster runs a slot migration in the background: for each stolen slot, N6 pulls keys from the old owner (Redis Cluster uses CLUSTER SETSLOT + MIGRATE ). During migration the old node keeps serving while the new one is filling up; when the arc is fully moved, a single atomic slot handoff switches ownership. This is why cluster resize is a bounded, background operation — the app never sees a stampede. 5.

Fault tolerance — gossip, quorum, and self-healing Every node picks a few random peers every second and exchanges a heartbeat table (Cassandra, Redis Cluster, Dynamo all do this). If node A hasn't seen a heartbeat from B in timeout , A marks B "PFAIL" (probably failed) and gossips this. When a quorum of nodes agree, B is marked "FAIL" and failover triggers. This decentralised approach avoids the single-point-of-failure of a central coordinator, at the cost of a few-second detection window. For tighter windows you use ZooKeeper or etcd to hold the membership authoritative — that's what Memcached-mcrouter and Twemproxy do. 6.

Cache patterns — the four you have to know Cache-aside (lazy loading) — app checks cache; on miss, reads DB, writes back. Simplest, most common. Downsides: cold-start latency and thundering herd on cache expire. Read-through — cache library owns the "on miss, fetch from DB" logic. Cleaner abstraction, but couples cache and DB. Write-through — writes hit cache and DB synchronously. Strong consistency, slower writes. Write-back / write-behind — writes hit cache; async flush to DB. Blazing writes, risk of data loss on crash. 7. Hot keys, thundering herd, and stampedes Two failure modes that always come up: Hot key — e.g. a viral tweet's like-count. Every request slams one physical node.

Fix: replicate hot keys to multiple nodes (client picks randomly), or use request coalescing — the first miss fetches, everyone else waits. Thundering herd on TTL expiry — a hot key expires; 10K threads simultaneously miss and hit the DB. Fixes: probabilistic early recomputation (refresh at expected miss time − ε), lease-based single-flight (Facebook's Memcached leases — first miss gets a lease token, everyone else waits), or stale-while-revalidate (return stale data while asynchronously refreshing). 8. Eviction policies When RAM fills up, something has to go. The classics: LRU — evict the least-recently-used. O(1) with a hashmap + doubly-linked list. Good general default.

LFU — evict the least-frequently-used. Better for stable working sets, worse for changing ones. TinyLFU / W-TinyLFU (Caffeine's default) — sketch-based frequency admission + LRU eviction. State-of-the-art hit ratio. TTL — evict on time, not on space. Complementary to the others. Random / FIFO — trivial, surprisingly close to LRU for uniform workloads (Redis allkeys-random ). 🧮 The DSA behind it Data structures & algorithms Most of the difficulty in a distributed cache is picking the right structure , not implementing anything clever.

Here's the shortlist an interviewer will probe: Where Structure / algo Why Complexity Ring lookup: hash(k) → node Sorted map (TreeMap / std::map / SkipList) or sorted array + binary search O(log V) to find the first vnode ≥ hash(k). V = total vnodes. O(log V) Key hashing MurmurHash3, xxHash, or SipHash Fast (~GB/s), well-distributed, non-cryptographic. Avoid MD5 (slow). O(len(k)) Alternative: bucketed lookup Jump consistent hashing Google's O(1)-memory algorithm; zero data structure, just an arithmetic recurrence. Downside: buckets must be numbered 0..N-1 (no arbitrary keys).

O(log N) time, O(1) space Alternative: rendezvous hashing Highest Random Weight (HRW) For each key, compute hash(k, node_i) for all nodes; pick the max. Simpler than a ring, better distribution, but O(N) per lookup. O(N) LRU eviction HashMap + doubly-linked list O(1) get + move-to-front + evict-from-tail. O(1) LFU eviction HashMap + min-heap of frequencies, or "buckets by count" Approximate LFU (Redis) uses a decaying counter — cheaper than a real heap. O(log N) / O(1) approx TinyLFU admission filter Count-Min Sketch + LRU Reject writes for keys unlikely to be re-accessed; retain the truly hot ones.

O(1) Membership check "is key possibly here?" Bloom filter Cut DB reads for keys we know are absent. O(k) hashes Failure detection Gossip protocol / SWIM Constant background bandwidth, ~log N rounds to reach everyone. SWIM adds indirect probes for accuracy. O(log N) convergence Anti-entropy across replicas Merkle trees Compare root hashes first, drill down only where they differ. Bandwidth proportional to divergence, not dataset size. O(log N) I/O to detect divergence Conflict resolution (multi-writer) Vector clocks / LWW timestamps Vector clocks detect concurrent writes; LWW just takes the highest timestamp (simpler, lossy).

O(N) size for N nodes The two that always come up: the sorted-map ring lookup (why not a hash-of-hashes? because you need "next node ≥ x", which is a range query), and Merkle trees for repair after a node comes back — a beautiful log-scale trick that syncs terabytes without shipping terabytes. ☁️ AWS implementation Mapping the design to AWS Component AWS service Why Managed cache cluster ElastiCache for Redis (cluster mode enabled) Consistent hashing across 16,384 slots, primary + up to 5 replicas per shard, Multi-AZ failover in ~15 s.

Deployment shape: an ElastiCache Redis Cluster with 10 shards × 3 nodes (1 primary + 2 replicas per shard) across 3 AZs. AWS partitions the 16 384 hash slots evenly across the shards — that's their form of consistent hashing (technically slot-based : slot = CRC16(key) mod 16384 ). When a primary dies, ElastiCache promotes a replica within ~15 s, updates DNS, and the client library refreshes topology. To scale, you add a shard — ElastiCache moves ~1/N of the slots to the new shard online, no downtime. 💻 C# implementation A minimal, correct consistent-hash client in C#.

It maintains a sorted map of virtual node positions → physical nodes , looks up "the first vnode ≥ hash(key)" with a binary search, and supports adding/removing nodes online. This is the trickiest part of a real client library — the network I/O is the easy bit. // ConsistentHashRing.cs — virtual-node ring with binary-search lookup using System.Collections.Concurrent; using System.Security.Cryptography; using System.Text; public sealed class ConsistentHashRing < TNode > where TNode : notnull { private readonly int _vnodesPerNode; private readonly SortedDictionary< uint , TNode > _ring = new (); private uint [] _sortedHashes = Array.Empty< uint >(); private readonly ReaderWriterLockSlim _lock

= new (); public ConsistentHashRing( int vnodesPerNode = 150) => _vnodesPerNode = vnodesPerNode; public void AddNode( TNode node) { _lock.EnterWriteLock(); try { for ( int i = 0; i < _vnodesPerNode; i++) _ring[Hash( $"{node}#{i}" )] = node; _sortedHashes = _ring.Keys.ToArray(); // already sorted (SortedDictionary) } finally { _lock.ExitWriteLock(); } } public void RemoveNode( TNode node) { _lock.EnterWriteLock(); try { for ( int i = 0; i < _vnodesPerNode; i++) _ring.Remove(Hash( $"{node}#{i}" )); _sortedHashes = _ring.Keys.ToArray(); } finally { _lock.ExitWriteLock(); } } // The primary owner of `key` = first vnode clockwise from hash(key) public TNode GetNode( string key) { _lock.EnterRead

Lock(); try { if (_sortedHashes.Length == 0) throw new InvalidOperationException( "empty ring" ); var h = Hash(key); var ix = Array.BinarySearch(_sortedHashes, h); if (ix < 0) ix = ~ix; // insertion point if (ix == _sortedHashes.Length) ix = 0; // wrap around return _ring[_sortedHashes[ix]]; } finally { _lock.ExitReadLock(); } } // The next N unique physical nodes clockwise — for replication.

public List< TNode > GetNodesForReplication( string key, int replicationFactor) { _lock.EnterReadLock(); try { var result = new List< TNode >(replicationFactor); var seen = new HashSet< TNode >(); var h = Hash(key); var ix = Array.BinarySearch(_sortedHashes, h); if (ix < 0) ix = ~ix; for ( int step = 0; step < _sortedHashes.Length && result.Count < replicationFactor; step++) { var node = _ring[_sortedHashes[(ix + step) % _sortedHashes.Length]]; if (seen.Add(node)) result.Add(node); // skip virtual-duplicate } return result; } finally { _lock.ExitReadLock(); } } // Fast, well-distributed 32-bit hash. MurmurHash3 would be even better; MD5 is used for clarity.

private static uint Hash( string key) { Span< byte > buf = stackalloc byte [16]; MD5.HashData(Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(key), buf); return BitConverter.ToUInt32(buf); } } // ---- Wiring it up as a cache client ---- public sealed class DistributedCacheClient { private readonly ConsistentHashRing < string > _ring = new (); private readonly ConcurrentDictionary< string , ICacheNode> _connections = new (); private const int N = 3; public async Task< string ?> GetAsync( string key) { var nodes = _ring.GetNodesForReplication(key, N); foreach ( var id in nodes) // try primary, fall through on failure { try { return await _connections[id].GetAsync(key); } catch (NodeUnavailableException) { continue ;

} } return null ; // all replicas down } public async Task PutAsync( string key, string value, TimeSpan ttl, int writeQuorum = 2) { var nodes = _ring.GetNodesForReplication(key, N); var tasks = nodes.Select(id => _connections[id].PutAsync(key, value, ttl)).ToList(); int acked = 0; while (tasks.Count > 0 && acked < writeQuorum) { var done = await Task.WhenAny(tasks); tasks.Remove(done); if (done.IsCompletedSuccessfully) acked++; } if (acked < writeQuorum) throw new QuorumException(acked, writeQuorum); } } What to point out in an interview when walking through this: (1) GetNodesForReplication skips virtual-node duplicates via the seen set — otherwise you'd "replicate" the key to the same physi

cal node three times; (2) writes use a WhenAny quorum loop so the call returns as soon as W replicas ack, not after all N; (3) reads try replicas in ring order so a single dead node just adds a few microseconds; (4) the ReaderWriterLockSlim keeps GET lock-free-ish under load — writes to the ring (rare) block; reads (billions) don't. In production you'd swap MD5 for MurmurHash3/xxHash and use ImmutableSortedDictionary for lock-free reads. ⚖️ Trade-offs, bottlenecks & likely follow-ups Scaling bottlenecks The first bottleneck is hot keys — no amount of consistent hashing helps if 40% of all requests target one key on one shard.

The fix is hot-key replication (put the same key on multiple shards, client picks randomly) or request coalescing in the client. The second is network — a single Redis shard on a c7g.4xlarge can push ~2 Gbps; beyond that you're fanning out across shards. The third is memory fragmentation — Redis's jemalloc allocator can end up with 20–30% wasted RAM under heavy churn; sizing needs a safety margin. Consistency trade-off Cache is fundamentally an AP system (CAP). We accept eventual consistency: a write may take a few ms to propagate to replicas, and cross-region replication is asynchronous.

If your app needs read-your-writes, you either use tunable quorum (W=R=2, N=3, so W+R>N) or read from the primary only. The trickiest bug in this space is cache-DB consistency — updating both non-atomically causes stale reads. The idiomatic fix is write-through or delete-then-DB-write (invalidate first) rather than update-then-update . Follow-ups you should expect Why consistent hashing and not just hash(k) % N ? Modulo hashing moves almost all keys when N changes (going from 10→11 relocates ~10/11 of the ring). Consistent hashing moves only ~K/N.

That's the difference between "add a node in the afternoon" and "add a node at 2 AM Sunday." Why virtual nodes? Doesn't one hash per node work? One point per node gives you dreadful variance — the largest shard can end up 2–3× the average. With ~100–200 virtual points per physical, the largest shard is only ~1.05× average. Vnodes also spread the recovery load: on a failure, the dead node's arcs get absorbed by many neighbours instead of doubling one. What happens when a cache node dies mid-request? Gossip flags PFAIL → FAIL in ~5 s. A replica is promoted primary via a mini-election. Client library retries the in-flight request against the next replica in the ring.

Meanwhile a fresh replica is spun up to restore N=3. All told, availability blip is a few seconds and no data is lost (assuming N ≥ 3 with quorum writes). How do you keep the cache in sync with the source DB? Two patterns. Write-through — every DB write goes through the cache client, keeping them coupled. Invalidation — the DB (via CDC / Kafka / Debezium) emits change events; a consumer deletes affected cache keys. Facebook's mcsqueal does the second at scale. The rule to memorise: delete, don't update — an invalidation is idempotent, an update-write can race.

What's the thundering-herd fix for a hot key expiring? Three viable answers: (1) single-flight / lease — first miss gets a "recomputing" lease, everyone else waits; (2) probabilistic early refresh — some fraction of requests before TTL trigger a background refresh; (3) stale-while-revalidate — return stale data instantly, refresh in background. Alternatives to a hash ring? Jump consistent hashing (Google, 2014) — O(1) memory, O(log N) time, arithmetic-only, no data structure. Downside: buckets are 0..N-1, not arbitrary. Rendezvous hashing (HRW) — hash(k, node) for every node, take the max. Slightly better distribution, O(N) per lookup.

Maglev (Google) — populates a fixed table with permutations; O(1) lookup, minimal disruption. Pick based on cluster size and lookup budget. How do you handle a cache-DB consistency race? Classic race: thread A reads DB, thread B writes DB and deletes cache, thread A writes stale value to cache. Fixes: (1) double-delete pattern (invalidate before AND after DB write, with a small delay); (2) versioned writes (only overwrite cache if incoming version > stored); (3) Facebook's lease tokens — cache hands out a lease on miss; only a client with the current lease can populate that key.

🗣️ Interview cheat sheet 30-second pitch: "I'd partition keys with consistent hashing on a 2³² ring using ~150 virtual nodes per physical node — that gives smooth distribution and moves only ~K/N keys on any scale event, versus 100% for modulo. Each key is replicated to the next N-1 unique physical nodes clockwise, with tunable N/W/R quorum. A gossip protocol detects node failures in ~5 s, promotes a replica, and rebalances only the affected arc. Cache-DB consistency uses delete-on-write invalidation via a CDC stream. Hot keys get single-flight leases to prevent stampedes.

On AWS this is ElastiCache Redis Cluster or DAX in front of DynamoDB." N=3 replicas with W=R=2 gives read-your-writes and 1-node fault tolerance. Gossip: heartbeat every 1s, fail after ~5s, failover ~15s (ElastiCache). 5 talking points that win the round Consistent hashing + vnodes — the pair, not just one. Vnodes are what make it actually work. K/N keys move — quote this fraction; it's the whole reason for the technique. Quorum N/W/R — W+R>N gives read-your-writes; picks are workload-dependent.

Failure detection is gossip, not a coordinator — no SPOF, ~5s convergence. System Design · Interview Prep Distributed File System Storing exabytes across thousands of failing machines — how GFS, HDFS, Colossus & Ceph split metadata from data to hit high throughput and durability. 🎯 Scenario 🧑‍🎓 Laymen 📋 Requirements 🏗️ Architecture 🎬 Animation 🔍 Deep-dive 🧮 DSA ☁️ AWS 💻 C# code ⚖️ Trade-offs 🗣️ Cheat sheet ❓ FAQ 📚 Sources 🎯 Real-world scenario What we're building & where it's used A distributed file system (DFS) presents a single logical namespace of files and directories that is physically spread across thousands of commodity machines.

To the application it looks like one giant disk; underneath, every file is chopped into large blocks, replicated or erasure-coded across many servers, and served in parallel. This is the storage substrate that big-data and cloud platforms are built on. The canonical family: Google File System (GFS, 2003) — the paper that started it all, built to store the web crawl and index for Search. HDFS — the open-source clone at the heart of Hadoop, powering analytics at nearly every large enterprise. Colossus — Google's GFS successor (2010) that removed the single-master bottleneck and now underpins Search, YouTube, Drive, Gmail, and all of Google Cloud (Cloud Storage, BigQuery, Filestore).

Ceph — the open-source unified store (object + block + file) used by OpenStack clouds and on-prem fleets. And the cloud managed services: Amazon S3 (object), EFS / FSx (file), and Azure Data Lake Storage . Companies build these because a single machine — no matter how big — cannot hold petabytes, cannot serve millions of concurrent readers, and will fail. The DFS turns a fleet of cheap, unreliable disks into one reliable, high-throughput, effectively-infinite volume. As the Colossus team puts it: "at Google scale, hardware is failing virtually all the time — not because it's unreliable, but because there's a lot of it." The DFS's whole job is to make that failure invisible.

🧑‍🎓 In laymen terms A movie studio's giant film archive spread across three warehouses Old movies were kept on long spools of film in metal cans. If a studio made hundreds of films every year, one warehouse couldn't hold them all — and a single fire could wipe out a century of cinema in one afternoon. So the big studios came up with a smart plan. First, they'd take each long film and cut it into shorter reels that fit into standard-sized cans. Then, for every single can, they'd make three identical copies and store them in three different warehouses across the country.

Finally, they kept a master index at the head office — a big book that says "Reel 4 of Casablanca is in Warehouse A shelf 12, Warehouse B shelf 5, and Warehouse D shelf 88." Now imagine you want to watch a movie. The studio doesn't hand you the whole thing from one warehouse — that would be slow. Instead, the head office tells five delivery trucks to pick up different reels from different warehouses at the same time , and you get the whole film almost instantly because everyone was pulling in parallel. If Warehouse B burns down tomorrow, no problem — the head office sees the gap, and quietly asks a fourth warehouse to make new copies from A and D. You never even notice.

That's exactly the trick behind the storage powering Dropbox , Google Drive , YouTube , and Netflix . Your holiday photo isn't sitting on one hard drive somewhere; it's chopped into small pieces, copied to three different buildings, and any two of them can still give you back the photo perfectly. So even though the hard drives break every single day — thousands of them — you never lose a single picture of your dog. 📋 Requirements & scale Requirements and back-of-the-envelope math Functional requirements Create / open / read / write / delete files within a hierarchical namespace (directories). Store very large files (GB → TB) and stream them efficiently.

Append (and in GFS, atomic concurrent record append ) — the dominant write pattern for logs and datasets. Return the locations of a file's data so clients can read directly from the machines that hold it. Non-functional requirements (the ones that shape the design) Durability — survive disk, machine, and rack failures with essentially zero data loss (target ~11 nines for S3-class systems). High throughput over low latency — optimized for large sequential scans, "even at the cost of latency" (GFS). Batch/analytics, not interactive random I/O. Availability — no single point of failure in the data path; fast automatic recovery.

Horizontal scalability — add machines to add capacity and bandwidth linearly. Consistency — a defined, well-understood model (not necessarily strict POSIX). Capacity estimation (a Colossus-scale cluster) Quantity Estimate Reasoning Cluster capacity ~1 exabyte (10¹⁸ B) A single Colossus cluster scales to exabytes over tens of thousands of machines. Machines 10,000–100,000 nodes Commodity servers, ~12–24 disks each. Block / chunk size 64 MB (GFS) · 128 MB (HDFS) Large blocks amortize seek cost and shrink metadata (see below). Metadata per block ~150 bytes HDFS NameNode rule of thumb — so 1 EB / 128 MB ≈ 8 billion blocks ⇒ ~1.2 TB of metadata.

This is exactly why a single in-memory master eventually breaks. Replication factor 3× (hot) or EC (10,4) ≈ 1.4× (cold) 3 copies tolerate 2 failures; Reed-Solomon (10,4) tolerates 4 failures at 1.4× overhead. Raw : usable ratio 3:1 with replication 1 EB usable ⇒ 3 EB of raw disk. EC cuts this to ~1.4 EB. Per-chunkserver read ~80–100 MB/s GFS benchmark ≈ one disk's throughput; aggregate scales with node count. Aggregate read throughput 10s of GB/s → TB/s GFS hit 583 MB/s across 342 nodes; since the master is off the data path, read bandwidth scales with the number of chunkservers.

The number to volunteer: "Metadata is tiny per block but the block count is what limits a central master — roughly 150 bytes × billions of blocks. That's the pressure that pushed GFS's single master to Colossus's distributed, BigTable-backed metadata." 🏗️ High-level architecture How the pieces fit together The single most important idea in the whole design: separate the control plane (metadata) from the data plane (bytes) . A client first asks the metadata service "which machines hold the blocks of this file?" — a small, cheap lookup. It then streams the actual data directly to and from the storage nodes , never routing bulk bytes through the metadata server.

This keeps the metadata node off the hot path, so read/write bandwidth scales with the number of storage nodes rather than being throttled by one coordinator. In GFS/HDFS terms: the Master / NameNode owns the namespace and the block→location map; the Chunkservers / DataNodes store the blocks and talk to clients directly. Storage nodes send periodic heartbeats (every 3s in HDFS) carrying block reports; if the master misses heartbeats for ~2 minutes it declares the node dead and re-replicates its blocks elsewhere. Writes are chained through a replication pipeline so a block flows node→node→node and is only acknowledged once all replicas have it.

Control plane (metadata) Data plane (bytes, direct) Replication pipeline Heartbeat / block report The read path, step by step Client asks the metadata service for the block handles and replica locations of /data/logs.txt at a given offset. Metadata service returns the block IDs and the set of storage nodes holding each replica (sorted by network proximity). Client connects to the nearest replica and streams bytes directly — the metadata node is now out of the loop. Client caches the block→location map briefly so subsequent reads skip the metadata round-trip.

The write (append) path Client asks the metadata service to allocate a new block; it picks replica nodes (rack-aware) and grants one replica a lease making it the primary . Client pushes the data to all replicas in a pipeline (A→B→C), decoupled from control flow to use full network bandwidth. Client sends the write request to the primary; the primary assigns a serial order and forwards it to secondaries. Once all replicas acknowledge, the primary acks the client. Any failure ⇒ client retries; the write is atomic only when all replicas succeed.

🔍 Component deep-dive Why blocks are huge (64–128 MB) A giant block size is a deliberate, load-bearing decision. First, it slashes metadata volume : at ~150 bytes of metadata per block, using 128 MB blocks instead of 4 KB OS pages reduces the number of metadata entries by ~30,000×, letting a single master's RAM hold the map for petabytes. Second, it amortizes disk seeks — for a workload of large sequential scans, one seek then a long streaming read is near-optimal disk behavior. Third, it lets a client hold a persistent TCP connection to a chunkserver and do many operations against the same block.

The cost: small files waste space and create hot blocks — DFSs are explicitly not built for millions of tiny files. The metadata bottleneck and how Colossus fixed it GFS used a single master holding all metadata in memory, with an operation log + periodic checkpoints for durability. This is beautifully simple and keeps metadata operations fast and strongly consistent — but it caps the cluster at whatever one machine's RAM and CPU can serve, and it's a recovery bottleneck. Google hit this wall (notably storing Search metadata).

Colossus replaced the single master with a horizontally scalable metadata service: Curators handle control operations and store the file-system metadata in BigTable (itself built on Colossus — a neat bootstrap). This "allowed Colossus to scale up by over 100× over the largest GFS clusters." HDFS took a different route to the same problem: HDFS Federation (multiple independent NameNodes, each owning a slice of the namespace) plus NameNode HA (an active/standby pair sharing an edit log via a quorum journal, with automatic failover). Replication, rack-awareness, and re-replication The default is 3 replicas .

Placement is rack-aware : HDFS puts two replicas on one rack and a third on a different rack. This balances two forces — keeping two copies close is cheap for the write pipeline's bandwidth, while the off-rack copy survives a whole-rack failure (a failed top-of-rack switch or PDU). When a node dies (missed heartbeats), the master notices its blocks are under-replicated and schedules re-replication from surviving copies to restore the factor of 3 — this background healing is what delivers durability despite constant hardware failure. Erasure coding for cold data 3× replication costs 200% overhead.

For colder data, systems switch to Reed-Solomon erasure coding : split data into k blocks, compute m parity blocks, and store all k+m . A common choice is RS(10,4) (used in Facebook's HDFS): 10 data + 4 parity survives any 4 simultaneous failures at only 1.4× overhead — versus needing 5× replication for the same fault tolerance. The trade-off is reconstruction cost : rebuilding one lost block requires reading k other blocks and doing math, which burns CPU and cross-node network. That's why EC is used for cold/archival data while hot data stays replicated for cheap reads and fast recovery.

Ceph & CRUSH — placement with no lookup table at all Ceph takes a radically different tack on the metadata bottleneck for data placement : it stores no central block→location map at all. Instead, the CRUSH algorithm (Controlled, scalable, decentralized placement) computes which OSDs (storage daemons) hold an object from the object's ID and a cluster map. Any client can calculate the location independently — zero lookups, no directory to become a chokepoint.

Ceph's Monitors maintain the authoritative cluster map; its MDS serves only POSIX filesystem names/inodes for CephFS (not data placement); and everything sits on RADOS , the underlying object store that also exposes S3-compatible object and RBD block interfaces. Consistency model These systems deliberately relax POSIX. GFS guarantees that a successful record append is written at least once atomically, but concurrent writes to overlapping regions can leave "consistent but undefined" data — the client is expected to tolerate duplicates and use checksums/record boundaries.

HDFS is simpler: write-once, read-many with append; a file has a single writer and readers see data only after a block is fully written/closed. The lesson for interviews: the file-system semantics are co-designed with the workload — append-mostly, large-scan analytics — rather than trying to be a general POSIX disk. 🧮 The DSA behind it Data structures & algorithms A DFS is a surprisingly rich bag of data structures. The namespace is a tree (or a flat hash map of full-path → inode, as GFS actually uses to avoid per-directory locking). The block map is a hash table from block-ID → replica set.

Durability of metadata comes from a write-ahead log (edit log) plus periodic checkpoints (fsimage) — the same pattern databases use. Data integrity relies on checksums (CRC32C) stored per block sub-chunk so silent disk corruption ("bit rot") is caught on read. And the heart of durability math is Reed-Solomon coding over a Galois field. Write-ahead log + checkpoint Metadata durability (edit log, fsimage) O(1) append; O(n) replay on recovery Survive master crash without losing recent ops; checkpoint bounds replay time. Consistent hashing / CRUSH Ceph data placement O(1) compute, no lookup Clients compute location; adding nodes moves minimal data; no central map. Reed-Solomon erasure code Cold-data durability Encode O(k·m); decode O(k²) per stripe Tolerate m failures at (k+m)/k overhead — far cheaper than replication. CRC32C checksums Per-block integrity O(block size) Detect silent corruption on every read; trigger repair from a good replica.

Heartbeat + failure detector Master ↔ storage nodes O(nodes) per interval Timeout-based liveness; drives re-replication and load balancing. Lease / primary election Write ordering per block O(1) Serializes concurrent mutations to a block without a global lock. Merkle-tree / scrubbing Background integrity (Ceph, S3) O(n) scan Continuously verify replicas match; detect & heal divergence. ☁️ AWS implementation Mapping the design to AWS On AWS you rarely build a DFS from scratch — you consume one of three managed families depending on the access pattern. The concepts map cleanly onto the components above.

DFS component AWS service Why Object store (S3-style, HTTP GET/PUT) Amazon S3 The canonical exabyte object store — 11 nines durability via replication across ≥3 AZs, flat key namespace, erasure-coded internally. Use for data lakes, backups, static content. POSIX shared file system (NFS) Amazon EFS Elastic, multi-AZ NFS mounted by many EC2/Lambda clients at once — the "shared network drive" use case. High-performance / specialized FS Amazon FSx (Lustre, NetApp ONTAP, Windows FS) FSx for Lustre gives HPC-grade throughput (100s GB/s) backed by S3 — the closest managed analog to a parallel DFS like GFS/HDFS.

Hadoop / HDFS workloads Amazon EMR (+ EMRFS on S3) Runs actual HDFS on the cluster's local disks, or EMRFS to treat S3 as the HDFS-compatible file system (decoupling storage from compute). Metadata / catalog DynamoDB / AWS Glue Catalog Scalable key-value metadata — the role BigTable plays for Colossus. Block storage (single-attach) Amazon EBS Network-attached block volumes — the RBD/D-server analog for a single instance. Membership / coordination Internal (S3 control plane) · self-managed ZooKeeper on EMR Leader election, config, and liveness — the heartbeat/lease machinery.

Deployment story to tell: "For analytics I'd decouple storage from compute — land raw data in S3 (durable, cheap, erasure-coded), catalog it in Glue , and run EMR /Spark or Athena against it via EMRFS. If a job needs a POSIX shared mount I'd use EFS ; for HPC-scale throughput, FSx for Lustre linked to the same S3 bucket. This mirrors the Colossus philosophy: a single durable storage pool underneath, many compute engines on top, control plane separate from data plane." 💻 C# implementation The two ideas most worth coding for an interview are (1) the metadata service that maps a file to its blocks and their replica locations, and (2) the durability math of Reed-Solomon-style erasure coding.

Here is a compact, idiomatic sketch of a NameNode-style metadata service plus the rack-aware placement and a simple XOR parity (RAID-4 style, the intuition behind Reed-Solomon). // ---- Metadata service: the control plane (NameNode / Master / Curator) ---- public sealed record BlockId ( long Value); public sealed class BlockInfo { public BlockId Id { get ; init ; } // replica locations, ordered by network proximity to the writer public IReadOnlyList < string > Replicas { get ; init ; } = Array .Empty< string >(); } public sealed class MetadataService { private const long BlockSizeBytes = 128L * 1024 * 1024; // 128 MB (HDFS default) private const int ReplicationFactor = 3; // path -> ordered

list of blocks that make up the file private readonly Dictionary < string , List < BlockId >> _fileToBlocks = new (); // blockId -> where its replicas live private readonly Dictionary < BlockId , BlockInfo > _blocks = new (); private readonly object _lock = new (); private long _nextBlockId = 1; private readonly IPlacementPolicy _placement; public MetadataService ( IPlacementPolicy placement) => _placement = placement; // WRITE control-op: allocate a new block and pick rack-aware replicas. public BlockInfo AllocateBlock ( string path) { lock (_lock) { var id = new BlockId (_nextBlockId++); var replicas = _placement. ChooseReplicas (ReplicationFactor); // e.g.

2 same-rack + 1 off-rack var info = new BlockInfo { Id = id, Replicas = replicas }; _blocks[id] = info; (_fileToBlocks. TryGetValue (path, out var list) ? list : _fileToBlocks[path] = new ()). Add (id); return info; // client now streams bytes DIRECTLY to these nodes } } // READ control-op: return block layout so the client reads direct from storage nodes. public IReadOnlyList < BlockInfo > GetBlockLocations ( string path) { lock (_lock) { if (!_fileToBlocks. TryGetValue (path, out var ids)) throw new FileNotFoundException (path); return ids. Select (id => _blocks[id]). ToList (); } } // Heartbeat handler: a dead node's blocks become under-replicated -> schedule repair.

public IEnumerable < BlockId > OnNodeDead ( string node) { lock (_lock) return _blocks.Values . Where (b => b.Replicas. Contains (node)) . Select (b => b.Id) . ToList (); // caller re-replicates each from a surviving copy } } // ---- Durability math: XOR parity (RAID-4) — the intuition behind Reed-Solomon ---- // Store k data blocks + 1 parity block = tolerate ANY 1 lost block for 1/k overhead.

public static class XorParity { public static byte [] ComputeParity ( IReadOnlyList < byte []> dataBlocks) { int len = dataBlocks[0].Length; var parity = new byte [len]; foreach ( var block in dataBlocks) for ( int i = 0; i < len; i++) parity[i] ^= block[i]; // XOR fold across all data blocks return parity; } // Reconstruct the ONE missing block by XOR-ing every surviving block (incl. parity).

public static byte [] Reconstruct ( IReadOnlyList < byte []> survivingBlocks) { int len = survivingBlocks[0].Length; var rebuilt = new byte [len]; foreach ( var block in survivingBlocks) for ( int i = 0; i < len; i++) rebuilt[i] ^= block[i]; // XOR is its own inverse return rebuilt; } } XOR parity tolerates only a single failure; real systems use Reed-Solomon (e.g. RS(10,4)) over a Galois field to survive m simultaneous losses. In production you'd reach for a battle-tested library rather than hand-rolling the field arithmetic — Jerasure or ISA-L (C/C++), or in .NET wrap ISA-L via P/Invoke; Backblaze also open-sourced a clean Java Reed-Solomon implementation worth reading.

The C# above is deliberately the intuition , not the production coder. ⚖️ Trade-offs, bottlenecks & likely follow-ups The metadata server is the classic bottleneck. A single master (GFS/HDFS) is simple and strongly consistent but caps namespace size at one machine's RAM and is a recovery risk. Fixes: HDFS Federation + HA (active/standby with quorum journal), or Colossus's fully distributed metadata in BigTable. Interviewers love to push here — be ready to explain why the single master survived so long (it's off the data path, so it only handles lightweight control ops) and what finally broke it (block-count growth). Small-file problem.

Huge blocks + per-block metadata means millions of tiny files explode metadata and waste space. Mitigations: pack small files into container formats (HAR, SequenceFile, Parquet), or use an object store with a flat namespace. Durability vs cost vs recovery speed. 3× replication = fast reads & simple recovery but 200% overhead; erasure coding = ~40% overhead but expensive, network-heavy reconstruction. The standard answer: replicate hot data, erasure-code cold data, and place replicas rack-aware so no single failure domain loses everything. Consistency vs performance.

Strict POSIX (fsync semantics, random overwrite, byte-range locking) is expensive at scale, so DFSs relax to write-once/append-mostly with at-least-once record append. Know the CAP framing: metadata operations are usually CP (consistent, may pause during failover); the data path favors availability and throughput. Q: Why is the block size so large (64–128 MB) instead of a normal 4 KB page? To shrink metadata (fewer block entries fit the whole map in the master's RAM) and to amortize disk seeks for large sequential scans. The cost is wasted space and hot blocks for small files — which is why a DFS isn't for millions of tiny files.

Q: How do you avoid the single master being a single point of failure? Persist metadata with a write-ahead edit log + periodic checkpoint; run active/standby with automatic failover (HDFS HA over a quorum journal); or eliminate the single master entirely — shard metadata across many servers backed by a scalable KV store (Colossus/BigTable) or compute placement algorithmically with no central map (Ceph/CRUSH). Q: How is data integrity guaranteed against silent disk corruption? Per-block CRC32C checksums verified on every read; background scrubbing continuously re-verifies replicas. A checksum mismatch triggers repair from a healthy replica or erasure-coded reconstruction.

Q: Why keep the metadata service off the data path? So aggregate read/write bandwidth scales with the number of storage nodes rather than being throttled by one coordinator. The client does one cheap lookup, then streams bytes directly to storage nodes — GFS scaled reads to 583 MB/s across 342 nodes precisely because the master isn't in the byte stream. 🗣️ Interview cheat sheet 30-second pitch: "A distributed file system stores one logical namespace across thousands of failing machines.

The key move is separating the control plane — a metadata service that maps files to large 64–128 MB blocks and their replica locations — from the data plane , where clients stream bytes directly to storage nodes. Blocks are replicated 3× (rack-aware) or erasure-coded ~1.4× for cold data; heartbeats detect failures and trigger background re-replication. GFS pioneered it with a single master; HDFS cloned it; Colossus removed the master bottleneck by sharding metadata into BigTable; Ceph computes placement with CRUSH and needs no central map at all." Numbers to quote Block size: 64 MB (GFS) / 128 MB (HDFS) ; metadata ≈ 150 B/block .

Replication: 3× (tolerate 2 failures) vs RS(10,4) = 1.4× overhead, tolerate 4 failures. Per-node read ≈ 80–100 MB/s ; GFS scaled to 583 MB/s over 342 nodes . Colossus: 100× metadata scaling over GFS; single cluster ≈ exabytes , tens of thousands of machines. Heartbeat every 3s ; dead after ~2 min of silence (HDFS). S3 durability target: 11 nines across ≥3 AZs. 5 talking points that win the round Control plane / data plane split — the reason it scales; metadata off the hot path. Large blocks — shrink metadata + amortize seeks; explain the small-file trade-off. Failure is the norm — heartbeats, re-replication, checksums, background scrubbing.

Replication vs erasure coding — hot vs cold data; overhead vs reconstruction cost. Evolution — single master (GFS/HDFS) → sharded metadata (Colossus) / CRUSH (Ceph); know why each step happened. ❓ FAQ — your follow-up questions Questions asked about this topic No follow-up questions yet — ask one about this topic and it'll be logged here with a compact answer. 📚 Sources A peek behind Colossus, Google's file system — Google Cloud Blog (2021): distributed metadata, Curators, D servers, BigTable, control/data-plane split. t: DNS: UDP vs TCP — System Design
x: That "one tiny lookup" happens trillions of times a day — Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1 alone answers on the order of two trillion queries daily. The protocol has to be blindingly fast, work through firewalls, survive packet loss, and now — under DNSSEC and IPv6 — carry payloads that no longer fit in a single UDP datagram. The classic interview question is: "Why does DNS use UDP? When does it switch to TCP?" The honest answer is DNS is hybrid : UDP on port 53 for the fast path, TCP on port 53 for the reliable path, and modern encrypted transports (DoT on 853, DoH on 443) layering TLS on top of TCP.

t: DNS: UDP vs TCP — System Design
x: The nuance is where a strong candidate wins: the 512-byte limit isn't really 512 anymore (EDNS0 pushed it to 1232/4096), the TC ("truncated") bit is the fallback signal, and RFC 7766 made TCP support mandatory for every DNS implementation in 2016. Real products this shapes: Cloudflare 1.1.1.1 , Google 8.8.8.8 , AWS Route 53 , Quad9 9.9.9.9 , every recursive resolver at every ISP, and the DNS-over-HTTPS clients built into Chrome, Firefox, iOS 14+, and Android 9+. Every one of them speaks both UDP and TCP — and they had to, the moment DNSSEC signatures made 512 bytes obsolete.

You need a phone book that maps names to addresses. That's exactly what DNS is: the phone book of the internet. Every website has a friendly name ( instagram.com ) and a number-y address ( 157.240.19.174 ) that computers actually use. Before your phone can open Instagram, it has to look up that address. Now imagine you had two ways to ask the phone book. Way #1 is a quick shout across a room : "Hey, what's Priya's address?" — someone shouts back instantly.

t: DNS: UDP vs TCP — System Design
x: It's fast, but if the answer is longer than one breath ("Priya lives at 42 Baker Street, Apartment 3B, London, and here's the doorbell code, the parking pass, and…") the shouter might not finish before running out of air. Way #2 is a proper phone call : you dial, say hello, ask the question, listen carefully to a long answer, and hang up. It's slower to set up — but it can carry a long, complicated reply reliably. DNS uses Way #1 (called UDP) by default because most answers are tiny — just an address.

t: DNS: UDP vs TCP — System Design
x: But when the answer is too big to shout in one breath (say, when the phone book is signed and stamped for security, or when a company is telling you which mail servers to use, and there are twelve of them), the phone book replies " my answer got cut off — call me back on the phone ". Your computer then dials up (that's TCP ) and asks the question again, patiently, over a real connection. Why bother with the shouting at all? Because speed matters enormously . Every time you tap a link, tap a photo, or open an app, one of these lookups happens. A single ISP handles millions of these per second — imagine placing a phone call for every single one. The building would collapse.

x: 🏗️ High-level architecture The full DNS resolution flow — and where TCP shows up A DNS query is not a single-hop conversation; it's a recursive walk through a tree of authorities. Your stub resolver (the OS library on your device) sends a query to a recursive resolver , usually run by your ISP, your VPN, or a public resolver (1.1.1.1, 8.8.8.8, Route 53 Resolver). The recursive resolver either returns a cached answer, or does the actual walk on your behalf: root name servers → TLD (.com, .in, .io) name servers → authoritative name server → answer . Every one of those hops is a UDP-first, TCP-fallback exchange.

The designers picked UDP for three reasons that still hold up: fewer packets , no per-connection state , and lower latency . A UDP query is exactly two datagrams — one out, one back. A TCP query requires a three-way handshake (SYN, SYN/ACK, ACK), then the query and response, then a four-way close (FIN, ACK, FIN, ACK) — roughly seven to nine packets on the wire.

t: DNS: UDP vs TCP — System Design
x: When you're a public resolver answering 100k+ QPS, that difference multiplies into gigabits of overhead. The stateless nature is arguably even more important. On UDP the server holds nothing between queries — no socket, no kernel buffer, no ESTABLISHED row in the connection table. That means a single Route 53 or BIND box can absorb bursts and DoS scans without collapsing under connection-tracker pressure. Cache hits (which dominate real traffic) are essentially "receive 40 bytes, memcpy an answer, send 60 bytes" — the kernel path is almost free. The 512-byte myth (and how EDNS0 fixed it) RFC 1035 §4.2.1 famously capped a DNS UDP payload at 512 bytes . Interviewers love this number.

t: DNS: UDP vs TCP — System Design
x: But the honest answer is that 512 has been effectively dead since RFC 6891 (EDNS0) in 2013. EDNS0 adds a pseudo-record called OPT to the additional section of every query, and inside OPT the client advertises how large a UDP response it can accept. Common values: 4096 — the RFC 6891 recommendation. Works on clean networks; risks IP fragmentation on hostile paths (firewalls dropping fragments). 1232 — the DNS Flag Day 2020 operator consensus. Chosen so a packet + IPv6 headers fits inside the 1280-byte IPv6 minimum MTU, guaranteeing zero fragmentation. 1400 / 1410 — Ethernet-frame-safe midpoint some operators used before Flag Day 2020.

t: DNS: UDP vs TCP — System Design
x: So when a modern interviewer asks "what's the UDP DNS limit", the correct answer is: 512 without EDNS0, typically 1232 in practice today, up to 4096 if you're aggressive — and if the answer still doesn't fit, we retry over TCP . The TC (truncated) bit and fallback Every DNS message has a 16-bit flags field in its header. Bit 6 is TC — "message was truncated". Any server sending a UDP response that would exceed the client's advertised buffer must set TC=1 and send whatever fits (or nothing meaningful). The client's rule is simple: if TC=1, discard, open a TCP connection, resend the same query . That's the entirety of the fallback protocol.

Zone transfers — always TCP When a secondary/replica name server needs to pull the current state of a zone from a primary, it does an AXFR (full transfer) or IXFR (incremental transfer, RFC 1995) — always over TCP. A zone can be megabytes of records; UDP simply can't carry it reliably. The primary streams records in order over a single TCP connection, and the secondary applies them atomically. This is the one case in DNS where UDP was never even attempted.

x: DNSSEC — why every large response is signed DNSSEC (RFC 4033/4034/4035) adds cryptographic signatures to DNS records so a resolver can verify that an answer wasn't spoofed. The signatures ( RRSIG ), public keys ( DNSKEY ), and denial-of-existence records ( NSEC / NSEC3 ) all live inline in DNS responses. The result: a DNSSEC-signed response is routinely 1–4+ KB , which blows straight past the 512-byte limit and even past the 1232-byte Flag-Day limit for larger zones. DNSSEC is why TCP fallback matters more today than it did in 1990. RFC 7766 — TCP is mandatory now Before 2016, some minimalist DNS implementations only supported UDP.

t: DNS: UDP vs TCP — System Design
x: RFC 7766 ended that: TCP support is now mandatory for every general-purpose DNS implementation — authoritative, recursive, and stub alike. RFC 7766 also blesses long-lived TCP connections (with edns-tcp-keepalive , RFC 7828), pipelining multiple queries on one TCP connection, and out-of-order responses matched by DNS Message ID. Modern encrypted transport — DoT and DoH DoT (DNS over TLS, RFC 7858) runs DNS inside TLS on port 853. It hides the query content from on-path observers and adds server authentication via TLS certificates. DoH (DNS over HTTPS, RFC 8484) goes further and disguises DNS as ordinary HTTPS traffic on port 443, indistinguishable from a web request.

x: Cloudflare, Google, Quad9, and Apple's iCloud Private Relay all offer DoH endpoints. Both are TCP-based (DoH is technically HTTP over TCP or QUIC). The latency cost is real — TLS handshake ≈ +2 RTTs on cold connect — but the privacy win is why they exist, and connection reuse amortises the handshake across thousands of subsequent queries. Why not just always use TCP? Because at scale, the numbers are brutal. A UDP query costs ~1 KB of in-flight memory. A TCP connection needs a socket, a send/receive buffer (typically 8 KB minimum each in Linux defaults), sequence number state, a slot in the connection tracker, and a file descriptor.

The UDP + spoofable source IP combination is a gift to attackers. A 40-byte query with a spoofed source can trigger a 3+ KB DNSSEC response aimed at the victim — a 60× amplification.

t: DNS: UDP vs TCP — System Design
x: Mitigations: rate-limiting (BCP 38 source-address filtering at ISPs), Response Rate Limiting (RRL) on authoritative servers, and the mandatory TCP fallback that RFC 7766 gives you (TCP requires a completed handshake, so you can't spoof the source). Fragmentation. A UDP response over 1500 bytes gets fragmented at the IP layer, and many firewalls silently drop fragments. That's why DNS Flag Day 2020 pushed everyone down to a 1232-byte EDNS0 buffer — enough for most answers, still small enough to never fragment on modern paths. Path MTU variance. IPv6 minimum MTU is 1280, IPv4 is 68 (theoretical) / 576 (practical).

t: DNS: UDP vs TCP — System Design
x: The 512-byte legacy limit was chosen precisely so a full DNS message would always survive a 576-byte MTU minus IP+UDP headers. Modern EDNS0 sizing is an ongoing operational compromise. Cache poisoning. Because UDP has no handshake, an attacker who can guess the DNS transaction ID and source port can inject a forged response. Kaminsky's 2008 attack made this practical. Mitigations: source port randomization , DNS cookies (RFC 7873), and — the real fix — DNSSEC-signed responses that clients can verify. Likely follow-up questions Q: Isn't DNS switching to TCP-only these days? No. UDP is still the default for every recursive+authoritative exchange.

t: DNS: UDP vs TCP — System Design
x: TCP-only would multiply memory and CPU cost per query 5–10×. What is shifting is client-to-resolver: DoT and DoH (both TCP-based) are increasingly the default at the browser and OS layer for privacy. Behind the resolver, UDP-first is still the norm. Q: How does the resolver decide the EDNS0 buffer size? Operator config, usually 1232 today (Flag Day 2020) or 4096 on clean private networks. It's advertised in every query's OPT record; if truncation still happens, the resolver may drop the advertised size on retry and eventually fall back to TCP. Q: Why is AXFR always TCP, but IXFR often UDP-tried first? IXFR (RFC 1995) sends only the diff since the secondary's last serial.

t: DNS: UDP vs TCP — System Design
x: If the diff is small enough to fit in a UDP packet, the primary may reply on UDP as an optimization. If the diff is bigger — or the primary chooses — the secondary falls back to TCP. AXFR is always TCP because a full zone is virtually always too big for UDP. Q: How does DoH differ operationally from DoT? DoT is easy to identify (port 853) and easy to firewall. DoH looks like ordinary HTTPS (port 443) — same TLS handshake, same ALPN as web traffic — so a network operator can't distinguish DNS traffic from a browser fetch without deep inspection. That's a privacy win for users and a governance headache for enterprise networks.

Negative-cache TTLs kick in so the resolver doesn't hammer a broken authoritative. Q: What did DNS Flag Day 2020 actually change? It got the major open-source servers and public resolvers (BIND, Unbound, PowerDNS, Cloudflare, Google, Quad9) to advertise 1232 bytes as their default EDNS0 buffer — eliminating IP fragmentation in the common path and pushing large-answer traffic to TCP where fragmentation is not an issue. 🗣️ Interview cheat sheet The 30-second pitch: "DNS is hybrid.

System Design · Interview Prep Memory Leaks in .NET Core / .NET Framework Yes, a garbage-collected runtime can still leak. Real production war stories, the five root causes, the retention-path detection workflow, and before/after C# fixes you can defend on a whiteboard. 🎯 Scenario 🧑‍🎓 Laymen 📋 Requirements 🏗️ Architecture 🎬 Animation 🔍 Deep-dive 🧮 DSA / GC ☁️ AWS 💻 C# code ⚖️ Trade-offs 🗣️ Cheat sheet ❓ FAQ 📚 Sources 🎯 Real-world scenario Why "we have a GC" is not the full story Every .NET engineer eventually gets paged for the same story: pods are healthy, latency looks fine — and then Kubernetes starts killing them every eight hours with an OOMKilled (137) .

CPU is idle, GC counters look calm, but the working set climbs 30 MB every hour until it hits the container limit. The garbage collector is doing its job perfectly; the problem is that something we wrote is still pointing at objects we no longer want . This is the .NET memory leak: not unreachable-and-unfreed (the C/C++ definition), but reachable-but-unwanted . The GC only reclaims objects nothing can point at. If a static field, an event delegate, a running timer, a captured closure, or a native handle keeps a reference alive, the object stays — and the graph it pins with it. These leaks have real names and real bug trackers behind them.

Simon Timms's 2016 "You're using HttpClient wrong" post is the reason IHttpClientFactory exists. Microsoft's ASP.NET Core memory doc walks through a PhysicalFileProvider native-handle leak filed as dotnet/aspnetcore#844 . StackExchange's Nick Craver blogs have chronicled cache-without-eviction bugs that grew Stack Overflow's servers by gigabytes overnight. The interview question isn't "what is a leak" — it's "tell me about one you found, and how" . 🧑‍🎓 In laymen terms The bathtub with a hidden drip Imagine your app is a bathtub .

Water flowing in is memory your program uses; the drain at the bottom is the janitor — in .NET we call it the garbage collector — who pulls the plug and lets the water out whenever the tub gets full. Most of the time this works beautifully. You fill the tub, the janitor drains it, you fill it again. Nobody thinks about plumbing. A memory leak is what happens when someone quietly leaves a rubber ducky floating in the tub. The janitor comes to drain, sees the ducky, and thinks, "someone still wants this" — so the water around the ducky stays. Every hour a new ducky gets left behind. The tub slowly fills, and eventually the whole thing overflows onto the floor.

In production, "overflows onto the floor" is a server crash at 3 AM. The tricky part is that the duckies aren't obviously garbage. They're things like a phone number you handed to a friend — you're done with the friendship, but the friend still has your number written on a slip of paper. As long as that paper exists, the janitor won't touch it. In code, that "slip of paper" is often an event subscription , a static cache , or a timer that nobody turned off . Real products fight this every day.

Instagram, Netflix, Stack Overflow, Azure services — every large .NET service has a story of a small piece of forgotten code that ate a few kilobytes per request until, three days later, machines started falling over. The fix is almost never "add more RAM"; it's find the slip of paper and tear it up . Here's the everyday example: imagine you sign up for a magazine and forget to cancel. Every month a new issue arrives. Your mailbox slowly fills. The postman keeps delivering — from his side, everything is working. That's exactly what a subscription-that-was-never-cancelled looks like inside a .NET app.

📋 Requirements & scale What "healthy" looks like — and the numbers to quote A leak conversation in an interview has a very specific rhythm: state the symptom, then quote the number, then propose the tool. Here are the numbers an interviewer expects you to volunteer. Setting / threshold Value Why it matters Large Object Heap (LOH) threshold 85,000 bytes Any allocation ≥ 85 KB skips SOH and lands on the LOH, which is only collected in Gen 2 and (historically) not compacted. A single byte[85_000] per request destroys throughput. Default HttpMessageHandler lifetime 2 minutes IHttpClientFactory rotates handlers so DNS changes are picked up. Set higher only if DNS is stable.

Ephemeral segment default (Server GC, 64-bit) ~1–4 GB per heap One heap per logical CPU. On a 512 MB container this can size wrong pre-.NET Core 3.0. Functional vs non-functional Functional: detect that memory is climbing; localise the retention path (which object roots the leak); apply the smallest fix that removes the root. Non-functional: do all that on a live pod without a restart (a restart hides the evidence), with tooling that ships with the .NET SDK, and with a repeatable playbook a junior can run at 3 AM. 🏗️ High-level architecture The .NET heap — the mental model interviewers listen for The whole conversation makes sense once you can draw the heap.

Objects are born on the Small Object Heap (SOH) in Gen 0 . Survive a collection → get promoted to Gen 1 . Survive again → Gen 2 , where objects live "forever" and only full collections reclaim them. Allocations ≥ 85,000 bytes skip SOH entirely and go on the Large Object Heap (LOH) . Pinned buffers (byte arrays used by native I/O) live on the Pinned Object Heap (POH) since .NET 5. Everything above is one .NET process; on top of that, roots — statics, running-thread locals, GC handles — anchor the graph the collector traces.

Gen 0 — most objects die here Gen 1 — buffer generation Gen 2 — leaks accumulate here LOH — 85 KB threshold POH — pinned The interview line: "A leak means an object graph is still reachable from a live root — a static, an event delegate, a running timer, or a native handle — even though logically we're done with it. Because it's reachable, the GC won't collect it. My job is to find that root and cut the reference." 🎬 Animation Watch the classic event-handler leak grow, then get cut The canonical .NET leak in eight steps.
