Every += adds a delegate to the manager's event, and the delegate's Target pins the subscriber — so even after the subscriber is "gone", the GC can't collect it. Watch Gen 2 climb. Then hit Reset and imagine the fix: an explicit -= in Dispose, or the weak-event pattern. ▶ Play Step → ← Back ↺ Reset Ready Press ▶ Play to start 🔍 The eight real-world scenarios you should be able to name An interviewer asking "tell me about a leak you've seen" wants concrete stories. These eight are the canon — each pulled from a real Microsoft doc, GitHub issue, or well-known engineering blog. Learn the symptom and the fix line for each. 1.

HttpClient socket exhaustion (the classic) Wrapping every outgoing call in using (var c = new HttpClient()) { … } looks textbook-correct — HttpClient is IDisposable , so of course you dispose it. But HttpClient owns a HttpMessageHandler , which owns a socket that stays in TIME_WAIT for ~240 s (Windows) after Dispose. Under load you exhaust ephemeral ports and start throwing SocketException . Simon Timms's 2016 post surfaced this; IHttpClientFactory in .NET Core 2.1 was the answer, pooling handlers and rotating them every 2 min so DNS changes are picked up. 2. Singleton HttpClient that never sees DNS changes The naïve "fix" is static readonly HttpClient _c = new() .

This solves sockets but creates a new bug (dotnet/runtime #18348): the underlying handler caches a resolved IP forever. A blue/green deploy or DNS failover looks broken on your side of the wire. Fix: IHttpClientFactory , or set SocketsHttpHandler.PooledConnectionLifetime . 3. Event handler leak (WiFiManager pattern) A long-lived publisher's event holds a delegate; the delegate's Target is your subscriber; the subscriber can never be collected. In WPF/Blazor/WinForms this manifests as pages/views that "still work" invisibly and mutate stale UI state. Fix: IDisposable + -= , or weak-event pattern. 4.

Static cache without eviction Microsoft's official "Debug a memory leak" tutorial ships this exact bug: a static CustomerCache : List<Customer> that grows on every request. In the tutorial, !dumpheap -stat reveals 206,770 String instances (~19 MB) and !gcroot walks straight back to the static list. Fix: IMemoryCache with SetSize + SizeLimit , or Redis with TTL. 5. LOH fragmentation from oversized buffers Any allocation ≥ 85,000 bytes lands on the LOH. Do that per-request and you trigger a Gen 2 collection every second and cut throughput in half — Microsoft's ASP.NET Core memory doc reproduces the chart.

ASP.NET Core's own ResponseCaching middleware chunks entries below 85 KB precisely to dodge the LOH. Fix: ArrayPool<byte>.Shared or MemoryPool<byte> ; return the buffer. 6. Native handle leak (PhysicalFileProvider #844) Some managed APIs open OS resources. new PhysicalFileProvider(TempPath).Watch("*.*") registers an inotify / ReadDirectoryChangesW handle. Miss the Dispose and the managed heap looks perfectly flat while private bytes and file-descriptor counts climb — a native leak masquerading as a happy .NET process. Fix: using the file provider, or hold one instance for the process. 7.

EF Core change-tracker retention A singleton or forgotten-scoped DbContext , or reading millions of rows without .AsNoTracking() , keeps every entity in the change tracker → the context turns into a giant hash-map that grows until pod eviction. Fix: scoped lifetime + AsNoTracking() for read paths. 8. Captive dependency (singleton captures scoped) You inject a scoped repository into a singleton service. The singleton is resolved once at startup and holds a reference to that first scope's DbContext, request-tenant, principal — everything — forever. Both the DI container and your monitoring will look normal. Fix: IServiceScopeFactory inside the singleton, or a scoped delegate factory.

🧮 The DSA / GC behind it How the collector actually works — and why that matters for finding leaks You cannot debug a leak without a working model of the tracing collector. .NET's GC is a generational mark-and-sweep with compaction . On collection it starts at the roots, does a graph walk marking every reachable object, then sweeps the unreachable ones and compacts the survivors so allocation stays a pointer bump. The five interview words: root , reachability , generation , promotion , and retention path .

Structure / algorithm Complexity Why it matters for leaks Tracing GC (mark-sweep-compact) O(live objects) per collection Cost scales with the surviving set, not the total heap — a leak that grows Gen 2 makes every full GC slower. Generational hypothesis Amortised O(1) per alloc Most objects die young → collecting Gen 0/1 is cheap and frequent; Gen 2 is rare and expensive. Card table (write barriers) O(1) per pointer write Lets a Gen 0 collection skip Gen 2 objects unless they point down to a young object. Reference graph traversal ( !gcroot ) O(V + E) SOS traces backwards from an object to a root — the single most valuable command for leak hunting.

Hash-set of live handles O(1) lookup How GCHandle pinned/weak references are tracked. ArrayPool<T> (bucketed free lists) O(1) rent/return Fixes LOH pressure by reusing buffers instead of allocating. The five words you must define Root — anything the runtime can point at without going through another managed object: static fields, JIT-tracked locals on live stacks, CPU registers, GC handles (incl. pinned), and the finalize queue. Reachability — the transitive closure of "pointed at by a root or by another reachable object". Only unreachable objects are collected. Generation — an age bucket. Gen 0 = new. Gen 1 = survived one GC. Gen 2 = survived two — treated as long-lived.

Promotion — surviving a collection moves you up one generation, up to Gen 2. Retention path — the chain of references from a root to a leaked object. This is what !gcroot prints. ☁️ AWS implementation Mapping .NET memory management to AWS operations Interviewers love this map — it proves you can run .NET at scale, not just write it. -mt <MT> # list instances of the offender > gcroot <addr> # THE command — retention path back to the root ⚖️ Trade-offs, bottlenecks & likely follow-ups Server GC vs Workstation GC. Server GC (default for ASP.NET Core) uses one heap and one GC thread per logical CPU — high throughput, larger ephemeral segments (~1–4 GB), but a bigger footprint. Workstation is lower-footprint and better for small containers or client apps. On a 512 MB Fargate task, forcing Workstation with <ConcurrentGarbageCollection>true</ConcurrentGarbageCollection> + <ServerGarbageCollection>false</ServerGarbageCollection> can be the right call. Compact-on-full-GC vs sweep-only.

Since .NET Core 3.0 the LOH can be compacted on demand ( GCSettings.LargeObjectHeapCompactionMode ). It's expensive — pauses can hit hundreds of ms — but it's the escape hatch when LOH fragmentation is real. The classic bottleneck sequence. Allocation rate too high → Gen 0/1 GCs frequent → objects survive into Gen 2 they didn't deserve → Gen 2 grows → full-GC pause grows → ALB health checks fail → tasks recycle → the surviving tasks take the traffic and start doing the same thing → thundering herd. How would you find a memory leak in production? Baseline with dotnet-counters on a live pod. If Gen 2 or working-set climbs while allocation rate stays flat, that's a leak.

Take two dotnet-gcdump snapshots ~5–10 min apart, diff them in Visual Studio or PerfView, follow the biggest positive-delta type, and run !gcroot on one instance to get the retention path back to a root. Fix the root, redeploy, watch the graph go flat. Why does .NET have leaks if it has a garbage collector? Because the GC only frees unreachable objects. A leak in .NET is reachable-but-unwanted : something we wrote is still pointing at an object we've logically finished with — a static field, an event delegate, a running timer, a captive closure, or a native handle. The GC is doing its job perfectly. Difference from a C++ leak? C++ leaks are unreachable-and-unfreed — you forgot to delete .

.NET leaks are reachable-and-unwanted — you forgot to -= or Dispose . Fix in C++ = smart pointers. Fix in .NET = cut the reference or add IDisposable + using . Why was IHttpClientFactory added? To fix two bugs at once. new HttpClient() per call exhausts sockets (TIME_WAIT). A static singleton fixes sockets but caches DNS forever. IHttpClientFactory pools handlers and rotates them every 2 min so DNS changes propagate — best of both. 🗣️ Interview cheat sheet "A .NET leak is reachable-but-unwanted — the GC can't collect an object something still points to. My job is to find the retention path back to the root and cut it.

The five roots that produce 90 % of leaks are statics, event delegates, timers, undisposed IDisposables, and native handles . I detect with dotnet-counters + two dotnet-gcdump s diffed; I confirm with !gcroot in SOS." The one-line definition — reachable-but-unwanted (vs C++ unreachable-and-unfreed). Five leak sources to name — static cache, event handler, timer, undisposed handle, captive dependency. Three numbers to quote — LOH threshold 85,000 bytes; handler lifetime 2 min; TIME_WAIT ~240 s Windows / 60 s Linux. The tool chain — dotnet-counters → two dotnet-gcdump s → diff → !gcroot .

The classic fix stories — IHttpClientFactory , weak-event pattern, ArrayPool , AsNoTracking , IMemoryCache with size limit. System Design · Interview Prep · Dynamo Paper §4–5 Dynamo: Consistent Hashing & the NWR Quorum How Amazon's 2007 Dynamo paper turns commodity boxes into an always-writeable, always-on key–value store — the ring, the preference list, sloppy quorums, hinted handoff, vector clocks — with an interview-ready walkthrough of sections 4 and 5. 🎯 Scenario 🧑‍🎓 Laymen 📋 Requirements 🏗️ Ring & NWR 🔍 Deep-dive 🧮 DSA ☁️ AWS 💻 C# ⚖️ Trade-offs 🗣️ Cheat sheet 🇮🇳 Jargon buster ❓ FAQ 📚 Sources 🎯 Real-world scenario What Dynamo is, and why it matters in an interview Dynamo is Amazon's 2007 highly-available, key–value store that powers services like the shopping cart, session state, and the best-se

ller list. It is the ancestor of Amazon DynamoDB , Cassandra , Riak , and Voldemort , and its ideas — consistent hashing, tunable NWR quorums, vector clocks, hinted handoff, Merkle-tree anti-entropy, gossip membership — are the standard vocabulary of any modern eventually-consistent store. The paper is a favourite interview springboard because it stitches six distinct techniques together to solve one very hard product problem: "the customer must never see a failed Add-to-Cart, even when disks are failing, network routes are flapping, or a whole datacenter goes dark." To hit that bar Dynamo deliberately drops strong consistency and lets the application clean up divergent versions later.

Sections 4 and 5 of the paper describe exactly how — and this page walks through them with the level of detail you need to whiteboard confidently. Real products built on this playbook: Amazon shopping cart , Netflix (originally on Cassandra), Instagram feed backfill (Cassandra), Discord messages (Cassandra → ScyllaDB), Uber geo-index, Twitter/X timeline delivery. Any time you hear "eventually consistent NoSQL", the ring and the NWR knobs behind the scenes are Dynamo's grandchildren. 🧑‍🎓 In laymen terms — a plain-English tour Imagine a very busy general store with many counters Picture a huge kirana store chain that sells lakhs of items across many outlets in one city.

Every customer expects to always be able to add an item to their cart, even if one outlet is closed for repairs, even if there's a small area power cut. The store makes a promise: "we will never say no to your cart addition." If two family members add different items at the same moment from different phones, the shop will keep both versions and let the family sort it out at checkout — better than losing an item. Now, where does each customer's cart live ? A single shop counter would collapse under lakhs of shoppers. So the chain does something clever: it draws a giant circular clock face and places every counter (server) at some hour on that circle.

When you arrive with your cart, they take your phone number , punch it through a formula that also lands on the clock, and whichever counter is next in clockwise order becomes your primary counter . The next two counters after that are your backups — every cart is written to three counters, so if one shuts down, the other two keep serving. Two more tricks make it robust: (1) writes are approved fast — as soon as 2 of the 3 counters have written your change, the shop says "done!" and you walk away. The 3rd catches up in the background. (2) If one of your 3 counters is temporarily closed, the shop doesn't refuse .

It writes to a spare counter with a Post-it note: "this belongs to counter A, hand it over when A opens." When A comes back, the Post-it is delivered. This is the whole secret behind Amazon's "Add to Cart never fails" guarantee. No jargon, just: circular seating chart + 3 copies + accept when 2 agree + Post-it for the missing one . 📋 Requirements & scale What Dynamo has to promise Functional Simple get(key) and put(key, context, value) — no joins, no queries, primary-key only. Objects are opaque blobs, usually < 1 MB . Nodes may join and leave without manual re-partitioning — incremental scalability .

Non-functional (the interviewer's favourite numbers) Metric Target from the paper Latency SLA 99.9% of get/put < 300 ms — measured at p99.9, not average Availability "Always writeable" — the shopping-cart service saw 99.9995% success over 2 years Typical N,R,W (3, 2, 2) — three replicas, quorum of two for read and write Scale unit Up to a few hundred nodes per Dynamo instance (each service runs its own) Divergent versions observed 99.94% of shopping-cart requests saw exactly 1 version; only 0.06% saw ≥2 Hashing MD5 of the key → 128-bit position on the ring These are the numbers to volunteer in an interview: 300 ms p99.9, N=3 R=2 W=2, MD5 128-bit, hundreds of nodes per instance, 99.9995% suc

cess. 🏗️ Ring architecture & the NWR quorum The ring, the preference list, and the quorum in one picture Every key k is hashed with MD5 to a 128-bit number. That number is a position on a logical ring whose full range is [0, 2 128 ) . Nodes are also placed on the ring — many times each, as virtual nodes — so load is spread evenly and heterogeneous hardware can carry more virtual nodes. To find the owner of k , walk clockwise from k 's hash until you hit the first node. That node is the coordinator ; the next N − 1 distinct physical nodes on the ring are the replicas. Together these N nodes are the preference list .

coordinator (B) replicas (C, D) hashed key position other nodes The NWR quorum — 3 knobs the client gets to tune Once you know where the N replicas live, Dynamo lets the application choose how many to wait for. Two knobs: W = how many replicas must acknowledge a write before it counts as success, R = how many must respond to a read. The paper's rule of thumb is R + W > N , which makes read/write sets overlap so a read will see the latest write.

W=2 write path (fan-out) ack path (2 needed) lagging replica — repaired later Config N R W Behaviour Common (shopping cart, session) 3 2 2 Balanced read/write, R+W>N ⇒ quorum Always-writeable (durability optional) 3 - 1 Never rejects a write; possible stale reads Read-heavy cache 3 1 3 Fastest reads, all replicas must ack writes 🔍 Component deep-dive 4.2 — Consistent hashing with virtual nodes The raw ring has two problems: nodes placed randomly give uneven ranges (some nodes get huge arcs, others tiny slivers), and a beefier server can't take extra load. Dynamo fixes both by giving each physical node many tokens (positions on the ring).

A powerful box gets more tokens; a small box gets fewer. When a node dies, its many small ranges get re-absorbed by many different neighbours, so no single neighbour gets crushed. When a new node joins, it steals slivers from many neighbours in parallel. 4.3 — Replication & the preference list Each key is replicated to N nodes. Because virtual nodes can put two tokens of the same physical box next to each other, the preference list is built by skipping until N distinct physical nodes are collected. And the list is longer than N — extra "spares" are pre-computed to cover failures (this is what makes hinted handoff cheap).

For datacenter failure resilience, the list is chosen so successive replicas live in different DCs . 4.4 — Vector clocks & conflict resolution Because writes can succeed with only W acknowledgements, two replicas can end up with divergent versions after a partition heals. Dynamo attaches a vector clock [(Sx, 1), (Sy, 2), …] — a list of (node, counter) pairs — to every version. If clock A dominates clock B on every entry, A is a descendant and B can be dropped ( syntactic reconciliation ). If neither dominates, both are returned to the client and the application merges them ( semantic reconciliation — for a shopping cart, "union of items").

Clocks are truncated at ~10 entries to keep them bounded. 4.5 — get() and put() execution A put(k, ctx, val) lands on any node; the receiver forwards it to the coordinator (first live node in k 's preference list). The coordinator bumps the vector clock, writes locally, and fans out to the other N−1 top-preference nodes. As soon as W−1 of them ack (plus its own local write = W total), the put succeeds. A get(k) similarly reads from N and waits for R responses; any divergent versions are returned to the caller with their contexts merged so the next put reconciles. 4.6 — Sloppy quorum & hinted handoff A "strict" quorum would block the write if a top-N node is down.

Dynamo instead does a sloppy quorum : if node A is unreachable, the write goes to the next healthy node D with a metadata "hint" naming A. D stores it in a side database; when A recovers, D transfers the hinted replicas back and deletes its copy. Result: writes never fail on transient failures, and durability is quickly restored. 4.7 — Anti-entropy with Merkle trees Hints only survive if D itself stays alive. For permanent drift, Dynamo runs Merkle-tree anti-entropy : each node maintains a Merkle tree per key range . Two replicas compare root hashes; if equal, done. If not, they descend only the disagreeing branches, minimising bytes transferred and disk reads.

Any leaves where the hashes differ pinpoint the exact keys that need syncing. 4.8 — Membership via gossip + seeds Adds/removes are explicit (an operator command) — Dynamo doesn't auto-remove a flapping node. The change is written to persistent store, then gossiped : every second each node picks a random peer and reconciles membership histories. A handful of well-known seed nodes anchor discovery so the ring can't logically split. Failure detection is purely local — "did B not answer my last few RPCs?" — no global agreement needed.

5 — Implementation notes worth quoting Each node has three components (all in Java): request coordination , membership & failure detection , and a pluggable local persistence engine (BDB Transactional, BDB Java Edition, MySQL, or an in-memory buffer with a persistent backing store). Coordination runs on a SEDA-style pipeline: each client request spawns a state machine — send N requests, wait for R (or W) responses, retry on timeout, reconcile divergent versions, respond, and then read-repair lagging replicas asynchronously. A neat trick from §5: the coordinator for a write is chosen to be the fastest replica from the preceding read , which both improves p99.9 and enables "read your writes".

Consistent hashing itself powers Amazon ElastiCache , memcached clients, Envoy 's ring-hash LB, and Vitess shard routing.

⚖️ Trade-offs, bottlenecks & likely interviewer follow-ups Why not use Paxos/Raft for strong consistency? A consensus round costs a round-trip to a majority for every write and cannot progress during partitions. The shopping cart cannot afford to reject an "Add to Cart" during a partition. Dynamo trades linearizability for availability, then pushes conflict resolution into the application. This is the CAP-theorem choice made explicit. Why MD5 and not SHA-256? Dynamo needs uniform distribution and speed, not cryptographic strength — the ring is inside a trusted datacenter, and there is no adversary crafting hash collisions.

MD5 is faster and 128 bits is more than enough entropy for the token space. What if two nodes coordinate concurrent writes on the same key? Both writes succeed with different vector clocks — say [(Sx,2),(Sy,1)] and [(Sx,2),(Sz,1)] . Neither dominates. The next reader gets both versions in the response context and must reconcile (for a cart, union the items; for a session, "last write wins" by timestamp). The paper reports 99.94% of shopping-cart requests still saw exactly one version. What are the real bottlenecks? (1) Gossip: full membership tables grow with N, limiting the design to a few hundred nodes per instance.

(2) Merkle-tree recomputation on membership churn — Strategy 3 (Q/S tokens with fixed partitions) fixed this in §6. (3) Foreground vs background contention — anti-entropy has to yield to live get/puts via admission control. Sloppy quorum vs strict quorum — does R+W>N still guarantee "read latest"? Not in a partition. Under a sloppy quorum, the "W" nodes that ack the write may not be in the top-N preference list at all — they might be spares holding hints. A subsequent read of R nodes could miss those hints and return a stale value. The guarantee is best-effort; strict overlap holds only when the top-N are all up.

How does datacenter failure work? The preference list is constructed so successive replicas fall in different DCs. Losing one DC still leaves 2 of 3 replicas alive, and a (3,2,2) quorum still passes. 🗣️ Interview cheat sheet 30-second pitch: "Dynamo is Amazon's always-writeable key–value store. Keys are placed on a consistent-hashing ring using MD5, each key is replicated to N=3 nodes forming a preference list, and writes succeed once W=2 replicas ack — R+W>N gives read-write overlap. When a replica is down, writes flow to a spare with a hint (sloppy quorum + hinted handoff), and Merkle-tree anti-entropy repairs permanent drift.

Conflicts are surfaced to the client via vector clocks and resolved semantically (e.g. cart union). It's the ancestor of DynamoDB and Cassandra." Numbers to quote: N=3, R=W=2, p99.9 < 300 ms, MD5 128-bit, 99.9995% availability, ~ hundreds of nodes/instance. Six techniques (Table 1): consistent hashing → replication → vector clocks → sloppy quorum + hinted handoff → Merkle-tree anti-entropy → gossip membership. Preference list : skip virtual nodes belonging to the same physical box; span multiple DCs. Write coordinator picked as fastest replica from previous read — improves p99.9 and enables read-your-writes.

Application, not the DB, resolves conflicts — shopping cart merges divergent versions. 🇮🇳 Jargon buster — Indian-context plain English The words on this page, decoded Every technical term the page uses, in one line of plain English plus one everyday Indian picture. Ideal for a quick re-read before you say them out loud. Consistent hashing A way to map keys to servers using a circular hash space so that adding/removing a server only reshuffles a tiny slice of keys, not everything. Like PIN-code-based delivery zones: adding a new delivery boy only reshuffles one colony, not the whole city.

Virtual node (vnode / token) One physical server pretends to be many small servers scattered on the ring so load is spread evenly and stronger boxes carry more. Same person manning multiple counters at an Aadhaar enrolment camp — the strong staff handle 3 counters, the trainee handles 1. Preference list The ordered list of N nodes responsible for a key — first is coordinator, next N-1 are replicas, plus a couple of spares for failures. Your primary emergency contact plus 2 backups plus 2 extras on your bank form — if the first can't be reached, they try the next in line.

Coordinator The node that orchestrates one put/get: assigns the version, fans out to the replicas, waits for the quorum, replies. The ward secretary who takes your application, sends copies to two offices, and hands you the receipt once both stamp it. Quorum (NWR) A rule that a write or read counts as successful only after a minimum number of replicas participate — R+W>N ensures the two sets overlap. A society decision needing at least 2 of 3 committee members' signatures — as long as any two agree, it stands. Sloppy quorum Instead of requiring the exact top-N nodes, Dynamo accepts writes on any N healthy nodes, so writes never fail during transient outages.

If your usual bank branch is closed, the cheque is still accepted at the nearest open branch and moved back later. Hinted handoff A temporary write sent to a stand-in node, tagged with the original recipient's name, and delivered once that node returns. The Amazon delivery boy leaves your parcel with the pharmacy next door and pastes a note — you pick it up when you're back home. Vector clock A list of (node, counter) pairs attached to a value so the system can tell whether one version descended from another or they diverged. A shared Google-Doc-style edit history saying "Ravi edited 3 times, Priya edited 1 time" — you can see if edits conflict or one followed the other.

Syntactic reconciliation The system itself can pick the newer version when one vector clock clearly dominates the other. No human judgement needed. Two versions of your Aadhaar update — one is newer on every field, obviously use that one. Semantic reconciliation The system returns both divergent versions to the application, which knows how to merge them meaningfully. Your mother added atta to the cart on one phone, you added ghee from another — the app just keeps both items in the final cart. Anti-entropy A background process that walks through replicas and pulls them back into agreement over time.

Monthly society ledger reconciliation — two secretaries sit and match register entries so both books agree. Merkle tree A tree of hashes where each parent hash summarises its children — lets two replicas compare huge datasets by exchanging one hash at a time. Comparing two thick railway timetables by first checking the front-page total, then only the chapters where totals differ, then only the rows in those chapters. Gossip protocol Each node picks a random peer every second and shares what it knows, so information spreads through the cluster like rumour. WhatsApp forwards in a family group — one aunty tells two, they tell four, and within minutes everyone in the extended family knows.

Seed node A well-known starting-point node whose address is in static config so a fresh node knows whom to gossip with first. The trusted "pandalji" whose phone number everyone in the wedding party has — new relatives arriving in town call him first. Read repair If a read reveals a lagging replica, the coordinator quietly pushes the fresh value to it on the way back — no separate job needed. While copying a document at a Xerox shop, the boy notices your neighbour's copy is older and hands them a fresh one for free. Read-your-writes A consistency guarantee that says once you write X, your very next read will see X (or newer).

You deposit ₹5,000 at the ATM and the very next mini-statement shows the balance — you shouldn't have to wait for it to appear. Eventually consistent All replicas agree eventually, given enough quiet time — but a reader mid-flight may see stale data. Your Aadhaar address update reflects on the online portal within minutes but on a printed KYC letter only after a few days — same info, delayed sync. p99.9 latency The response time by which 99.9% of requests are served — a much stricter target than the average. Not "average IRCTC page loads in 3 seconds" but "999 out of every 1,000 clicks respond within 3 seconds" — the hard promise.

SEDA architecture A server design where each request flows through a pipeline of stages, each with its own queue and thread pool, so back-pressure is localised. A passport office where your form moves from token counter → biometrics → verification → payment, each with its own queue. Back-pressure When a downstream stage is slow, it signals upstream to slow down so queues don't explode. The billing counter at Big Bazaar tells the entrance guard to hold customers when the checkout queue is too long. BDB (Berkeley DB) / RocksDB Embedded key-value libraries a service links into its own process for fast local storage.

Like keeping your own steel almirah at home instead of renting a bank locker — no round-trip to a separate building. Zero-hop DHT Every node knows the full routing table, so a request goes directly to the right node in one network hop — no chain of forwards. Direct-dial STD calls instead of asking the operator to connect you through three exchanges. ❓ FAQ — your follow-up questions Questions asked about this topic No follow-up questions yet — ask one about this topic and it'll be logged here with a compact answer. 📚 Sources DeCandia et al., "Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store" , SOSP 2007 — the primary source.

System Design · Interview Prep How Amazon DynamoDB Works The internals of AWS's serverless NoSQL database: partitioning by hash, Multi-Paxos replication, single-digit-ms latency at any scale, and how to design tables for it. 🎯 What it is 🧑‍🎓 Laymen 📋 Guarantees & limits 🏗️ Architecture 🔍 Deep-dive 🧮 DSA ☁️ Capacity & features 💻 C# code ⚖️ Trade-offs 🗣️ Cheat sheet ❓ FAQ 📚 Sources 🎯 What it is & where it's used A serverless key-value store that never slows down DynamoDB is AWS's fully-managed NoSQL database that delivers consistent single-digit-millisecond latency at any scale — whether your table holds a kilobyte or a petabyte, whether you do ten requests a second or twenty millio

n. It descends from the 2007 Dynamo paper (the internal Amazon key-value store born from a Christmas-shopping outage), but the original Dynamo was disliked internally because teams still had to run and scale it themselves. DynamoDB, launched in January 2012, kept Dynamo's core ideas (consistent hashing, replication, tunable consistency) and removed all the operational burden — no servers, no manual sharding, no patching. It powers the shopping cart and many core services at Amazon.com, and externally backs things like Snapchat's Memories, Disney+ watchlists, Lyft ride state, and countless session/leaderboard/IoT workloads.

Interviewers ask about it because it forces you to think differently: unlike a relational database, DynamoDB makes you design your table around your access patterns first — get that wrong and no amount of scaling saves you. Explaining why it stays fast (the partitioning + replication model) and how to model data for it is the whole game. 🧑‍🎓 In laymen terms A library with a million drawers and a magic sorting hat Imagine the world's largest library, but instead of shelves it has a million tiny drawers lined up along a giant wall. When you walk in with a book to file — say a note about your grandmother's birthday — you don't wander around looking for space.

You hand the book to a little assistant at the door who wears a magic sorting hat . The hat looks at the title of your book, whispers a number, and tells you "drawer number seven-hundred-and-forty-two, second row." You put the book in, done. Someone else walks in with a completely different book — the hat tells them "drawer number two-thousand-nine-hundred-and-eleven." Nobody ever has to fight over the same drawer. Now here's the beautiful part. Because everyone gets sent to a different drawer, a thousand people can file books at the same time without bumping into each other.

If suddenly ten million people show up, the library just builds more drawers along the wall and the hat starts pointing to those too. Nothing slows down. This is how Amazon's giant online store keeps working even during a huge Black Friday sale — every shopping cart is filed in its own little drawer. To make sure nothing is ever lost, the library secretly makes three copies of every drawer , kept in three different buildings across the city. If one building burns down, your book is still safe in the other two.

And when you go back to fetch your grandmother's birthday note, you again walk in the door, tell the hat the title, and it whispers the drawer number — you walk straight to it in one step. No searching, no wandering. The one big rule is: you have to tell the hat in advance what titles you'll be searching by . If you file a book under "birthday note" but later try to find it by "grandmother's name," the hat shrugs — it wasn't told to remember that. This is why people who use DynamoDB spend a lot of time thinking about how they'll search before they store anything.

📋 Guarantees, and the numbers to quote What DynamoDB promises — and its hard limits The value proposition is predictable performance : latency stays flat as you scale because data is spread across many small partitions, each independently served. Durability comes from synchronous replication across three Availability Zones ; availability targets are 99.99% (single region) and 99.999% (global tables). 400 KB max item size 10 GB max data per partition 3,000 RCU max reads/partition/sec 1,000 WCU max writes/partition/sec 3 AZs synchronous replicas Unit Definition RCU (Read Capacity Unit) 1 strongly-consistent read/sec, OR 2 eventually-consistent reads/sec, for items up to 4 KB .

(Transactional reads cost 2×.) WCU (Write Capacity Unit) 1 write/sec for items up to 1 KB . (Transactional writes cost 2×.) These three per-partition ceilings — 10 GB, 3,000 RCU, 1,000 WCU — are the key mental model: whenever a partition crosses any of them, DynamoDB automatically splits it into more partitions. That's the whole scaling story in one sentence. 🏗️ Architecture Request routers, partitions, and Paxos replication A request flows through two tiers. First it hits a stateless request router — it authenticates, checks the metadata service to learn which partition owns your key, verifies you have capacity (admission control), and forwards the request.

Second, it lands on the right storage node . Every partition is replicated to three storage nodes across three AZs , forming a replication group . One replica is the leader , elected via Multi-Paxos ; the leader handles all writes and strongly-consistent reads, then replicates the write to the peers. A write is acknowledged once a quorum (the leader + at least one peer) has durably persisted it to its write-ahead log. request path Paxos replication metadata lookup Behind the scenes there are also log replicas (write-ahead-log-only nodes) that let DynamoDB restore a full replica quickly after a failure without a heavy copy, and an auto-admin service that continuously splits/moves partitions.

The genius is that every layer is horizontally scalable and stateless where possible — routers scale out freely, storage scales by adding partitions. 🔍 Component deep-dive Partition keys and how data is placed Every item has a partition key (PK) , optionally plus a sort key (SK) . DynamoDB runs the partition key through an internal hash function ; the hash determines which partition stores the item. Items sharing a PK live together on one partition, sorted by SK — which is what makes Query (fetch all items for one PK, optionally a SK range) so fast: it's a B-tree lookup within a single partition.

Choosing a high-cardinality, evenly-accessed partition key is the single most important design decision, because it spreads load uniformly. Consistency options Reads come in two flavors. A strongly consistent read goes to the leader and always returns the latest write. An eventually consistent read (the default, and half the cost) hits any of the three replicas at random — so there's roughly a "1-in-3 chance" of reading a value from a replica that hasn't yet received the very latest write during the brief replication window. This is the CAP/PACELC dial in action: DynamoDB is PA/EL — it favors availability and low latency, offering strong consistency only as an opt-in, single-region choice.

Hot partitions & adaptive capacity The classic failure mode is a hot partition : a bad key (e.g., partitioning by "today's date" so all writes hit one partition) concentrates traffic and throttles even though the table has spare capacity. DynamoDB fights this with adaptive capacity (instantly borrows unused capacity for hot partitions), burst capacity (banks up to 5 minutes of unused throughput), and split-for-heat (isolates a hot key onto its own partition). But you should still design keys to avoid hotspots — write sharding (append a random suffix #1..#N to the PK) is the standard fix for an unavoidably hot key.

Secondary indexes To query by an attribute that isn't the primary key, you add an index. A Local Secondary Index (LSI) keeps the same PK but a different SK (must be created at table creation, shares the partition's throughput). A Global Secondary Index (GSI) has a completely different PK/SK and is effectively a separate, asynchronously-maintained copy of the table (eventually consistent, its own capacity). A "log propagator" keeps indexes updated. Because each index adds write cost, a table is capped at a handful — favor GSIs for flexible query patterns.

🧮 The DSA behind it Hashing, B-trees, quorums, and Merkle trees Structure / algorithm Where it's used Why Hash function on PK Placing items into partitions O(1) routing; spreads data uniformly across the keyspace. (Modern DynamoDB uses range-based partition assignment over the hash space rather than a pure consistent-hash ring.) B-tree Storage engine within a partition Sorted by sort key ⇒ O(log n) point lookups and efficient range scans (the Query operation). Multi-Paxos Replication group leader election & log agreement Keeps 3 replicas consistent and picks a new leader in ~seconds if the leader's 1.5 s heartbeat is missed. See consensus .

Quorum (W=2 of 3) Durable write acknowledgement ACK after a majority persists to the write-ahead log ⇒ survives one AZ loss with no data loss. Merkle trees / anti-entropy Detecting & repairing replica divergence Cheaply compares replicas and syncs only the differing ranges (inherited from Dynamo). Write-ahead log Every storage & log replica Durability: replay the log to recover; log replicas restore a failed node fast. Capacity math worked example Say you store 6 KB items and need 500 strongly-consistent reads/sec. Each read rounds up to ceil(6/4) = 2 RCU, so you need 500 × 2 = 1,000 RCU . For 200 writes/sec of 2 KB items: ceil(2/1) = 2 WCU each ⇒ 400 WCU .

Being able to do this arithmetic out loud is a common interview checkpoint. ☁️ Capacity modes & ecosystem features Provisioned vs on-demand, and the surrounding toolkit Feature What it does When to use On-demand capacity Pay per request; scales instantly to any traffic, zero capacity planning. Spiky/unknown traffic, new apps, serverless. Provisioned + Auto Scaling Set target RCU/WCU; autoscaler adjusts to utilization. Predictable traffic where you want lower cost. DynamoDB Streams Ordered change log of item mutations (24 h), consumed by Lambda. CDC, event-driven fan-out, aggregations, replication. Global Tables Multi-region active-active replication, last-writer-wins conflict resolution.

Low-latency global apps, regional DR (99.999%). DAX In-memory write-through cache; microsecond reads. Read-heavy, hot-item workloads. TTL Auto-expire items by timestamp attribute (free). Sessions, ephemeral data. Transactions TransactWriteItems — ACID across up to 100 items in one region. All-or-nothing multi-item updates. The deployment norm: pick on-demand unless you can prove steady traffic, enable PITR (point-in-time recovery), front hot reads with DAX , wire Streams → Lambda for anything reactive, and reach for Global Tables only when you truly need multi-region.

💻 C# implementation — single-table design in action The idiomatic DynamoDB pattern is single-table design : store multiple entity types in one table using overloaded, prefixed keys so related items co-locate under one partition key and one Query fetches an entire aggregate. Here's modeling a user and their orders, then reading them in a single round-trip with the AWS SDK for .NET. // Single-table design: PK groups an aggregate, SK distinguishes entity type. // PK = "USER#123" SK = "PROFILE" -> the user row // PK = "USER#123" SK = "ORDER#2024-..." -> that user's orders var client = new AmazonDynamoDBClient (); // --- Write a profile and an order atomically (all-or-nothing) --- await client.

TransactWriteItemsAsync ( new TransactWriteItemsRequest { TransactItems = new () { new () { Put = new Put { TableName = "AppTable" , Item = new () { [ "PK" ] = new ( "USER#123" ), [ "SK" ] = new ( "PROFILE" ), [ "name" ] = new ( "Santosh" ) }}}, new () { Put = new Put { TableName = "AppTable" , Item = new () { [ "PK" ] = new ( "USER#123" ), [ "SK" ] = new ( "ORDER#2024-06-01#a91" ), [ "total" ] = new AttributeValue { N = "42.00" } }}} } }); // --- One Query returns the profile AND every order in a single partition read --- var resp = await client.

QueryAsync ( new QueryRequest { TableName = "AppTable" , KeyConditionExpression = "PK = :pk" , // hits exactly one partition -> fast ExpressionAttributeValues = new () { [ ":pk" ] = new ( "USER#123" ) }, ConsistentRead = false // eventually consistent = cheaper (½ RCU) }); // resp.Items now holds the PROFILE row + all ORDER# rows, sorted by SK. Alternatives worth naming: the higher-level DynamoDBContext (object mapper) for simple CRUD, PynamoDB /boto3 in Python, and PartiQL (SQL-like syntax) if the team prefers SQL. But the key skill is the data model , not the SDK — design keys around your access patterns before writing any code.

⚖️ Trade-offs, bottlenecks & likely follow-ups "How does DynamoDB scale to millions of requests?" By partitioning: data is hashed across many partitions, each capped at 10 GB / 3,000 RCU / 1,000 WCU. Cross any ceiling and it auto-splits. Stateless request routers scale out independently. Latency stays flat because each partition is small and independently served. "What's a hot partition and how do you fix it?" A poorly-chosen key concentrates traffic on one partition and throttles despite spare table capacity. Fixes: choose a high-cardinality key, write-shard by appending a random suffix, or lean on adaptive capacity + split-for-heat.

Prevention via key design beats relying on the automatic mitigations. "Strongly vs eventually consistent reads?" Strong reads go to the Paxos leader and always see the latest write, cost 1 RCU/4 KB, single-region. Eventual reads hit any replica, cost ½ RCU, and may briefly return stale data during the replication window. Default is eventual. "When is DynamoDB the wrong choice?" When you need ad-hoc queries, complex joins, or flexible analytics — its access patterns must be known up front. For those, use Aurora/RDS, or stream to Redshift/OpenSearch/S3+Athena for analytics.

"LSI vs GSI?" LSI = same partition key, alternate sort key, shares partition throughput, must exist at table creation, supports strong reads. GSI = entirely different key, async/eventually consistent, own capacity, can be added anytime. Prefer GSIs for flexibility. 🗣️ Interview cheat sheet 30-second pitch: "DynamoDB is a serverless NoSQL store giving single-digit-ms latency at any scale. Items are hashed by partition key across many partitions, each capped at 10 GB, 3,000 RCU, 1,000 WCU — cross a ceiling and it auto-splits. Each partition is replicated across 3 AZs with a Multi-Paxos leader that handles writes and strong reads; writes ACK on a quorum.

It's a PA/EL system — availability and low latency first, strong consistency as an opt-in. You design the table around access patterns using single-table design and pick a high-cardinality key to avoid hot partitions." Numbers: 400 KB item, 10 GB/partition, 3,000 RCU & 1,000 WCU/partition, 3 AZs. RCU = 4 KB strong read; WCU = 1 KB write. Placement: hash(PK) → partition; items with same PK sorted by SK ⇒ fast Query . Replication: 3 AZ replicas, Multi-Paxos leader, quorum write ACK, log replicas for fast recovery. Consistency: eventual (default, ½ cost, any replica) vs strong (leader). CAP = PA/EL. Hot partition = the #1 pitfall → high-cardinality key + write sharding.

Toolkit: on-demand vs provisioned, Streams→Lambda, Global Tables, DAX, TTL, transactions, single-table design. ❓ FAQ — your follow-up questions Questions asked about this topic No follow-up questions yet — ask one about this topic and it'll be logged here with a compact answer. 📚 Sources Amazon DynamoDB — Wikipedia Elhemali et al. — "Amazon DynamoDB: A Scalable, Predictably Performant, and Fully Managed NoSQL Database Service" (USENIX ATC 2022) DeCandia et al.

x: So Git periodically (on git gc , on push, or when loose objects pile up) rolls many objects into a single packfile ( .pack ) with a companion index ( .idx ) that maps each SHA to a byte offset. Inside the pack, similar objects are delta-compressed : Git stores one version in full and the others as deltas against it, and deltas can chain. A clever twist: it stores the newest version intact and older versions as deltas, since you most often read recent data. This is why .git stays remarkably small even for huge histories. x: Git's smart protocol does it in three moves. (1) Ref advertisement : the server lists all its refs with their SHAs and its capabilities. (2) want/have negotiation : the client sends want <sha> for tips it lacks and have <sha> for commits it already owns, so the two sides discover their common ancestor . (3) Packfile transfer : the server computes exactly the objects reachable from the wants but not the haves , packs them on the fly, and streams them. Push is the mirror image ( send-pack ↔ receive-pack ), with all-zero SHAs signaling ref creation or deletion. This content-addressed, negotiate-the-difference design is precisely what makes Git distributed rather than client-server.

x: The primary key lookup is easy: hash the key, jump to the right shard, done. The interesting problem is secondary access . If a table of 500 million movies is partitioned by movie_id , then a query like WHERE genre = 'Crime' has no idea where the data lives — the partition key isn't in the predicate. What now? This is one of the most common real-world tension points in distributed databases, and interviewers love it because it forces you to reason about writes, reads, consistency, and latency all at once. The two answers are Local Secondary Index (LSI) and Global Secondary Index (GSI) , and picking wrong turns a 5 ms point read into a 200 ms scatter-gather nightmare.

x: Every serious partitioned system faces this: DynamoDB ships both LSI and GSI as first-class features. Cassandra and ScyllaDB only ship local indexes and warn you about the scatter-gather cost. MongoDB lets you build indexes on any field, but on a sharded collection those are per-shard indexes underneath. PostgreSQL 's partitioned tables build one child index per partition — no truly global index. Elasticsearch , Vitess , CockroachDB , Spanner — all have to answer this question. The pattern is universal. 🧑‍🎓 In laymen terms (for a beginner) Explaining this at a dinner party Imagine you own a huge library with 500 million books.

x: One building can't hold that many, so you rent 10 warehouses across the city and split the books by their catalog number — books 1 to 50 million go to warehouse 1, 50 to 100 million to warehouse 2, and so on. If someone asks for "book 137,842,301," you look at the catalog number, know instantly it's in warehouse 3, and drive straight there. Easy. But then a librarian asks: "give me all mystery novels." Uh oh. Mystery novels aren't grouped together — they're scattered across all 10 warehouses. You have two choices, and this is the whole story. Choice A — the little card catalog in each warehouse. You put a small card index at every warehouse listing only the mysteries in that warehouse.

x: Cheap to keep updated (a new mystery arrives at warehouse 4, you just update warehouse 4's index). But to answer "give me all mysteries," you have to send 10 messengers to 10 warehouses , wait for them all to come back, then combine the answers. Slow. Choice B — one giant master catalog for mysteries. You build a separate index in its own building, organized by genre. All the mysteries in the world are listed in one place. Now "give me all mysteries" is a single trip — fast. But every time a new book arrives at any warehouse, you must also send an update to the master catalog building. And if you demand this update happens immediately , every book delivery becomes slow.

x: That's the whole trade-off. Choice A = cheap writes, slow "search everywhere" reads . Choice B = fast reads, expensive writes . Real systems like Amazon's DynamoDB let you pick either one — and if you pick wrong, your app either can't keep up with new orders or takes forever to search. Concrete example: Netflix has a movies table split across 100 machines by movie_id . If Netflix wants to show you "all Crime movies released in 2024," a local-index setup would ask all 100 machines and merge — maybe 200 ms. A global-index setup keeps a separate table organized by genre , so the same query hits just one machine — 5 ms.

Support secondary queries on non-partition-key attributes (e.g. genre , email , status ) without full-table scans.

A query that filters only on the indexed attribute hashes that attribute's value and jumps directly to one GSI partition — no fanout, no coordinator merge. The catch: every write to the base table must also flow to the correct GSI partition, which lives on a different node group.

Almost every production system takes the pragmatic escape hatch: update the GSI asynchronously . The base write commits fast, an internal replicator streams the change into the GSI, and readers accept eventual consistency (typically sub-second, up to minutes under load). The scatter-gather tax on LSI cross-partition reads Suppose we have 100 shards and each shard's p99 latency is 20 ms. The mean latency of a scatter-gather is not 20 ms — it's the maximum of 100 independent 20 ms samples.

Range partitioning — used by HBase, Bigtable, Spanner. Keeps range scans efficient but is more prone to hot spots. Scatter-gather merge When a coordinator receives ordered result streams from N shards, merging is exactly a k-way merge problem — the same one you'd solve with a min-heap of size N. Complexity is O(K · log N) for K total results across N shards. This is why the query planner cares deeply about pushing filters and sorts down into each shard before merging.

GSI makes writes expensive (or eventually consistent) and pure-secondary reads cheap. There is no free lunch — you're moving the cost around, not eliminating it. Failure modes Straggler shards on LSI reads. One slow shard drags the whole query to its p99.

x: Mitigation: hedged requests (send to a replica after 95 ms), circuit-break slow shards, or degrade to partial results with an explicit "incomplete" flag. GSI backfill lag under bursty writes. Async replicators fall behind, and the "1-second lag" turns into a "5-minute lag." Mitigation: rate-limit writes into the GSI, over-provision the GSI's throughput, or read from the base table for read-your-writes. Hot GSI partition. Skewed indexed attribute → one GSI partition eats all traffic. Mitigation: composite key (append a bucket/user hash to the indexed attr), or shard the GSI writes explicitly. Index corruption drift.

Likely interviewer follow-ups Why is a scatter-gather query on 100 shards slower than 100× a single-shard read? Because latency is dominated by the slowest shard, not the average. Even if the mean shard responds in 20 ms, the max of 100 samples has a much fatter tail — often 3–5×. Add coordinator merge overhead and network jitter, and the "parallel" fanout is bottlenecked by tail latency.

x: If GSIs are eventually consistent, when would you ever want an LSI? When you need strong consistency on a secondary read but always have the partition key in the query. Example: fetching an order's payment attempts by orderId + attemptStatus . The partition key is always known, and you can't afford a stale read of "payment successful" that hasn't propagated to a GSI yet. Why does PostgreSQL force the unique constraint to include the partition key? Because PostgreSQL only supports local indexes on partitioned tables. It can enforce uniqueness inside a single partition (its local index will refuse duplicates), but it has no global index to enforce uniqueness across partitions.

t: Indexes on Partitioned & Sharded Data — System Design
x: Forcing the constraint to include the partition key means two duplicate rows would necessarily land on the same partition, where the local index catches the collision. Could you build a synchronous GSI? What's the cost? Yes — every base write becomes a distributed 2-phase commit across the base partition and the GSI partition. You get strong consistency but roughly 2× the write latency and a new failure mode: if the GSI is unavailable, the base write blocks. DynamoDB deliberately chose eventual consistency for GSIs to preserve base-table write availability.

x: How would you handle a query needing multiple indexed attributes — say genre AND year ? Options: (1) build a composite GSI with partition key genre and sort key year — one hop, no fanout. (2) fall back to two lookups + intersection (expensive and pointless if either result set is large). (3) push the workload to a search engine like OpenSearch, which is designed for multi-attribute queries. The rule: if it's a hot query, model the composite key upfront; DynamoDB rewards single-purpose indexes over general-purpose ones. Where do you see this in Cassandra? Cassandra's native secondary indexes are effectively LSIs — an index per node covering only that node's data.

x: That's why the community warns against them for high-cardinality attributes: a query without the partition key becomes a coordinator-driven fanout to every node. The preferred pattern is a manual denormalized table keyed on the query attribute — literally hand-building a GSI. SASI and Materialized Views moved the needle but still don't give you a true global index. 🗣️ Interview cheat sheet The 30-second pitch: Once you partition a table by a primary key, any query that doesn't include that key has no locality. Two answers: Local Secondary Index co-locates a small index inside every shard — cheap writes, but pure secondary queries scatter-gather across all shards.

x: Global Secondary Index re-partitions the table by the indexed attribute onto its own node group — pointed reads, but writes now touch two shards and must be async or 2PC. Pick LSI when writes dominate or the partition key is always in the query; pick GSI when the indexed attribute is your dominant read path. The words that win the round: "scatter-gather," "tail latency amplification," "write amplification," "eventual consistency," "hot partition on the GSI." System Design · Interview Prep Design Instagram A photo/video sharing app with a personalized feed at billion-user scale — the canonical "media + social graph + fan-out feed" interview question. 🎯 Scenario 🧑‍🎓 Laymen 📋 Requirements 🏗️ Architecture 🔍 Deep-dive 🧮 DSA ☁️ AWS 💻 C# code ⚖️ Trade-offs 🗣️ Cheat sheet ❓ FAQ 📚 Sources 🎯 Real-world scenario What we're building & where it's used Instagram lets a user snap a photo or record a short video, add a caption, and publish it to their followers, who then see it in a scrollable, personalized home feed .

Underneath a deceptively simple UI sit three hard problems that show up in almost every large consumer app: storing and delivering huge amounts of immutable media cheaply and fast, modeling a massive social graph (who follows whom), and assembling a per-user feed from the posts of everyone you follow — quickly, for hundreds of millions of people at once. The same architectural spine powers Facebook, Twitter/X, TikTok, Pinterest, Snapchat, and LinkedIn. That is exactly why interviewers love it: it forces you to reason about a read-heavy workload (people scroll far more than they post), the classic fan-out-on-write vs.

fan-out-on-read trade-off, object storage plus a CDN for blobs, and how you shard a relational database when a single box can no longer hold the data. The real Instagram famously scaled to 14M+ users with a tiny team on Django, PostgreSQL, Redis and Amazon S3 before Facebook acquired it — a reminder that the fundamentals, done well, take you a very long way. 🧑‍🎓 In laymen terms Your own private magazine, freshly printed every second Think about what Instagram actually is: two billion people take pictures, and two billion people want to see pictures — but only from the handful of friends and celebrities they care about. Nobody wants to see everyone's photos. That's the whole trick.

Imagine a giant printing press in the sky. Every time your friend Priya posts a beach photo, the press immediately prints a copy into your personal magazine — and into the personal magazines of everyone else who follows her. Same for your cousin's dog, your college batch group, the food blogger you follow. When you open the app, you're not searching through a huge pile of "everyone's photos." You're just flipping through your own custom magazine that was already assembled for you. That's why it feels instant. But there's a catch : some people, like Cristiano Ronaldo , have 640 million followers .

If the printing press tried to stamp his photo into 640 million magazines the moment he posts, it would jam. So Instagram plays a clever mixed game — for ordinary people (a few hundred followers), it stamps the photo into everyone's magazine instantly. But for superstars, it does the opposite : their photos sit in one central spot, and when a fan opens their app, Instagram quickly runs over and mixes in the latest superstar posts on the way. The photos themselves? They're not on Instagram's main computers. They live in a giant, cheap warehouse called S3 — basically Amazon's endless attic.

And to make them appear in your feed in a blink no matter where you are on the planet, Instagram keeps small copies of the popular photos in warehouses close to you — one in Mumbai, one in Frankfurt, one in São Paulo. Your phone grabs the picture from the nearest warehouse, not the original one. The really hard part is that all of this — write once, be seen a million times, feel instant — has to hold together while people upload a hundred million photos every single day . 📋 Requirements & scale Requirements and back-of-the-envelope math Functional requirements Upload media — post a photo or video with a caption. Follow / unfollow other users (a directed social graph).

Home feed — see a reverse-chronological (or ranked) feed of posts from people you follow, with low latency. View a user's profile — their posts in reverse-chronological order. (Extensions) likes, comments, search, stories, notifications — mention them, then scope them out to stay focused. Non-functional requirements Highly available — feed should never be "down"; availability > strict consistency. Low latency — feed loads in < 200–500 ms; media renders instantly via CDN. Durable — an uploaded photo is never lost (11 nines of durability on object storage). Eventually consistent — it's fine if your new post takes a few seconds to appear in every follower's feed.

Read-heavy — design for a ~100:1 read:write ratio. Back-of-the-envelope (numbers to volunteer) Assume 500M daily active users out of ~1B total. Say ~100M posts/day (a mix of photos and videos). These round numbers are what interviewers want you to state up front and reason from. Quantity Estimate How we get it Daily active users 500M Given assumption Posts / day ~100M ~0.2 posts per DAU Write QPS (uploads) ~1,200/s avg, ~6k/s peak 100M ÷ 86,400 s; ×5 peak factor Read:write ratio ~100:1 Scrolling ≫ posting Feed-read QPS ~120k/s avg, ~600k/s peak Write QPS × 100 Photo size ~2–3 MB (≈0.5 MB post-compress) Given / typical New media / day ~100–200 TB/day 100M × avg blob size + thumbnails/transco

des Storage / year tens of PB → hundreds of PB with video Daily × 365, ×replication Metadata / year ~tens of GB of rows 100M/day × ~0.5 KB row × 365 The headline takeaway to say out loud: "The bytes live in blob storage + a CDN; the database only stores small metadata rows and the graph. Media storage is the cost/bandwidth problem; feed generation is the latency/fan-out problem." 🏗️ High-level architecture How the pieces fit together Clients talk to an API gateway / load balancer that routes to stateless microservices. The write path and the read path are deliberately separated.

On upload, the client gets a pre-signed URL and pushes the raw bytes directly to object storage (bypassing our servers), then the Post service writes a small metadata row and drops an event on a queue. A fan-out worker consumes that event and pushes the new post ID into the Redis feed-cache list of each follower ("fan-out on write"). On read, the Feed service simply reads the pre-computed list of post IDs from Redis, hydrates them with metadata, and returns CDN URLs for the media — so the scroll is a couple of fast cache lookups, not a giant join.

write / async fan-out read / feed path media (blob + CDN) data stores The two paths, step by step Upload: client asks Post service for a pre-signed URL, uploads raw bytes straight to S3, then confirms — Post service writes a metadata row (author, caption, media key, timestamp, a globally-unique post ID) and emits a "new post" event. Process: a worker generates thumbnails / transcodes video into multiple resolutions, storing them back in S3 behind the CDN. Fan-out: the fan-out worker looks up the author's followers in the graph store and prepends the post ID to each follower's Redis feed list (capped, e.g. latest 500–1000).

Read feed: Feed service reads the pre-computed post-ID list from Redis, batch-hydrates metadata from cache/DB, and returns items with CDN media URLs — the client streams the bytes from the nearest edge. 🔍 Component deep-dive Media storage — never put blobs in your database Photos and videos are large, immutable, and served by the millions per second — a perfect fit for object storage (S3) , not a relational DB. The DB stores only a small row with the S3 object key . Uploads go directly from client to S3 via a pre-signed URL so our app servers never touch the bytes, and downloads go through a CDN that caches media at edge locations near the user.

This is what makes media "render instantly" — the bytes travel the shortest possible network path, and origin (S3) load stays low because of high cache-hit ratios. Feed generation — fan-out on write vs. fan-out on read This is the heart of the interview. Fan-out on write (push): when you post, we immediately write the post ID into every follower's precomputed feed list in Redis. Reads are then O(1) — dirt cheap and fast — at the cost of expensive writes and storage duplication. Fan-out on read (pull): we store nothing precomputed; at read time we gather recent posts from everyone you follow and merge them.

Writes are cheap, but reads are expensive (a merge across hundreds of authors on every scroll). The production answer is hybrid . Use push for the common case (most users have a modest follower count), but for celebrities with tens of millions of followers, fanning out a single post to 50M lists is catastrophic (the "hot key" / thundering-herd problem). So for those high-fan-out accounts we switch to pull : their posts are not pushed; instead, at read time the Feed service merges the viewer's precomputed list with a fresh pull of the few celebrities they follow. Best of both worlds.

The social graph & sharding Follows are a directed graph stored as adjacency lists ( followers(userId) → [followerIds] and following(userId) → [...] ). Everything is sharded by user ID so one user's data lives on one shard. That means a globally unique, roughly time-sortable post ID matters a lot: Instagram's real solution was a 64-bit ID minted in Postgres that packs a millisecond timestamp, the shard ID, and a per-shard sequence number — so IDs sort by time and encode where the row lives, with no central coordinator. Caching & hot keys Multiple cache layers: the CDN for media, Redis for feed lists, and Memcached/Redis for hot metadata (post rows, user profiles, follower counts).

Hot keys (a viral post, a celebrity profile) are mitigated with request coalescing, short TTLs, and replicas. The DB sits behind all of this and mostly serves cache misses and writes. 🧮 The DSA behind it Data structures & algorithms The design looks like plumbing, but each choice is a deliberate data-structure decision: Redis list / sorted set per user — the precomputed feed. A capped list gives O(1) prepend and O(1) range-read of the latest N. A sorted set keyed by timestamp (or a ranking score) lets you keep it ordered and trim the tail cheaply. k-way merge with a min/max-heap — fan-out-on-read and the hybrid merge combine posts from many authors in timestamp order.

Push the newest post from each of the k sources into a heap and pop the max repeatedly: O(N log k) to produce N feed items. 64-bit time-sortable IDs (Snowflake-style) — [41 bits ms timestamp | 13 bits shard | 10 bits sequence] . Distributed, collision-free, and monotonic-by-time so a feed can be ordered by ID alone. Adjacency lists for the follow graph — the natural structure for "get all followers of X" in O(degree). Consistent hashing to map user ID → shard/cache node, so adding capacity moves only a small slice of keys. Bloom filter — a compact "have you already seen this post?" check to de-duplicate the feed without a DB round-trip.

API entry API Gateway / ALB TLS, auth, routing, throttling to stateless services.

Compute (services) ECS/EKS or Lambda Stateless Post/Feed/Graph services that scale horizontally. Media blobs Amazon S3 11 nines durability, cheap, direct pre-signed uploads; origin for CloudFront. Media processing Lambda / MediaConvert Thumbnails + video transcoding into multiple bitrates, triggered by S3 events. Metadata store DynamoDB (or Aurora/RDS sharded) Post/user rows keyed by ID; DynamoDB gives auto-sharding + predictable latency. Feed cache ElastiCache for Redis Precomputed per-user feed lists; O(1) prepend/range-read. Hot-read acceleration DAX / ElastiCache Microsecond reads for hot profiles/posts, shielding the DB.

Async fan-out SQS / SNS / Kinesis (or MSK) Decouple upload from fan-out; absorb spikes; retry safely. Search / discovery OpenSearch Hashtag, caption, and user search. Observability CloudWatch Metrics, alarms on feed latency and queue depth. Deployment: clients hit CloudFront/API Gateway; stateless containers on ECS/EKS across multiple AZs sit behind an ALB and auto-scale on CPU/queue depth. Uploads flow client→S3 directly; an S3 event fires a Lambda to transcode; a "new post" message goes to SQS, and fan-out workers (ECS/Lambda) update ElastiCache. DynamoDB holds metadata with on-demand capacity, and everything replicates across AZs (and Regions for the media/CDN layer) for availability.

shardId = shardId; public long NextId () { lock (_lock) { var ms = DateTimeOffset.UtcNow.ToUnixTimeMilliseconds(); if (ms == _lastMs) { _seq = (_seq + 1 ) & MaxSeq; if (_seq == 0 ) while ((ms = DateTimeOffset.UtcNow.ToUnixTimeMilliseconds()) <= _lastMs) { } // spin to next ms } else _seq = 0 ; _lastMs = ms; return ((ms - Epoch) << (ShardBits + SeqBits)) | (_shardId << SeqBits) | _seq; } } } // ---- 2.

FollowerCountAsync (authorId); if (followerCount > CelebThreshold) return ; // celebrity → pulled at read time await foreach ( var follower in _graph. GetFollowersAsync (authorId)) { await _redis.

LPushCappedAsync ($ "feed:{follower}" , postId, FeedCap); } } // Read path: merge precomputed feed with fresh posts from followed celebrities. public async Task< List < Post >> GetFeedAsync ( long userId, int limit = 30 ) { var pushedIds = await _redis. LRangeAsync ($ "feed:{userId}" , 0 , limit * 2 ); var celebs = await _graph. GetFollowedCelebritiesAsync (userId); var pulledIds = await _posts. RecentPostIdsAsync (celebs, limit); // IDs are time-sortable → merge & take newest. (heap for true k-way merge) var merged = pushedIds. Concat (pulledIds) . Distinct () . OrderByDescending (id => id) . Take (limit); return ( await _posts. HydrateAsync (merged)).

ToList (); // attach CDN URLs } } In other stacks you'd reach for the same shapes: Redis LPUSH / LTRIM for the capped list, a real min-heap for the k-way merge (e.g. PriorityQueue<T> in .NET), and Twitter's open-source Snowflake or a DB sequence for IDs. ⚖️ Trade-offs, bottlenecks & likely follow-ups The celebrity fan-out problem. Pure push dies on accounts with tens of millions of followers — one post triggers tens of millions of writes and a latency spike. The hybrid (push for the masses, pull for celebrities) is the standard answer; be ready to name the follower threshold as a tunable. Consistency vs. availability.

We choose availability and eventual consistency (a post appearing a few seconds late is fine), but a user must always see their own post immediately — so on read we can splice the user's own recent posts in even before fan-out finishes ("read-your-writes" for the author). Storage & bandwidth are the dominant cost. Video multiplies everything; you transcode into multiple bitrates and lean hard on CDN cache-hit ratio and tiered/cold storage (S3 Glacier) for old media. Hot keys & thundering herds on viral content — solved with request coalescing, multiple cache replicas, and short TTLs. "How do you keep the feed fast at 500M users?" Precompute it.

Reads become O(1) Redis lookups; the expensive work happens asynchronously off the write path. "What breaks first as you scale, and how do you shard?" The single DB. Shard by user ID with consistent hashing, and use time-sortable Snowflake IDs that encode the shard so you never need a global lookup. "How do you order the feed — chronological or ranked?" Start chronological (sort by ID). To rank, store a score in a Redis sorted set and compute it from engagement signals; the structure is the same, only the sort key changes.

"How does upload not overload your servers?" Pre-signed URLs — the client uploads bytes straight to S3; our servers only handle the small metadata write and enqueue processing. 🗣️ Interview cheat sheet 30-second pitch: "Media lives in S3 behind a CDN; the DB only holds small metadata rows and the follow graph. I separate the write and read paths: uploads go straight to S3 via pre-signed URLs and enqueue an async fan-out that pushes post IDs into each follower's precomputed Redis feed list. Reads are then O(1) cache lookups.

I use a hybrid fan-out — push for normal users, pull for celebrities — to dodge the hot-key problem, and shard everything by user ID with time-sortable Snowflake IDs." Numbers to quote: 500M DAU, ~100M posts/day, ~100:1 read:write, feed < 200–500 ms, media = the storage/bandwidth cost, feed = the fan-out/latency cost. Talking point 1: Blobs in object storage + CDN; never in the DB. Talking point 2: Fan-out on write for cheap reads; hybrid to survive celebrities. Talking point 3: Pre-signed uploads keep bytes off your servers. Talking point 4: Shard by user ID; Snowflake IDs sort by time and encode the shard.

Talking point 5: Availability > consistency; eventual consistency, but read-your-writes for the author. ❓ FAQ — your follow-up questions Questions asked about this topic No follow-up questions yet — ask one about this topic and it'll be logged here with a compact answer. 📚 Sources Hello Interview — Instagram System Design breakdown GeeksforGeeks — Design Instagram (system design interview) Instagram Engineering blog — real production architecture (Django, PostgreSQL sharding, Snowflake-style IDs, Redis, S3) High Scalability — Instagram architecture write-ups Generated by the design-research skill · researched via web search · open via localhost

API requests carry the access token in the Authorization: Bearer header; each microservice (or the API gateway) verifies the signature locally against the auth service's public key — no database, no network hop. When the access token expires, the client silently exchanges the refresh token for a new pair ( rotation ).

What a JWT actually is A JWT is three Base64URL segments joined by dots: header.payload.signature . The header names the algorithm (e.g. {"alg":"RS256","typ":"JWT"} ). The payload holds claims — registered ones like iss (issuer), sub (subject/user id), aud (audience), exp (expiry), iat (issued-at), jti (token id), plus custom claims like roles/scopes.

x: The signature is computed over base64(header) + "." + base64(payload) with a key. Crucially, the payload is signed, not encrypted — anyone can read it, so never put secrets in a JWT . Verification means recomputing/validating the signature and checking exp / aud / iss ; if it passes, the claims are trustworthy without a database. 2. Sessions (stateful) vs JWT (stateless) — the core decision The classic alternative is a server-side session : on login you store a session record and hand the client an opaque session id cookie; every request looks the session up in Redis. This gives instant revocation (delete the row) but adds a store lookup to every request.

t: JWT & User Login Flow — System Design Interview
x: A JWT flips it: the token is self-describing so any service verifies it locally — perfect for microservices and horizontal scale — but you lose easy revocation because there's no server record to delete. The mature answer is the hybrid you see everywhere : stateless access JWTs for the hot path + a stateful refresh token store for the revocation lever. 3. Access token vs refresh token The access token is short-lived (5–15 min), sent on every request, and deliberately not checked against a database — its short TTL is what bounds damage if stolen. The refresh token is long-lived (days–weeks), sent only to the /refresh endpoint, and is tracked server-side so it can be revoked.

x: When the access token expires the client quietly swaps the refresh token for a fresh pair, so the user never notices. 4. Refresh token rotation & reuse detection Best practice (Auth0/OAuth BCP): every refresh issues a brand-new refresh token and invalidates the old one — rotation. The server tracks a token family . If an already-used refresh token is ever replayed, that means someone stole it, so the server invalidates the entire family , forcing re-authentication. This turns a stolen refresh token from a persistent backdoor into a one-shot that trips an alarm. 5.

x: The revocation problem (the #1 follow-up) "If JWTs are stateless, how do you log someone out immediately?" You can't un-issue a signed token, so you use one of: (a) short access-token TTL so it self-expires in minutes; (b) a denylist — cache the jti of revoked tokens in Redis until their exp , and have the gateway check it (reintroduces a small stateful lookup, but only for the denylist); or (c) revoke at the refresh layer — kill the refresh token so no new access tokens can be minted, and let the current one die within minutes. Most systems combine (a) + (c), adding (b) only for high-security "kill it now" needs. 6.

x: RS256 (asymmetric) signs with a private key and lets anyone verify with the public key — so the Auth Service holds the private key and every microservice verifies independently. That's why real fleets use RS256 (or ES256) and publish keys via a JWKS endpoint. OAuth2 is the delegation framework ("let this app act for me"); OpenID Connect layers identity on top and defines the ID token (itself a JWT). "Login with Google" is OIDC Authorization Code + PKCE: you redirect to Google, get a code, exchange it for tokens, verify Google's ID token, then mint your own.
