System Design · Interview Prep Load Balancer The single front door that fans traffic across a fleet — L4 vs L7, round-robin vs consistent hashing, health checks, session affinity, and how to make the load balancer itself fault-tolerant. 🎯 Scenario 🧑‍🎓 Laymen 📋 Requirements 🏗️ Architecture 🎬 Animation 🔍 Deep-dive 🧮 DSA ☁️ AWS 💻 C# code ⚖️ Trade-offs 🗣️ Cheat sheet ❓ FAQ 📚 Sources 🎯 Real-world scenario What we're building & where it's used A load balancer is the single public endpoint that sits in front of a fleet of servers, accepts every incoming request, and decides which backend gets it.

It is the piece that lets an application scale beyond one machine, survive machine failures, deploy new versions safely, and terminate TLS in one place. Every large product you use is behind one: Netflix in front of its edge tier, Amazon in front of its retail API, WhatsApp in front of its chat servers, Uber in front of its dispatcher, GitHub in front of its API, your bank in front of its login page. The load balancer answers three related questions at once. How do we present one address to millions of clients? Give clients one DNS name resolving to the LB. How do we survive a server crash? Health-check every backend and stop sending it traffic within seconds.

How do we scale horizontally? Add another backend, register it with the LB, done. It also solves several bonus problems: TLS termination, WAF integration, cross-zone routing, canary/blue-green rollout, and hiding backend IPs from the world. This is a classic interview question because it touches almost every distributed-systems concept: consistent hashing, health checks, session state, HA/failover, DNS, CAP trade-offs, and the difference between transport-layer (L4) and application-layer (L7) routing. Whether a candidate can whiteboard "here's how one request reaches one server, and here's what happens when that server dies" is a strong signal for senior-level system-design roles.

🧑‍🎓 In laymen terms Explain it like I've never written code Imagine a huge, popular restaurant . There's one entrance, one host at the door — and behind them, thirty identical kitchens ready to cook. Every diner walks up to the same host, and the host quietly points them to a table near whichever kitchen has the shortest queue. Diners never see the kitchens. They never know which one cooked their meal. They just see the door, order their food, and eat. That host is the load balancer . The kitchens are the servers. The magic isn't in the cooking — it's in the calm, invisible dispatch . Because the host spreads customers evenly, no single kitchen gets slammed while others sit idle.

If one kitchen catches fire, the host stops sending anyone that way and diverts them to the others — the restaurant keeps serving without anyone noticing. Now think about the tricky parts: How does the host know which kitchen is free? They quietly check every few seconds — "you still cooking? still cooking? still cooking?" — and if a kitchen doesn't respond, they mark it "closed" until it recovers. That's a health check . What if you're mid-meal at kitchen 7 and order dessert? The host remembers you and sends you back to the same kitchen so your table isn't split up. That's session affinity .

What if the host themselves gets sick? A second host is standing right there, watching, ready to take over the exact moment the first one steps away. That's high availability . Without it, the whole restaurant would grind to a halt every time the host sneezes. Every big website — Netflix, Amazon, WhatsApp, Uber, Instagram, your bank — is really a restaurant with tens of thousands of kitchens and a small army of hosts at the door working together. You just never notice, because they're doing the whole job in about one millisecond, forever.

📋 Requirements & scale Requirements and back-of-the-envelope math Functional requirements Accept incoming connections on one virtual IP / DNS name and forward each to a healthy backend server. Support multiple algorithms for target selection: round-robin, weighted, least-connections, IP-hash / consistent-hash. Run active health checks against each backend and remove failing targets from the pool within seconds. Optionally provide session affinity (sticky sessions) so a client keeps hitting the same backend. Terminate TLS at the edge for L7 mode; pass through TCP/UDP for L4 mode. Emit rich metrics and logs for every request/connection: latency, status, target, health-check state.

Non-functional requirements Very high availability. The LB itself must not be a single point of failure — active/active across zones, DNS failover, floating VIP. Extremely low latency added. Sub-millisecond for L4, single-digit ms for L7. Millions of requests per second and tens of millions of concurrent connections at scale. Graceful drain on backend removal so in-flight requests complete. Observability — every routing decision explainable. Back-of-the-envelope Dimension Typical number Why Peak RPS handled by one AWS ALB / NLB Millions of req/sec (elastic) ELB auto-scales; capacity is not a fixed limit for well-warmed LBs.

Latency added by L4 (NLB) ~100 µs Just a flow-hash lookup + packet forward — near line rate. Latency added by L7 (ALB / HAProxy) ~1–5 ms p50 TLS termination + HTTP parsing + policy eval. Concurrent connections per node ~1M with tuned kernel Ephemeral ports, file descriptors, and RAM per connection govern it. Health-check interval 5–30 s Too fast burns backend CPU; too slow leaves users hitting dead nodes. Unhealthy threshold 2–3 consecutive fails Balance false positives vs time-to-eject. Connection drain timeout 30–300 s Long enough for streams to finish, short enough not to stall deploys. Cross-zone LB fan-out 3 AZs typical Loss of one AZ leaves 2/3 capacity live.

🏗️ High-level architecture How the pieces fit together A production load balancer is not one box — it's a tier . DNS resolves the LB name to multiple load-balancer node IPs (one per zone). Each node runs the routing logic: parse the request, look up the target group, select a healthy backend using the configured algorithm, forward the packet or the HTTP request, and record the result. A separate health-check subsystem pings each backend on a schedule and updates the routing table when a target flips healthy/unhealthy. A control plane handles configuration updates, TLS certs, and target registration without dropping in-flight traffic.

Client LB data plane Healthy backend Ejected backend Health-check probe Control plane 🎬 Animation Watch the core mechanic run, step by step The animation walks through a request landing on the LB, being routed to Server B via least-connections, a health check catching Server C going down, and a subsequent request being routed around the failure — the whole "what makes an LB an LB" cycle in one frame. ▶ Play Step → ← Back ↺ Reset Ready Press ▶ Play to start 🔍 Component deep-dive L4 vs L7 — the fundamental split A Layer 4 load balancer operates at the transport layer. It sees TCP/UDP packets, not HTTP requests.

It picks a backend using a flow hash — a hash of (src_ip, src_port, dst_ip, dst_port, protocol) — and forwards every packet in that flow to the same target for the connection's lifetime. It doesn't parse anything above TCP. This makes it extremely fast (microseconds of added latency), protocol-agnostic (works for anything over TCP/UDP: TLS, MQTT, gRPC-over-TCP, database protocols), and blind to application semantics. A Layer 7 load balancer terminates the TCP connection itself, parses the HTTP request, and routes based on content : the URL path, host header, cookies, method, query string.

This is what lets you say "requests to /api/v2/* go to the v2 fleet" or "requests with cookie canary=1 go to the canary pods." The trade-off is TLS + HTTP parsing add latency (single-digit ms) and expose it to HTTP-level attacks. Modern L7 LBs (envoy, nginx, HAProxy, ALB) also do TLS termination, WebSocket upgrade, HTTP/2 fan-out, and connection multiplexing. The routing algorithms Round Robin Cycle through the pool in order. Simple, memoryless, ignores load. Fine when backends are identical and requests are uniform. Weighted Round Robin Assign weights; bigger boxes get more turns. Handles heterogeneous fleets and canary ramps.

Least Connections Pick the backend with the fewest open connections right now. Best for long-lived or variable-length requests. Least Response Time Combine "fewest connections" with recent p50 latency. Actively steers away from struggling backends. IP Hash / Source Hash Hash client IP → same backend. Cheap session affinity without cookies. Breaks under NAT. Consistent Hashing Backends and keys on a ring; keys go clockwise to the next node. Adding/removing a backend disturbs only 1/N keys — vital for caches. Power of Two Choices Pick two random backends, take the less loaded. Near-optimal load balance at O(1) cost and no shared state.

Maglev / Rendezvous Consistent-hash variants used by Google and CDNs for stateless, memory-friendly, symmetric routing. Health checks Health checks are the LB's truth signal about the fleet. They come in two forms. Active health checks are probes the LB sends on a schedule — a TCP SYN , a TLS handshake, or an HTTP GET /healthz — and grade each backend. Passive checks watch real traffic and eject a backend that starts returning 5xxs or timing out (outlier detection). A well-tuned LB uses both.

Key parameters: interval (how often we probe — 5–30 s), timeout (how long to wait for a response — a few seconds), unhealthy threshold (consecutive failures before ejection — usually 2 or 3), and healthy threshold (consecutive successes before re-admission). Every parameter is a trade-off between false positives and time-to-detect. Session affinity (sticky sessions) Sometimes the backend keeps state per user — a shopping cart, a game session, an SSE stream. The LB then needs to send the same user back to the same server. Two approaches: cookie-based stickiness (the LB injects a cookie like AWSALB=<target-id> and honors it) or IP-hash / source-affinity .

Cookies are more precise; IP-hash breaks when many clients share an IP (mobile CGNAT, corporate proxies). Both come at the cost of load imbalance — you're overriding the algorithm's judgment. The best answer is often "make the backend stateless and don't need affinity." High availability of the LB itself The load balancer is the front door — if it dies, everything dies. Production LBs achieve HA through redundancy at every layer . Multiple LB nodes run in parallel, one per availability zone; the DNS returns all their IPs so clients naturally shard across them.

Inside a single VIP, ECMP (equal-cost multi-path routing) or a floating VIP managed by keepalived/VRRP lets a peer take over an address within milliseconds. Managed services like AWS ELB do this transparently; self-hosted setups (HAProxy + keepalived, nginx + Consul + BGP) reproduce the pattern. TLS termination and connection lifecycle Terminating TLS at the LB centralises certificate management (one cert, not one per backend), lets the LB inspect HTTP for routing, and offloads crypto from backends. Some architectures prefer re-encryption (mTLS to backends) for defense in depth.

Long-lived connections (WebSocket, gRPC streaming) need connection draining : when a backend is deregistered, the LB stops sending new traffic to it but lets existing streams finish for up to 5 minutes. 🧮 The DSA behind it Data structures & algorithms Under the hood, a load balancer is a small stack of very classical CS. Every routing decision must be O(1) or O(log N) — millions per second per node. Round-robin counter — a single atomic integer modulo N. O(1) selection; the "hello world" algorithm. Min-heap on active connections — least-connections uses a heap keyed by connection count, giving O(log N) select and O(log N) increment/decrement on connect/disconnect.

Consistent hash ring — nodes and keys hashed onto a 32-bit or 64-bit ring; a request finds "the next node clockwise" via binary search on a sorted array of hash points. O(log N) lookup, and adding/removing a backend disturbs only 1/N of keys. Used everywhere from Cassandra to memcached to Envoy's ring-hash LB. Maglev hashing — Google's improvement: a fixed-size lookup table where every entry maps to a backend and each backend gets a near-equal share. O(1) lookup; small disruption on membership changes; symmetric across nodes so any LB gets the same answer for the same 5-tuple. Rendezvous / HRW hashing — for each request key, compute hash(key, node_i) for every backend, take the max.

O(N) but stateless and easy to reason about — used in some CDNs and cache tiers. Bloom filter of drained IDs — to answer "is this connection stuck to an old backend?" with a tiny memory footprint during rolling deployments. Ring buffer of health-check results — per backend, the last K probe outcomes. Sliding window O(1) decides "unhealthy" once ≥ threshold in the buffer are failures. Concurrent hash map — flow table mapping 5-tuple → backend, so every packet of an established TCP flow is routed to the same target without recomputing the hash.

Service Layer Best for Key traits ALB — Application Load Balancer L7 HTTP/HTTPS/gRPC APIs, path- and host-based routing, canaries, WAF integration. HTTP/2, WebSockets, Lambda targets, header/cookie routing, redirects, fixed responses, TLS termination + re-encrypt. NLB — Network Load Balancer L4 Extreme throughput, static IPs, non-HTTP protocols, PrivateLink endpoints. Millions of RPS, ~100 µs added latency, preserves source IP, per-AZ static IP, QUIC support, flow-hash routing. GWLB — Gateway Load Balancer L3+L4 Inserting third-party virtual appliances (firewalls, IDS) transparently into the traffic path. GENEVE encapsulation, route-table reachability, flow-symmetry, no proxying.

CLB — Classic Load Balancer L4/L7 Legacy EC2-Classic; new designs should not use it. Deprecated in favor of ALB/NLB for new workloads. Component AWS service Why DNS in front of the LB Route 53 (alias record) Health-checked, latency-based or geo routing; multi-region failover. Global anycast entry point Global Accelerator Static anycast IPs + AWS backbone for fast, deterministic entry into regional LBs. Public HTTPS API ALB + ACM cert TLS termination, HTTP/2, path routing, WAF association. Ultra-low-latency TCP/UDP NLB PrivateLink source, gaming/streaming, database front-end.

Compute targets EC2 / ECS / EKS / Lambda ALB supports Lambda targets; both ALB and NLB support IP and instance targets. Health checks Target-group health checks + Route 53 checks Two layers: LB-local for target ejection, Route 53 for regional failover. Autoscaling behind LB Auto Scaling group attached to target group Backends scale in/out with traffic; the LB always sees the current set. Traffic inspection AWS WAF + Shield Bot filtering, rate limiting, DDoS protection sitting on top of ALB. Observability CloudWatch + Access logs to S3 Per-target metrics, request logs for forensics.

Concretely: for a typical web API, put an ALB in front of an EKS or ECS service with WAF attached; front it with Route 53 alias record; deploy the ALB across at least three AZs. For a stateless TCP service (game server, MQTT broker), use an NLB and preserve source IP so backends see real clients. For a global product, add Global Accelerator so users hit the nearest AWS edge and traverse the AWS backbone the rest of the way. NLB and ALB both auto-scale and hide the load-balancer HA plumbing behind a single DNS name.

The bones above are what tools like YARP (Microsoft's reverse proxy), Envoy , and HAProxy implement — just faster and in C++/Rust. ⚖️ Trade-offs, bottlenecks & likely follow-ups Where a load balancer hurts It's still a bottleneck. Every packet flows through it, so its throughput ceiling is your ceiling. Solution: run many LB nodes and let DNS or ECMP fan out across them. AWS ELB does this transparently; self-hosted needs BGP or Anycast to scale beyond one box. L7 costs latency. Parsing HTTP and terminating TLS adds ~1–5 ms. If you don't need content-based routing, use L4 and preserve simplicity + speed. Sticky sessions kill load balance.

Once a user is stuck to a warm backend, the algorithm can't rebalance them. Preferred fix: externalize session state (Redis, DynamoDB) and make backends stateless. Rebalancing is disruptive without consistent hashing. A modulo-N hash sends 100% of traffic to different backends when N changes. Consistent hashing (or Maglev) limits disturbance to 1/N — mandatory for cache tiers. Health checks lie. A backend can pass /healthz while its downstream DB is broken. Add deep health checks that exercise dependencies, and use passive outlier detection on real traffic to catch what active probes miss. Thundering herd on backend restart.

When a large backend comes back healthy, least-connections routes a burst to it. Mitigate with slow start — the ALB supports this natively — where a new target ramps up over 30–900 s. Likely interview follow-ups When would you pick NLB over ALB? Sub-millisecond latency, non-HTTP protocols (MQTT, gRPC over raw TCP, gaming UDP), static IPs, or you need to expose the service through PrivateLink. Otherwise ALB, because content-based routing and Lambda targets are worth the extra ms. Why consistent hashing for caches specifically? Cache hit rate depends on the same key going to the same node. With plain modulo, adding one node invalidates ~ (N-1)/N of the cache.

Consistent hashing invalidates only ~ 1/N , keeping hit rates high through fleet changes. How does the LB avoid being a single point of failure? Redundant nodes across AZs, DNS with multiple A records, and a floating VIP (VRRP/keepalived) or ECMP so a peer takes the address within milliseconds. Managed LBs (ELB) handle all of this behind one DNS name. What happens to in-flight requests when you deregister a target? Connection draining — the LB stops sending new work but lets existing streams finish for up to a configurable timeout (30 s to 5 min). Only then is the target actually torn down. How do you handle sticky sessions without breaking scale? Best answer: don't.

Push session state to Redis or a signed cookie, keep backends stateless. If you must, use LB-generated cookies (not IP-hash) so you're immune to NAT and can drain cleanly. Round-robin vs least-connections vs power-of-two — when do they diverge? Uniform request cost → round-robin is fine. Highly variable request cost (WebSockets, long-poll, mixed API) → least-connections wins. Massive fleets where global state is expensive → power-of-two-choices gives near-least-connections quality with no shared state. Global Accelerator vs Route 53 latency routing — what's the difference? Route 53 answers DNS with the closest regional LB's name.

Global Accelerator gives you a fixed anycast IP and moves traffic onto the AWS backbone at the nearest edge, reducing internet-path variance. Use Accelerator when clients don't cache DNS well or you need instant regional failover. 🗣️ Interview cheat sheet The 30-second pitch: "A load balancer is the single-endpoint dispatcher in front of a horizontal fleet. Clients hit one DNS name; the LB picks a healthy backend using an algorithm — round-robin for uniform workloads, least-connections for variable ones, consistent hashing for cache affinity — and forwards the request.

It runs continuous health checks to eject failed backends, terminates TLS, supports sticky sessions when needed, and is itself made HA by running redundant nodes across AZs with DNS or floating VIPs. On AWS: ALB for HTTP with content routing, NLB for extreme L4 throughput, GWLB for appliance insertion, Route 53 in front for regional failover." Numbers to quote: NLB ~100 µs added latency, ALB single-digit ms; millions of RPS per LB; ~1M concurrent conns per node; health checks 5–30 s interval, 2–3 fails to eject; drain 30–300 s. Five talking points that win the round: L4 vs L7: transport-layer flow hashing vs application-layer content routing — pick by latency vs feature need.

Algorithms: RR, weighted RR, least-connections, consistent hash, power-of-two — name them and know which fits which shape of load. Health checks + connection draining: how a failed node is ejected fast and a deregistered node dies gracefully. The LB's own HA: multi-AZ nodes, DNS spread, VIP failover — the front door must not be a SPOF. AWS mapping: ALB / NLB / GWLB / Global Accelerator / Route 53 — which for which job. Words to say: "flow hash", "5-tuple", "consistent hashing ring", "connection draining", "slow start", "outlier detection", "sticky sessions via LB cookie".

System Design · Concurrency · Solution Architect Playbook Locking & Concurrency Control in Distributed Systems A field guide for choosing between optimistic, pessimistic, row-level, distributed, atomic-update, and versioning strategies — with the real-world scenarios that make each one the right answer, and the interview traps that make them the wrong one.

🎯 Problem 🧑‍🎓 Laymen 📋 Approaches 🏗️ Big picture 🎬 Animation 🔍 Each mechanism 🎬 Scenarios 💥 Failures 🧭 Decision matrix 🪤 Interview traps 💻 C# code 🗣️ Cheat sheet ❓ FAQ 📚 Sources 🎯 The problem Two things want to change the same thing at the same time Every real system eventually hits the same shape of bug: two requests arrive concurrently, both read the same value, both make an independent decision, and both write. The second write silently overwrites the first — money vanishes, inventory goes negative, five copies of a "daily report" email land in the customer's inbox, or a table row shows a state that neither user actually asked for.

This is the concurrency problem, and it doesn't care whether you have one server, five servers, or five hundred. The concurrency literature offers a small toolbox: optimistic locking (let everyone work, verify before saving), pessimistic locking (lock the resource before touching it), row-level database locks , distributed locks across servers via Redis or ZooKeeper, advisory locks for cross-transaction coordination, atomic database operations that dodge locking altogether, and versioning / compare-and-swap / ETag patterns for stateless APIs. Each is right somewhere. Each is disastrous somewhere else. This page is the map.

Every mechanism is explained the same way: what problem it solves, its mental model, an architecture diagram, one crisp production scenario, and where it fails. Then a decision matrix and a decision tree bring it all back together. The goal is not to be able to say what optimistic locking is — it is to look at a new problem and instantly answer "which mechanism, why, and what fails if we pick wrong?". 🧑‍🎓 In laymen terms Five ways to share one whiteboard Imagine a whiteboard in a shared office. Ten people occasionally walk up, read what's there, erase some part, and write something new. If two of them arrive at once, one person's changes disappear.

How do we prevent that? Pessimistic locking is the most obvious answer — put a padlock on the whiteboard. Whoever arrives first turns the key, does their edit, then unlocks. Everyone else stands in a queue. Nothing gets lost, but the queue can be slow and if the first person faints while holding the key, nobody moves. Optimistic locking is more relaxed. Everyone photocopies the whiteboard, walks off to their desk, edits their copy in peace, then comes back. Before they write anything on the real board, they check: "is the board still exactly the way it was when I photocopied?" If yes, they write.

If someone else has edited it in the meantime, they throw their copy away, take a fresh photocopy, and redo the edit. Fast when conflicts are rare, wasteful when they aren't. Atomic operations are cleverer still — instead of locking the whole board, you tell it: "if the current number is 1, subtract 1". The board handles the check and the write in one indivisible motion. No lock. No photocopy. This is what a good database engine does on your behalf when you write UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE qty > 0 . Distributed locks are for when the whiteboard is on a different floor and multiple offices want to edit it.

Now you need one shared padlock that every office can see — usually a Redis key. Whoever writes their name on the padlock first owns it for a while. Versioning / ETag is the postal-mail version of optimistic locking. Every version of the board is stamped with a number. When you mail in your edit, you also mail in the version you were editing. The board only applies your edit if that version is still the latest. Every real product uses several of these together. Gmail's drafts are optimistic (last-save-wins, with conflict UI). Payment systems are pessimistic on money rows. Instagram inventory decrements are atomic. Kubernetes scheduling is distributed-lock territory.

The trick is not knowing what each does — it's knowing which to reach for. 📋 The 8 approaches at a glance Every mechanism in one table Mechanism Mental model Where it lives Best for Pain Optimistic locking "Verify before save" App + DB (Version col) Rare conflicts, UI edits Retries under contention Pessimistic locking "Lock, then modify" DB row lock Short critical section on scarce row Blocks readers, deadlock risk Row-level DB lock SELECT … FOR UPDATE Inside a transaction Reserving a single resource Long transactions kill throughput Atomic DB operation "Check + write in one query" DB engine Counters, inventory, balances Only works for expressible predicates Distributed lock (Redis) "One w

inner across N servers" Redis / ZooKeeper / etcd Cross-server coordination (jobs, singletons) Async replication, no fencing, complex DB advisory lock Application-defined named lock Postgres / SQL Server Cross-transaction coordination inside one DB Tied to one DB, connection-scoped Compare-and-Swap / Version "Only write if version = X" DB / cache / DynamoDB Stateless services, DynamoDB Same conflict cost as optimistic locking ETag / If-Match Optimistic over HTTP REST APIs Concurrent editors of a document Requires clients to send the header Two rules of thumb before we dive in. First, reach for an atomic DB operation first — the fewer explicit locks in your design, the fewer failure modes.

Second, distributed locks are a coordination tool, not a correctness tool — always pair them with an idempotency ledger if the outcome must be exactly-once. 🏗️ Big picture Where each mechanism sits in a real stack The two "sides" of concurrency control are the data layer (where the resource actually lives) and the application layer (where the caller decides how to touch it). Locks can live on either side; usually the answer is the one closer to the resource. The picture makes one thing obvious. Row-level, atomic, versioning, and advisory locks all live inside the database — they are natural, transactional, and safe.

Distributed locks live outside the database in Redis / etcd / ZooKeeper — they exist precisely because the database cannot help coordinate work between servers that aren't touching the DB (like "only one pod runs the nightly job"). ETag is optimistic locking translated to HTTP . Pick the layer closest to where the actual conflict happens. 🎬 Animation The inventory race — three strategies, one shared row Stock = 1. Customer A and Customer B both hit "Buy" at the same time. Watch how the same race plays out under three designs: no locking (lost update), pessimistic lock (blocking wait), and atomic update (one query wins, no lock).

▶ Play Step → ← Back ↺ Reset Ready Press ▶ Play to start 🔍 Every mechanism — concept, architecture, and one scenario 1. Optimistic locking — "let everyone work, verify before saving" Concept. Nobody blocks. Two users can open the same row and edit it side-by-side. When one of them clicks Save, the server checks whether the row is still the way it was when they opened it. If yes, save. If not, the save is rejected and the user reloads. Called optimistic because it assumes conflicts are rare and does not pay any locking cost upfront. Scenario — two edits to the same customer row. User A opens Customer 1001 and changes the phone. User B opens the same row and changes the address.

Both saved rows started as Version = 10 . The application issues: -- Optimistic UPDATE embeds the previously-read version UPDATE Customer SET Address = 'Mumbai' , Version = 11 WHERE CustomerId = 1001 AND Version = 10; The first request lands. RowsAffected = 1 . The second lands moments later — the row is now Version 11, so the WHERE clause matches nothing. RowsAffected = 0 . The app returns a 409 Conflict; the client reloads and re-applies. No locks were held during editing, so a user could take three hours in the form and not block anyone. 2. Pessimistic locking — "lock, then modify" Concept. Before I read the row, I claim it. Anyone else who tries to read it with intent-to-write must wait.

Guarantees no conflict but at the cost of throughput. Called pessimistic because it assumes conflicts are common and pays the coordination cost upfront. Scenario — the last hospital appointment slot. One slot remains at 10 AM. Two receptionists on two servers both click "Book". Server A begins a transaction and issues SELECT … FOR UPDATE , which places a row lock. Server B issues the same statement moments later — its request queues inside the DB until Server A commits.

Server A DB row: appointment 123 │ │ │ BEGIN │ │ SELECT * FROM Appointment │ WHERE Id = 123 FOR UPDATE ────────▶ lock granted │ (verify slot available) │ │ UPDATE Appointment SET userId = A │ │ COMMIT │ │ ────────────────────────────────────▶ lock released │ │ Server B │ │ BEGIN │ │ SELECT * FROM Appointment │ WHERE Id = 123 FOR UPDATE ────────▶ WAIT for A │ │ │ ← Server A commits ← │ │ ────────────────────────────────────▶ lock granted, sees userId=A │ (slot no longer available) │ │ ROLLBACK │ Syntax differs by engine: -- Postgres / MySQL SELECT * FROM Appointment WHERE Id = 123 FOR UPDATE; -- SQL Server SELECT * FROM Appointment WITH (UPDLOCK, ROWLOCK) WHERE Id = 123; -- Oracle SELECT * F

ROM Appointment WHERE Id = 123 FOR UPDATE; Rules. Hold the lock as briefly as possible — a transaction that lingers on a hot row destroys throughput. Never call external services (SMTP, payment gateway, HTTP APIs) while holding a row lock. Match lock ordering across code paths to avoid deadlocks. 3. Database row-level locking — pessimistic, done right Row-level locking is the granular form of pessimistic locking. Modern engines (Postgres, MySQL InnoDB, SQL Server) default to per-row locks rather than table locks, so contention only happens on the exact rows being modified.

Lock escalation (row → page → table) is the pathological failure mode when too many rows are locked in one transaction — beware bulk updates without a batching strategy. 4. Atomic database operations — the "no lock at all" option Concept. Express both the check and the write in one SQL statement, and let the engine handle the concurrency. This is the cheapest correct answer for inventory decrement, account debit, quota consumption — any pattern shaped as "if the value satisfies X, change it".

-- Inventory decrement — DB engine serialises writes to the same row UPDATE Inventory SET Quantity = Quantity - 1 WHERE ProductId = 101 AND Quantity > 0; -- rowsAffected = 1 → purchase allowed -- rowsAffected = 0 → out of stock — reject purchase Why prefer this over pessimistic locks? No lock is explicitly held by application code; the DB acquires and releases a very short internal lock on the affected row for the duration of one UPDATE . Application timeouts, client crashes, and GC pauses cannot leave a lock behind. Common atomic idioms: Conditional increment/decrement — inventory, credits, seats. Insert-if-not-exists — INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING (Postgres) or a UNIQUE constraint.

Great for idempotency ledgers. Conditional update on state — UPDATE order SET status='PAID' WHERE id=@id AND status='PENDING' . State-machine transitions. DynamoDB conditional writes — ConditionExpression: attribute_not_exists(pk) or ConditionExpression: version = :v . 5. Distributed locking — coordinate work across servers Concept. Sometimes the resource you want to protect is not a database row — it's an action . "Only one of our five pods runs the nightly report." "Only one process rebuilds the cache." Row locks and atomic updates cannot help because the resource is a job, not a row.

A distributed lock is a shared coordination primitive — a Redis key, an etcd lease, a ZooKeeper ephemeral znode — that only one caller across the whole cluster can own at a time. Scenario — five app servers, one nightly report. All five have the same code and the same cron. At 00:00 each server races to Redis with: # One atomic write. NX = only if not exists. PX = expire in 30 s. SET daily-report-lock <unique-token> NX PX 30000 Redis awards the lock to exactly one caller and returns OK ; the others receive nil and skip. The winner runs the job, then releases the lock atomically: -- Safe release: DEL only if the stored token still equals mine.

if redis.call( "GET" , KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then return redis.call( "DEL" , KEYS[1]) else return 0 end Every option matters: SET — the write. Redis is single-threaded, so evaluation of NX + write is one indivisible step. NX — "only if the key does not exist" — this is the mutual-exclusion primitive. PX 30000 — lease expiration in milliseconds. A crashed owner cannot hold the lock forever. <unique-token> — a 128-bit random value identifying this specific execution . Not the hostname. 6.

Why the unique token is not optional Consider the timeline where Server A's job overruns: t=0 A acquires lock (token=A-uuid, TTL=30s) t=30 Redis TTL expires → lock auto-deleted t=30 B acquires the same key (token=B-uuid) t=40 A finishes its work t=40 A calls DEL daily-report-lock ⚠ would erase B's lock! Solution: A releases only if the stored value equals its own token. But even a client-side GET -then- DEL is unsafe — another owner can intervene between the two commands. Redis's Lua execution is atomic on the single-threaded event loop, so the GET + DEL +comparison happen indivisibly. That is why the release is a Lua script, not two client calls. 7.

Lock renewal — the watchdog If the job may take longer than the TTL, run a background thread that renews the lease every TTL/3 seconds, but only if the token still matches: -- Compare-and-renew if redis.call( "GET" , KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then return redis.call( "PEXPIRE" , KEYS[1], ARGV[2]) else return 0 end With TTL = 30 s and renewal every 10 s, you tolerate two consecutive missed ticks (network blip, brief Redis slowness) before losing the lock. If renewal fails, the owner must treat the lock as lost and abort the job — do not "keep going and hope". This is precisely what Redisson's watchdog does. See our companion page for the full nightly-job walkthrough.

Failure modes to alert on: network partition (renewal fails), application pause (GC / stop-the-world) longer than the TTL, Redis primary failure with async replication lag, and process crash between "did the work" and "wrote the completion row". Distributed locking is genuinely harder than DB locking — combine with an idempotency ledger if you need exactly-once outcomes. 8. Database advisory locks — named locks inside your DB Concept. Postgres and SQL Server expose application-defined named locks: your app calls pg_advisory_lock('nightly-report'::hashtext) and the DB serialises all callers who ask for the same name.

Great for coordinating actions inside a single DB deployment when the "resource" isn't a specific row. -- Postgres — session-scoped advisory lock SELECT pg_advisory_lock(hashtext( 'nightly-report' )); -- do the work SELECT pg_advisory_unlock(hashtext( 'nightly-report' )); -- Postgres — transaction-scoped variant (auto-releases at commit) SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext( 'nightly-report' )); -- SQL Server EXEC sp_getapplock @Resource = 'nightly-report' , @LockMode = 'Exclusive' ; -- work EXEC sp_releaseapplock @Resource = 'nightly-report' ; Best for: lightweight cross-transaction coordination in a single-DB deployment. Less operational overhead than adding Redis just for this.

Not great for: multi-service coordination where the DB isn't the common denominator (use Redis / etcd) or when the DB itself is the bottleneck. 9. Compare-and-Swap · RowVersion · ETag — optimistic in three costumes The same idea shows up under different names depending on the layer: Layer Name Wire form Application ↔ SQL DB Version column UPDATE … WHERE Version = @old Application ↔ SQL Server RowVersion / rowversion Auto-incremented per row; used same way Application ↔ DynamoDB Conditional writes ConditionExpression: version = :old Client ↔ REST API ETag / If-Match HTTP 412 Precondition Failed on stale Kernel primitive CAS (compare-and-swap) Atomic CPU instruction; foundation of lock-free d

ata structures ETag in REST — the wire trace. A first-class citizen of HTTP: GET /customers/1001 HTTP/1.1 <-- 200 OK ETag: "v15" { "id": 1001, "address": "Bangalore", "phone": "…" } PUT /customers/1001 HTTP/1.1 If-Match: "v15" { "address": "Mumbai" } <-- 200 OK if the resource is still v15 ETag: "v16" <-- 412 Precondition Failed if some other client updated it to v16 in the meantime Conceptually identical to WHERE Version = 15 — expressed at the HTTP layer so a stateless client can participate in the concurrency control.

🎬 Full production scenarios — what to actually build Payment flow — never hold a lock across a slow external call An order service reserves inventory, then calls a payment gateway. The gateway takes 5–20 seconds on the slow path. The wrong design holds a database row lock the whole time: BAD: BEGIN TX SELECT … FROM Inventory WHERE product = 42 FOR UPDATE ← lock held qty -= 1 call Stripe /charges (takes 10 s) ← still holding lock if success then commit else rollback COMMIT Ten seconds of held lock across the entire product's peak traffic will melt the DB.

The fix is a reservation state machine — commit the "reserved" state to the DB (releasing the lock), call the gateway, then transition state: GOOD: BEGIN TX UPDATE Inventory SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE product = 42 AND qty > 0 ← atomic INSERT INTO Reservation (order_id, product, expires_at) … COMMIT ← lock released call Stripe /charges (async, off-lock) if paid: BEGIN TX UPDATE Order SET status='PAID' WHERE id=? AND status='RESERVED' UPDATE Reservation SET status='CONFIRMED' … COMMIT else: ← payment failed / timed out BEGIN TX UPDATE Inventory SET qty = qty + 1 WHERE product = 42 UPDATE Reservation SET status='RELEASED' … COMMIT State transitions: Available → Reserved → Payment Pending → Paid →

Confirmed , with the escape hatch Reserved → Payment Failed → Reservation Released . Every transition is an atomic conditional UPDATE. This pattern is what powers real-world checkout at Amazon, Shopify, Bookmyshow, etc. Combine with a Saga if the workflow crosses microservices. REST document editing — ETag is the whole answer Two editors open PUT /docs/42 . Server returns ETag: "v9" . Both edit locally. Editor A saves first; server responds 200, ETag now "v10" . Editor B saves; server compares If-Match: "v9" against current "v10" , returns 412. Client reloads, offers a diff/merge to the user. No server-side lock, no timeouts, works across mobile clients on slow networks.

Kubernetes: exactly-one leader across pods Not a DB row problem, so Redis / etcd is the right layer. Kubernetes itself uses etcd leader election for the controller manager, scheduler, and every operator that must be a singleton. Applications typically use a Redis lock or a lease object. Same "unique-token + TTL + safe release" pattern applies. 💥 Failure modes — how each mechanism breaks and recovers # Failure What happens Recovery / mitigation 1 Server crashes holding a DB lock DB detects the connection is gone and releases the lock automatically at connection close. Nothing to do — DB engine handles it. Keep transactions short so recovery is fast.

2 Server crashes holding a Redis lock TTL is the safety net. Lock auto-expires; a later run acquires cleanly. Always set PX . Keep TTL longer than expected work time; use watchdog for long jobs. 3 Redis lock expires before work completes Two "owners" for a brief window — potential duplicate side effects. Watchdog to renew lease; idempotency ledger to absorb duplicates; fencing tokens for stronger correctness. 4 Network partition between app and Redis Renewal fails; app thinks it still owns the lock but Redis has expired it. Owner must detect renewal failure and stop the work (fail-fast). Do not keep going. 5 DB transaction times out DB rolls back; row lock released; caller sees an error.

Retry with exponential backoff; shorten transactions; index the WHERE columns. 6 Two services think they own the same lock (split-brain) Concurrent writes to the resource. Fencing tokens; use ZooKeeper/etcd if the SLA requires stronger safety. 7 Deadlock Two transactions each hold what the other wants → circular wait. DB detects and aborts one; retry the loser. Consistent lock ordering prevents most. 8 Optimistic locking hot-conflict Retries pile up on a hot row → user-visible latency and errors. Move to atomic UPDATE or (as a last resort) a short pessimistic lock for the truly hot row.

Deadlock — the classical picture Transaction A Transaction B │ │ Lock Row 1 Lock Row 2 │ │ Wait for Row 2 ←──── Wait for Row 1 A owns Row1 ─────► wants Row2 ▲ │ ← DB deadlock detector aborts one │ transaction; the other proceeds B owns Row2 ─────► wants Row1 Prevention. Always acquire multi-row locks in a consistent order (e.g. by primary key ascending). Prefer atomic single-row updates when possible. Keep transactions short so the window for cycles is small. Alert on deadlock rate; a spike almost always indicates a bug in lock ordering or a missing index that turned a "row lock" into a "scan + range lock".

🧭 Decision matrix — which mechanism for which problem Scenario Preferred mechanism Why (and what to avoid) User profile update from a form Optimistic locking (Version / ETag) Conflicts rare; users may edit for minutes — never hold a DB lock. On conflict, 409 + reload. Configuration / document editing ETag / If-Match Same as above but expressed at the HTTP layer. Appointment reservation (scarce slot) Atomic conditional update, else short pessimistic lock UPDATE … SET userId=@me WHERE slot=@s AND userId IS NULL — no need for FOR UPDATE. Inventory decrement Atomic UPDATE … SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE qty > 0 Never read-then-write. DB engine handles concurrency internally.

Prevent duplicate scheduled job across pods Distributed lock (Redis / etcd) Not a DB row problem; you need cross-server coordination. Pair with idempotency ledger. Prevent duplicate API request Idempotency key Client sends a UUID; server stores the response for that key and re-returns it on retry. No lock needed. Financial account update DB transaction + atomic conditional update Serial ACID guarantees. Never span accounts in a single lock — use a two-phase / Saga. Long-running business workflow State machine + Saga Do NOT hold locks across the workflow. Each step is an atomic state transition. Concurrent REST edits to a resource ETag + If-Match 412 Precondition Failed → client reload/merge.

Leader election / singleton runner etcd / ZooKeeper lease Real consensus; fencing tokens available; used by Kubernetes itself. Prevent thundering herd on cache miss Distributed lock (short TTL) or single-flight per key One request rebuilds the cache; others wait for it. Analytics counter increments Atomic INCR (Redis) or approximate counter (HLL) Never lock a counter row; you'll serialise your write traffic to a single row. The correct question is not "which lock?" but "does this need a lock at all?". Atomic updates, unique constraints, idempotency keys, message queues, state machines, and Sagas replace locks in more scenarios than most engineers realise.

🪤 Common system-design interview traps "I'll use a Redis distributed lock for every concurrency problem." This is the biggest tell of an inexperienced answer. Redis locks are a coordination primitive for actions that span servers — nightly jobs, cache warmup, singleton runners. For single-row concurrency, an atomic UPDATE or a short pessimistic row lock is safer, simpler, and doesn't add a coordination service to the failure surface. "I'll hold a database lock while calling the payment gateway." This will melt production. External calls take seconds; row locks take microseconds. Never combine them.

Use a reservation state machine — commit the "reserved" state, release the lock, then call the gateway, then transition state. "I'll set the Redis TTL to 10 minutes to be safe." A long TTL means a crashed owner wedges the system for 10 minutes before recovery. Set the TTL just longer than expected work + one renewal cycle. Use a watchdog to renew rather than a giant fixed TTL. "I'll just call DEL when done." Not without ownership validation. If your work overran the TTL, the lock now belongs to someone else, and your DEL just released their lock. Always use the Lua compare-and-DEL script. "A distributed lock gives me exactly-once processing." It does not.

If you acquire the lock, send an email, then crash before writing "done", the next run acquires and re-sends. Locks prevent concurrent execution; idempotency ledgers prevent duplicate outcome. Use both. "I read the row, then update it — that's enough." Classical lost update. In-between your read and your write, someone else has done the same. Move to an atomic UPDATE with a predicate, or add a Version column for optimistic locking. "I'll just use SERIALIZABLE isolation everywhere." You just made the DB single-threaded on any dataset the two transactions touch. Retry storms and abort rates will spike. Match isolation level to the specific data conflict, not the app globally.

"HttpOnly cookies prevent all attacks, so we don't need CSRF tokens." (For completeness — not a locking trap, but often asked together.) HttpOnly prevents JS from reading the cookie. CSRF uses the browser's auto-attach behaviour, which HttpOnly doesn't affect. Different problem, different control. "Distributed lock in Redis is safe even during failover." Redis replication is asynchronous. A lock written on the primary that isn't yet on the replica can be lost after failover — briefly, two owners can hold the same lock. For correctness-critical workloads use etcd / ZooKeeper (Raft / ZAB consensus) or add a fencing token that the resource itself enforces.

Optimistic locking — Dapper / EF Core with a Version column // ----------------------------------------------------------------------- public async Task < bool > UpdateCustomerAsync ( Customer c) { const string sql = @" UPDATE Customer SET Address = @Address, Phone = @Phone, Version = Version + 1 WHERE CustomerId = @Id AND Version = @Version" ; var affected = await _db.ExecuteAsync(sql, c); return affected == 1; // false → tell the caller to reload and retry } // ----------------------------------------------------------------------- // 2.

Pessimistic locking — SELECT … FOR UPDATE inside a transaction // ----------------------------------------------------------------------- public async Task ReserveAppointmentAsync ( Guid apptId, Guid userId) { using var tx = _db.BeginTransaction( IsolationLevel .ReadCommitted); var row = await _db.QuerySingleAsync< Appointment >( "SELECT * FROM Appointment WHERE Id=@id FOR UPDATE" , new { id = apptId }, tx); if (row.UserId is not null ) { tx.Rollback(); throw new ConflictException (); } await _db.ExecuteAsync( "UPDATE Appointment SET UserId=@u WHERE Id=@id" , new { u = userId, id = apptId }, tx); tx.Commit(); } // ----------------------------------------------------------------------- // 3.

Atomic UPDATE — the recommended default for inventory / counters // ----------------------------------------------------------------------- public async Task < bool > TryDecrementStockAsync ( int productId) { const string sql = @" UPDATE Inventory SET Quantity = Quantity - 1 WHERE ProductId = @pid AND Quantity > 0" ; return ( await _db.ExecuteAsync(sql, new { pid = productId })) == 1; } // ----------------------------------------------------------------------- // 4.

Redis distributed lock — SET NX PX + Lua safe release // ----------------------------------------------------------------------- public async Task < string ?> TryAcquireAsync ( string key, TimeSpan ttl) { var token = Guid .NewGuid().ToString( "N" ); bool ok = await _redis.StringSetAsync( key, token, expiry: ttl, when: When .NotExists); return ok ? token : null ; } public Task ReleaseAsync ( string key, string token) => _redis.ScriptEvaluateAsync( @"if redis.call('GET', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then return redis.call('DEL', KEYS[1]) else return 0 end" , new [] { ( RedisKey )key }, new RedisValue [] { token }); // ----------------------------------------------------------------------- // 5.

HTTP ETag — ASP.NET Core minimal-API endpoint // ----------------------------------------------------------------------- app.MapPut( "/customers/{id}" , async ( int id, HttpRequest req, CustomerRepo repo) => { var current = await repo.GetAsync(id); var incoming = req.Headers.IfMatch.ToString().Trim( '"' ); if (incoming != $ "v{current.Version}" ) return Results .StatusCode(412); // Precondition Failed var updated = await req.ReadFromJsonAsync< Customer >(); var saved = await repo.SaveWithOptimisticLockAsync(updated!, current.Version); return saved ? Results .Ok().WithHeader( "ETag" , $ "\"v{current.Version + 1}\"" ) : Results .StatusCode(412); }); // ----------------------------------------

------------------------------- // 6. Postgres advisory lock — one-liner via Dapper // ----------------------------------------------------------------------- await _db.ExecuteAsync( "SELECT pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext(@name))" , new { name = "nightly-report" }); // … work inside the same transaction; lock releases at commit Six mechanisms, one file. The point is not the specific library — it's that each mechanism collapses to a few lines when you pick the right one, and to hundreds of lines of retry logic and bug reports when you pick the wrong one.

🗣️ Final mental model — the decision tree you memorize Multiple requests modifying the same thing? │ ▼ Can the operation be expressed as a single atomic DB query? │ │ Yes No │ │ Atomic UPDATE ▼ Conflicts rare? │ │ Yes No │ │ Optimistic Need short exclusive access? (Version / │ ETag) ▼ Pessimistic (FOR UPDATE) Different servers must coordinate a job / action? │ ▼ Distributed lock (Redis / etcd) + idempotency ledger Long-running business workflow with external calls? │ ▼ State machine / Saga — do NOT hold locks Duplicate request retries from clients? │ ▼ Idempotency key — no lock needed Say this in the interview.

"I default to an atomic UPDATE when the operation can be expressed as a single predicate — inventory, counters, state transitions. When the conflict window is longer than a query, I use optimistic locking with a Version column, or ETag/If-Match if the concurrency crosses HTTP. Pessimistic FOR UPDATE is reserved for genuinely scarce rows where the critical section is short and inside one transaction. Distributed locks come out only when the resource isn't a DB row — nightly jobs, singletons, cache warmup — and I always pair them with an idempotency ledger because a lock alone does not give exactly-once.

And I never hold a lock across an external call — that's what reservation state machines and Sagas are for." The 5 lines that win the round "Atomic UPDATE first, lock only if you can't." "Optimistic when conflicts are rare, pessimistic when they aren't." "Distributed lock is for actions across servers, not rows in a DB." "Lock ≠ exactly-once. Combine with idempotency." Every time you load Facebook, the page stitches together "hundreds of pieces of information from the social graph" — who your friends are, which posts they made, who liked and commented on them, which pages they follow — and it must render "on the fly in a few hundred milliseconds." If there are three billion people using it, those tiny questions add up to millions of them every single second .

x: Nobody can answer that many questions from a filing cabinet — it would be like a librarian sprinting to the basement stacks for every visitor. The whole place would collapse. So the trick is this. Imagine a busy town clerk's office. All the official records — birth certificates, marriage records, deeds — are stored in tall filing cabinets in the back room . Those are the truth, and they never lie.

t: Meta TAO — The Social Graph Store — System Design

When you walk up to the counter, 99 out of 100 times your answer is already on a sticky note — you get it instantly and walk away happy. Only the odd, unusual question makes the clerk actually walk to the back room. The magic part: when someone adds a new friend, the clerk writes it down in the filing cabinet first (so it's permanent), then updates the sticky notes on every counter around the world .

Everything else follows from that." 🏗️ High-level architecture How the pieces fit together TAO is a two-tier, write-through caching layer over a sharded MySQL backing store , organized logically as a tree per region. Clients never touch MySQL directly; they talk to the nearest cache.

t: Meta TAO — The Social Graph Store — System Design
x: The tree has two cache tiers within each region: follower caches (what clients connect to) and a smaller set of leader caches that sit in front of MySQL. Reads are served from RAM at the follower tier; on a miss, the request climbs the tree (follower → leader → MySQL) and the answer is filled back down, populating each tier on the way. Geographically, each shard has one primary (master) region . All caches in a region share the local MySQL replica for reads, so reads are always local and fast.

t: Meta TAO — The Social Graph Store — System Design
x: Writes are the interesting part: a write goes up to the leader; if the local region is a secondary for that shard, the leader forwards the write to the primary region's leader, which applies it to the primary MySQL. MySQL's own replication then streams the change back out to the secondary regions' databases. Because TAO is write-through , the cache is updated as the write reply propagates back down the tree — so the follower that issued the write reflects it immediately (read-after-write for that client). t: Meta TAO — The Social Graph Store — System Design
x: MySQL's InnoDB buffer pool assumes spatial locality (rows near each other on disk are accessed together), but Facebook's access pattern is creation-time locality — recently created items are hottest regardless of where they sit on disk. Worse, many queries check for relationships that don't exist (does A like B?), and those negative lookups polluted the block cache. On top of that, product engineers had to manually keep two different data models (objects in MySQL rows, cached blobs in memcache) in sync — error-prone and slow to build on. TAO makes the cache graph-aware so it understands objects, edges, counts, and inverse edges natively.

t: Meta TAO — The Social Graph Store — System Design
x: Two cache tiers: leaders and followers Splitting the cache into followers (many, client-facing) and leaders (few, database-facing) is a deliberate scaling move. Followers absorb the raw read volume close to clients; leaders serialize access to each shard's MySQL and act as a coordination point. The leader is the single writer per shard within a region, which lets it de-duplicate concurrent misses (the "thundering herd" — a thousand followers all missing the same hot key ask the leader, which issues one database read) and it's the place from which cache invalidations are broadcast to followers after a write. This two-level fan-in is why a single hot celebrity object doesn't melt MySQL.

t: Meta TAO — The Social Graph Store — System Design
x: Sharding the graph Data is partitioned into hundreds of thousands of shards , each living in one logical MySQL database, and an object's id encodes its shard. Associations are co-located with their source object's shard so that a node's edge list is served from one place. Because shards are fine-grained, TAO can migrate or clone a hot shard to spread load and smooth spikes without resharding the world — the standard answer to "what about a celebrity with 100M followers?" Consistency model TAO chooses eventual consistency by default — a deliberate CAP-theorem trade favoring availability and latency at global scale.

x: In the old days it was a single giant shop that sold everything — clothes, groceries, medicines, phones. If the electricity broke in one corner, the whole shop went dark. That's a monolith . Modern malls are different: they're made of many small independent shops. You get more variety, one shop can renovate without closing the others, and no single problem shuts everything down. That's microservices . But now the mall has new problems, and each pattern on this page is the mall's fix for one of them. How does a visitor find the phone shop when it keeps changing floors? There's a directory near the entrance — that's service discovery .

t: Microservices Patterns — Service Discovery, API Gateway, BFF, Sidecar, Circuit Breaker, Bulkhead, Strangler Fig, Service Mesh
x: How do you avoid making the visitor walk from shop to shop? There's a concierge at the entrance who takes their whole order and dispatches to the right shops — that's the API Gateway . What if the mobile shopper wants a smaller lighter menu than the counter walker? You give each type of shopper their own personal concierge — that's Backend for Frontend . What if the electrician's shop is failing today? A helper standing next to every shop handles all the boring but universal stuff — power, plumbing, security cameras — the same way for every shop, in every language. That's the Sidecar .

t: Microservices Patterns — Service Discovery, API Gateway, BFF, Sidecar, Circuit Breaker, Bulkhead, Strangler Fig, Service Mesh
x: What if too many shoppers rush into a broken shop and the crowd starts blocking other shops? A fuse box automatically trips and diverts them; when the shop looks healthy again, the fuse lets a trickle through, then reopens. That's the Circuit Breaker . How do you make sure a busy problem in the food-court doesn't drain all the mall's staff away from the electronics section? You put separate teams of staff on each floor , so a stampede in one place can't empty out another. That's the Bulkhead , named after the sealed compartments on a ship.

x: What about the old giant shop that still handles half the sales — can we replace it without shutting the mall for a year? Yes: build new small shops around it and slowly move each aisle , so shoppers barely notice. Eventually the old shop has nothing left to sell and you tear it down. That's the Strangler Fig , named after a vine that grows around a tree until only the vine is left. And finally, when the sidecars, the fuse boxes, the retries, the security cameras and the concierge all become too much to configure per-shop, you build a city-wide plumbing and electric grid that every shop just plugs into. That's the Service Mesh .

Named after the sealed watertight compartments of a ship's hull — if one floods, the ship stays afloat. Mechanism. Partition resources so a fault in one part cannot drain another. System Design · Interview Prep Multi-Tenancy Serving thousands of customers from one system — without them ever seeing each other, stealing each other's resources, or making the ops team weep. 🎯 Scenario 🧑‍🎓 Laymen 📋 Requirements 🏗️ Architecture 🎬 Animation 🔍 Deep-dive 🧮 DSA ☁️ AWS 💻 C# code ⚖️ Trade-offs 🗣️ Cheat sheet ❓ FAQ 📚 Sources 🎯 Real-world scenario What we're building & where it's used Multi-tenancy is the discipline of running one software system that serves many independent customers — called tenants — from shared infrastructure while keeping each tenant's data, load, and failures walled off from the others.

A tenant is an organization , not a user; a company with 500 employees is one tenant with 500 users. It is the defining architectural pattern of SaaS: without it there is no SaaS, there is only a hosting business that manually clones one stack per customer. Every product you use for work is multi-tenant. Slack, Salesforce, GitHub, Notion, Stripe, Datadog, Zoom, HubSpot, Shopify — each is one running system serving millions of orgs. Companies build multi-tenant systems because the economics are transformational: a shared stack costs a fraction of a dedicated one, ships features to everyone at once, and lets a two-engineer team run a business with a million customers.

The catch is that if you get isolation wrong even once, one customer sees another customer's data — a business-ending event. So multi-tenancy is really a conversation about how much you share and how you enforce the boundaries when you share . The interview question is almost never "design multi-tenancy" in the abstract. It's usually embedded in a bigger question — "you're building a SaaS analytics platform, walk me through your tenancy model" — and the interviewer is watching whether you reach for the industry taxonomies (silo/pool/bridge, database-per-tenant vs sharded), name the tradeoffs, and handle the follow-ups on noisy neighbours, cost attribution, and blast radius.

🧑‍🎓 In laymen terms The plain-English version Imagine you rent apartments for a living. You have a building with many families living in it. All of them share the front door, the elevator, the plumbing, and the roof — but each family has their own locked apartment with their own key. That's multi-tenancy. One building, many families, and no family ever wanders into another family's kitchen. Now think about a company like Slack . Your company uses Slack. So does the company across the street, and 10 million other companies. Slack didn't build 10 million separate copies of Slack. They built one Slack — one building — and gave each company a "locked apartment" inside it.

When you open Slack, some invisible check figures out which company you belong to and only shows you your company's messages. If that check ever failed, you'd see someone else's private messages. That would be the end of Slack. So the check has to be perfect. The hard parts are what happen when families share things. If one family throws a huge party, does everyone else lose water pressure? If one family calls the elevator constantly, does everyone wait? If the roof leaks, does every family get wet? Real software has the same problems. If one customer runs a giant report at 3am, other customers shouldn't feel it. If one customer's data corrupts, others shouldn't be affected.

If one customer gets hacked, others shouldn't spill. Some customers pay a lot more money. For them, you might build a private house instead of an apartment — dedicated everything. It costs more, but they get all the water pressure to themselves and nobody can hear their music. Big banks and hospitals often get the private house. Small startups happily share the building. A tiny example: your two-person startup and IBM both use Slack. Your startup lives in a "shared apartment" — cheap, fine. IBM might live in a dedicated wing with its own elevator. Slack's job is to make both of you feel like you're the only tenant on the planet, even though you're technically breathing the same air.

📋 Requirements & scale Requirements and back-of-the-envelope math Functional requirements Tenant onboarding — create a new tenant in seconds; provision users, initial config, quotas. Data isolation — a user of tenant A must never read or write data of tenant B, at any layer. Tenant context on every request — every request carries a verifiable tenant_id ; every query is scoped to it. Per-tenant quotas / rate limits — noisy tenants must not degrade quiet tenants. Tier-based isolation — free / pro / enterprise get different isolation levels. Cost attribution — cost per tenant is knowable (for pricing, capacity planning, churn analysis).

Tenant lifecycle — offboarding (delete all data, GDPR), tier migration (pool → silo), export. Non-functional requirements Isolation guarantee : zero cross-tenant reads/writes — treated as a P0 breach. Blast radius : one failing tenant / one failing cell must not take down the fleet. P99 fairness : enterprise tenants see stable P99 even during flash-sale-scale spikes from other tenants. Elasticity : onboarding a tenant is O(seconds), not O(days). Capacity — a mid-sized SaaS example Metric Value Why Tenants 50,000 orgs (98% pool, 2% silo) Power law — enterprise is few but pays most. Users total ~5 M Avg 100 users/tenant. QPS (aggregate) ~50 K 1 req/s per active user, 10% concurrency.

P99 per tenant read ≤ 100 ms Standard interactive SaaS. Storage/tenant 10 GB avg, 5 TB p99 Long-tail tenants dominate storage. Fleet DB size ~500 TB Requires sharding — no single Postgres fits. Shard fanout ~480 logical shards over ~32 physical DBs Same order as Notion's real numbers. Cell size (blast radius) ~2 K tenants / cell Slack-style cellular isolation. Volunteer these numbers unprompted. "50 K tenants, power-law distributed, so I'll pool the small 98% and silo the enterprise 2%; that shapes every other choice from routing to billing." Interviewers reward math you bring before they ask.

🏗️ High-level architecture How the pieces fit together The classic multi-tenant SaaS architecture is a shared control plane (identity, onboarding, billing, observability) sitting in front of a tenant-aware data plane whose isolation level varies by pricing tier. On every request the flow is: client → edge (TLS, WAF) → identity (validate JWT, extract tenant_id ) → API gateway (per-tenant rate limit, tier lookup) → services (execute business logic scoped to tenant_id ) → data (either the shared pool table with row/item-level policies, or the dedicated silo database for enterprise tenants).

Async traffic — notifications, exports, ETL — flows through queues that carry the tenant tag so downstream workers can preserve isolation. The load-bearing decision is which components pool and which silo . Microsoft's Azure Architecture Center calls isolation a continuum, not a binary — you can pool the UI/app tier while siloing the data tier, or the other way around, depending on what actually causes noisy-neighbour pain. In practice, the app tier is almost always pooled (compute is cheap and stateless), while the data tier is where the isolation model lives.

Pool data plane (shared) Silo data plane (dedicated) Cell / control plane Async plane The three canonical isolation models 🏰 Silo Dedicated resources per tenant. No noisy neighbours, trivial cost attribution, simple to enforce. But hits account/quota ceilings and costs ~linearly. Best for enterprise / regulated tenants. 🌉 Bridge Mix per microservice. Regulatory + noisy-neighbour sensitivity pushes a service to silo; agility + cost pushes to pool. Most real SaaS ends up here. 🏢 Pool Shared everything, keyed by tenant_id . Cheapest, most agile, hardest to isolate. Requires fine-grained IAM / row-level security. Best for free/pro tiers.
