Press ▶ Play. ▶ Play Step → ← Back ↺ Reset Ready Press ▶ Play to start 🔍 Component deep-dive 1. Tenant identification & routing Every request must carry a verifiable tenant identity . The industry-standard pattern (from AWS's serverless SaaS reference) is: the identity provider — Amazon Cognito, Auth0, Okta — authenticates the user and issues a JWT with tenant_id and tier as custom claims .

Downstream services trust the JWT signature and read the claims from a shared library (a Lambda Layer in AWS-speak). This means the tenant context is attached to the request itself — you never trust a client-supplied header, and you never make a network call to look up who the user's tenant is. Every service downstream — API gateway, business services, workers, background jobs — receives the tenant context and scopes every operation to it. 2. Tenant isolation is not authentication This is the single most-repeated point in the AWS SaaS Lens, and the point interviewers use to separate strong candidates from weak ones.

An authenticated, authorized user can still cross tenant boundaries if you rely on authorization alone. AuthN answers "who are you"; AuthZ answers "what can you do"; isolation answers "which tenant's slice of the world can you touch". You need a separate mechanism — application-layer scoping, row-level security, dynamically minted IAM policies — that binds every resource operation to the request's tenant context. A breach of this boundary is treated as a P0 event: business-ending. 3. Data isolation strategies Data isolation runs on a spectrum. From most-shared to most-isolated: Shared table + tenant_id column — cheapest. Every query filters by tenant. Bug in one query = cross-tenant leak.

Postgres Row-Level Security (RLS) policies push the guard into the database so even a raw query can't escape the tenant. DynamoDB uses dynamodb:LeadingKeys IAM conditions to achieve the same at the storage engine. Shared DB + schema-per-tenant — Postgres schemas, MySQL databases. Cleaner separation, still one DB engine, migrations run N times. Database-per-tenant (in elastic pool) — Azure SQL and RDS both support this. Isolation is at the storage engine, cost sharing is at the pool. Scales to 100 000+ databases per Azure SQL instance. Silo — dedicated DB cluster — enterprise tier. Own VPC, own KMS key, own IAM boundary. Trivial isolation, expensive. 4.

Sharding — the real production pattern Notion runs Postgres in the pooled model but hit the limits of one machine. Their solution — the pattern most large SaaS reach — is application-level sharding on workspace_id (their tenant key) into 480 logical shards across 32 physical databases, colocating all block data for a workspace on one shard to preserve transactional consistency within a tenant while avoiding cross-shard joins. This is the sweet spot between pool and silo: shared engine, but tenant data is physically grouped. 5. Noisy-neighbour mitigation The whole reason silo exists is to eliminate noisy neighbours.

In pool mode you fight it with three tools: Per-tenant token buckets — Stripe's rate limiter runs 4 layers: per-user request rate, per-user concurrent-requests, fleet-wide load shedder, and a burst limiter. Keyed by tenant. Shuffle sharding — assign each tenant a random subset of workers so any two tenants overlap on ≤ 1 worker. A tenant that saturates its subset only affects a tiny fraction of others. AWS's canonical technique from the Builders' Library. Cell-based architecture — divide the fleet into fixed-size cells (say ~2 K tenants each). A cell's failure is confined to its tenants. Slack moved to this after a June 2021 AZ outage; each us-east-1 AZ is now a cell. 6.

Blast radius & cellular design The largest architectural upgrade a maturing SaaS makes is cellular . Instead of one global fleet where a bad deploy breaks everyone, you deploy N identical cells, each serving a bounded set of tenants. Roll out to one cell first, watch it, then the rest. A poison pill from tenant Q blows up cell 3 only; cells 1, 2, 4…N are fine. 7. Cost attribution Silo makes cost trivial — infrastructure tags per tenant → billing report. Pool makes it hard — you have to instrument every request with the tenant tag and aggregate telemetry back.

AWS's Split Cost Allocation Data and per-tenant CloudWatch dimensions are the standard tools; underneath, you're just tagging every metric and log line with tenant_id . 8. Onboarding & tier migration Onboarding in pool mode is a row in the tenants table — milliseconds. Onboarding a silo tenant is a Terraform / control-plane workflow that spins up a dedicated stack — minutes. The hardest operation is tier migration , e.g. pool → silo when a Standard tenant upgrades to Enterprise. You provision the silo stack, run a background copy of the tenant's data, dual-write for a window, then cut reads over and stop the pool writes.

No downtime, no lost writes — this is what shipped-in-production SaaS teams get paid to do right. 🧮 The DSA behind it Data structures & algorithms Multi-tenancy is not one algorithm — it's a stack of small, tenant-keyed data structures that show up everywhere. Data structure / algorithm Where it lives Complexity Why Consistent hashing ring Router → shard mapping. hash(tenant_id) % ring . O(log N) lookup Adding a shard remaps only K/N tenants, not all of them. Token bucket Per-tenant rate limiter. O(1) per request Bursty but bounded — matches real API traffic. Shuffle sharding Worker pool assignment. O(1) per tenant Combinatorial isolation: pick S of W workers → P(overlap) ≈ C(W-S,S)/C(W,S).

Cellular routing Tenant → cell map (in tenant registry). O(1) lookup Bounded blast radius; deployable in ripples. Bloom filter "Does tenant X even exist here?" hot-path guard. O(k) per lookup Skip the DB on unknown tenants — cheap negative check. LRU / LFU cache Tenant metadata cache (tier, quotas, shard). O(1) get/put Every request needs this — must be sub-millisecond. B-tree / composite index Pool table: (tenant_id, entity_id) . O(log N) scan Leading column = tenant_id → tenant's data physically contiguous. Priority queue Background jobs (billing, exports) ordered by tier. O(log N) Enterprise jobs don't wait behind free-tier jobs.

Circular buffer / sketch (Count-Min) Per-tenant usage counter for billing/alerts. O(1) update Approximate but sub-linear in memory — 50 K tenants fits. Interview-critical: the two data structures interviewers probe most are the tenant → shard router (consistent hashing or range map) and the per-tenant rate limiter (token bucket). Be able to whiteboard both in 90 seconds. Shuffle sharding — the one clever bit AWS's foundational multi-tenant idea. If you have W workers and give each tenant S of them at random, then two tenants overlap on all S workers with probability C(S, S) / C(W, S) . For W = 8, S = 2 → 1/28 . For W = 100, S = 4 → 1/3.9 M .

A single bad tenant can only take out its S workers, and every other tenant still has W − S good ones. It's isolation without dedicated hardware — the math does the walling off. ☁️ AWS implementation Mapping the design to AWS AWS publishes a canonical serverless SaaS reference (2021, still cited). Below is that reference distilled and generalized to non-serverless deployments. Component AWS service Why Identity + JWT Amazon Cognito Emits tenant_id and tier as JWT custom claims. Multi-user-pool option for silo tenants. Edge + rate limiting API Gateway + WAF Per-key rate limits and usage plans map onto per-tenant. WAF for L7 filtering.

Authorizer Lambda authorizer (shared Lambda Layer) Extracts JWT claims, injects tenant context, mints scoped STS credentials for the request. Pool compute Lambda or ECS/EKS Stateless services scaled by aggregate load; tenant_id in the request. Silo compute (enterprise) Dedicated ECS/EKS cluster in tenant VPC Full network + IAM boundary. Own KMS key per tenant. Pool data DynamoDB shared table, PK = tenant_id dynamodb:LeadingKeys IAM condition enforces item-level isolation at the storage engine. Pool relational data Aurora / RDS Postgres with Row-Level Security RLS policy scopes every row to current_setting('app.tenant_id') .

Silo data Dedicated RDS / Aurora cluster per tenant One DB per enterprise tenant, own KMS key, own VPC subnet group. Object storage S3 with prefix-per-tenant + bucket policy s3:prefix IAM condition scopes list/get/put per tenant. Async / eventing SQS + EventBridge + Kinesis / MSK Every message tagged with tenant_id ; consumers preserve isolation downstream. Cache ElastiCache Redis with tenant-prefixed keys tenant_id:entity:id . Multi-shard for hot tenants. Cost attribution CloudWatch dimensions + Cost Allocation Tags + Split Cost Allocation Data Silo → tag resources by tenant. Pool → tag every metric/log emission.

Observability CloudWatch Logs + X-Ray with tenant dimension Every log/trace carries tenant_id . Dashboards per tenant. Tenant control plane Step Functions + Terraform / CDK Silo tenant onboarding = state-machine driving IaC apply. Pool onboarding = one DynamoDB Put. AWS reference flow, in one paragraph Client hits API Gateway. A Lambda authorizer verifies the Cognito-issued JWT, pulls tenant_id and tier out of custom claims, and generates a short-lived STS credential scoped by a dynamically constructed IAM policy that uses dynamodb:LeadingKeys = tenant_id .

That credential is handed to the Lambda business logic, which reads from a shared DynamoDB table where the partition key is the tenant id. If the same JWT had a tier=Platinum claim, the authorizer would route to a dedicated Lambda + DynamoDB + Cognito pool that lives in a tenant-specific VPC and is invisible to pool tenants. Async writes fan out through EventBridge with the tenant tag; downstream workers scope everything to that tag.

💻 C# implementation Three of the most-asked reference snippets: (1) middleware that extracts the tenant from a JWT and puts it in the request context, (2) per-tenant token-bucket rate limiter backed by Redis, and (3) tenant-scoped repository using EF Core global query filters. Together they cover the request→service→DB path. 1. Tenant context middleware — extract from JWT, fail-closed // ASP.NET Core middleware. Runs on every request. Extracts tenant_id + tier // from a verified JWT and stashes it in a scoped ITenantContext. Downstream // code is REQUIRED to use ITenantContext — never a client header.

public sealed class TenantContext : ITenantContext { public string TenantId { get ; init ; } = "" ; public string Tier { get ; init ; } = "pool" ; // pool | silo } public sealed class TenantContextMiddleware { private readonly RequestDelegate _next; public TenantContextMiddleware ( RequestDelegate next) => _next = next; public async Task Invoke ( HttpContext ctx, ITenantContextAccessor acc) { // The JWT is already validated by [Authorize] earlier in the pipeline. // We just pull the trusted claims. If any are missing, 401 — fail closed.

var user = ctx.User; var tenant = user.FindFirst( "tenant_id" )?.Value; var tier = user.FindFirst( "tier" )?.Value ?? "pool" ; if ( string.IsNullOrEmpty (tenant)) { ctx.Response.StatusCode = StatusCodes .Status401Unauthorized; await ctx.Response. WriteAsync ( "missing tenant claim" ); return ; } acc.Current = new TenantContext { TenantId = tenant, Tier = tier }; // Tag every log line for this request so observability aggregates by tenant. using ( LogContext . PushProperty ( "tenant_id" , tenant)) using ( LogContext . PushProperty ( "tier" , tier)) { await _next(ctx); } } } 2.

Per-tenant token-bucket rate limiter (Redis-backed) // Atomic Lua script: refill bucket at rate r, take 1 token, return 0 if empty. // Runs in Redis under one RTT — safe under contention across service replicas. public sealed class TenantRateLimiter { private const string LUA = @ " local key = KEYS[1] local rate = tonumber(ARGV[1]) -- tokens/sec local capacity = tonumber(ARGV[2]) local now = tonumber(ARGV[3]) -- ms local b = redis.call('HMGET', key, 'tok', 'ts') local tok = tonumber(b[1]) or capacity local ts = tonumber(b[2]) or now local delta = math.max(0, now - ts) tok = math.min(capacity, tok + (delta * rate / 1000.0)) local allowed = 0 if tok >= 1 then tok = tok - 1; allowed = 1 end re

dis.call('HMSET', key, 'tok', tok, 'ts', now) redis.call('PEXPIRE', key, 60000) return allowed " ; private readonly IDatabase _redis; public TenantRateLimiter ( IConnectionMultiplexer mux) => _redis = mux. GetDatabase (); public async Task < bool > TryAcquireAsync ( string tenantId, int ratePerSec, int capacity) { var key = $"rl:{tenantId}" ; var now = DateTimeOffset .UtcNow.ToUnixTimeMilliseconds(); var res = ( int )( long ) await _redis. ScriptEvaluateAsync ( LUA, new [] { ( RedisKey )key }, new RedisValue [] { ratePerSec, capacity, now }); return res == 1; } } 3. EF Core global query filter — tenant-scoped repository // Every entity carries a TenantId.

The global query filter appends // `WHERE TenantId = @current` to EVERY query — so a forgotten filter // in a repo can't leak. Belt AND suspenders: DB-side RLS on top for depth. public class AppDb : DbContext { private readonly ITenantContextAccessor _tenant; public AppDb ( DbContextOptions < AppDb > o, ITenantContextAccessor t) : base (o) => _tenant = t; public DbSet < Invoice > Invoices => Set < Invoice >(); protected override void OnModelCreating ( ModelBuilder mb) { mb.Entity< Invoice >(). HasQueryFilter (i => i.TenantId == _tenant.Current!.TenantId); } // Also stamp TenantId on inserts — never trust the caller.

public override Task < int > SaveChangesAsync ( CancellationToken ct = default ) { var tid = _tenant.Current!.TenantId; foreach ( var e in ChangeTracker. Entries < Invoice >()) if (e.State == EntityState .Added) e.Entity.TenantId = tid; return base . SaveChangesAsync (ct); } } Note on "belt and suspenders": the EF query filter is application-side. It's convenient but a bad LINQ query using IgnoreQueryFilters() can bypass it. In production, pair it with a database-side guarantee — Postgres RLS or DynamoDB LeadingKeys . Two independent walls. Interviewers love this answer.

Other-language notes Same shapes in other stacks: Spring / Java — Hibernate @FilterDef + @Filter ; Django — a tenant-scoped model manager; Node / Prisma — a middleware that injects where: { tenantId } before every query. Redis Lua for the rate limiter is language-agnostic and is what Stripe, GitHub, and Cloudflare all publicly describe. ⚖️ Trade-offs, bottlenecks & likely follow-ups The one tradeoff that rules them all Isolation strength vs economies of scale. Every other decision — noisy neighbours, cost attribution, blast radius, onboarding cost — falls out of this.

Silo maximises isolation and sacrifices scale economics; pool maximises economics and sacrifices isolation guarantees; bridge picks per microservice. Common bottlenecks Hot tenant — one tenant is 50× the traffic of the median. In pool mode they'll saturate whatever shard they're on. Cure: shuffle-shard them, or graduate them to silo. Pool DB write hotspot — pool tables with tenant_id as the leading key are fine for reads but a hot tenant creates a hot partition. Cure: composite key ( tenant_id + hash-suffix ) or move to database-per-tenant. Silo account limits — AWS has quota ceilings on VPCs, IAM roles, RDS instances per account. Hit them at ~1 K silo tenants.

Cure: multi-account (AWS Organizations), one account per ~500 silo tenants. Cross-tenant analytics — the CFO wants "total signups this quarter across all tenants". Pool table is easy; silo means fanning out queries to N tenant DBs. Cure: ETL every tenant into a shared analytics warehouse (with tenant tag), never query silos live for cross-tenant analytics. Failure modes to name unprompted Leak via a forgotten WHERE tenant_id = ? — the classic P0. Answer: RLS at the DB, plus code-review checklist, plus contract tests. Bad deploy blows up all tenants at once — cellular deploy + canary cell. Poison message from tenant Q clogs the queue for everyone — per-tenant DLQ, tenant-aware retry policy.

Enterprise tenant's silo DB is slow → looks like the whole product is slow to their execs — silo P99 SLO is per-tenant, not fleet-wide. Likely interviewer follow-ups (with 30-second answers) "What if a pool tenant grows so big they need to become a silo tenant — how do you migrate them without downtime?" Provision the silo stack. Snapshot + streaming replicate the tenant's data into it. Enter a dual-write window where writes go to both. Cut reads over to silo, verify parity. Stop writes to pool, delete pool data. Feature-flag the whole thing so you can roll back at any step.

"How do you rate-limit tenants fairly when quiet tenants can't predict what noisy ones will do?" Per-tenant token buckets sized to their tier, plus a fleet-wide load shedder that kicks in when aggregate load threatens SLO. Weighted fair queueing between tiers. That's Stripe's public model. "How do you enforce isolation if a bug in your ORM lets a query drop the tenant filter?" Never rely on the ORM alone. Two independent walls: application-side (query filter / repository middleware) and database-side (Postgres RLS or DynamoDB LeadingKeys). A single bug breaks one wall, not both.

"How do you know what each tenant costs?" Silo: tag every resource with tenant_id , use AWS Cost Allocation Tags and Split Cost Allocation Data. Pool: instrument requests with a cost proxy (DB rows read, S3 bytes stored, Lambda ms) tagged per tenant, roll up nightly. It's an approximation, but it's defensible. "What's your blast-radius story?" Cellular. Fixed-size cells, deployable independently, tenants pinned to cells. A blast is confined to one cell of ~2 K tenants — that's how Slack survives AZ failures. 🗣️ Interview cheat sheet 30-second pitch: "Multi-tenancy is a spectrum from silo (dedicated per tenant) to pool (shared with tenant_id keys), with bridge as the practical mix.

Tenant isolation is separate from authN/authZ — the JWT carries tenant_id + tier as custom claims, every service scopes to it, and I use two independent walls: application-side query filters plus a database-side guarantee like Postgres RLS or DynamoDB LeadingKeys. Small tenants share a pooled Aurora + DynamoDB, enterprise tenants get siloed stacks. I contain blast radius with cellular deploys, contain noisy neighbours with per-tenant token buckets and shuffle sharding, and attribute cost via CloudWatch tenant dimensions." Numbers to quote Azure SQL DB-per-tenant scales to 100 000+ databases per instance .

Notion runs Postgres in 480 logical shards over 32 physical DBs , sharded by workspace_id. Slack cellularized after the June 30 2021 AZ outage ; each us-east-1 AZ is a cell. Stripe runs 4 rate limiters : per-user request, per-user concurrent, fleet load-shedder, burst. Shuffle sharding: W=100, S=4 → P(two tenants share all workers) ≈ 1 in 3.9 M . Five talking points that win the round "Isolation is a spectrum, not a binary — I decide per tier and per component." "Tenant isolation ≠ AuthN/AuthZ.

An authenticated user can still cross tenants." "Two independent walls: app-side query filter + DB-side RLS / LeadingKeys." "Blast radius contained via cellular architecture; noisy neighbours via shuffle sharding + per-tenant token buckets." "Cost is easy in silo, requires per-request telemetry in pool — I'd tag every log, metric, and message with tenant_id from day 1." ❓ FAQ — your follow-up questions Questions asked about this topic No follow-up questions yet — ask one about this topic and it'll be logged here with a compact answer. 📚 Sources Microsoft Learn — Multitenant SaaS Patterns (Azure SQL Database) — the three-pattern taxonomy and scale numbers (100 K+ DBs per instance).

In under a second, each of you has to hear music.

t: Design a Music Streaming Platform (Spotify) — System Design
x: Not "loading… loading…" — actual sound. How on earth does one company pull that off? Here's the trick: Spotify doesn't keep all its songs in one giant warehouse in California and pipe them to your phone. That would be like everyone in the world calling the same pizza shop — the phone line would jam. Instead, Spotify runs thousands of tiny jukeboxes tucked into cities all over the planet — often inside your own phone company's building. When you tap play, your phone asks the nearest jukebox first. It almost always has the song, because that jukebox is quietly stocked with whatever's trending near you — the top hits in your country, your saved playlists, your morning workout mix.

t: Design a Music Streaming Platform (Spotify) — System Design
x: The songs themselves are also chopped into small three-second chunks , like a book split into single pages. Your phone grabs one page, starts reading (playing) it, and quietly fetches the next page in the background. If your train dips into a tunnel, you're never stuck mid-page — the next few pages are already in your pocket. And if the signal gets bad, Spotify quietly slips you a lower-quality version of the next page so the music never stops, then upgrades again when your wifi comes back. The really hard part isn't the audio at all — a song is only about 4 megabytes, which is nothing. The hard part is finding what you want among 100 million songs .

That's the computer noticing which songs other people-like-you keep replaying, then quietly slipping them onto your playlist. Control-plane calls (search, playlists, "give me the stream URL for track X") hit stateless microservices backed by databases and caches. When the user presses play, the metadata/streaming service returns a signed, expiring CDN URL ; the client then pulls the audio directly from the CDN edge , chunk by chunk — origin is bypassed on a cache hit.

Metadata (small, structured, must be fresh) goes through your services and databases. Audio (large-ish, immutable, cacheable) goes straight through the CDN and never touches your app servers on a cache hit. Keeping them separate is what lets the system scale — say this explicitly in the interview.

t: Design a Music Streaming Platform (Spotify) — System Design
x: 🔍 Component deep-dive Audio ingestion & transcoding pipeline When a label uploads a master track, an async pipeline (triggered off a queue) transcodes it into multiple codecs and bitrates — e.g. Ogg Vorbis at 96/160/320 kbps and AAC at 128/256 kbps, plus FLAC for lossless — and segments each into small chunks. Spotify streams up to 160 kbps Vorbis on free and 256 kbps AAC / up to 24-bit FLAC on Premium. Outputs are written to blob storage (S3) as the origin and pushed/warmed into the CDN. This is done once per track and is embarrassingly parallel, so a queue + worker fleet (or serverless) handles it. The result is immutable objects with content-hash keys — perfect for caching.

t: Design a Music Streaming Platform (Spotify) — System Design
x: Streaming: chunks + adaptive bitrate Playback uses chunked, adaptive streaming — the same idea as HLS/DASH for video, applied to audio. The client fetches a manifest, then pulls small time-slices (a few seconds each). If the network degrades, it switches down to a lower bitrate for the next chunk (ABR), avoiding rebuffering; on seek, it jumps to the chunk covering that timestamp instead of re-downloading. To hit sub-250 ms start latency, the client requests a short low-bitrate opening chunk first, prefetches the next track in a playlist, and caches recently-played audio locally. Byte-range requests over HTTP against the CDN are the workhorse.

Because the catalog is ~200 GB and mostly static, caching hit rates are extremely high. User activity — plays, likes, listening history — is append-heavy and huge, so it goes into a horizontally-scalable store like Cassandra (an AP, write-optimized choice ) rather than the relational metadata DB. Audio is immutable and the same popular tracks are played millions of times, giving near-100% cache hit rates. CDN edges serve bytes close to users at low latency and offload origin/bandwidth. Your app servers only handle small metadata calls. "How do you get instant playback (low start latency)?" Chunked streaming with a short low-bitrate opening chunk, client-side prefetch of the next track, local caching of recent audio, and edge delivery.

System Design · Interview Prep Design Netflix 260M+ subscribers, ~98% of traffic served from a private CDN inside your ISP, and a play button that has to feel instant on every screen in the world. 🎯 Scenario 🧑‍🎓 Laymen 📋 Requirements 🏗️ Architecture 🎬 Animation 🔍 Deep-dive 🧮 DSA ☁️ AWS 💻 C# code ⚖️ Trade-offs 🗣️ Cheat sheet ❓ FAQ 📚 Sources 🎯 Real-world scenario What we're building & where it's used We're designing a global on-demand video-streaming service with a curated catalog — a service that ingests studio masters, transcodes them into hundreds of device-specific renditions, delivers those bytes to a viewer in Nairobi or Nagoya with sub-second startup, and personalizes every

homepage row for every profile. This is the archetype for Netflix , and closely related to Amazon Prime Video , Disney+ , Hulu , HBO Max , Apple TV+ , and Hotstar/JioCinema . Netflix differs from YouTube in one critical way: the catalog is curated and finite , not user-uploaded — which changes the CDN math dramatically. Companies build this because streaming has replaced broadcast television , and doing it well is the difference between a Sunday-night binge and an angry churn.

The design touches every core distributed-systems primitive: a globally-distributed CDN (which Netflix famously operates itself as Open Connect), multi-region caching (EVCache on Memcached), distributed databases (Cassandra for viewing history, MySQL for billing), massive asynchronous pipelines (Kafka at 8 M events/sec peak), and a personalization stack that ranks the entire catalog per user per session. It's a favorite interview question because a good answer proves you can reason about the whole stack — not just a REST endpoint. 🧑‍🎓 In laymen terms Explained without any tech words The everyday problem. You come home, kick off your shoes, sit on the couch, and press play on a movie.

It starts in about a second, looks crisp, and doesn't stutter — no matter whether you're in Tokyo, Toronto, or a small town in South Africa. That is genuinely magical, and the entire business of Netflix is making that one second feel effortless for hundreds of millions of people at the same time. The story of one tap. When you press play, Netflix doesn't fly the movie to you from a warehouse in California — that would take too long. Instead, Netflix has quietly shipped little fridges of hard drives (yes, real physical boxes) into your internet provider's building down the road, and it fills them up overnight with the movies most people in your neighborhood are likely to watch.

So when you press play, the movie is not travelling across the ocean — it's coming from a box that is maybe a mile from your couch. That's why it starts so fast. The homepage magic. Before you even press play, Netflix has to decide which shows to show you . The homepage rows — "Trending Now," "Because You Watched…," "Top 10 in your country" — are not the same for anyone else. Netflix ran a giant matching game in the background all day, guessing which rows would tempt you the most, and even picked a different thumbnail image for the same show based on what it thinks you find eye-catching. All of that had to be ready the millisecond you opened the app. The hard part.

The tricky bit is Sunday evening in every timezone . Everyone finishes dinner, everyone wants to watch, and suddenly Netflix is the biggest single tenant on the entire internet — at peak, more than a tenth of the world's internet traffic is Netflix videos moving through the pipes. If they got it even slightly wrong — one crashed database, one overloaded cache — you'd see a spinning circle instead of a show, and you'd cancel your subscription. The whole design is built around never showing that spinning circle , even when small pieces break in the background.

📋 Requirements & scale Requirements and back-of-the-envelope math Functional requirements Browse a curated catalog, with personalized rows and search. Stream on 2 200+ device types with adaptive bitrate (HLS/DASH). Resume exactly where you left off — on any device. Recommend what to watch next, personalize every row and every thumbnail. Manage profiles, subscriptions, billing. Ingest studio masters, transcode into 1 100+ device-specific renditions per title. Non-functional requirements Startup latency < 1 second — the "TTFF" (time to first frame) target. Availability > strong consistency everywhere except billing. A stale view count is fine; a stuck play button is fatal.

Global reach : viewers on every continent, on 3G to gigabit fiber. Read-heavy : ~9:1 read/write ratio on viewing history alone; on catalog metadata, closer to 10 000:1. Peak-heavy : evening prime-time in each region is ~5–8× the daily average. Back-of-the-envelope (Netflix-scale) Metric Estimate How we got there Subscribers ~260 M globally Public 2024 figure. Hours streamed / day ~250 M+ hours ~5 hours/week × 260 M / 7. Peak concurrent streams ~40 M+ globally at prime time Multiple public estimates. Avg stream bitrate ~3.65 Mbps SD 500 kbps up to 4K ~15 Mbps; weighted avg. Peak egress bandwidth ~150–200 Tbps aggregate 40 M × ~4 Mbps.

Two costs dominate: egress bandwidth at peak and storage of thousands of renditions per title across the CDN . That's why Netflix runs its own CDN (Open Connect) — buying that egress from a commercial CDN would be untenable at their scale. 🏗️ High-level architecture How the pieces fit together The whole system splits into three planes . The control plane runs on AWS: microservices behind the Zuul gateway, EVCache in front of Cassandra and MySQL, Kafka for events. Its job is to answer "who are you, what can you watch, where did you leave off, what should we recommend?" — and to hand the client a signed manifest URL .

The data plane is Open Connect : Netflix's own CDN, with servers embedded directly inside ISPs and IXPs. It stores the transcoded video and serves 98%+ of playback bytes without ever touching AWS. The offline plane is the ingest+transcode pipeline plus the ML/recommendation training pipeline — everything that runs on Spark and EMR while you sleep. Sync API call (control plane) Video bytes (data plane) Async / offline The magic move is that the two planes only meet once, at manifest time . The client asks AWS "what should I play, and where's my personalized homepage?" — AWS returns metadata + a manifest URL. From that moment on, every byte of video comes from Open Connect, never from AWS.

That's how Netflix keeps its AWS bill tractable and its startup latency low. 🎬 Animation Watch a play request run, step by step This walks through the full path of pressing "play" on a Netflix title: browse (control plane) → manifest (control plane) → segments (Open Connect data plane) → adaptive bitrate as network changes. Notice how AWS is completely out of the loop after the manifest hop. ▶ Play Step → ← Back ↺ Reset Ready Press ▶ Play to start 🔍 Component deep-dive 1. Open Connect — a private CDN inside your ISP Netflix built its own CDN because the commercial CDNs of 2011 couldn't handle its egress economics.

Open Connect deploys physical appliances — OCAs (Open Connect Appliances) — in two places: embedded inside ISP networks (free of charge to qualifying ISPs, over 1 000+ ISP partners ), and clustered at internet exchange points (IXPs) via settlement-free interconnect (SFI). Each OCA is packed with HDDs and NVMe SSDs, and each is prefilled during the ISP's off-peak window (usually 2–6 AM local) with the titles most likely to be watched in that region the next day. When you press play in Tokyo, the bytes are already sitting on a box a mile from your couch. Netflix reports the CDN hit rate at ~98% — only ~2% of playback traffic escapes back toward AWS.

This is the single biggest reason startup latency (TTFF) is under a second: the bytes never travel far. 2. Streaming — DASH/HLS adaptive bitrate at rendition-level extreme fan-out Every title is transcoded into ~1 100–1 200 renditions : resolutions from 240p through 4K HDR, codecs H.264 (broad), H.265/HEVC (bandwidth-efficient), VP9 (older Android), AV1 (newer), audio in dozens of languages and multiple bitrates (stereo, 5.1, Atmos), plus subtitles. Netflix uses per-title encoding and per-shot encoding — running an optimization to find the best bitrate ladder for each individual title (a talky drama needs fewer bits than a Marvel action sequence).

At playback, the client uses DASH or HLS adaptive bitrate : it measures its own bandwidth and buffer level and switches rendition between segments. This is why a viewer whose Wi-Fi drops from strong to weak sees the picture dim slightly instead of buffering. 3. Startup latency — how to make TTFF < 1 second Reducing time-to-first-frame is a design theme, not one component.

Key techniques: (a) the manifest is tiny — a few KB — and can be fetched from AWS in ~100 ms via anycast + regional caching; (b) segments are pre-warmed in the OCA closest to you before you even open the app — the "top 10 in your country" is on the local box; (c) parallel probes at manifest time — the client fires off connections to multiple OCAs and races them; (d) the first segment is intentionally short (2–4 s vs 6–8 s later segments) so the buffer fills fast; (e) the initial rendition is chosen conservatively — start at a bitrate the client is likely to sustain, then ratchet up.

In an interview, name these five tactics: "manifest, prewarm, parallel probes, short-first-segment, conservative-first-bitrate." 4. Caching — EVCache and the "cold cache is worse than no cache" problem EVCache is Netflix's open-source wrapper around Memcached. It's designed for the failure mode Netflix cares about: cold caches during a region failover . Writes are propagated to all replica nodes and cross-region; reads hit only the nearest cluster. This means the cache is full and warm on both coasts , so when a region evacuates, the incoming region doesn't stampede Cassandra. Metadata caches (title info, homepage rows) commonly hit > 99%.

This pattern — write-fan-out, read-local — is the reason Netflix can survive an entire AWS region failure without visible impact to the user. 5. Distributed databases — Cassandra + MySQL, each for a specific reason Cassandra holds the write-heavy, eventually-consistent workloads: viewing history (~9:1 write:read), user activity, playback events. Netflix runs 50+ Cassandra clusters, 500+ nodes , with the biggest cluster handling 250 000 writes per second . To keep viewing-history reads fast, Netflix splits it into a LiveVH (recent, uncompressed rows) and CompressedVH (older rows, compressed and denser) — a classic hot/cold tier.

MySQL is reserved for the strongly-consistent workloads: billing, subscriptions, payment. Netflix runs MySQL master-master with InnoDB and cross-region read replicas; failover is DNS-driven via Route 53. 6. Event pipeline — Kafka, at eye-watering scale Every play, pause, scrub, rating, and click flows into Kafka: ~500 billion events per day, peak 8 million events per second, ~24 GB/s, ~1.3 PB/day . Consumers include: the recommendation feature store (real-time signals), Elasticsearch (for on-call ops and CS tooling), the analytics warehouse (S3 → Spark → Redshift-equivalent), and the QoE (quality-of-experience) telemetry pipeline that measures whether that spinning circle ever appeared.

Kafka being the "spinal cord" of the data plane is a common answer at Netflix-scale interviews. 7. Recommendations — two-stage ranking + contextual bandits + artwork personalization The recommendation problem at Netflix is not just "what should the user watch next" — it's "which rows should be on the homepage, in what order, with what titles in each row, and which thumbnail image for each title." The high-level architecture is a two-stage funnel : (1) candidate generation narrows the ~15 000-title catalog to a few thousand per profile using collaborative filtering, embeddings, and content-based signals; (2) ranking — a heavier GBDT/neural model — orders those candidates using rich features

(device, time of day, session context, freshness). On top of ranking sits a contextual bandit for row ordering and for thumbnail personalization : Netflix has multiple thumbnail images per title and learns which image drives clicks for which taste cluster. Training runs on Spark; online serving is a low-latency service in every region. Model retraining is daily; real-time signals (this session's clicks) feed a feature store so the recommendations adapt as you browse. 8. Handling peak traffic — autoscale, chaos-test, and cache-warm Netflix does not scale reactively — it scales predictively .

Traffic is highly seasonal (evenings in each region + weekends + release windows), so services are pre-scaled before evening prime time. Chaos engineering ( Chaos Monkey, Simian Army, ChAP ) constantly kills nodes and even entire regions in production to prove the failover paths still work. Regional evacuations are practiced monthly. The zone-based load balancer is two-tier — DNS round-robin across zones, then round-robin across instances within a zone — so a zone loss doesn't cascade. Combined with the full cross-region cache in EVCache, the failure of an entire AWS region is a non-event for the viewer.

🧮 The DSA behind it Data structures & algorithms Under every subsystem is a specific algorithm doing the heavy lifting. Naming them signals depth. Component Structure / algorithm Why chosen & complexity Playback ID / session Snowflake-style 64-bit IDs Time-sortable, unique without coordination. O(1). Segment lookup on watch Consistent-hashed key-value on (titleId, resolution, segmentIndex) OCA finds segment in O(1); consistent hashing keeps mapping stable on scale-out. Adaptive bitrate Rate + buffer PID controller (BOLA/BBA-style) Smooth switches; O(1) per segment on the client.

Per-title / per-shot encoding Convex-hull optimization over (bitrate, quality) with VMAF Finds the tightest ladder for that title's complexity — offline, O(#shots × #bitrates). CDN prefill Popularity forecast (per-region top-N) + Zipf weighting The head of the distribution is 90%+ of watches, so prefilling top-N gets you most of the way. Cache eviction (EVCache) LRU / LFU inside Memcached slabs O(1) amortized; hot metadata never evicted. Viewing history Wide-row Cassandra by userId; time-sorted; TTL on LiveVH Write-heavy 9:1 ratio; append-only + tombstones handled by compaction.

Candidate generation (recs) Approximate nearest neighbor over user+item embeddings (HNSW/FAISS) Sub-linear (~O(log N)) over the catalog vs O(N) brute force. Ranking (recs) Gradient-boosted trees + deep neural net Bounded O(features × candidates) with candidates capped ~500. Row ordering & thumbnails Contextual multi-armed bandit (LinUCB / Thompson sampling) Balances exploit (known winners) with explore (test new artwork). O(1) per impression. Search / autocomplete Inverted index + trie (Elasticsearch) Prefix match O(k); ranking layer atop the postings. Trending / real-time popularity Count-min sketch, HyperLogLog for uniques Sub-linear memory, tight-bounded approximation. O(1) update.

The one to remember: Zipf-driven CDN prefill . The reason Open Connect hits 98% is not clever caching — it's that 90% of watches concentrate on 10% of titles, and Netflix ships those bytes to your ISP overnight. ☁️ AWS implementation Mapping the design to AWS Netflix runs its control plane on AWS across multiple regions, but the CDN (Open Connect) is Netflix-owned hardware, not AWS. If you re-implement Netflix's design entirely on AWS (a common interview follow-up), you'd replace Open Connect with CloudFront. Here is the mapping. Component AWS service Why DNS / geo-routing Route 53 (latency-based / geolocation) Sends the viewer to the nearest region; failover on health.

API gateway Zuul on EC2 / EKS (or API Gateway if fresh build) Auth, canary, throttling, dynamic routing. Microservices EKS / ECS Fargate (Spring Boot / Java) Netflix runs Java on EC2; either works. Service discovery Eureka (internal); AWS Cloud Map is the managed alternative Client-side load balancing via Ribbon. Cache EVCache on ElastiCache Memcached (or DAX for DynamoDB) Write-fan-out across AZs and regions; read-local. Warm on failover. Viewing history / activity Amazon Keyspaces (managed Cassandra) or self-hosted C* on EC2 Write-heavy 9:1; wide-row user-partitioned. Billing / subscriptions Aurora MySQL (multi-master) or RDS MySQL ACID compliance; failover via Route 53.

Search & ops Amazon OpenSearch (managed Elasticsearch) Search, log analytics, CS tooling. Event bus Amazon MSK (Kafka) or Kinesis Data Streams Handles play/pause/QoE events at multi-GB/s. Master originals + rendition staging S3 with Cross-Region Replication 11 nines durability; source-of-truth for the catalog. Cold storage S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval Older / rarely-served titles. Transcode farm AWS Elemental MediaConvert or EMR/EKS with FFmpeg on g5/inf2 1 100+ renditions per title, GPU-accelerated. CDN (if not Open Connect) CloudFront + Origin Shield ~600 PoPs; regional edge cache collapses origin fill. Analytics / ML training Kinesis Firehose → S3 → EMR Spark → Redshift / Athena Feeds daily model retrain, QoE dashboards. Recs online serving SageMaker endpoints + OpenSearch k-NN (or MemoryDB Redis vector) ANN candidate gen + real-time ranking. Chaos engineering AWS Fault Injection Simulator (managed Simian-Army-style) Kill nodes, AZ, region on schedule to prove the design. Deployment story : services run active-active across 3 AWS regions (Netflix uses us-east-1, us-west-2, eu-west-1).

Route 53 latency-based routing pins users to the nearest region; a regional evacuation just flips the health check and cache-warm-elsewhere ensures no thundering-herd on the surviving regions. S3 replicates masters cross-region so a regional loss cannot destroy the catalog. On the data plane, either Open Connect appliances in ISPs (Netflix's actual setup) or CloudFront with Origin Shield (the AWS-native equivalent) serves 95–98% of playback bytes locally.

💻 C# implementation Two pieces of the design in C#: (1) the playback authorization endpoint that reads user state from EVCache/Cassandra and returns a signed manifest URL, and (2) a compact ABR (adaptive bitrate) selector the player uses to pick the next segment. These two together are the seam between the control plane and the data plane — exactly what an interviewer wants you to code.

In Open Connect this is BGP + DNS // steering; on AWS you'd let CloudFront do it automatically.

This is the whole handoff to the CDN. var manifestUrl = SignedUrl.Build( host: ocaHost, path: $"/manifests/{titleId}/master.m3u8" , ttl: TimeSpan.FromHours( 6 ), userId: userId); return Results.Ok( new { titleId, manifestUrl, resumeSec, drmLicenseUrl = "https://drm.netflix.example/widevine" }); }); app.Run(); Client-side ABR selector (segment-by-segment) // Buffer-based ABR: choose the next segment's bitrate based on how much // buffer we already have + measured throughput.

This is the algorithm // running inside every Netflix client to keep playback smooth without // buffering. Similar in spirit to BOLA/BBA published algorithms. public sealed class AbrSelector { private readonly int [] _ladderKbps; // e.g. [400, 1200, 3000, 6000, 12000] private double _emaKbps = 2000 ; // EWMA of measured throughput private const double Alpha = 0.3 ; // smoothing factor public AbrSelector ( int [] ladderKbps) => _ladderKbps = ladderKbps; // Called after each segment download completes.

public void ObserveSegment( long bytes, TimeSpan elapsed) { var kbps = (bytes * 8.0 ) / (elapsed.TotalSeconds * 1000 ); _emaKbps = Alpha * kbps + ( 1 - Alpha) * _emaKbps; } // Pick the bitrate for the next segment. public int PickBitrateKbps( double bufferSec) { // Safety headroom: never request a bitrate above 80% of measured throughput. var ceiling = _emaKbps * 0.8 ; // If buffer is tiny (< 8s), be very conservative — avoid the rebuffer cliff. // If buffer is fat (> 30s), we can afford to reach for the top of the ladder.

var allowanceFactor = bufferSec switch { < 8 => 0.6 , < 15 => 0.8 , < 30 => 1.0 , _ => 1.2 }; var target = ceiling * allowanceFactor; // Pick the highest rung of the ladder we can afford. var pick = _ladderKbps[ 0 ]; foreach ( var r in _ladderKbps) if (r <= target) pick = r; return pick; } } Two shapes to notice. The authorization endpoint is thin — cache first, DB fallback, mint a signed URL, return. That's it. The real complexity lives on the client : bitrate selection, segment prefetch, decoder buffer management. This is the correct division of labor for a streaming service — put the intelligence at the edge where the network conditions are actually known.

⚖️ Trade-offs, bottlenecks & likely follow-ups Where it can break The three real bottlenecks are evening prime-time egress in a single metro (solved by prefilled OCAs), Cassandra hot partitions from a global superstar profile (solved by wide-row bucketing and TTL'd LiveVH), and recommendation freshness lag — training is daily but users expect instant reactions to their behavior (solved by real-time features and contextual bandits on top of the stale ranker). A subtle failure mode: a rendition that's bad but shipped everywhere — Netflix mitigates this by rolling out new encodes gradually and A/B-testing quality metrics (VMAF) against real users.

Consistency vs availability Everything user-facing chooses availability . Viewing history, resume positions, view counts, likes are all eventually consistent — you might see a title show up on two devices' "continue watching" rows a few seconds apart. Billing is the exception: it lives in MySQL with ACID semantics because charging you twice would be worse than a spinning circle. In an interview, name this split: "read paths are AP; the money path is CP." Likely follow-up questions (with crisp answers) Why did Netflix build its own CDN instead of using Akamai or CloudFront? Egress economics at their scale.

Netflix is ~10-15% of North American peak internet traffic; commercial CDN pricing on that volume was untenable. Open Connect also gives them tighter control over prefill, telemetry, and codec rollouts — they own the whole video path. How does an OCA know what to prefill? Netflix runs a daily popularity forecast per region using recent viewing patterns and release calendars. Each OCA gets a manifest of what to prefill overnight; content moves from the tier-2 regional cluster to the OCA during ISP off-peak hours. What happens if a whole AWS region goes down? Route 53 fails DNS over to the surviving region(s); Zuul + microservices are already running there active-active.

The critical trick is EVCache is write-fan-out cross-region , so the surviving region's cache is already warm — no thundering herd against Cassandra. How does Netflix personalize thumbnails? Each title has several thumbnail candidates. A contextual multi-armed bandit per user cluster tests which image drives the most clicks. Explore vs exploit is tuned per session — you might see the same title with a different thumbnail depending on which taste cluster you're in. Why is the first HLS segment shorter than later segments? To fill the buffer fast and start playback in under a second. A short first segment costs a bit more manifest overhead but earns a huge TTFF win.

Subsequent segments are longer (6–8s) for cache-hit efficiency and fewer HTTP requests. Why Cassandra for viewing history — not DynamoDB? Wide-partition user-keyed workloads with a 9:1 write:read ratio; also, historical reason — Netflix adopted Cassandra pre-DynamoDB maturity. On a fresh AWS build, DynamoDB with adaptive capacity would be a perfectly good substitute. How does chaos engineering fit in? Netflix continuously runs Chaos Monkey (kills instances), Chaos Kong (evacuates regions), and ChAP (chaos experiments in production) so failure paths never atrophy. Regional evacuation is practiced monthly; that's how they can promise no visible impact from an AWS region loss.

🗣️ Interview cheat sheet "Netflix separates the control plane (AWS microservices, EVCache, Cassandra, MySQL) from the data plane (Open Connect appliances embedded in ISPs and IXPs). The client hits Zuul, gets homepage rows from a personalized ranker, and receives a signed manifest URL — that is the last time AWS is in the loop. Every subsequent byte comes from an OCA a mile from the viewer, hit rate ~98% . Startup latency is under a second because segments are pre-warmed nightly . Peak traffic is handled by predictive pre-scaling, cross-region cache warm, and chaos-tested failover .

Recommendations are a two-stage funnel (candidate + rank) topped with a contextual bandit for row ordering and thumbnails. Choose availability over consistency everywhere except billing." Numbers to quote ~260 M subscribers ; ~40 M peak concurrent streams . Open Connect ~98% hit rate ; only ~2% of playback bytes hit origin. Kafka: 500 B events/day, 8 M events/s peak, 1.3 PB/day . Cassandra: 50+ clusters, 500+ nodes, 250 K writes/sec on the biggest cluster . ~1 100–1 200 renditions per title across resolutions/codecs/audio/subtitles. 2 200+ device types supported. Startup latency target: < 1 s TTFF .

Five talking points that win the round " Open Connect is what makes this possible — a private CDN inside 1 000+ ISPs, prefilled nightly using a popularity forecast." " The two planes only meet at the manifest. AWS answers 'what to play'; Open Connect delivers the bytes." " EVCache is write-fan-out cross-region so a regional failover doesn't cold-cache and stampede Cassandra." " Recs are a two-stage funnel : ANN candidate → GBDT/DNN rank, with a contextual bandit on top for row ordering and thumbnails." " Chaos engineering is a first-class citizen — Chaos Monkey/Kong constantly kills things so failover paths never atrophy." ❓ FAQ — your follow-up questions Questions asked about this topic No

To send anything — a photo, a message, a video call — the postal service has to solve seven separate problems , and every one of the topics on this page is one of those problems. First, the mail has to physically travel — a truck on a road, a plane in the air, or a signal on a wire (this is the physical and data-link layer ).

So there's a giant phonebook that translates "whatsapp.com" into an actual address — that phonebook is DNS . Once you know the address, you have to decide how careful the delivery should be. If you're sending a legal contract, you want a courier who guarantees delivery, has a signature on arrival, and re-sends anything lost — that's TCP .

The letter itself — the shape of the request and answer — is written in a shared language called HTTP . When you want the letter to be secret , you put it inside a sealed, tamper-proof envelope — that's HTTPS . Every envelope has a small tamper-check sticker on it — if the sticker looks scratched, the receiver throws the letter out. That sticker is a checksum . Finally, big companies don't want everyone knocking on their front door.

x: When production says "the network is broken", OSI turns it into a specific accusation: "the client got a TCP RST from the LB, so it's a Layer-4 problem", or "the TLS handshake fails with unknown_ca , so it's a Layer-6 issue". Real systems implement the tighter 4-layer TCP/IP model, but interviewers ask about the 7-layer OSI because its finer granularity makes it easier to point at exactly what broke. x: When you're picking infrastructure, the key question is which layer does this thing operate at? An AWS Network Load Balancer is L4 (TCP-only, fast, protocol-agnostic). An AWS Application Load Balancer is L7 (understands HTTP, can route on Host / Path / cookies, can terminate TLS). A service mesh like Istio uses L4 for connection handling but adds L7 for mTLS and traffic policy. Modern reality: layer boundaries have blurred. TLS lives ambiguously between L5 and L6. QUIC is technically L4 (transport) but bundles TLS 1.3 and reliability. gRPC is L7 but rides HTTP/2 which is also L7. Don't get stuck on where exactly a protocol lives; know why you're naming it. 2.

x: IP Address — routing coordinates, not identity An IP address is a location for a network interface, not an identity for a machine or a user. IPv4 uses 32 bits (~4.3 billion addresses, exhausted); IPv6 uses 128 bits with a common /64 subnet size. Real systems typically deploy dual-stack : both an A record (IPv4) and an AAAA record (IPv6) point at the same service. In cloud VPCs, the private ranges from RFC 1918 (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16) are used internally, and a NAT gateway or LB is what makes the service reachable from the public internet. CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing) is how modern networks slice address space.

t: Networking Fundamentals — OSI, IP, TCP/UDP, HTTP/HTTPS, DNS, Checksums, Proxy
x: Notation is network/prefix-length : 10.0.0.0/16 means "the first 16 bits identify the network, the last 16 bits identify hosts" — 65 536 addresses. Routers use longest prefix match : if two routes cover the same destination, the more specific one (larger prefix) wins. NAT keeps IPv4 alive by rewriting private source IPs to a shared public IP as traffic leaves the network. It works beautifully for outbound, painfully for inbound (you need port forwarding or a load balancer). NAT is why the true client IP arrives in the X-Forwarded-For / Forwarded header rather than the TCP source field — and why rate-limiting purely by IP is dangerous: an entire CGNAT block might share one public address. 3.

x: TCP vs UDP — the "what if data is late or missing?" question The single best framing for TCP vs UDP is "what should the application do when data is late, lost, duplicated, or reordered?" . TCP answers: "I'll hide all of that from you — you get an in-order byte stream and I retransmit whatever gets lost." UDP answers: "here's your datagram, good luck, deal with loss yourself." TCP opens with a three-way handshake (SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK), then guarantees ordered delivery, retransmits on loss, and applies flow control (receiver window) and congestion control (sender adjusts rate). Header is 20 bytes base.

t: Networking Fundamentals — OSI, IP, TCP/UDP, HTTP/HTTPS, DNS, Checksums, Proxy
x: Suffers from head-of-line blocking : a lost segment freezes later bytes in the buffer even if they arrived. That's why HTTP/2 didn't solve everything and HTTP/3 moved to UDP. UDP has no handshake, no reordering, no retransmission, 8-byte header. Perfect for real-time media (a lost 20 ms of audio doesn't matter — a fresh frame is already on the way), DNS (a single query fits in one packet; if it's lost, ask again), and modern QUIC / HTTP/3. QUIC is the plot twist: built on UDP but adds TLS 1.3, retransmission, congestion control, and multiplexed streams — all in userspace.

t: Networking Fundamentals — OSI, IP, TCP/UDP, HTTP/HTTPS, DNS, Checksums, Proxy
x: Its killer features are 1-RTT (or 0-RTT resumption) connection setup and connection migration , so your call survives a WiFi-to-cellular switch. When an interviewer asks "TCP or UDP?", the real 2026 answer is often "QUIC — because I want TCP-like reliability without TCP head-of-line blocking". 4. HTTP / HTTPS — the application-layer contract HTTP is a request-response protocol: method + target line, headers, optional body. It's stateless at the protocol level — every request should carry enough context to be understood on its own. Methods have two important properties: safe (no side-effect, e.g. GET, HEAD) and idempotent (calling twice = calling once, e.g. GET, PUT, DELETE).

t: Networking Fundamentals — OSI, IP, TCP/UDP, HTTP/HTTPS, DNS, Checksums, Proxy
x: POST is neither safe nor idempotent by default, which is why retrying a POST needs an idempotency key. Status codes matter because they define the client's next move. 2xx = success. 3xx = follow the redirect / use cache. 4xx = don't retry blindly — you did something wrong. 5xx = server is broken; safe to retry with backoff, but only if the request is idempotent. The pair 502 vs 504 is a classic interview question: 502 Bad Gateway means the reverse proxy got a broken response from upstream; 504 Gateway Timeout means the reverse proxy didn't hear back in time. HTTPS wraps HTTP inside TLS.

x: The TLS 1.3 handshake takes 1-RTT: ClientHello (SNI + ALPN + supported ciphers) → ServerHello + Certificate + ephemeral ECDHE key share → client verifies chain + derives keys → encrypted HTTP begins. Forward secrecy is guaranteed by ephemeral DH. TLS 1.3 also supports 0-RTT for repeat connections, but replay-vulnerable, so use only for idempotent reads. HTTP versions: HTTP/1.1 is text-based, one request per TCP connection (or serialized with keep-alive) — a slow response blocks the connection. HTTP/2 is binary and multiplexes many streams over one TCP connection but still suffers TCP-layer head-of-line blocking.

x: HTTP/3 runs over QUIC (UDP) with per-stream loss recovery and connection migration. HTTP/2 server push turned out to be a bad idea and is effectively deprecated. 5. DNS — the internet's phonebook DNS translates human names into IP addresses. When you visit google.com , your OS asks a recursive resolver (your ISP's, or a public one like 8.8.8.8 or 1.1.1.1). If the resolver doesn't have a cached answer, it walks the hierarchy: root nameserver → TLD nameserver (for .com ) → authoritative nameserver for google.com . The authoritative server hands back an A record (IPv4) or AAAA record (IPv6). The whole thing usually completes in tens of milliseconds because of caching.

t: Networking Fundamentals — OSI, IP, TCP/UDP, HTTP/HTTPS, DNS, Checksums, Proxy
x: Every DNS record has a TTL (time-to-live) telling downstream caches how long they may reuse the answer. Long TTLs are cheaper but make cutovers slow; short TTLs make cutovers fast but multiply query volume. Most production systems use 60-300 s TTLs for A records and much longer for stable records like MX or NS. DNS's underrated superpower is traffic steering : geo-routing, latency-based routing, weighted round-robin, health-check-driven failover. AWS Route 53, Cloudflare, Akamai FastDNS all do this. Your netflix.com resolves to a completely different IP address depending on where you are — that's DNS deciding for you which CDN edge is closest.

x: DNS is stateless UDP by default (single-packet request/response on port 53). Large responses fall back to TCP:53. Modern deployments use DoT (DNS over TLS) or DoH (DNS over HTTPS) to hide queries from network operators. DNSSEC adds authenticity: authoritative servers sign records so resolvers can verify they weren't tampered with — but adoption is patchy. 6. Checksums — integrity, not authenticity A checksum is a compact value computed from a block of data; you recompute it on the receiver and compare. It's how Ethernet frames, IPv4 headers, TCP segments, and UDP datagrams detect accidental corruption on the wire.

t: Networking Fundamentals — OSI, IP, TCP/UDP, HTTP/HTTPS, DNS, Checksums, Proxy
x: IPv6 dropped the IP-layer checksum because L2 and L4 already provide integrity, and doing it once at each layer is enough. The key distinction to volunteer: checksums catch accidents; they do not stop adversaries . A CRC-32 is fast and hardware-accelerated (CRC-32C in particular) and reliably catches burst bit-flips — perfect for a lossy WiFi link. But if an attacker modifies the payload, they can also recompute a valid CRC. So a checksum gives you integrity ("did the bytes change accidentally?"), not authenticity ("did the right person send them?").

t: Networking Fundamentals — OSI, IP, TCP/UDP, HTTP/HTTPS, DNS, Checksums, Proxy
x: When authenticity matters, use a cryptographic hash (SHA-256, BLAKE3) as a fingerprint (Git object IDs, container image digests), or better, an HMAC (shared-secret keyed hash — great for webhook signatures) or a digital signature (asymmetric — anyone with the public key can verify, only the private-key holder can sign — great for signed package releases). MD5 and SHA-1 should not be used where security matters. 7. Proxy vs Reverse Proxy — same box, different side of the door The single-sentence definition: a forward proxy is on the client's side, a reverse proxy is on the server's side . Both sit between clients and servers, but they exist for opposite reasons.

t: Networking Fundamentals — OSI, IP, TCP/UDP, HTTP/HTTPS, DNS, Checksums, Proxy
x: A forward proxy is your outbound gatekeeper — corporate egress filtering, content blocking, audit logging, or plain caching for many clients. A reverse proxy is the server's front door — one stable public endpoint that hides a farm of backends behind it. Everything modern lives behind a reverse proxy. NGINX, HAProxy, Envoy, Caddy, Traefik for self-hosted; Cloudflare, Fastly, AWS ALB, GCP HTTPS LB, Azure App Gateway for managed. In a K8s cluster, an ingress controller is a reverse proxy. In a service mesh, every sidecar (Envoy under Istio, linkerd-proxy) is a reverse proxy for that pod.

x: What do reverse proxies actually do? TLS termination , load balancing , routing (host/path/header), caching , compression , WAF , rate limiting , auth-token check , logging & tracing . The other big distinction: L4 vs L7 proxies . An L4 proxy (an NLB, or NGINX in stream mode) forwards TCP/UDP bytes without opening them — fast, protocol-agnostic, works for anything. An L7 proxy (an ALB, NGINX HTTP mode) reads HTTP requests, so it can route on host name, URL path, method, header, or JWT claim. You pay for that intelligence with latency and CPU.

Also: when a proxy is in front, the backend sees the proxy's IP as the source. Preserve the true client identity in X-Forwarded-For and only trust that header from proxies you control. 🧮 The DSA behind it Data structures & algorithms hiding inside Networking looks like a plumbing topic, but every layer runs an algorithm.

TCP hides loss at the cost of head-of-line blocking; UDP exposes loss but never freezes a stream. HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3: HTTP/3 wins under packet loss and network changes; HTTP/2 wins where UDP is blocked (some corporate firewalls). L4 vs L7 load balancer: speed & protocol-agnosticism vs routing intelligence. NLB for gRPC/TCP passthrough, ALB for host/path routing. DNS TTL length: short = agile failover, more query load; long = cheap, slow to change.

CRC vs cryptographic hash: speed vs tamper resistance. CRC for accidental bit-flips; SHA-256/HMAC for anything an attacker might touch. Common interviewer follow-ups "Why does DNS use UDP instead of TCP?" A typical DNS query and response each fit in one packet (~50–100 bytes), so the ~1 RTT TCP handshake would be pure overhead. UDP is 8-byte header and connectionless — if a query is lost, the resolver just asks again.

x: DNS falls back to TCP when the response is larger than 512 bytes (zone transfers, DNSSEC-signed records). "What's the difference between 502 and 504?" Both come from a reverse proxy. 502 Bad Gateway = the proxy contacted the upstream and got a broken/invalid response back (e.g., connection reset, malformed HTTP). 504 Gateway Timeout = the proxy contacted the upstream and never heard back within the timeout. The debugging move is opposite: 502 → check upstream logs / crash; 504 → check upstream load / slow downstream / bad timeout config.

x: "Would you use an NLB or an ALB for your service?" NLB (L4) when I want minimum latency, protocol-agnostic passthrough, preserved source IP, or when running non-HTTP protocols like raw TCP, gRPC-over-h2c, or MQTT. ALB (L7) when I need host- or path-based routing, cookie stickiness, WAF, or TLS termination with modern cipher suites. In a modern web service the answer is usually "CloudFront in front of ALB in front of ECS" — you get edge caching plus L7 routing plus health checks.

x: "How would you prevent tampering on a webhook?" HMAC-SHA256 the payload with a shared secret, put the tag plus a timestamp in a header, and validate on the receiver with a constant-time compare and a small replay window (say 5 minutes). Never rely on the checksum alone — a plain checksum has no key, so an attacker can recompute it after modifying the payload. "You have a service that sees traffic drop after a deployment even though the app is fine. First guess?" Something in the path is misclassifying traffic.

"Client IP shows up as the load balancer's IP in the backend logs — why?" The reverse proxy terminated the client TCP connection and opened a new one to the backend, so the backend sees the proxy's IP. The true client IP is forwarded in the X-Forwarded-For header (or Forwarded , or via Proxy Protocol at L4). Only trust that header from proxies you control — anyone can send it.

System Design · Interview Prep · FAANG favourite 📰 Design a News Feed (Twitter / Facebook Timeline) Show each user a fresh, ranked stream of posts from the people they follow — at hundreds of thousands of reads per second. The classic test of the fan-out trade-off and the celebrity problem . 🎯 Scenario 🧑‍🎓 Laymen 📋 Requirements 🏗️ Architecture 🔍 Deep-dive 🧮 DSA ☁️ AWS 💻 C# code ⚖️ Trade-offs 🗣️ Cheat sheet ❓ FAQ 📚 Sources 🎯 Real-world scenario What we're building & where it's used A news feed (a.k.a. timeline) is the scrolling, reverse-chronological-or-ranked list of posts you see when you open Twitter/X, Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn, or Reddit .

The system takes the content published by everyone a user follows and assembles a personalised, ordered stream — fast enough that the feed is already waiting the instant the app opens. It's a top-tier FAANG interview question because it forces you to confront the central tension of social systems head-on: do you do the expensive work when a post is written, or when a feed is read? It's deceptively simple to state ("show me posts from people I follow, newest first") but every real product hits the same walls: the volume is brutally read-heavy (people scroll far more than they post), a single celebrity post must reach tens of millions of followers, and the feed must feel instant .

Interviewers love it because the obvious first design (query everyone you follow at read time) collapses at scale, and the "correct" design (push posts into precomputed timelines) collapses for celebrities — so you're forced into a hybrid and have to defend the boundary. Say this up front: "This is a read-heavy feed-generation problem. The core decision is fan-out-on-write versus fan-out-on-read, and the right answer at scale is a hybrid that pushes for normal users and pulls for celebrities." 🧑‍🎓 In laymen terms The personal magazine already waiting on your doormat Imagine every morning a magazine lands on your doormat, and it's a personal magazine — put together just for you .

It only contains pages from the friends, family, celebrities, and shops you actually care about. Your neighbour, who follows different people, gets a completely different magazine. When you open Instagram or Twitter or Facebook, this is exactly what you're doing — picking up your personal, freshly-assembled magazine. Now here's the puzzle. You have hundreds of millions of readers , and each of them wants their magazine to be ready the instant they touch the app . If we tried to assemble each magazine on the spot — running out to every friend's house, checking what they posted, and stapling it together in that one second — the whole thing would freeze.

So the clever people running the app do the work earlier . Every time your friend posts a photo, a little worker in the background quietly slides a copy into every magazine that follows her . Your feed isn't built when you open the app — it was pre-assembled bit by bit through the day. But here's the twist. What if your friend is Cristiano Ronaldo, with 600 million followers ? Sliding a copy of his photo into 600 million magazines takes hours. So the trick is: for a normal person like your school friend, we push their post into everyone's magazine right away.

For a giant celebrity, we do the opposite — we leave the post sitting on their doorstep, and when you open your app, we quickly run and grab the celebrity's latest before showing you the page. Push for normal people, pull for the celebrities. Nobody waits. And if you haven't opened Instagram for six months? They stop building your magazine altogether until you come back. That's how a few servers keep half a billion people happy. 📋 Requirements & scale Requirements and back-of-the-envelope math Functional requirements Publish a post — a user creates a post; it must reach all their followers' feeds. Read the feed — return a paginated, ordered list of posts from the people a user follows.

Follow / unfollow users (defines the social graph that drives the feed). Optional: ranking (relevance, not just time), media, likes/comments counts. Non-functional requirements Low latency on read — the feed should render in well under a second (target ~200 ms server-side); this is the experience that matters most. High availability — feeds should always load; eventual consistency is acceptable (a post arriving a few seconds late is fine). Massive read scale — reads dominate writes by a large factor. Eventual consistency & durability — never lose a published post, but it can propagate asynchronously.

Capacity estimation (numbers to quote — Twitter-scale) Anchor on 100 million active users and 500 million posts/day . Everything else follows: Metric Estimate Derivation Active users 100 million given Posts / day 500 million (~15B/month) given Write QPS (posts) ~6,000 posts/sec 500M ÷ 86,400s Read QPS (feed reads) ~100,000 reads/sec 250B read requests/month ÷ 2.5M Read : write ratio ~16 : 1 (and higher at peak) 100k reads vs 6k writes Fan-out deliveries ~60,000/sec (5B/day) avg 10 followers reached per post Tweet/post size ~10 KB (incl.

media id) 8B id + 32B user + 140B text + ~10KB media ref New content / month ~150 TB (~5.4 PB / 3 yr) 15B posts × 10 KB The punchline: "Writes are modest (~6k/sec) but each write fans out to many timelines, and reads are enormous (~100k/sec). So I optimise the read path to be a near-O(1) cache lookup by precomputing timelines on write — except where fan-out itself becomes the bottleneck." 🏗️ High-level architecture How the pieces fit together There are two paths, and the whole interview hinges on separating them.

On the write path , a user publishes a post: it's written durably to the Post store, then a Fan-out Service (driven by a message queue) looks up the author's followers and pushes the post id into each follower's precomputed home-timeline cache . On the read path , opening the app is cheap: the Feed Service reads the user's ready-made timeline (a list of post ids) straight from Redis in roughly O(1), then "hydrates" those ids into full posts via the Post and User services. Because the heavy lifting happened asynchronously at write time, the read is fast. The exception is the celebrity : pushing one post to 50 million timelines is hugely expensive and slow.

So for high-follower accounts the system skips fan-out and instead pulls their recent posts at read time and merges them into the requesting user's feed. That hybrid — push for the masses, pull for celebrities — is the design's centrepiece. Synchronous read Async fan-out (write) Precomputed timeline (push) Celebrity pull (merge) Walk it verbally: "Publish → durable Post DB → event on a queue → Fan-out Service expands the follower list and writes the post id into each follower's Redis timeline. On read, the Feed Service grabs the precomputed id list from Redis, pulls in celebrity posts separately, merges and ranks, hydrates the ids into full posts, and returns a page.

The queue decouples the slow fan-out from the fast publish acknowledgement." 🔍 Component deep-dive 1. Fan-out on write (push model) — the default When a user posts, the Fan-out Service looks up their followers and inserts the new post id at the head of each follower's home-timeline list in Redis. Reads then become trivial: the timeline is already built. The cost is paid on write and it's an O(number-of-followers) operation — 1,000 followers means 1,000 cache writes. This is ideal because most users have modest follower counts and reads vastly outnumber writes, so doing work once on write saves it on millions of reads. 2.

Fan-out on read (pull model) — for celebrities For an account with tens of millions of followers, pushing one post to every timeline would generate tens of millions of writes and can take minutes to complete — unacceptable. So we don't fan out celebrity posts at all . Instead, at read time, the Feed Service fetches the recent posts of the (few) celebrities a user follows and merges them into the feed. This shifts a little work to the read path but avoids the write explosion. 3. The hybrid (what you actually propose) Combine them: push for normal users, pull for celebrities , using a follower-count threshold (e.g. > ~1M followers, tunable).

A user's final feed = their precomputed pushed timeline ∪ recent posts pulled from the celebrities they follow , then merged and ranked. This is the answer FAANG interviewers are listening for. 4. Timeline cache & the inactive-user optimisation Home timelines live in a Redis cache as lists of post ids (cheap: ids, not full posts), capped at a few hundred entries per user. To save memory, only active users' timelines are kept warm; if someone has been inactive for, say, 30+ days, their timeline is dropped and lazily rebuilt from the database on next login by querying who they follow. This stops you from fanning out to tens of millions of dormant accounts. 5.

Ranking Pure reverse-chronological is the simple version. Real feeds rank by relevance — recency, affinity to the author, engagement (likes/comments velocity), and media type — typically scored by an ML model at read time over the candidate set. Mention it as an extension; keep the core design chrono + pluggable ranker. 🧮 The DSA behind it Data structures & algorithms Fan-out (scatter): expanding one post to N follower timelines — the defining operation; O(N) writes, done async on a queue.

k-way merge with a min/max-heap: merging the pushed timeline with several celebrity post-streams into one ordered feed is exactly a k-way merge of sorted lists — a heap keyed on timestamp/score pops the next item in O(log k). Redis list / sorted set (ZSET): the home timeline is a capped list of post ids, or a sorted set scored by timestamp/rank for O(log n) insert and O(1) head reads. Hash maps: the follower/following graph and the id→post hydration are hash lookups (O(1) average). Cursor / keyset pagination: "load more" uses a cursor (last post id/score), not OFFSET, so paging stays O(page) regardless of depth.

API entry / routing API Gateway or ALB Auth, throttling, routing to services. Feed / Post / Fan-out services ECS/EKS Fargate (or Lambda) Stateless, autoscaling microservices; ECS for steady high QPS. Home-timeline cache ElastiCache for Redis Lists/ZSETs of post ids — the precomputed timelines, O(1) reads. Post store DynamoDB (or Cassandra) Write-heavy, horizontally sharded by post id; single-digit-ms reads. Social graph (follows) DynamoDB follower/following adjacency lists; partition by user id. Fan-out queue Kinesis / SQS (+ SNS) Decouples slow fan-out from fast publish; buffers spikes. Media blobs S3 Durable object store; served via CloudFront.

Ranking / search OpenSearch + SageMaker Candidate search + ML relevance scoring. Deployment story: CloudFront/Route 53 → API Gateway → Fargate services. A publish writes to DynamoDB and drops an event on Kinesis; Fan-out consumers read the follower adjacency list from DynamoDB and write post ids into ElastiCache Redis timelines. On read, the Feed Service reads the Redis timeline, pulls celebrity posts from DynamoDB/Redis, k-way-merges, hydrates post bodies (DynamoDB, media via S3/CloudFront), and returns a cursor-paginated page. Inactive timelines are evicted and rebuilt on demand. 💻 C# implementation The heart of the system is the hybrid fan-out on publish and the merge on read.

GetFollowersAsync (post.AuthorId)) await _timelineCache.
