GetRecentByAuthorsAsync (celebs, limit); // c) k-way merge by score (timestamp/relevance) using a max-heap var heap = new PriorityQueue<PostRef, long> (); // key = -score → max-heap foreach ( var r in pushed. Concat (pulled)) heap. Enqueue (r, -r.Score); var top = new List<PostRef> (limit); while (heap.Count > 0 && top.Count < limit) top. Add (heap. Dequeue ()); // d) hydrate ids → full posts in one batched multiget return await _postStore. HydrateAsync (top.

Select (r => r.Id)); } Other tools / languages: the same design ships in Java/Spring or Go ; the timeline cache could be Redis ZSETs; the queue could be Kafka; the post store Cassandra (Twitter's real choice) instead of DynamoDB. ⚖️ Trade-offs, bottlenecks & likely follow-ups The central trade-off: fan-out-on-write makes reads cheap and writes expensive (great because reads dominate), while fan-out-on-read makes writes cheap and reads expensive. The hybrid picks per-user by follower count. The main bottleneck is the Fan-out Service under celebrity posts and "thundering herd" events; the queue + the pull-for-celebrities rule are what tame it.

Consistency vs availability: feeds are eventually consistent (AP) — a post may take a few seconds to appear in all timelines, which is fine. Never block a publish on full fan-out; acknowledge the write after the durable store + queue enqueue. Q: Push or pull — which and why? A: Hybrid. Push (fan-out on write) for normal users so reads are O(1) cache hits; pull (fan-out on read) for celebrities to avoid tens of millions of writes per post. Threshold on follower count. Q: How do you handle a celebrity with 100M followers? A: Don't fan out their posts at all. Fetch their recent posts at read time and merge into each requesting feed; cache those hot posts aggressively since many users want them.

Q: A user follows 5,000 people — how is the read still fast? A: Their timeline is precomputed in Redis, so the read is a single capped list fetch, not 5,000 queries. Only the handful of celebrities they follow are merged in at read time. Q: Why keep only post ids in the timeline cache? A: Memory. Ids are tiny; storing full posts ×N timelines would explode RAM. Hydrate ids to bodies in a batched multiget at read time. Q: What about inactive users? A: Don't fan out to them. Evict dormant (e.g. 30-day) timelines and rebuild lazily from the DB on next login.

Q: New follow — do you backfill? A: Optionally merge the newly-followed user's recent posts into the timeline (a small pull), rather than rebuilding everything. 🗣️ Interview cheat sheet 30-second pitch: "A news feed is a read-heavy feed-generation problem. I precompute each user's home timeline by fanning out posts on write into a Redis list of post ids, so reads are O(1) cache hits. For celebrities , fanning out to tens of millions is too expensive, so I don't push — I pull their recent posts at read time and k-way-merge them into the feed.

That hybrid, plus an async fan-out queue, eviction of inactive timelines, and cursor pagination, gives instant feeds at ~100k reads/sec while keeping writes sane. It's eventually consistent (AP) — a post can land a few seconds late." Numbers to quote 100M users · 500M posts/day · ~6k write QPS · ~100k read QPS (~16:1 read:write) ~60k fan-out deliveries/sec (avg 10 followers/post) · ~150 TB new content/month Celebrity threshold ≈ 1M followers (tunable) · timelines capped at a few hundred ids 5 talking points that win the round Push vs pull framed as the core trade-off — and choose hybrid . Celebrity problem → pull + merge, not fan-out.

Store ids, not posts , in the timeline cache; hydrate on read. Async fan-out via a queue ; ack publish early → AP/eventual consistency. System Design · Interview Prep Notification System A push/email/SMS delivery pipeline built for reliability at billions of messages a day — with queues, retries, priorities, and idempotency baked in. 🎯 Scenario 🧑‍🎓 Laymen 📋 Requirements 🏗️ Architecture 🎬 Animation 🔍 Deep-dive 🧮 DSA ☁️ AWS 💻 C# code ⚖️ Trade-offs 🗣️ Cheat sheet ❓ FAQ 📚 Sources 🎯 Real-world scenario What we're building & where it's used A Notification System is the shared platform inside a company that any internal team calls to reach a user through email, SMS, push notification, in-app banner, or WhatsApp .

When Amazon sends you "your order has shipped," when Uber pings your phone that the driver is 2 minutes away, when Slack emails you a magic-login link, when your bank texts a one-time password — they all funnel through a notification service that looks like a single "send" API to callers but is really a distributed pipeline of queues, workers, retries, rate limiters, and third-party vendor integrations behind it. Every large product needs one because reaching users reliably is surprisingly hard . Third-party gateways (Twilio, SendGrid, APNs, FCM) go down. Users disable channels. OTPs must arrive in seconds while a marketing blast can wait an hour.

A duplicate push at 3am is a customer-support ticket. And volumes are enormous — LinkedIn sends billions of notifications monthly, Facebook well over 30 billion a day at peak, so the system must absorb massive spikes without dropping a single high-priority message. This is a classic staff-level interview scenario because it hits every core distributed-systems concept: async processing, at-least-once delivery, deduplication, backpressure, priority queues, rate limiting, and observability .

You'll see the design pattern reused everywhere: AWS SNS , Google Cloud Pub/Sub , Twilio , OneSignal , Braze , Airship , Amazon Pinpoint , and every in-house notification platform at Netflix, Uber, LinkedIn, Meta, Airbnb, and Flipkart. 🧑‍🎓 In laymen terms Explained without the jargon Imagine your bank has one giant post-office inside its building. Whenever any department — the credit-card team, the loans team, the fraud team — needs to tell a customer something, they don't run to the customer themselves.

They drop a slip of paper into the post-office chute that says "tell Priya her card was charged $45." The post-office does all the messy work of actually reaching Priya — figuring out whether she prefers a text message, an email, or the little bell icon in the bank's app; making sure the message doesn't go out twice; slowing down promotional flyers if the post-office is already busy handling urgent fraud alerts. That's a notification system. Any part of the company can say "tell user X, thing Y" and walk away confident the message will arrive. Here's why it's harder than it sounds.

First, the mailman isn't your employee — you rely on the phone company for texts and Apple/Google for phone notifications. They sometimes have bad days. Second, some messages are on fire and some are lukewarm — a login code you're waiting for right now cannot wait behind five million marketing emails ahead of it in line. Third, the same slip sometimes gets dropped in the chute twice because a computer somewhere got nervous and retried — but Priya must not get charged-notice twice. Fourth, you can't spam anyone — even if six teams want to ping the same customer in five minutes, the system has to be polite. You've used systems like this every single day.

When WhatsApp buzzes your phone , when Uber texts your OTP , when Amazon emails your invoice , when your bank flashes a low-balance alert — it all came through a post-office like this. The interesting design work is: how do you build a post-office that handles ten billion slips a day , never loses an urgent one, never sends the same slip twice, and gracefully slows down when the phone company is having a bad hour? A tiny example. At 8:03 AM Priya taps "Login" on her bank app. At 8:03:00.4 the login service drops a slip: "SMS OTP 4821 to Priya, urgent." The post-office puts it in the express lane , texts Twilio, and Priya's phone buzzes by 8:03:02.

Meanwhile a marketing job dumped 3 million promotional emails into the slow lane at 8:00 AM — those are still calmly draining through in the background, one batch at a time, and Priya's OTP jumped right past them because the express lane never gets stuck. 📋 Requirements & scale Requirements and back-of-the-envelope math Functional requirements Accept notification requests from any internal service via a simple POST /notifications API. Support multiple channels: email, SMS, mobile push (APNs/FCM), in-app, WhatsApp . Respect per-user channel preferences and unsubscribe/opt-out state. Support priority tiers — e.g.

critical (OTP, security), transactional (order shipped), promotional (marketing blast). Provide a template engine with placeholders and localization (i18n). Support scheduled and bulk notifications. Track delivery status and expose it via an API (queued → sent → delivered → opened). Non-functional requirements Reliability : at-least-once delivery for every notification; no silent drops. Idempotency : same request ID sent twice → user is notified exactly once. Low latency for critical messages: p99 < 5 s end-to-end for OTP. High throughput : absorb bulk campaign spikes without slowing down critical traffic.

Availability : 99.99% for the ingest API; degraded delivery is preferable to rejecting requests. Extensibility : adding a new channel or vendor should not require redesign. The flow of one request: a caller service (e.g.

the Orders service) calls POST /notifications with a JSON body containing request_id , user_id , template_id , data , and priority . The ingest API validates the schema, deduplicates against a Redis cache keyed by request_id , and drops the message onto one of three priority-partitioned Kafka topics ( notif.critical , notif.transactional , notif.promo ). Downstream, a Notification Router service consumes each topic (critical topic has the largest consumer group so it drains fastest), fetches the user's channel preferences from a preferences store, checks per-user and per-tenant rate limits in Redis, and expands the request into one message per target channel.

Each channel message goes onto its own channel queue (SQS or Kafka partition). Channel workers read from their queue, render the template, call the third-party gateway with a timeout, and on failure re-enqueue with an exponential-backoff delay. After N retries, the message goes to a Dead Letter Queue for later inspection or manual replay. Every message emits a tracking event (queued/sent/delivered/failed) to a Kafka topic consumed by an analytics pipeline that lands rows in Cassandra + a Kinesis stream feeding real-time dashboards.

We follow one OTP from ingest to the user's phone, watch a low-priority marketing message queue up in parallel, see a duplicate get deduplicated, and — for drama — one Twilio call fails and re-tries with exponential backoff before succeeding. ▶ Play Step → ← Back ↺ Reset Ready Press ▶ Play to start 🔍 Component deep-dive 1. Ingest API — the deduplication front door The Notification API is a thin, stateless service behind an API Gateway.

It performs three cheap checks and then returns immediately with a 202 Accepted . First, it authenticates the caller (mTLS or short-lived JWT). Second, it validates the schema and rejects malformed requests. Third, and most importantly, it enforces idempotency by consulting Redis with the caller-supplied request_id : SET nx:req:{id} 1 EX 86400 NX . If the key already exists, we treat the request as a duplicate and drop it. This is the primary defence against double sends caused by client retries. Fast-path latency stays under 20 ms so callers can call it synchronously with confidence. 2.

Priority-partitioned queues A single FIFO queue would let a 5-million-row marketing job block an urgent OTP. Instead we run separate Kafka topics per priority tier (or SQS FIFO queues with a priority attribute if you prefer SQS). Consumers on the critical topic get a large consumer group (say, 200 pods), transactional gets 100, promo gets 20. Because Kafka guarantees no head-of-line blocking across topics, the critical lane drains at its own pace irrespective of promo backlog. A common alternative — a weighted round-robin consumer — reads from all three but skews 70/25/5 in favor of higher priority. 3.

Notification Router Consumes from all priority topics, resolves the user, and fans out to per-channel queues. It hits three stores per message: (a) User Preferences DB — which channels the user allows, quiet hours, opt-out flags; (b) Redis rate-limit — token bucket per user (say, 20 promo msgs/day) and per tenant; (c) an optional de-throttle cache to suppress duplicate content sent within N minutes. If a user opted out of email but allows push, only the push message is emitted. The router is where policy lives. 4. Rate limiter We use a token-bucket algorithm in Redis with Lua-atomic decrement — the standard implementation for high-cardinality rate limits.

Two dimensions of buckets are enforced simultaneously: per-user (protects the recipient from spam) and per-tenant / per-vendor (protects our vendor quotas — Twilio, SES). When a bucket is empty, the message is deferred back to the topic with a delay, not dropped, so it eventually gets through. 5. Channel workers & retry mechanism Each channel has its own pool of workers matched to the vendor's rate limits. The worker fetches a message, renders the template, and calls the vendor with a strict timeout (email 5 s, SMS 3 s, push 2 s). On any 5xx or timeout it invokes the retry loop: exponential backoff with jitter , capped at ~5 attempts.

The delay formula is min(cap, base × 2^attempt) + random(0, jitter) . Delayed messages are re-enqueued to a delay queue (SQS delay queue, or Kafka with a scheduled-consumer pattern). After the retry budget is exhausted, the message goes to a Dead Letter Queue and an alert fires; operators can inspect and manually replay from the DLQ. 6. Idempotency in the delivery worker Even with front-door dedup, the worker must be idempotent because Kafka guarantees at-least-once. Before calling the vendor the worker checks (and writes) a marker in Redis keyed on the notification's message_id : SET sent:{id} 1 EX 3600 NX .

If a duplicate message arrives after the first has already been dispatched, the worker skips the vendor call. For vendors that also accept an idempotency key (Twilio does), we forward it too — belt and braces. 7. Notification tracker & analytics Every state transition (queued, sent, delivered, failed, opened, clicked) emits a small event to a Kafka topic. A stream processor lands them in Cassandra partitioned by user_id, day — write-optimized, cheap seeks by user. A parallel branch feeds a real-time dashboard (deliveries/sec, DLQ growth, vendor latencies). 8. Template & personalization service Templates live in an object store with a metadata table (S3 + DynamoDB).

The router resolves template_id + locale and hands the worker a rendered payload, or defers rendering to the worker to save router CPU. Personalization tokens ( {{first_name}} ) get filled in from the request's data field. 🧮 The DSA behind it Data structures & algorithms Even though this looks like glue code between queues and vendors, the interesting engineering hides in a handful of well-known algorithms — get these right and the whole system behaves .

⚖️ Trade-offs, bottlenecks & likely follow-ups The main tension in a notification system is between reliability and cost . At-least-once delivery is easy; exactly-once is not — it requires end-to-end idempotency and monotonic message IDs, and you pay for it with more Redis, more state, more code. Most teams pick at-least-once + strong idempotency and call it a day, because a user rarely notices a duplicate SMS as much as they notice a missing OTP. The failure mode you are most likely to interview on is vendor outage : SES silently drops your throughput to 1k/s, your queue backs up, DLQ grows, and users see delayed emails.

The escape hatch is multi-vendor fallback — route to Twilio if SNS SMS is degraded, use SendGrid if SES rate-limits — driven by circuit breakers that observe error rates per vendor. Two other classic gotchas: hot users (a celebrity account gets 10,000 events at once — you need per-user rate limiting and partition-aware sharding to avoid one Kafka partition owning all the traffic) and token invalidation (an iOS app is uninstalled → APNs returns 410 Gone; the worker must remove that device token from the preferences store, otherwise it wastes vendor calls forever).

Likely interview follow-ups How do you achieve exactly-once delivery? You approximate it with at-least-once + idempotency: ingest-time dedup on request_id , worker-side dedup on message_id before the vendor call, and pass an idempotency key to the vendor when they support it (Twilio, Stripe, some SES flows do). True exactly-once across independent networks is impossible; users won't notice the difference if idempotency is airtight. What if the third-party vendor is down for an hour? The circuit breaker opens after N consecutive failures and stops calling the vendor; messages accumulate in the channel queue (harmless — queues are durable) or fan out to a secondary vendor.

Once the breaker sees healthy probes it half-opens and drains the backlog. For truly urgent messages you can hot-swap to a fallback provider (SNS ↔ Twilio) on the fly. How would you scale to 10× traffic tomorrow? Ingest API and channel workers auto-scale horizontally — Kafka gets more partitions on the critical topic, SQS is elastic by default, Redis moves to cluster mode. The real bottleneck is vendor quotas , not us: negotiate higher SES/Twilio limits, buy more phone-number pools for SMS, add device-token sharding for push. Also expect the tracking store to be the next thing to feel it — pre-shard Cassandra with an extra partitioning dimension.

How do you handle scheduled or time-zone-aware sends? A separate scheduler service stores scheduled jobs in a sorted set / min-heap keyed on send_at . A tight loop pops due entries every second and injects them into the priority topics. For time-zone-aware sends, store the user's TZ in preferences and resolve send_at per user at enqueue time. How do you prevent notification storms after a bug? Two guardrails. First, a global kill-switch per tenant/template — flipping a flag in DynamoDB causes the router to drop matching messages instantly. Second, a per-user cooldown maintained in Redis (max N msgs / hour); anything above it gets rejected and logged.

In practice: also have an on-call runbook for "purge Kafka topic X" and rehearse it. Why not just use SNS or SendGrid directly and skip building this? Small startups do exactly that. You start needing this system when: (a) you have >1 channel per user (choice logic), (b) you need per-user preferences and unsubscribes across channels, (c) you need centralized rate-limiting, dedup, and analytics, (d) you have compliance rules (quiet hours, GDPR opt-out) that must be enforced uniformly. Below that scale, SNS/SendGrid is fine.

Channel workers call the vendor with a 3-attempt exponential-backoff-with-jitter retry, dead-letter after that, and everything emits tracking events to Cassandra. Idempotency is enforced twice — ingest and worker — using Redis SET NX. That gives at-least-once delivery, priority isolation, and no duplicate sends." System Design · Interview Prep Transactional Outbox Pattern How to update your database and publish an event atomically — the go-to answer when a FAANG interviewer asks "how do you avoid the dual-write problem?" 🎯 Scenario 🧑‍🎓 Laymen 📋 Requirements 🏗️ Architecture 🔍 Deep-dive 🧮 DSA ☁️ AWS 💻 C# code ⚖️ Trade-offs 🗣️ Cheat sheet ❓ FAQ 📚 Sources 🎯 Real-world scenario What we're building & where it's used Almost every event-driven system at scale eventually hits the same wall.

A service handles a command — say "place order" — and it must do two things: (1) write the new order row to its own database, and (2) publish an OrderPlaced event to a message broker (Kafka, SQS, RabbitMQ) so that downstream services — payments, inventory, notifications, analytics — can react. The interviewer's trap is this: these are two separate systems, and there is no shared transaction across them. If you commit the DB row and then crash before publishing, the rest of the company never learns the order exists. If you publish first and the DB rollback fires, you've told everyone about an order that doesn't exist.

This is the famous dual-write problem , and the transactional outbox pattern is the canonical, battle-tested answer. The core idea is deceptively simple: don't write to two systems — write to one. Inside the same local database transaction that saves your business data, you also insert a row into an outbox table describing the event you want to publish. Because it's one transaction, it's all-or-nothing: the order and its "please publish this" record commit together or roll back together. A separate background process — the message relay — later reads the outbox and forwards those events to the broker, retrying until they land.

This pattern is everywhere in production: it's a first-class feature of Debezium (Red Hat's CDC platform), it underpins how companies like Uber, Netflix, Airbnb, Shopify, and DoorDash keep their microservices consistent, and it's the recommended alternative to distributed transactions in Chris Richardson's Microservices Patterns and Sam Newman's books. If you can whiteboard it and defend the trade-offs, you've demonstrated the single most important reliability pattern in event-driven architecture. 🧑‍🎓 In laymen terms The waiter's notepad trick Picture a busy restaurant. You order a paneer tikka.

The waiter has to do two things: (1) update the bill on your table, and (2) run to the kitchen and tell the chef. Both have to happen — no bill without a dish, no dish without a bill. But what if the waiter writes the bill, then trips on the way to the kitchen and forgets? You get charged, no food arrives. What if he tells the chef first, then his pen runs out and he never writes the bill? You eat free. Now here's the clever trick real restaurants actually use. The waiter carries one notepad . On a single page, he writes both : "Table 7: paneer tikka, ₹280" AND "Kitchen: make one paneer tikka." He tears the page — one single action — and drops it in a box.

Then a separate helper comes along, picks up the paper, and walks the "make one paneer tikka" half to the kitchen. If the waiter trips, the whole page is either torn or not torn — never half. Either both things happen or neither does. That's the outbox pattern , and it's how big websites keep their promises. Say you pay for a train ticket on IRCTC . The website has to: (1) mark your seat as booked in the database, and (2) tell the SMS system to text you the PNR. If it tries to do both separately, one might fail — you'd get a seat with no confirmation SMS, or an SMS with no seat. Disaster.

So instead, in one single write , the website scribbles both the booking AND a little sticky note that says "please send an SMS to +91-98…" into the same table. Then a background helper program quietly walks over, picks up the sticky note, and hands it to the SMS system — retrying until the SMS actually sends . If the whole website crashes right after you paid, the sticky note is still safely there, waiting to be delivered when things come back up. The catch : the SMS might arrive a few seconds late, and if the helper is clumsy it might send the same SMS twice — so the receiving side has to be smart enough to ignore duplicates.

But you'll never get "money taken, no seat, no message." That's the whole point. 📋 Requirements & scale Requirements and back-of-the-envelope math This is a pattern , not a product, so "requirements" means the reliability properties you must guarantee. The interviewer wants to hear you name them precisely, because each one drives a design decision. Functional requirements An event is published if and only if the business transaction commits (no phantom events, no lost events). Downstream consumers eventually receive every event — eventual consistency across service boundaries. Events for the same aggregate/entity are delivered in commit order .

Non-functional requirements Durability — a crash of the service, relay, or broker must never drop an event. At-least-once delivery — we accept possible duplicates and make consumers idempotent, rather than paying for true exactly-once. Low added latency — publishing should trail the commit by milliseconds, not minutes. No 2PC — we must not require distributed transactions between DB and broker. Back-of-the-envelope: does the outbox table become a bottleneck? Suppose an e-commerce service does 5,000 writes/sec at peak, each producing one event.

That's 5,000 extra INSERT s/sec into the outbox — trivial for Postgres/MySQL, which comfortably handle tens of thousands of small inserts per second, especially since they piggyback on an existing transaction (no extra round-trip). The numbers interviewers expect you to reason about: Quantity Estimate Why it matters Extra write amplification 1 outbox INSERT per business txn Same transaction → ~0 extra round-trips; negligible Outbox row size ~0.5–2 KB (id, type, aggregate, JSON payload, timestamp) Payload dominates; keep events lean Relay latency (polling) poll interval (e.g.

100 ms–1 s) Tunable; trades DB load vs freshness Relay latency (CDC / log tailing) ~10–99 ms (two-digit ms, per Debezium/Postgres WAL) Near-real-time, no polling load Table growth at 5k/s ~432M rows/day if never purged Must delete/archive after publish, or the table explodes Purge strategy DELETE on publish, or TTL/partition drop Keeps the hot table tiny and indexes fast The number to volunteer: "The outbox adds one small INSERT per transaction — negligible write cost — and with log-based CDC the end-to-end publish latency is two-digit milliseconds .

The only real operational concern is housekeeping : at 5k writes/sec the table would grow ~430M rows/day, so I purge published rows or use a log-only outbox." 🏗️ High-level architecture How the pieces fit together The flow has two independent halves connected only through the database. On the write path (solid arrows), the service opens one local transaction, writes the business row and the outbox row, and commits — atomically. On the relay path (dashed arrows), a separate process observes the outbox (by polling it or by tailing the DB's transaction log) and publishes each event to the broker, marking it done only after the broker acknowledges.

Consumers read from the broker and apply idempotency to tolerate the duplicates that at-least-once delivery inevitably produces. write path (one local TX) async relay path (at-least-once) outbox table Client calls the service ( POST /order ). Service opens one local DB transaction and writes both the orders row and an outbox row, then COMMIT . Atomic — no partial state possible. The message relay observes the new outbox row (polling query, or transaction-log tailing via CDC). Relay publishes the event to the broker and waits for the broker's ack. On ack, the relay marks the outbox row published (or deletes it). If it crashed before this step, it republishes on restart → at-least-once .

Consumers read from the broker and deduplicate using the event ID / log offset before applying side effects. 🔍 Component deep-dive 1. The outbox table schema The outbox is an ordinary table in the same database as your business data — that co-location is the whole point, because it's what makes the shared transaction possible. A typical schema: CREATE TABLE outbox ( id UUID PRIMARY KEY , -- event id (dedup key for consumers) aggregate_type VARCHAR , -- e.g. 'Order' → routes to a topic aggregate_id VARCHAR , -- e.g. order id → Kafka partition key (ordering!) event_type VARCHAR , -- e.g.

'OrderPlaced' payload JSONB , -- the serialized event created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now(), published_at TIMESTAMPTZ -- NULL = not yet relayed (polling mode) ); The aggregate_id is doing double duty: consumers need it, and the relay uses it as the broker partition key so that all events for one order land on the same partition and stay ordered. 2. The message relay — polling vs. log tailing (the key decision) This is where interviewers push hardest, because it's the real engineering trade-off. There are two ways to get events out of the outbox: (a) Polling Publisher.

A background job runs SELECT * FROM outbox WHERE published_at IS NULL ORDER BY created_at LIMIT N on a timer, publishes each row, then marks it published. Simple, works on any database, easy to reason about. The downsides: it adds constant query load, forces a latency-vs-load trade-off via the poll interval, and — subtly — ordering can be wrong . Because a row is written when a transaction starts its insert but only becomes visible when it commits , two concurrent transactions can commit in a different order than their created_at /sequence suggests, so a naive poller can even skip a row that committed late. You mitigate with SELECT ...

FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED for safe concurrent workers and careful ordering logic. (b) Transaction Log Tailing (CDC) — usually preferred. Instead of querying the table, a tool like Debezium reads the database's write-ahead log (Postgres WAL, MySQL binlog). Every committed insert to the outbox appears in the log in exact commit order , so ordering is correct by construction, there's no polling load, and latency drops to two-digit milliseconds . This is what most large-scale deployments use. The cost is operational complexity — you now run and monitor a CDC connector and (often) Kafka Connect.

Interview power move: "I'd start with a polling relay for simplicity, but at scale I'd move to log-based CDC with Debezium — it gives correct ordering for free from the commit log and cuts latency to tens of milliseconds without loading the database." 3. Delivery semantics & idempotent consumers The relay gives at-least-once delivery: if it publishes to the broker and then crashes before recording success, it will republish on restart. (Brokers deliver at-least-once anyway, so this is rarely a new burden.) Therefore consumers must be idempotent . Two standard techniques: Dedup journal (UUID): the consumer stores the IDs of processed events and drops anything it's seen.

Simple, but you must decide how long to retain IDs (too short → miss a late duplicate; too long → the journal bloats). Monotonic watermark (better): store only the highest offset/LSN seen and reject anything ≤ it. Use the transaction-log offset (Postgres LSN, Kafka offset) — not a database sequence, which isn't reliably monotonic across concurrent transactions. 4. Housekeeping At high write rates the outbox grows fast, so you must prune it: delete rows on successful publish, run a periodic cleanup, or partition by day and drop old partitions. A neat CDC trick: INSERT then DELETE the outbox row in the same transaction — CDC still captures the insert from the log, but the table stays empty.

Postgres goes further with pg_logical_emit_message() , writing the event straight to the WAL with no table at all ("log-only outbox"). 🧮 The DSA behind it Data structures & algorithms The outbox pattern isn't algorithm-heavy, but a strong candidate names the data structures that make it correct and the abstractions each component is really an instance of.

workers, no double-send Lets N relays drain the table concurrently without contention The deepest insight to state out loud: the outbox turns a distributed-transaction problem into a single-node log-ordering problem. Ordering and durability come "for free" from the database's own transaction log — the same mechanism that already guarantees ACID — rather than from an expensive cross-system coordinator like two-phase commit. ☁️ AWS implementation Mapping the design to AWS On AWS the pattern maps cleanly, and the relay choice mirrors the polling-vs-CDC decision above. The managed sweet spot is Aurora/RDS → DynamoDB isn't needed → DMS or Lambda relay → SNS/SQS/Kinesis/MSK .

For SQL shops, Aurora + DMS (or Debezium on MSK Connect) → MSK/Kinesis is the direct analog of the classic Postgres-WAL-to-Kafka design.

💻 C# implementation The heart of the pattern is one method: save the entity and the outbox record in a single EF Core SaveChanges (one transaction). Then a separate polling relay drains the outbox. This is the correct, idiomatic .NET version. // ---------- 1. The outbox row ---------- public class OutboxMessage { public Guid Id { get ; set ; } = Guid .NewGuid(); // dedup key public string AggregateId { get ; set ; } = "" ; // partition key → ordering public string EventType { get ; set ; } = "" ; public string Payload { get ; set ; } = "" ; // serialized JSON public DateTime CreatedAt { get ; set ; } = DateTime .UtcNow; public DateTime ? PublishedAt { get ; set ; } // null = pending } // -

--------- 2. Write path: business row + event in ONE transaction ---------- public async Task PlaceOrderAsync( Order order) { _db.Orders.Add(order); // Same DbContext → same SaveChanges → same transaction. Atomic! _db.Outbox.Add( new OutboxMessage { AggregateId = order.Id.ToString(), EventType = "OrderPlaced" , Payload = JsonSerializer .Serialize( new { order.Id, order.Total }) }); await _db.SaveChangesAsync(); // commit both, or neither — no dual write } // ---------- 3.

Polling relay: drain the outbox, publish, mark done ---------- public async Task RelayLoopAsync( CancellationToken ct) { while (!ct.IsCancellationRequested) { // FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED lets many relay workers run safely in parallel. var batch = await _db.Outbox .FromSqlRaw( @"SELECT * FROM outbox WHERE published_at IS NULL ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 100 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED" ) .ToListAsync(ct); foreach ( var msg in batch) { // Event Id is the idempotency key — consumers dedup on it.

await _broker.PublishAsync(msg.EventType, msg.AggregateId, msg.Payload, msg.Id, ct); msg.PublishedAt = DateTime .UtcNow; // crash before this ⇒ republish (at-least-once) } await _db.SaveChangesAsync(ct); if (batch.Count == 0) await Task .Delay(200, ct); // backoff when idle } } // ---------- 4. Idempotent consumer: watermark / dedup on event Id ---------- public async Task HandleAsync( Guid eventId, string payload) { if ( await _seen.ExistsAsync(eventId)) return ; // already processed → drop duplicate // ... apply side effect ...

await _seen.RecordAsync(eventId); // mark processed (same TX as side effect) } The one bug interviewers look for: publishing inside a different transaction, or publishing before SaveChanges . The whole pattern collapses unless the business write and the outbox write share one commit. In .NET that means: same DbContext , one SaveChangesAsync . Alternatives worth a sentence: instead of hand-rolling the relay, production teams use Debezium (log-based CDC) or a library like MassTransit , whose built-in Transactional Outbox does exactly this within its message-consumer pipeline.

⚖️ Trade-offs, bottlenecks & likely follow-ups Why not just use two-phase commit (2PC)? Because the broker often can't participate in an XA transaction (Kafka, SQS don't), 2PC couples the service to the availability of both systems, blocks on the coordinator, and scales poorly. The outbox deliberately trades strong cross-system atomicity for local atomicity plus eventual consistency — the right trade for microservices. Why accept at-least-once instead of exactly-once? True exactly-once across a DB and a broker requires distributed coordination that's expensive and fragile.

At-least-once + idempotent consumers gets you effectively-once results at a fraction of the cost, and brokers already force you to handle duplicates. Bottlenecks & failure modes Outbox table bloat — the #1 operational issue. Solve with purge-on-publish, partition-drop, or a log-only outbox. Polling load & latency — polling adds DB load and floor latency; CDC removes both but adds infra. Ordering under concurrency — commit order ≠ insert/sequence order; rely on the log (LSN) or a per-aggregate partition key, not created_at . Relay is a moving part — it must be HA; use leader election or SKIP LOCKED so multiple relays don't double-publish or stall.

Developer discipline — someone can forget to write the outbox row. Enforce via a repository/UoW abstraction or domain-event dispatch so it's automatic. Q: How do you guarantee ordering of events? A: Use the transaction log (WAL/binlog) which is in commit order, and key the broker partition by aggregate_id so all events for one entity stay on one ordered partition. Don't trust a DB sequence or timestamp — they aren't monotonic across concurrent commits. Q: What if the relay publishes but crashes before marking the row published? A: On restart it republishes — that's the at-least-once guarantee. Consumers dedup on the event id / offset watermark, so the duplicate is harmless.

Q: Polling vs CDC — which and why? A: Polling for simplicity and any-DB portability; CDC (Debezium/DynamoDB Streams) for correct ordering from the log, no polling load, and ~10–99 ms latency. I default to CDC at scale. Q: How is this different from event sourcing? A: Event sourcing makes the event log the source of truth and rebuilds state from it. The outbox keeps current-state tables as truth and merely uses a table/log to reliably publish events. The outbox is a smaller, additive change; event sourcing is a whole storage philosophy. Q: How does this relate to the Saga pattern? A: Sagas coordinate a multi-service business transaction through a chain of local transactions + events.

The outbox is how each saga step reliably emits its event/command — sagas are a primary reason the outbox exists. 🗣️ Interview cheat sheet 30-second pitch: "To update my database and publish an event atomically without 2PC, I use the transactional outbox. In the same local transaction that writes the business row, I insert a row into an outbox table. A separate relay — polling, or better, log-based CDC like Debezium — reads the outbox and publishes to the broker with at-least-once delivery, and consumers dedup on the event id.

This solves the dual-write problem: the event is published if and only if the transaction commits." Name the enemy: "dual-write problem" — two systems, no shared transaction. One transaction: business row + outbox row commit together or not at all. Relay = polling vs CDC: CDC (WAL/binlog, Debezium, DynamoDB Streams) wins at scale — correct ordering, ~ms latency, no polling load. Delivery = at-least-once + idempotent consumers: dedup by UUID journal or monotonic offset/LSN watermark. Ordering: from the commit log + partition-by-aggregate-id — not from timestamps or DB sequences. Don't forget housekeeping: purge/partition the outbox, or go log-only ( pg_logical_emit_message ).

Numbers to quote: one small INSERT per txn (negligible), CDC latency two-digit ms, table grows ~430M rows/day at 5k writes/s if unpruned. ❓ FAQ — your follow-up questions Questions asked about this topic No follow-up questions yet — ask one about this topic and it'll be logged here with a compact answer. 📚 Sources Chris Richardson — Pattern: Transactional Outbox (microservices.io) Gunnar Morling — Revisiting the Outbox Pattern (Decodable) microservices.io — Polling Publisher & Transaction Log Tailing Debezium — Outbox Event Router documentation AWS Prescriptive Guidance — Transactional outbox pattern Generated by the design-research skill · researched via web search · open via localhost

System Design · Interview Prep Database Sharding & Partitioning How one big database becomes many — the classic scaling move that every large system eventually makes, and every interviewer eventually asks about. 🎯 Scenario 🧑‍🎓 Laymen 📋 Requirements 🏗️ Architecture 🎬 Animation 🔍 Deep-dive 🧮 DSA ☁️ AWS 💻 C# code ⚖️ Trade-offs 🗣️ Cheat sheet ❓ FAQ 📚 Sources 🎯 Real-world scenario What we're solving & where it's used You started with a single PostgreSQL or MySQL box and it served you beautifully — until traffic climbed, tables grew to hundreds of millions of rows, indexes stopped fitting in RAM, backups started taking hours, and a single hot query could freeze the whole application.

The classic answer is partitioning (split the data into smaller pieces) and eventually sharding (put those pieces on different physical machines ). This is how every large system — Instagram, Discord, Slack, Shopify, Notion, Uber, Pinterest, Figma, YouTube — keeps its database responsive as it grows past what any single server can hold. The video this page is based on — Database Sharding and Partitioning by Arpit Bhayani — frames it exactly this way: partitioning is logically splitting a big table into smaller pieces (still on one machine), and sharding is physically distributing those pieces across independent database servers so read and write throughput scale horizontally.

The distinction is small in wording but massive in operational impact: partitioning is a query-planner optimization; sharding is a distributed-systems commitment. Interviewers love this topic because a good answer proves you understand the whole ladder — vertical scaling → read replicas → caching → partitioning → sharding — and can articulate when to pull each lever, not just how . The wrong answer is "just shard everything"; the right answer names the shard key, the strategy, the resharding pain, and the cross-shard query trap before the interviewer has to ask.

🧑‍🎓 In laymen terms Explaining it to someone who's never touched a database Imagine you run a giant library that started with a single, beautiful room full of books. At first, one librarian at the front desk could handle everyone — someone walks in, asks for "Harry Potter," she walks to the shelf, finds it, hands it over. Simple. Now imagine your library becomes wildly popular. Fifty people show up every second asking for books. Your one librarian is running around, sweating, dropping things. The room itself is packed floor to ceiling — you literally can't fit more shelves in it. What do you do? You open more rooms.

But now you have a problem: if the books are randomly scattered across ten rooms, every request means checking every room. So instead, you agree on a rule for where each book lives. Maybe: "books whose title starts with A–E go in Room 1, F–J in Room 2, K–O in Room 3…" Now a visitor asking for "Harry Potter" is sent straight to Room 2, and the other nine rooms don't even know the request happened. Each room has its own librarian. Everyone's fast again. That's sharding . Each "room" is a separate database server, each "rule for where things live" is called a shard key , and the person at the front door who sends you to the right room is a router .

Instagram does this with your photos, WhatsApp does this with your chats, Uber does this with rides — the trick is exactly the library trick, just with computers. The hard parts, in plain English: (1) picking a bad rule means one room gets slammed while the others sit empty (imagine everyone asks for "Harry Potter" — poor Room 2). (2) Some questions can't be answered from one room — "how many books do we have in total?" — so you have to walk to every room and add up. And (3) once you've split things up, merging them back or changing the rule is a nightmare , because you have to physically move millions of books between rooms without closing the library.

Think of it as: one giant filing cabinet → many smaller filing cabinets, each in a different room, with a receptionist who knows exactly which cabinet holds your file. That's the whole idea. Everything else is engineers arguing about the receptionist's algorithm. 📋 Requirements & scale When sharding is (and isn't) the right answer Sharding is not a first move — it's the last big lever you pull before you're in true "large-system" territory. Interviewers expect you to name the ladder of cheaper alternatives you'd try first, then justify why sharding is unavoidable. The scaling ladder (try these before sharding) Rung What it does Ceiling 1.

Vertical scale Bigger box: more RAM, faster NVMe, more cores. ~1–2 TB working set; expensive at the top end. 2. Read replicas Async replicas serve reads; primary takes writes. Read-heavy only; writes still bottlenecked on primary. 3. Caching Redis / Memcached in front of the DB. Great for hot keys, useless for uncached queries. 4. Partitioning Split one table into many smaller tables inside one DB. Same machine limits — CPU, RAM, disk I/O. 5. Sharding Split across many DBs on many machines. Near-infinite; complexity explodes. Signals it's time to shard Data doesn't fit on one box. Working set exceeds ~1 TB and the index no longer fits in RAM. Writes overwhelm the primary.

Read replicas don't help — you need write parallelism. Backups & DDL become impossible. A single table migration takes 12 hours and locks the app. Blast radius is unacceptable. One noisy tenant can freeze all tenants; you need physical isolation. ne migration incident scar 🏗️ High-level architecture How the pieces fit together The core architecture has four moving parts: the application (which knows nothing about physical shards), a shard router / proxy (which knows exactly which shard holds which key), a set of shards (independent DB clusters, each often replicated for HA), and a metadata / config store (which holds the shard map — key ranges or hash-bucket-to-shard assignments). A write for user u42 flows: app → router → hash( u42 ) → shard 3 → primary → replicas. A cross-user query (e.g. "top posts across the platform") requires scatter-gather : the router fans the query out to every shard, waits for all responses, merges them.

The two axes of splitting to keep separate in your head: Vertical partitioning Split a wide table by columns — put hot columns ( user_id, name, email ) on one server and cold ones ( bio, avatar_blob, prefs_json ) on another. Reduces row width and I/O per read. Common inside a single DB. Horizontal partitioning (a.k.a. sharding) Split a table by rows — users 1–10M on shard 1, users 10M–20M on shard 2, etc. Each shard has the same schema , different subsets.

This is what people usually mean by "sharding." 🎬 Animation Watch a shard route resolve, step by step This animation shows the single most important flow: a request for user u42 enters the router, the router hashes the key, consults the shard map, and forwards the request to exactly one shard. Then we show the hot-shard failure mode and a resharding split — the two things every interviewer probes. ▶ Play Step → ← Back ↺ Reset Ready Press ▶ Play to start 🔍 Component deep-dive Partitioning vs sharding — the strict definition Arpit's key clarification (and the one interviewers reward): partitioning is a logical split; sharding is a physical distribution .

Partitioning a table into monthly chunks inside one PostgreSQL keeps everything on one machine — the query planner just prunes irrelevant partitions. Sharding takes those partitions and puts them on different boxes with independent CPU, RAM, storage, and network. Sharding is horizontal partitioning, but not all horizontal partitioning is sharding. The four sharding strategies 1) Range-based sharding Assign contiguous key ranges to shards: user_id 0–10M → S1 , 10M–20M → S2 . Perfect for range queries (give me all orders from Jan–Mar) because they hit one or two shards. The killer downside: skew .

If new users are always assigned the highest ID, the last shard becomes a hot write shard while shard 1 sees nothing. Time-series data is famously bad at this — the "current day" partition takes every write. 2) Hash-based sharding shard = hash(shard_key) mod N . This spreads writes evenly and needs no lookup table — the router computes the shard from the key. The trade-off: range queries are broadcast (every shard has some of the requested rows), and changing N is catastrophic because almost every key moves. The fix is consistent hashing , which limits the moved fraction to roughly 1/N . 3) Directory-based sharding A lookup table maps shard_key → shard_id .

Maximum flexibility — you can move any key anywhere, add shards dynamically, target hot users. The cost: the lookup service becomes a hot path on every request and a potential single point of failure. In practice the map is cached aggressively on the router (a "shard cache" in Instagram parlance). 4) Geo-based sharding Shard key encodes region: EU users on EU shards, US users on US shards. Great for latency (users hit the nearest data center) and compliance (GDPR data residency). It's really just range-based sharding with a geographic dimension. The classic pain is the traveling user — someone flies from Berlin to New York and their data is still on eu-central-1.

Shard key selection — the highest-leverage decision Nothing you do later can save a bad shard key. Two properties matter: High cardinality. The key must have far more distinct values than the shard count. Sharding by country_code caps you at ~200 shards forever. Even frequency. If 30% of your traffic is one tenant, that tenant creates a permanent hot shard no matter which strategy you use. The best keys are also request-correlated — the key naturally appears in every query. Instagram shards by user_id because virtually every request is "show me user X's stuff." A payment system might shard by merchant_id . Never shard by an auto-increment ID and never by a low-cardinality enum.

The hot-shard problem A hot shard is when one shard receives disproportionate traffic — a celebrity user, a viral product, a Black-Friday tenant. Sharding alone doesn't fix it because the hot key by definition maps to one shard. Real defenses: replicate hot keys (fan reads across replicas of that shard), split further (subdivide the hot user's data by another dimension — e.g. per-post shards for a celebrity), or write-buffer and coalesce (batch writes to that key). This is the follow-up interviewers always ask, and "consistent hashing" alone is not a full answer. Resharding without downtime The most feared operation.

The typical pattern (used by Instagram, Discord, Slack) is double-writes : (1) launch new shards, (2) dual-write every mutation to old and new, (3) backfill historical data online, (4) shadow-read the new shards and compare, (5) cut reads over, (6) stop writing to old. This takes weeks and requires idempotent writes and a killswitch. Consistent hashing dramatically reduces the size of the move but does not eliminate the ceremony. Cross-shard queries Any query without the shard key becomes a scatter-gather : fan out to all shards, wait for all responses, merge. Latency = slowest shard , not average.

Two mitigations: (a) denormalize / duplicate — maintain a global secondary index in a separate store (Elasticsearch, DynamoDB GSI) so "search all users by email" doesn't need to hit every shard; (b) embrace approximate answers — pre-aggregated counters, sketch data structures (HyperLogLog). Cross-shard transactions Multi-key ACID transactions across shards are essentially impossible cheaply. Real systems fall back to Saga pattern (compensating actions), 2PC (slow, blocking, availability-hostile), or outbox + event sourcing (asynchronous eventual consistency). This is one of the biggest costs of sharding, and interviewers ask about it.

🧮 The DSA behind it Data structures & algorithms that make sharding work 1) Modulo hashing The naive baseline: shard = hash(key) % N . Beautiful simplicity — O(1) lookup, no memory. But when N changes from 4 to 5, virtually every key remaps: ~80% of your data moves. That's the primary reason large systems don't use plain modulo. 2) Consistent hashing Place shards on a ring of hash values 0..2³²−1. A key hashes to a point on the ring; it belongs to the next shard clockwise. Adding a shard only takes over the arc between it and the next-clockwise shard — only K/N keys move, not K . Use virtual nodes (each physical shard owns 100–200 points on the ring) to smooth out uneven arcs.

Used by DynamoDB, Cassandra, Riak, ElastiCache Redis. Ring (simplified, 3 shards, hashes 0..99) 0 ─── 33 ─── 66 ─── 99 \ | | [S1] [S2] [S3] keys 34..66 → S2 add S4 at 50 → only keys 34..50 move from S2 to S4 3) Rendezvous (HRW) hashing For each key, compute hash(key, shard_i) for every shard i and pick the shard with the highest hash. Adds only 1/N movement on shard changes, no ring, no virtual nodes. Simpler correctness proof; used in load balancers and CDN routing. 4) B-Tree indexes (per shard) Each shard is still a normal database — B-Trees on the primary key, secondary indexes, WAL. Sharding doesn't replace them, it multiplies them.

Total index memory across shards grows sub-linearly with data because each shard's index fits in that shard's RAM. 5) Bloom filters for existence checks Before scattering "does user@example.com exist?" to N shards, ask a Bloom filter maintained per shard (or globally). A Bloom filter says "definitely not on this shard" with zero false negatives, saving expensive fan-out. Complexity table Operation Sharded lookup Notes Point read by shard key O(1) route + O(log N) index probe The happy path — this is what you optimize for. Point read without shard key O(N) fan-out Every shard queried; latency = slowest reply. Range query on shard key (range sharding) O(few shards) Cheap when ranges align.

Range query (hash sharding) O(N) fan-out Hash destroys locality. Add one shard (modulo hash) O(all data moved) Nearly full reshuffle. Add one shard (consistent hash) O(K/N) keys moved The whole reason consistent hashing exists. Cross-shard join O(N × M) or forbidden Usually done in app layer or denormalized upstream. ☁️ AWS implementation Mapping the design to AWS AWS gives you two paths: use a managed sharded database (DynamoDB, Aurora Limitless, Redshift, Keyspaces) where AWS hides sharding from you, or build sharding at the application layer on top of RDS/Aurora clusters. Both are valid interview answers — you should be able to defend either.

Component AWS service Why Managed sharded key-value DynamoDB Partition-key sharding is baked in. Auto-splits hot partitions, adaptive capacity redistributes throughput. You never see the shards. Managed sharded SQL Aurora + app-layer sharding or Aurora Limitless Aurora Limitless does automatic sharding for PostgreSQL-compatible clusters. Otherwise, run N Aurora clusters and shard in your app. Managed columnar analytics Redshift Distribution keys and sort keys are shard-and-partition primitives for OLAP. Wide-column at scale Keyspaces (Cassandra) Partition-key sharding across regions; global tables for geo.

Shard router / proxy RDS Proxy + app-layer routing, or ProxySQL on EC2 Connection pooling and failover; actual shard resolution is done in app code. Shard map / config store DynamoDB or Parameter Store , cached in ElastiCache Small, read-heavy, needs strong consistency on updates. Hot-key defense DAX (DynamoDB) or ElastiCache Redis in front of RDS Cache absorbs read spikes on celebrity keys. Backups & PITR per shard RDS Automated Backups , DynamoDB PITR Sharded backups scale linearly — no more 12-hour monolithic snapshots. Change data capture (for resharding) DMS + Kinesis or DynamoDB Streams Enables online migration and dual-write validation.

A canonical AWS deployment for a self-sharded relational stack: an ECS/EKS fleet running your API with a shard-routing library, an ElastiCache Redis that holds the shard map plus hot-key cache, N × Aurora clusters (each with a writer + 2 read replicas), a small DynamoDB table as the authoritative shard-map source, and DMS ready to spin up whenever a reshard is planned. All traffic enters through ALB → API Gateway . Observability (per-shard QPS, p99, storage) lives in CloudWatch + Managed Grafana . If you can defend this diagram in five sentences, you've passed the AWS half of the interview.

💻 C# implementation — a minimal shard router Below is a self-contained C# reference: a consistent-hash ring, a shard resolver that supports both modulo-hash and consistent-hash strategies, and a routing entry-point. It's intentionally small — a real one adds virtual nodes (already included), weight, replica awareness, health checks, and a shard-map store — but this is the code you should be able to sketch on a whiteboard in an interview. using System; using System.Collections.Generic; using System.Linq; using System.Security.Cryptography; using System.Text; // 1) A shard descriptor — in real life this holds a connection string, replica list, region, etc.

public sealed record Shard ( string Id, string ConnectionString); // 2) The abstraction — every strategy answers "which shard owns this key?" public interface IShardRouter { Shard Resolve ( string shardKey); } // 3) Naive modulo hashing — great for interviews to explain the "why not this?" case. public sealed class ModuloRouter : IShardRouter { private readonly List < Shard > _shards; public ModuloRouter ( IEnumerable < Shard > shards) => _shards = shards.ToList(); public Shard Resolve ( string shardKey) { var h = Stable64(shardKey); var idx = ( int )((h & long .MaxValue) % _shards.Count); return _shards[idx]; } // SHA-1 → first 8 bytes → long.

Deterministic across processes (Object.GetHashCode is NOT). internal static long Stable64 ( string s) { using var sha = SHA1.Create(); var b = sha.ComputeHash(Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(s)); return BitConverter.ToInt64(b, 0); } } // 4) Consistent-hash ring with virtual nodes. Adding/removing a shard moves only ~K/N keys. public sealed class ConsistentHashRouter : IShardRouter { private readonly SortedDictionary < long , Shard > _ring = new (); private readonly int _vnodes; public ConsistentHashRouter ( IEnumerable < Shard > shards, int vnodes = 150 ) { _vnodes = vnodes; foreach ( var s in shards) AddShard(s); } public void AddShard ( Shard s) { for ( int i = 0 ; i < _vnodes; i++) { var point =

ModuloRouter.Stable64($ "{s.Id}#{i}" ); _ring[point] = s; } } public void RemoveShard ( string shardId) { var victims = _ring.Where(kv => kv.Value.Id == shardId).Select(kv => kv.Key).ToList(); foreach ( var k in victims) _ring.Remove(k); } public Shard Resolve ( string shardKey) { if (_ring.Count == 0 ) throw new InvalidOperationException ( "No shards registered" ); var h = ModuloRouter.Stable64(shardKey); // Walk clockwise: first ring key >= h; wrap around if past the end. foreach ( var kv in _ring) if (kv.Key >= h) return kv.Value; return _ring.First().Value; } } // 5) Usage.

In production, wrap this in a decorator that reads shard-map version from // ElastiCache/DynamoDB so that a live reshard can update the ring without redeploying. public static class Demo { public static void Main () { var shards = new [] { new Shard ( "s0" , "..." ), new Shard ( "s1" , "..." ), new Shard ( "s2" , "..." ), new Shard ( "s3" , "..." ), }; IShardRouter router = new ConsistentHashRouter (shards); var shard = router.Resolve( "user:u42" ); Console.WriteLine($ "u42 → {shard.Id}" ); // consistent across processes } } Language alternatives.

Discord published its version of this in Elixir (Cassandra-backed sharding); Instagram's original was Python calling PostgreSQL with a hand-rolled Python shard_id % N . In Go, look at Vitess (YouTube's MySQL sharding layer). In Java, look at Apache ShardingSphere. All of them have the exact same shape as the code above — a hash function, a shard map, and a router. ⚖️ Trade-offs, bottlenecks & likely follow-ups The costs you pay the moment you shard You lose cheap joins — anything crossing shards has to be done in the app layer or via a denormalized secondary index.

You lose global unique constraints — no single database can enforce "email must be unique across all users"; you need a separate uniqueness service or a dedicated shard for unique-index tables. You lose auto-increment IDs — you need a distributed ID generator (Snowflake, UUIDv7, KSUID). You lose easy transactions — anything spanning shards is Saga or 2PC. You lose operational simplicity — N times the pagers, N times the disk-full alerts, N times the version-upgrade coordination.

The bottlenecks that persist Sharding does not fix these on its own: (1) the router or proxy tier can become the new bottleneck if it's synchronous and single-threaded; (2) the shard-map store is read on every request — cache it and expect thundering herds when it invalidates; (3) cross-region latency if shards live in different regions; (4) tail latency — with N shards and slow-tail request rate p , the probability at least one shard is slow is roughly 1 − (1−p)ᴺ , which is why scatter-gather queries have exponentially worse p99 as N grows.

Common interviewer follow-ups (and crisp answers) "What's the difference between partitioning and sharding?" Partitioning is a logical split of a table into pieces (usually inside one database, exploited by the query planner). Sharding is a physical split of those pieces across multiple independent database servers. Sharding is horizontal partitioning + operational separation. "How do you pick a shard key?" Two properties: high cardinality (so it can support many shards) and even distribution (so no shard gets disproportionate traffic). Ideally the key is also present in nearly every query, so most reads/writes are single-shard.

Instagram picks user_id ; a marketplace might pick merchant_id . "Why not just modulo hash?" Because changing shard count remaps almost every key. Consistent hashing or rendezvous hashing move only ~K/N keys when N changes, which is critical for online resharding. "What if one shard becomes hot?" Split it (subdivide by a secondary dimension), replicate hot keys behind a cache like DAX/Redis, and add write coalescing. Sometimes the correct answer is to give the hot tenant a dedicated shard. "How do you reshard without downtime?" Dual-write to old and new shards, backfill history in the background, shadow-read to verify, then cut reads over and stop writing to old.

Requires idempotent writes and CDC (DMS or DynamoDB Streams). "How do you handle queries that don't include the shard key?" Either denormalize into a secondary index (Elasticsearch or a DynamoDB GSI keyed by the alternate field), or scatter-gather across all shards. Fan-out is O(N), latency is set by the slowest shard. "Cross-shard transactions — how?" Sagas with compensating actions are the pragmatic answer. 2PC is technically possible but slow and hurts availability. Outbox pattern + event sourcing is common for eventual consistency.

"When would you NOT shard?" When vertical scaling still has headroom, when the workload is read-heavy (replicas are cheaper), when the data fits in ~1 TB, when the join graph is dense, or when the cost of losing ACID and easy operations outweighs the throughput win. 🗣️ Interview cheat sheet 30-second pitch: "Partitioning is splitting a table logically; sharding is putting those partitions on physically separate databases. Pick a shard key with high cardinality and even distribution — often user_id or tenant_id . Use consistent hashing so adding a shard only moves 1/N keys.

Design around single-shard queries: cross-shard fan-out kills p99, cross-shard transactions require sagas, and hot shards need targeted mitigation like key-splitting or caching. Reshard online with dual-writes, CDC, and shadow-reads." Numbers to quote: one Postgres box handles ~10k–50k QPS and ~1 TB; keep each shard's index in RAM; typical fleets are 16/64/256/1024 shards. The four strategies: range, hash (with consistent variant), directory, geo — each with its own hot-shard failure mode. Shard key rules: high cardinality, even frequency, request-correlated. Bad keys are permanent. The three losses on day one: joins, global unique constraints, easy transactions. Plan replacements upfront.

The three hardest ops: resharding, hot shards, cross-shard queries.
