System Design · Interview Prep Rate Limiter Protecting a service from abuse, runaway scripts & traffic spikes — the algorithms (token bucket, sliding window), the distributed Redis design, and how Stripe does it in production. 🎯 Scenario 🧑‍🎓 Laymen 📋 Requirements 🏗️ Architecture 🎬 Animation 🔍 Deep-dive 🧮 DSA ☁️ AWS 💻 C# code ⚖️ Trade-offs 🗣️ Cheat sheet ❓ FAQ 📚 Sources 🎯 Real-world scenario What we're building & where it's used A rate limiter controls how many requests a client may make to a service in a given window of time, rejecting or delaying the excess.

It's the bouncer at the door of an API: it protects the service from being overwhelmed — whether by a malicious flood (DoS/brute-force), a buggy client stuck in a retry loop, a scraper, or just an unexpected traffic spike — and it enforces fair usage so one noisy tenant can't starve everyone else. It's one of the most common system-design interview questions precisely because it's everywhere and it forces you to reason about algorithms, state, concurrency, and distributed coordination in a small space. Real examples: Stripe rate-limits its payments API and says its request limiter alone "has rejected millions of requests this month" — largely runaway test-mode scripts.

Twitter/X caps tweets (e.g. 300 per 3 hours); the Google Docs API allows ~300 read requests per user per 60 seconds; GitHub , Cloudflare , and every major cloud API do the same. The universal signal for "you've been limited" is HTTP 429 Too Many Requests (and 503 when the server itself is shedding load). Why companies invest in it: without a limiter, a single client can degrade or take down a shared service, drive up infrastructure cost, and ruin the experience for everyone. A good limiter is also a graceful-degradation tool — under overload you shed the least-important traffic first and keep the critical paths (like "create a charge") alive.

🧑‍🎓 In laymen terms The bouncer with a bucket of tokens Imagine a very popular club with a strict bouncer. The rule of the night is simple: "You get 100 free drink tokens. Come back when you run out." Every time you order a drink, the bouncer takes one token out of your hand. When your fist is empty, he smiles politely and says "come back in 30 seconds." Slowly — say, one token per second — the bouncer quietly slips new tokens back into your hand, so you're never permanently cut off. That's it. That's a rate limiter . Now, why does every big website need this bouncer? Picture what happens on IRCTC at 10 AM when Tatkal train tickets open.

Twenty million people mash the "Book Now" button at the same instant. If the website tried to serve everyone at once, it would keel over and nobody gets a ticket. Worse: one person could write a small robot to click the button a thousand times a second and hog every seat. The bouncer's job is to say, "Sorry — you personally get 5 clicks per second, no matter how fancy your script is." The bucket analogy also handles bursts nicely. Say you're a well-behaved app and you haven't made any requests for 30 seconds. Your bucket has quietly filled back up to 100 tokens. Now you suddenly need to send 20 requests at once — maybe a page just loaded. No problem! You have plenty of tokens saved up.

This is why real websites use the "bucket of tokens" idea instead of a rigid "no more than 5 per second, ever" rule — it lets honest users burst when they need to, but stops abusers cold. There's a tricky part though. A website like Stripe or GitHub doesn't run on one computer — it runs on thousands . If each computer keeps its own bucket, a clever attacker could hit computer A with 100 requests, then computer B with 100 more, then C, and effectively cheat. So all the bouncers have to share one central scoreboard (usually a super-fast in-memory store called Redis ) so everyone agrees on how many tokens you have left.

That shared scoreboard has to answer in less than a millisecond or the bouncer becomes the bottleneck. That's the whole engineering challenge in one sentence: a bouncer fast enough to never slow down the party. 📋 Requirements & scale Requirements and back-of-the-envelope math Functional requirements Limit requests per client identity (API key, user id, or IP) to N per time window . Return HTTP 429 when the limit is exceeded, ideally with a Retry-After and rate-limit headers ( X-RateLimit-Remaining , -Reset ). Support different rules per endpoint / tier (a free user vs. an enterprise user; a cheap GET vs. an expensive POST).

Allow controlled bursts above the steady rate (flash-sale traffic) without permanently raising the limit. Non-functional requirements (the ones that shape the design) Low latency — the check sits in front of every request, so it must add well under ~1 ms. Distributed correctness — the limit must hold across a fleet of servers, not per-instance. High availability & fail-open — if the limiter's datastore is down, legitimate traffic should still flow (Stripe explicitly catches exceptions so a Redis outage doesn't block traffic). Memory efficiency — millions of distinct clients ⇒ per-client state must be tiny.

Accuracy — avoid the boundary-burst problem where 2× the limit slips through at a window edge. Capacity estimation (a mid-size API gateway) Quantity Estimate Reasoning Peak throughput ~100,000 req/s Every request does one limiter check ⇒ 100k limiter ops/s. Distinct clients ~10 million keys API keys + user ids + IPs being tracked. State per client (token bucket) ~20–40 bytes Just {tokens, last_refill_timestamp} — a few numbers. Total limiter memory ~200–400 MB 10M × ~30 B — easily fits one Redis node's RAM. Redis op cost 1 atomic Lua call/req Redis does ~100k+ ops/s per node; shard by key if beyond that. Added latency budget < 1 ms In-region Redis round-trip; co-locate to stay sub-ms.

The number to volunteer: "Token-bucket state is just two numbers per client — tokens left and last refill time — so 10 million clients is only a few hundred MB. That's why the whole limiter fits in one Redis node's RAM and each check is a single atomic operation." 🏗️ High-level architecture How the pieces fit together The rate limiter is a middleware check that runs before your business logic — usually in the API gateway or a thin filter in front of the app servers. The critical design decision is where the counter lives . Per-instance in-memory counters are fast but wrong in a fleet (10 servers × limit N = 10N allowed).

So the counter state moves to a shared, fast datastore — almost always Redis — and the check must be a single atomic operation (a Lua script or INCR + EXPIRE ) so concurrent requests across many servers can't race past the limit. The flow: a request arrives, the gateway extracts the client identity, and asks the limiter "is this client under its limit?" The limiter atomically updates the client's bucket/counter in Redis and returns allow/deny. On allow , the request proceeds; on deny , the gateway short-circuits with 429 and a Retry-After . If Redis is unreachable, the design fails open — allow the request rather than take down the whole API.

Allowed request flow Atomic limiter check Rejected → 429 The request path Request hits the gateway; middleware derives the client key (API key / user id / IP) and the applicable rule. Middleware runs one atomic op in Redis (Lua script): refill the bucket by elapsed time, try to take a token. Token available → decrement, return allow ; request proceeds to app servers. Bucket empty → return deny ; gateway responds 429 with Retry-After and rate-limit headers. If Redis errors/timeouts → fail open (allow) so the limiter never becomes the outage.

🎬 Animation Watch the token bucket work, step by step The token-bucket algorithm is the industry-default rate limiter — Stripe, AWS API Gateway, and countless others use it. This animation shows exactly how it behaves: tokens dripping in at a steady rate up to a capacity, requests consuming a token to be allowed, and requests bouncing off with a 429 when the bucket runs dry. Use Play to watch the sequence, or Step → / ← Back to inspect each frame. ▶ Play Step → ← Back ↺ Reset Ready Press ▶ Play to watch the token bucket in action. 🔍 Component deep-dive: the five algorithms The heart of this interview is knowing the algorithms cold — how each works, its memory cost, and its burst behavior.

Here they are, weakest to strongest. 1. Fixed Window Counter Split time into fixed windows (say, 1-second buckets). Keep one counter per client per window; increment on each request; reject once it exceeds the limit, then reset at the next window. Pros: trivially simple, one integer of memory, easy in Redis ( INCR + EXPIRE ). Con — the boundary burst: a client can send the full limit at the very end of one window and again at the start of the next, pushing 2× the limit through in a fraction of a second. Good enough for coarse quotas, dangerous for tight protection. 2.

Sliding Window Log Store a timestamp for every request in a sorted set; to decide, drop timestamps older than the window and count what remains. Pros: perfectly accurate, no boundary burst. Con: memory grows with request volume — you store every single request timestamp — so it's expensive for high-traffic clients. Great accuracy, poor scalability. 3. Sliding Window Counter (the sweet spot) A hybrid: keep the current and previous fixed-window counts and weight the previous window by how much of it still overlaps the sliding window. Estimated count = curr + prev × (overlap fraction) . Pros: smooths the boundary burst almost as well as the log, but with fixed, tiny memory (two counters).

This is the algorithm most production systems reach for when they want accuracy without the log's cost. 4. Token Bucket (the industry favorite) A bucket holds up to b tokens and refills at rate r (one token every 1/r seconds; overflow is discarded). Each request removes one token; if the bucket is empty, the request is non-conformant (rejected or queued). The genius is controlled bursts : a client that's been quiet accumulates up to b tokens and can spend them in a burst (a flash sale), but the long-run average is still capped at r . Memory is just {tokens, last_refill} .

This is what Stripe uses — they note clients "can always spread out their requests a bit more," and they layer a burst allowance on top for real-time spikes. It's the default answer to "which algorithm?". 5. Leaky Bucket Requests enter a queue and are processed ("leak out") at a constant rate . Overflowing the queue drops requests. Pros: perfectly smooth, jitter-free output — ideal for traffic shaping a downstream that needs steady load. Con: it doesn't allow bursts and adds queueing latency; it's a shaper, not really a burst-friendly limiter. Token bucket is its "mirror image" and is usually preferred for APIs.

Making it distributed & atomic The single hardest part in a fleet is the race condition : two servers read "1 token left" simultaneously and both allow. The fix is to make the read-modify-write atomic . In Redis this means a Lua script (executed atomically on the server) that does refill-and-take in one shot, or INCR + EXPIRE for fixed windows. You also decide between centralized (one Redis, exact but a round-trip per request) and local-token / sticky approaches (each node gets a slice of the budget for lower latency, at the cost of some accuracy).

Stripe runs it on Redis (self-hosted or ElastiCache) and explicitly designs to fail open , ships kill switches , and dark-launches new limiters to see what would be blocked before enforcing. Stripe's four-layer production model (worth quoting) Request rate limiter — caps requests/sec per user; the primary defense. Rejects millions/month, mostly runaway scripts. Concurrent requests limiter — caps in-flight requests (e.g. 20 at once) to protect CPU-heavy endpoints from retry storms. Fleet usage load shedder — reserves a % of the fleet for critical methods; sheds non-critical traffic with 503 when it exceeds its allocation.

Worker utilization load shedder — last line of defense in incidents: sheds by priority tier (test mode → GETs → POSTs → critical). 🧮 The DSA behind it Data structures & algorithms Under the hood these are small, elegant data-structure choices, and the interviewer wants to hear the memory/accuracy trade-off for each. The token bucket is just arithmetic on two numbers; the sliding window log is a sorted set; the sliding window counter is a clever weighted estimate. Algorithm Data structure Memory / client Burst behavior & notes Fixed window 1 integer counter (+TTL) O(1) — tiny Allows 2× at boundary; simplest.

Sliding window log Sorted set of timestamps O(requests in window) Exact, no burst; memory-heavy. Sliding window counter 2 integer counters O(1) — tiny Smooths boundary burst; best accuracy-per-byte. Token bucket {tokens, last_refill_ts} O(1) — ~2 numbers Controlled bursts up to b ; avg capped at r . Industry default. Leaky bucket FIFO queue + drain timer O(queue size) Smooth output, no burst, adds latency; a shaper. The token-bucket math With refill rate r tokens/sec and capacity b : the long-run average request rate is bounded by r , while the maximum burst is governed by bucket depth b .

Formally, if M is the peak arrival rate, the max burst duration is T_max = b / (M − r) (for M > r ) and max burst size B_max = T_max × M . The elegant trick: you don't run a timer to add tokens — you lazily compute refill on each request as tokens = min(b, tokens + (now − last_refill) × r) . That's why the check is O(1) and needs no background job. ☁️ AWS implementation Mapping the design to AWS On AWS you can get a rate limiter three ways: fully managed at the edge, managed at the API layer, or self-built on Redis for full control (the Stripe approach). Pick by how much customization you need.

Component AWS service Why Edge / L7 rate limiting AWS WAF (rate-based rules) + CloudFront Block floods by IP/header before they reach your origin — cheapest DDoS-style protection. Per-API-key throttling API Gateway usage plans + throttling Built-in token-bucket throttling (rate + burst) per API key; zero code for standard quotas. Custom distributed limiter ElastiCache for Redis + Lua The Stripe-style token bucket when you need per-endpoint/per-tier rules and burst logic. Atomic Lua = no races. Limiter logic host Lambda authorizer or ECS/EKS middleware Run the check in a Lambda authorizer on API Gateway, or as filter middleware in your service.

Serverless counter store DynamoDB (atomic counters, TTL) Alternative to Redis when you want no cache cluster to manage; conditional writes give atomicity, TTL auto-expires windows. Overload / load shedding ALB + Auto Scaling + priority queues ( SQS ) Shed low-priority traffic (503) and scale out; mirrors Stripe's fleet/worker shedders. Metrics & tuning CloudWatch Dark-launch: log what would be blocked, tune thresholds before enforcing. Deployment story to tell: "For coarse abuse protection I'd start with AWS WAF rate-based rules at CloudFront and API Gateway usage-plan throttling — no code, token-bucket built in.

When I need per-tier rules and burst allowances like Stripe, I'd build a token bucket in ElastiCache Redis driven by an atomic Lua script, invoked from a Lambda authorizer or service middleware, and I'd fail open if Redis is unreachable. I'd dark-launch via CloudWatch to tune thresholds, and keep the WAF/load-shedder layer as the last line of defense during incidents." 💻 C# implementation Here's a correct, idiomatic token bucket in C# — first the single-node version showing the lazy-refill math, then the crucial note on making it atomic in a distributed fleet with Redis + Lua. // Thread-safe, single-node token bucket. State is just two numbers per client.

public sealed class TokenBucket { private readonly double _capacity; // b: max tokens (burst size) private readonly double _refillPerSec; // r: tokens added per second private double _tokens; // current tokens private long _lastRefillTicks; // last update (Stopwatch ticks) private readonly object _gate = new (); public TokenBucket ( double capacity, double refillPerSec) { _capacity = capacity; _refillPerSec = refillPerSec; _tokens = capacity; // start full ⇒ allow an initial burst _lastRefillTicks = Stopwatch . GetTimestamp (); } // Returns true = allowed (a token was taken); false = rejected (429). public bool TryConsume ( double cost = 1.0) { lock (_gate) { long now = Stopwatch .

GetTimestamp (); double elapsed = (now - _lastRefillTicks) / ( double ) Stopwatch .Frequency; _lastRefillTicks = now; // LAZY refill: add tokens for the elapsed time, capped at capacity. _tokens = Math . Min (_capacity, _tokens + elapsed * _refillPerSec); if (_tokens >= cost) { _tokens -= cost; // conformant: take the token(s) return true ; } return false ; // non-conformant: no tokens left } } } // ---- Distributed: the check MUST be atomic across the fleet. ---- // A per-instance lock is NOT enough — 10 servers would allow 10x. // Run this Lua on Redis; it does refill+take in ONE atomic step, keyed by client.

private const string TokenBucketLua = @" local key = KEYS[1] local rate = tonumber(ARGV[1]) -- tokens per second (r) local capacity = tonumber(ARGV[2]) -- bucket size (b) local now = tonumber(ARGV[3]) -- current time (seconds, from caller) local cost = tonumber(ARGV[4]) local b = redis.call('HMGET', key, 'tokens', 'ts') local tokens = tonumber(b[1]) or capacity local ts = tonumber(b[2]) or now tokens = math.min(capacity, tokens + (now - ts) * rate) -- lazy refill local allowed = tokens >= cost if allowed then tokens = tokens - cost end redis.call('HMSET', key, 'tokens', tokens, 'ts', now) redis.call('EXPIRE', key, math.ceil(capacity / rate) + 1) -- reclaim idle keys return allowed and 1 or

0 " ; public async Task < bool > TryConsumeDistributedAsync ( IDatabase redis, string clientKey) { try { var res = ( long ) await redis. ScriptEvaluateAsync (TokenBucketLua, new RedisKey [] { $ "rl:{clientKey}" }, new RedisValue [] { 50, 100, DateTimeOffset .UtcNow.ToUnixTimeSeconds(), 1 }); return res == 1; } catch ( RedisException ) { return true ; // FAIL OPEN: never let the limiter cause the outage (Stripe's rule) } } The two takeaways an interviewer wants: (1) the lazy refill ( min(capacity, tokens + elapsed × rate) ) means no background timer — the bucket is recomputed on demand in O(1); and (2) in a distributed setting the read-modify-write must be atomic , which the Redis Lua script

guarantees because Redis runs it single-threaded to completion. Note the catch → return true : failing open is a deliberate availability choice. .NET's built-in System.Threading.RateLimiting (with TokenBucketRateLimiter ) is the production library for the single-node case. ⚖️ Trade-offs, bottlenecks & likely follow-ups Accuracy vs. cost. Sliding window log is exact but memory-hungry; fixed window is cheap but allows boundary bursts; sliding window counter and token bucket are the pragmatic middle. State the trade-off explicitly and recommend token bucket (bursts) or sliding window counter (strict smoothing) as your default. Centralized vs. distributed accuracy.

One Redis is exact but adds a network round-trip and is a potential bottleneck/SPOF; per-node local budgets are fast but approximate (each node allows its slice). The usual answer: centralized Redis with atomic Lua, sharded by client key if you outgrow one node, with local caching only if latency demands it. The race condition is the classic follow-up. Two servers checking "1 token left" concurrently must not both succeed — hence atomic Lua / INCR , not read-then-write in app code. Fail-open vs. fail-closed.

If the limiter store dies, do you block everything (safe for the backend, terrible for users) or allow everything (Stripe's choice — the limiter must never be the outage)? For most APIs, fail open. For protecting a fragile downstream, you might fail closed on specific critical paths. Clock skew & what key to limit on. Distributed nodes have skewed clocks — pass a single authoritative time (or use Redis's clock in the script). And choose the identity carefully: IP is easy but punishes users behind NAT/proxies and is spoofable; API key/user id is fairer but requires auth to happen first.

Q: Which algorithm would you choose and why? Token bucket by default — O(1) memory (two numbers), it allows controlled bursts (good for flash sales), and its average is cleanly capped at the refill rate. If I need to strictly smooth traffic with tiny memory and no bursts, sliding window counter. Stripe uses token bucket. Q: How do you enforce one global limit across 50 servers? Move the counter to a shared store (Redis) and make the check a single atomic operation — a Lua script that refills and takes a token in one step, keyed by client. Per-instance counters would multiply the effective limit by the server count.

Q: What happens when Redis goes down? Fail open — catch the error and allow the request, so the limiter never becomes the point of failure (Stripe does exactly this). Optionally degrade to a coarse per-node local limit as a backstop. Q: How do you avoid the fixed-window boundary burst? Use sliding window counter (weight the previous window by its overlap) or token bucket — both spread the limit continuously instead of resetting hard at a window edge, so a client can't push 2× through the boundary. 🗣️ Interview cheat sheet 30-second pitch: "A rate limiter is middleware in the gateway that caps requests per client per window and returns 429 on excess.

The five algorithms are fixed window (cheap, boundary-burst bug), sliding window log (exact, memory-heavy), sliding window counter (cheap + accurate), token bucket (allows controlled bursts — the industry default, what Stripe uses), and leaky bucket (smooth shaper). In a fleet the counter lives in Redis and the check is a single atomic Lua script so concurrent servers can't race past the limit. State is just two numbers per client, so millions of clients fit in one Redis node. And it fails open — the limiter must never be the outage." Numbers to quote Token-bucket state ≈ 2 numbers (~30 B) per client ⇒ 10M clients ≈ few hundred MB.

Reject signal: HTTP 429 (client limited) / 503 (server shedding). Fixed window flaw: up to 2× the limit at the boundary. Stripe: request limiter rejects millions/month ; concurrent limiter set to e.g. 20 in-flight . Real limits: Twitter 300 tweets/3h , Google Docs API ~300 reads/user/60s . 5 talking points that win the round Token bucket — controlled bursts, O(1) state, lazy refill; the default pick. Atomicity — Redis Lua kills the race condition across the fleet. Boundary burst — name it as the fixed-window flaw; fix with sliding window counter. Fail open — availability over strictness; the limiter can't be the SPOF.

System Design · Interview Prep Redis — Architecture & Purpose What Redis is, how it works internally, the deployment topologies, and the real reasons companies reach for it. A one-stop revision page. 🎯 Scenario 🧑‍🎓 Laymen 📋 Requirements 🏗️ Architecture 🎬 Animation 🔍 Deep-dive 🧮 DSA ☁️ AWS 💻 C# code ⚖️ Trade-offs 🗣️ Cheat sheet ❓ FAQ 📚 Sources 🎯 Real-world scenario What Redis is, and where it's used Redis (Remote Dictionary Server) is an open-source, in-memory data-structure store.

It's the Swiss Army knife of the data layer — used as a cache , a session store , a pub/sub bus , a rate-limiter backend , a leaderboard engine , a distributed lock , a message queue , and even a primary datastore for latency-critical workloads. It answers most operations in < 1 ms at 100k+ ops/sec per node , which is why almost every large-scale system has a Redis tier somewhere in the stack.

Real products that rely on it: Twitter caches timelines in Redis, Stack Overflow serves nearly every page from it, GitHub uses it for job queues, Snapchat uses it for real-time messaging, Instagram uses it for feed and counters, Uber uses it for driver-location and geo queries, and Discord uses it for presence. Managed offerings — AWS ElastiCache , Amazon MemoryDB , GCP Memorystore , Azure Cache for Redis , Redis Cloud — are among the largest revenue lines for cloud providers.

In an interview, "add Redis" is the single most defensible way to justify sub-second reads, offload the database, and unlock features (leaderboards, sessions, pub/sub, rate limits) that would take weeks to build on top of a relational DB. 🧑‍🎓 In laymen terms Explain it like I have never coded Imagine a busy coffee shop. Every time someone orders "the usual", the barista could go to the storeroom, unlock it, find the recipe folder, flip to the customer's page, and read it. That would work — but with a queue of 200 people, it's painfully slow. So the barista keeps a whiteboard right beside the counter .

On it are the last 500 customers' usual orders, written in big letters, ready to read at a glance. When Alice walks in, the barista just looks at the board and shouts "cappuccino, oat milk" — no trip to the storeroom, no unlocking, no flipping through folders. Redis is that whiteboard. The storeroom is your database (Postgres, MySQL, DynamoDB), and Redis is the fast-glance surface sitting next to the counter.

Because it's a whiteboard and not a filing cabinet, three things follow: (1) it's much faster — a glance versus a walk; (2) it can lose data if the shop catches fire — a whiteboard isn't fireproof, so most people also keep the folders in the storeroom; and (3) it's small — you can't fit a million customers' orders on it. So Redis is used for the hot data — the stuff you look up again and again in the next few minutes. Redis also does more than just remember answers.

It can count things instantly ("how many people liked this photo?"), keep a ranked scoreboard ("who's #1 on the leaderboard right now?"), broadcast messages to many listeners at once ("new order came in — anyone free?"), and act as a traffic cop that says "sorry, you've asked 100 times this minute, come back later" (rate limiting). Every one of these is a tiny problem a database can technically do, but a whiteboard does it a thousand times faster. Almost every app you use has one of these whiteboards behind the scenes: Instagram remembers your feed there, Uber remembers where the nearby drivers are, Twitter remembers your timeline, WhatsApp remembers who's currently online.

When you tap something and the answer comes back instantly , there's a good chance a Redis whiteboard just answered you. 📋 Requirements & scale What Redis is optimized for (and what it isn't) Redis is not a general-purpose database — it's a data-structure server that keeps everything in RAM and speaks a very simple TCP protocol (RESP). That single decision is where most of its performance comes from, and it also defines the boundaries of what you should ever use it for. Functional Sub-millisecond GET / SET on primitive types and rich data structures (strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, streams, bitmaps, HyperLogLog, geo). Atomic multi-command scripting via Lua or Functions .

Pub/sub messaging and Streams (Kafka-lite). Server-side TTL / expiration on every key. Optional persistence (RDB, AOF, or both) and replication for durability. Non-functional (typical single-node targets) Dimension Typical target Latency (p99) < 1 ms local, < 5 ms same-AZ Throughput 100k – 1M ops/sec per node (pipelined) Memory per node 16 GB – 256 GB (bounded by RAM) Max key/value size 512 MB per value (practical limit ~ MB) Cluster max size 1 000 nodes (recommended); 16 384 hash slots Durability 0 s – 1 s data loss (AOF everysec) up to fully durable (fsync always) Back-of-the-envelope for interview: "a single Redis node comfortably handles 100k ops/sec at < 1 ms p99.

With Redis Cluster (16 384 hash slots) we shard horizontally across N masters — a 6-node cluster gives us ~600k ops/sec and roughly 6× the memory." 🏗️ High-level architecture How Redis is put together Redis is famously simple: one process, one main thread, one event loop . Every command lands on that thread, runs to completion, and the reply is queued back out. There's no lock contention because there are no other threads competing for the data structures. The main thread is helped by a small pool of I/O threads (Redis 6+) that read/write sockets, and by background threads that do fsync, close-on-write, and lazy freeing of large objects — but the command execution itself is single-threaded.

That's why every command in Redis is atomic by construction. request path single-threaded core persistence replication HA / sharding Around the core sit three orthogonal concerns: persistence (should this data survive a restart?), replication (do we need a hot standby?), and topology (single node, Sentinel-managed HA pair, or a sharded Cluster?). You pick each independently based on the workload.

Core data structures — the real reason Redis is different Redis isn't a KV store where the value is opaque bytes. Every key points to a typed data structure whose native operations run server-side.

That single fact removes one round-trip per operation and is why Redis crushes Memcached on non-trivial workloads. Type Backed by Common commands Signature use case String SDS (dynamic byte array) GET / SET / INCR / SETEX cache, counters, bitmaps Hash listpack (small) / hashtable HSET / HGET / HINCRBY object-per-key (user:42 → {name, email, …}) List quicklist (linked list of listpacks) LPUSH / RPOP / BLPOP queues, timelines Set listpack / hashtable SADD / SISMEMBER / SINTER tags, unique visitors, "friends of friends" Sorted Set (ZSet) skip-list + hashtable ZADD / ZRANGEBYSCORE leaderboards, priority queues, time-series Stream radix-tree of entries XADD / XREADGROUP append-only log, consumer

groups (Kafka-lite) Bitmap string as bit array SETBIT / BITCOUNT daily active users, feature flags per user HyperLogLog probabilistic (12 KB) PFADD / PFCOUNT cardinality of billions with 0.81% error Geo ZSet + geohash GEOADD / GEOSEARCH "drivers within 2 km" — Uber-style 2. The single-threaded event loop The main thread runs an epoll -based reactor. Sockets are non-blocking; when one is ready, its command is parsed, executed against the key-space, and the reply is written back. Because everything happens on one thread , transactions ( MULTI/EXEC ) and Lua scripts are trivially atomic — there is no other thread to interleave with.

The tradeoff: a single slow command blocks every other client . KEYS * , giant LRANGE , or DEBUG SLEEP can freeze the entire node. In production you use SCAN instead of KEYS , cap value sizes, and offload lazy-free work to background threads. 3. Persistence — RDB vs AOF RDB (snapshots) Point-in-time binary dump of the whole key-space ( dump.rdb ). Triggered by save 60 1000 -style rules or BGSAVE . Redis fork() s a child; the child writes while the parent keeps serving — uses copy-on-write. Pros: compact, fast restart, great for backups/DR. Cons: can lose the last few minutes of data; fork() can stall multi-GB instances for hundreds of ms.

AOF (append-only file) Every write command appended to a log in RESP format. fsync policies: always (safest, slowest), everysec (default — at most 1 s loss), no (OS decides). Auto-rewrites (multi-part in Redis 7+) compact the log into a fresh base + increments. Pros: up to 1-second durability, replayable, easy to inspect and repair with redis-check-aof . Cons: larger files, slower restarts, extra CPU for rewriting. Best of both: enable both. On restart Redis prefers the AOF (more complete); RDB snapshots go to S3 for disaster recovery. For a pure cache where you don't care about loss, disable both. 4. Replication Redis replication is asynchronous by default .

A replica connects and issues PSYNC with its offset and replication ID; if the master still has the missed bytes in its replication backlog, it streams just those (partial resync). Otherwise it triggers a full sync — RDB snapshot streamed to the replica, followed by the backlog. Replicas can chain (replica-of-a-replica). Because replication is async, the client sees a write ack before the replica has seen it — a master crash can lose the last few ms of writes. WAIT numreplicas timeout exists to make a write wait for replicas, but it's still best-effort, not synchronous consensus. 5.

Topologies — pick one Topology What it gives you What it can't Standalone Simplest — one process, optional replicas No auto-failover, no sharding, RAM-bound Sentinel Auto-failover of a primary/replica pair; clients learn the new primary via Sentinel Not horizontal — one shard's worth of data Cluster Sharding across N masters via 16 384 hash slots; each shard replicated; gossip-based membership; MOVED/ASK client redirects Multi-key ops must share a {hashtag} ; no cross-slot transactions; async replication still means small write loss on failover 6. Memory management & eviction Redis enforces maxmemory .

When it's hit, it applies the maxmemory-policy : noeviction — writes fail; reads still work. Safe for a primary datastore. allkeys-lru / allkeys-lfu — evict the least-recently- or least-frequently-used key across all keys. Standard cache policy. volatile-lru / volatile-lfu / volatile-ttl — same, but only among keys with a TTL. allkeys-random / volatile-random — cheap and dumb. Redis uses an approximated LRU/LFU — it samples a few candidates and evicts the worst — because a strict LRU list would cost too much memory. In production, always set maxmemory + a policy . An unbounded Redis is a Redis that OOM-kills itself. 7.

Redis vs Memcached (the classic interview follow-up) Dimension Redis Memcached Data model Rich types (hash, list, set, zset, stream…) Only opaque strings Threading Single-threaded core + I/O threads Multi-threaded Persistence RDB + AOF None Replication / HA Async replicas, Sentinel, Cluster None built-in (client-side sharding only) Pub/Sub, Streams, Lua, Geo Yes No When to prefer Almost always today Pure LRU cache of small strings at very high throughput 🧮 The DSA behind it Why Redis is fast — the data structures at play The performance and the feature list both come from the fact that Redis picks a textbook data structure for each type and exposes its native operations verbatim.

Redis type Underlying DSA Complexity of hot ops String SDS (Simple Dynamic String) — length-prefixed, binary-safe GET / SET / STRLEN — O(1) Hash Listpack when small, hashtable (chained, incremental rehashing) when large HGET / HSET — O(1) List Quicklist — a linked list of listpacks (compact + cache-friendly) LPUSH / RPOP — O(1); LRANGE — O(N) Set Listpack / hashtable SADD / SISMEMBER — O(1); SINTER — O(N·M) Sorted set Skip list + hashtable side index ZADD / ZRANGE — O(log N); ZSCORE — O(1) Stream Radix tree of macro-nodes of packed entries XADD — O(1) amortized; XREAD — O(log N + M) Bitmap String as bit array SETBIT / GETBIT — O(1); BITCOUNT — O(N) HyperLogLog 12 KB dense/sparse probabilist

ic structure PFADD / PFCOUNT — O(1), 0.81% std. error Geo Sorted set keyed by 52-bit geohash GEOSEARCH — O(N + log M) Key-space Hashtable (2 tables + incremental rehash so no rehash stalls) Key lookup — O(1) Expiry Second hashtable of key→ttl + active-expire cycle sampling Amortized O(1) The clever bits: incremental rehashing (never stall on a resize), listpacks (tightly packed byte blobs for small objects — 30% memory savings), skip lists (simpler than balanced trees, same asymptotics, easier concurrency), and 16 384 hash slots (small enough to bitmap efficiently, big enough to shard fine-grained).

Cheapest managed option. ElastiCache Serverless Auto-scaling Redis with per-GB-hour + per-request pricing; no node sizing Spiky or unpredictable workloads where you don't want to right-size clusters. Front the app with API Gateway → Lambda / ECS Fargate. Cluster-mode ElastiCache Redis with 3 shards × 2 replicas across 3 AZs. Encryption at rest (KMS) and in transit (TLS). Client uses a smart cluster client (StackExchange.Redis with ConnectionMultiplexer , or Lettuce for JVM).

Snapshots exported to S3 daily; CloudWatch alarms on CurrConnections , Evictions , ReplicationLag , DatabaseMemoryUsagePercentage . For write-durability, use MemoryDB instead. 💻 C# implementation The de-facto Redis client in .NET is StackExchange.Redis — it multiplexes many logical operations over a single TCP connection per endpoint, so you keep exactly one ConnectionMultiplexer for the app's lifetime and share it. e notes an interviewer will probe: (a) reuse one ConnectionMultiplexer — creating one per request is the #1 misuse; (b) Lua scripts execute atomically because the event loop is single-threaded — that's the whole point of using EVAL for the rate-limiter; (c) the {userId} hash tag forces all keys sharing that tag onto the same slot so multi-key ops work in Cluster mode. ⚖️ Trade-offs, bottlenecks & likely follow-ups Use Redis when… You need sub-millisecond reads and can afford RAM. You want counters, leaderboards, geo, sets, TTLs — server-side. You need a pub/sub or stream bus without spinning up Kafka. You need a distributed lock or rate limiter that's actually atomic.

Avoid Redis when… Working set doesn't fit in RAM — RAM is 10–100× the cost of disk. You need multi-key transactions across shards — Cluster doesn't support them. You need strong durability + strong consistency — plain Redis loses writes on failover (use MemoryDB if you must keep the API). You need rich queries (joins, aggregations) — use a real DB or a search engine. Common bottlenecks Big keys. A 500 MB hash blocks the event loop when it's touched. Split large objects; use UNLINK instead of DEL . Hot keys. One key (e.g. a global counter) can saturate a single shard. Use per-partition sub-keys and aggregate. Fork stalls.

RDB snapshots and AOF rewrites fork() — on large instances this can stall for hundreds of ms. Use replicas for snapshotting or disable persistence on the primary. Async replication loss. A master crashing after ack loses the un-replicated tail. Use WAIT for critical writes or move to MemoryDB. Eviction storms. Reaching maxmemory without a policy stalls writes. Always set allkeys-lfu for caches. Likely follow-up questions (and short answers) Why is Redis single-threaded, yet fast? In-memory data + non-blocking I/O + no lock overhead makes the CPU the bottleneck, and a single core happily pushes 100k+ ops/sec.

You scale out with sharding (Cluster) or up with more nodes, not more threads on one node. Redis vs Memcached? Memcached is a pure LRU cache of opaque strings, multi-threaded. Redis has rich data types, persistence, replication, pub/sub, streams, Lua, and clustering. Today, prefer Redis unless you have a pure hot-string cache and want the simpler ops. Can Redis be a primary datastore? Yes, but understand the durability model. With AOF everysec you can lose 1 s of writes; on failover, unreplicated writes are gone. If the app can't tolerate that, use Amazon MemoryDB (multi-AZ synchronous journal) or accept Redis is a cache tier only.

How does Redis Cluster shard? Every key is hashed with CRC16 modulo 16 384 — the resulting slot lives on exactly one master. Clients cache the slot→node map; a MOVED reply means "resharded, refresh the map". Multi-key commands need all keys to share a {tag} so they hash to the same slot. How do you build a distributed lock? Simple: SET lock:X uniqueId NX PX 30000 — atomic acquire with TTL. Release with a Lua script that only deletes if the value still matches your uniqueId. For higher safety across nodes, the Redlock algorithm acquires the lock on a majority of independent masters, but its safety is famously debated (Kleppmann vs antirez) — for a single Redis, the simple pattern is enough.

Redis Pub/Sub vs Streams? Pub/Sub is fire-and-forget — subscribers connected at publish time get the message, no history. Streams are an append-only log with consumer groups, offsets, and replay — think Kafka-lite. Use Pub/Sub for notifications; use Streams for anything a subscriber might miss. 🗣️ Interview cheat sheet "Redis is a single-threaded, in-memory data-structure server. One event loop, no locks — that's why every command is atomic and every op is sub-millisecond. It ships strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, streams, bitmaps, HyperLogLog and geo natively, so features like leaderboards, rate limiters, and pub/sub are one command away.

Persistence is optional (RDB snapshots + AOF log), replication is async, and we shard with Redis Cluster's 16 384 hash slots. In production it's the cache tier, the session store, the rate limiter, the distributed lock, and often the pub/sub bus — but never the durable source of truth unless we swap it for MemoryDB." Numbers: 1 ms p99, 100k ops/sec/node, 16 384 slots, 512 MB max value . Persistence: RDB (compact, some loss) + AOF (durable, larger) — enable both. Topologies: Standalone → Sentinel → Cluster — pick by need for HA and sharding. Eviction: always set maxmemory + allkeys-lfu for caches. Cluster ops: multi-key needs {hashtag} ; no cross-slot txns; MOVED/ASK redirects.

And once you scale beyond one node, how do you coordinate across processes when Redis itself has no atomic cross-node primitive? That's what "how Redis handles concurrency" is really asking, and it splits cleanly into two questions. Within a single Redis instance , concurrency is solved by not having any — the event loop processes one command at a time, so every command is inherently atomic.

The event loop uses I/O multiplexing (epoll on Linux, kqueue on macOS): a single thread waits on many client sockets simultaneously and wakes up whenever any of them is readable. It then reads the command, executes it in memory (dictionary lookup, list push, whatever), writes the reply back to the socket, and returns to the wait. Nothing runs in parallel with the command — no other client can observe a partial state, and no lock is needed. This is exactly like Node.js's design, and it's why "single-threaded" is not a scaling weakness for the type of workload Redis targets.

The event loop executes them one at a time in receive order. Each is atomic — no other client sees a partial state.

The elegant consequence: every individual Redis command is atomic by definition, so a single INCR counter under contention from a million clients never loses an increment. Why is it fast, then? Two reasons: (1) data lives in RAM, so each operation is sub-microsecond; and (2) the loop never blocks on I/O — epoll_wait returns readiness events for many sockets, and Redis handles each in turn. MULTI / EXEC / DISCARD — batching commands atomically Redis's version of a transaction is optimistic and simple : MULTI starts a queue, subsequent commands are stashed (not run), and EXEC runs them all as one indivisible unit — no other client can interleave. Isolation is trivial because the event loop runs the whole batch before any other command. There's no partial visibility. Combined with MULTI/EXEC, this is optimistic locking — a check-and-set equivalent that never blocks. The client reads the current value, decides what to write, and executes; if someone else got there first, EXEC returns nil and the client retries. # Classic conditional decrement — subtract 10 if balance ≥ 10, else fail.

x: Redlock — a lock across N independent Redis masters Single-node SET NX PX fails safety under Redis failover : replication is asynchronous, so if the master accepts a lock, then dies before replicating, the replica promoted in its place has no record of the lock — two clients can now hold it. To close that gap, Redlock (proposed by Redis creator Salvatore Sanfilippo) requires the client to acquire the lock on a majority of N independent Redis masters (N is typically 5, so 3 acquisitions needed): Client generates a unique random token. Client records the current time T₀ , then attempts SET NX PX on each of the N Redis instances with a short per-instance timeout.

x: Client computes elapsed time Δ = now − T₀ . Success requires: (a) it got the lock on ≥ ⌊N/2⌋+1 nodes, AND (b) Δ < the TTL. His prescription: use a real consensus system (ZooKeeper, etcd, Chubby) and, most importantly, enforce fencing tokens — the lock service issues a monotonically increasing token on each acquisition, and the protected resource rejects any write with a smaller token. Redlock has no fencing tokens. The practical takeaway: for efficiency locks (avoiding duplicate work, e.g. "only one cron runs the report at a time"), single-node SET NX PX is fine — an occasional double-run is annoying, not catastrophic.

Everyone else who arrives, reads the whiteboard, sees someone else's name is already there, and quietly walks away. Only the twin whose name is on the board actually prints and mails the letter. That whiteboard is Redis — a super fast shared notepad that every server on the internet can look at.

x: The "write your name if the board is empty" trick has an official name in Redis: SET key value NX . NX just means "only if nobody else has written here yet". Two very natural worries come up: 1. What if the twin who wrote their name faints? They will never rub their name off and everyone else is blocked forever. Solution: they don't just write their name, they write " this claim expires in 30 seconds ". If they faint, the note peels itself off the wall. In Redis this is PX 30000 — the note lives 30 seconds and then vanishes on its own. 2.

t: Redis Distributed Lock — Daily Scheduled Job — System Design
x: What if the twin is slow and the note expires while they are still printing? Then another twin might see the empty board, write their name, and start printing too. Now we have two workers again. There are two fixes here that experienced engineers combine: renew the note every 10 seconds while you are still working (the "watchdog"), and also keep a receipt book that says "the letter for Grandma on Tuesday has already been mailed" — so even if a second twin sneaks past the whiteboard, the receipt book stops them from mailing a duplicate. The whiteboard rule is called a distributed lock . The receipt book is called idempotency .

x: Lock acquisition — one atomic command The correct primitive is a single atomic write: # Redis SET daily-report-lock <unique-token> NX PX 30000 Every option matters: daily-report-lock — the resource being protected. One key per (job, scope). For per-tenant isolation the key becomes daily-report-lock:{tenantId}:{yyyy-MM-dd} . <unique-token> — a random 128-bit value (UUID v4, or 16 bytes from a CSPRNG) that identifies this specific execution . Not the hostname — because the same host may retry after a crash and must not match a lease it no longer owns. NX — "only set if the key does not exist". This is the mutual-exclusion primitive.

x: Redis evaluates NX and the write in a single, indivisible operation because the server is single-threaded. PX 30000 — expiration in milliseconds (30 seconds). This is the lease. If the owner crashes or gets network-partitioned, Redis will auto-delete the key and the next scheduler run can proceed. Redis returns OK to exactly one client and nil to everyone else. Losers must not retry immediately — they simply skip the job. 2.

If the crash happens after SET but before EXPIRE , the key exists with no TTL — a permanent lock. The next night, the job is blocked forever until an operator manually runs DEL . This is one of the most common outages in real systems, which is why Redis added the combined SET ... NX PX form back in Redis 2.6.12. 3.

Suppose Server A acquires with token A-uuid , its job runs long, the 30 s TTL elapses, Redis deletes the key, Server B (next scheduler tick or another server) acquires with token B-uuid , and then Server A finishes and calls DEL daily-report-lock . Server A just deleted Server B's lock, and now a third server can grab it. Two concurrent owners for the same resource — precisely what we were trying to prevent. The fix is to release only if the stored value still equals your own token.

x: But even that has to be atomic — a client-side "GET, compare, DEL" is still a TOCTOU race because Server B could acquire the lock between your GET and your DEL. Redis exposes atomic multi-command sequences via Lua: -- Redis EVAL: atomic compare-and-delete if redis.call( "GET" , KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then return redis.call( "DEL" , KEYS[1]) else return 0 end Because the Redis server is single-threaded, this whole script runs without any other command interleaving. The lock is released exactly when the caller still owns it, and no-ops otherwise. This is the "safe release" pattern from the Redis documentation. 4. The classic race — long job vs.

The Lua script is the fence. 5. Long-running jobs — the watchdog / lease-renewal pattern The other half of the fix is never letting the lease expire while you are still working . Set a short TTL for safety in case of a crash, but have a background thread renew it periodically as long as the job is alive.

Server A owns lock (token = A-uuid, ttl = 30s) │ ▼ Every 10 seconds a watchdog thread runs: │ ▼ Lua: if GET key == A-uuid then PEXPIRE key 30000 else 0 │ ┌──┴──┐ │ │ match no match / GONE │ │ ▼ ▼ renew STOP · abort work · alert TTL The renewal cadence is a rule of thumb: renew at 1/3 of the TTL . Fencing tokens — the fix for the fix Layman version. The lock says "you're allowed to work now".

t: Redis Distributed Lock — Daily Scheduled Job — System Design
x: A fencing token says "you're allowed to work now — and here is a number that proves you're the latest allowed worker". Every downstream system checks the number and refuses to accept work from an older number, even if you show up with the right token, because a newer worker has already been through. Technical version. Each successful lock acquisition returns a monotonically increasing integer along with the lock. The lock owner attaches this number to every write it performs (email send, DB update, S3 put). The downstream service — the SMTP relay, the DB, the S3 API — remembers the highest token it has seen for this resource, and rejects any request whose token is smaller.

When your SET NX PX lands on the primary, Redis returns OK before the write has been propagated to replicas.

x: Concurrent primitive — Compare-And-Set (CAS) SET NX PX is a CAS on a single Redis key: "if the current value is nil, set this new value with this TTL, atomically". Redis's single-threaded command loop is what makes it atomic in O(1) time without any explicit locking on the server side. This is the same primitive that underlies lock-free algorithms and DynamoDB conditional writes ( ConditionExpression: attribute_not_exists(pk) ). Lease-based mutual exclusion Rather than the classical "lock until released" primitive from OS textbooks, distributed systems use leases — the lock has a time bound. A lease is a lock with a TTL, plus a renewal protocol.

The interesting property is total order : every acquisition gets a token strictly greater than any previously issued one. x: Redis SET NX PX is arguably the simplest distributed lock money can buy — one line of code, sub-ms latency, works for 99% of "avoid duplicate cron" problems. What you buy for that simplicity is a lock that can silently disappear during a failover, and a lock that gives you no fencing token. For efficiency use cases this is fine; for correctness use cases it is not. TTL length. Short TTL protects against crashed owners (lock recovers fast) but risks premature expiration. Long TTL is safer for long jobs but wedges the system longer after a crash. The compromise is short TTL with watchdog renewal : 30 s TTL, renew at 10 s, tolerate one lost tick.

x: Do we still need idempotency if we have a lock? Yes — always. The lock protects "concurrent execution"; idempotency protects "duplicate business outcome". They cover different failure modes. Combining both is what makes the design actually correct. Lock granularity. One global lock ( daily-report-lock ) is simple but serializes 100 K users into one server per minute — the job cannot be sped up by adding servers. A per-tenant lock ( daily-report-lock:{tenantId}:{date} ) partitions the work naturally and lets many servers work in parallel. Prefer per-tenant unless there's a reason not to. Bottlenecks Redis is a single point. Multi-AZ replication reduces blast radius but doesn't eliminate it.

x: Redlock or ZooKeeper if the SLA requires it. Global lock serializes work. Fix with per-tenant keys. The scheduler racing itself. The interview asks us to keep the scheduler on every server; the "real production" fix is to move to a central EventBridge scheduler + SQS FIFO and stop racing altogether. Downstream throttling. SES has send-rate quotas — even without duplicates, hammering it at midnight from 100 K parallel workers will get you throttled. Rate-limit at the worker side. Interview follow-ups & short answers Why not SETNX + EXPIRE ? Two commands are not atomic together. If the client crashes between them, the key has no TTL and the lock becomes permanent.

x: SET NX PX is one atomic write. Why the Lua release script instead of GET-then-DEL? GET-then-DEL is a TOCTOU race. Between the GET and the DEL another client can acquire the lock and you'll delete their key. Lua runs atomically on Redis's single-threaded loop, so the compare-and-delete is indivisible. What if the job takes longer than TTL? Use a watchdog: renew the TTL every TTL/3 seconds with a Lua "renew only if my token still matches" script. If a renewal fails, the owner treats the lock as lost and aborts. This is exactly what Redisson's watchdog does.

x: Can this send zero emails? Can it send two? It can send zero if the owner crashes after acquiring but before sending — the next scheduler tick retries. It can send two if the owner sends the email, then crashes before marking the ledger, and the lease expires and a new owner runs before the ledger row lands. The idempotency ledger is what makes "at most one" hold in practice. What if Redis fails over? Async replication means a lock written on the old primary may not be on the new one. Two servers could hold the "same" lock briefly. The idempotency ledger (strongly consistent — DynamoDB conditional write or a UNIQUE index in Postgres) absorbs that duplicate.

x: If we cannot tolerate any duplicate, we move off Redis to ZooKeeper/etcd. What is a fencing token and why isn't Redis enough? A monotonically increasing number issued at lock-acquire time, checked at the resource — the resource rejects writes with a token older than the highest one it has seen. Redis doesn't natively provide monotonic tokens because a single-node counter isn't fault-tolerant. Consensus systems (ZooKeeper's zxid, etcd's mod_revision) give you one for free.

t: interview: Redis Distributed Rate Limiter — System Design
x: In a distributed system that same map is twenty independent counters — the load balancer sprays requests across boxes, so a user who has already spent all 100 requests on server A can happily continue on server B and still look "under the limit" on both. Local memory is the wrong place for shared state. The classic fix is to move the counter into a shared, in-memory store that every application server can hit with sub-millisecond latency: Redis . Redis gives you exactly what a rate limiter needs — atomic operations ( INCR , EXPIRE , ZADD , sorted sets), TTL for automatic cleanup, and Lua scripting so a "read, decide, write" sequence executes as one indivisible unit.

x: Once the counter lives in Redis, all twenty servers are agreeing on the same source of truth: one rate-limit:user:101:2026-08-22T10:15 key, one atomic increment, one decision. Every serious API service you use has this in front of it: Stripe runs four layers of token-bucket limiters on Redis and rejects millions of requests a month; GitHub , Twitter , Cloudflare , and AWS API Gateway all publish 429s under the same design. It is a top-3 interview question at Amazon, Google, Meta, and Stripe because it touches distributed state, atomicity, algorithm choice, HA trade-offs, and the CAP conversation — all in a single, contained problem.

t: interview: Redis Distributed Rate Limiter — System Design
x: If Priya walks up for her 101st coffee, the barista sees her tally is full and politely says "come back at 11:00." Now the shop gets popular and opens twenty checkout counters . Priya can walk up to any counter, and no barista knows what the others have already served her. If each counter keeps its own private tally sheet, Priya could get 100 coffees at counter 1, then another 100 at counter 2, and so on. Twenty tally sheets can't enforce one rule. This is exactly the situation for a website with many servers. The fix is beautifully simple: put one shared tally sheet on the wall in the middle of the shop.

t: interview: Redis Distributed Rate Limiter — System Design
x: Every barista, at every counter, must run to the same wall, put a mark next to Priya's name, and check that she hasn't crossed 100 marks in the current hour. Because the sheet lives in one place, all twenty counters agree on the same count. The "wall" in a real system is a lightning-fast in-memory scratchpad called Redis , and the marks are just numbers that get automatically wiped after an hour so the sheet doesn't fill up forever. There's a hard part everyone misses on the first try. Two baristas can walk to the wall at the same instant , both read "99", both think "one more is fine", both put a mark, and now Priya has 101 with the wall reading 100.

t: interview: Redis Distributed Rate Limiter — System Design
x: The counters were not talking to each other . So we don't ask the wall "what's the count?" and then write — we ask it " add one and tell me the new number " as a single unbreakable action. That way even if a thousand baristas rush the wall at the same nanosecond, they each get a unique number: 99, 100, 101, 102… and everyone past 100 is turned away. This "add-then-return" step is the atomic core of the whole idea, and it is why Redis is the go-to answer. You've used this every day.

Every request runs an atomic INCR ; if the resulting value is ≤ 100, allow it. Set a TTL of 60–61 seconds so old windows evaporate on their own. t: interview: Redis Distributed Rate Limiter — System Design
x: Redis processes commands one at a time on a single thread per shard, and INCR is a single command — no two concurrent increments can ever produce the same return value. Every server sees a unique, monotonically increasing counter for that user's window. That is the whole distributed-consensus story reduced to one command. The atomicity bug you must call out: INCR then EXPIRE as separate commands is a subtle bug. If the app crashes or the network drops between the two, the counter has been incremented but has no TTL , so the key lives forever. Do them together in a Lua script ( see below ) or inside MULTI/EXEC .

x: Also, only set the TTL when the counter is first created ( count == 1 ); do not reset it on every increment or the window will silently slide forward. 2. The Fixed-Window Boundary Burst Problem Fixed window looks tight but has a well-known hole. Suppose the limit is 100/min. A user sends 100 requests in the last second of window 1 (say 10:00:59), then 100 more in the first second of window 2 (10:01:00). Each individual window is at exactly 100 — both under the limit — but the user has effectively done 200 requests in ~2 seconds . Interviewers love this trap because it feels correct until you look at a two-second slice.

x: The fix is to never let the application make the decision — let Redis make it atomically. INCR is atomic. Better yet, wrap the entire "increment + expire + limit-check + return remaining" flow in a Lua script and call it via EVALSHA . Redis executes the whole script under its single-threaded event loop; nothing can interleave. Race conditions and atomic Lua Redis Lua is the interview power move . Because a user's requests can be load-balanced to any of the N servers. Each local counter only sees a fraction of the traffic, so 100 rpm easily becomes 100 × N rpm in aggregate. Shared state is not a nice-to-have here; it's required. Q. Why Redis specifically? A. Four properties in one package: sub-millisecond latency, atomic single-command primitives ( INCR , ZADD ), first-class TTL for automatic cleanup, and Lua for multi-op atomicity.

t: interview: Redis Distributed Rate Limiter — System Design
x: Add horizontal scaling via Cluster and multi-AZ HA via ElastiCache — you rarely find that combination elsewhere. Q. Is Redis INCR really atomic across a cluster? A. Atomic within a shard — which is where the key lives. Redis is single-threaded per shard; each command runs to completion before the next starts. Two clients incrementing the same key can never observe the same return value. Q. What if the INCR succeeds and the EXPIRE fails? A. The counter has no TTL and lives forever, leaking memory. The fix is to combine the two into a single Lua script (or MULTI/EXEC ), and only set the TTL when the counter was freshly created ( if count == 1 ).

t: interview: Redis Distributed Rate Limiter — System Design
x: Don't refresh the TTL on every increment — that would slide the window forward indefinitely. Q. When would you pick sliding window over token bucket? A. When you need strict rolling-window enforcement — e.g., "at most 5 login attempts in any 60-second sliding window." Token bucket allows short bursts by design, which is undesirable for auth. For "at most 100 req/min on average with small bursts okay", token bucket wins. Q. How do you handle a Redis failover during traffic? A. Async replication means a few writes may be lost on promotion, so a user may briefly get a handful of extra requests. That's acceptable for rate limiting (advisory, not correctness-critical).

t: interview: Redis Distributed Rate Limiter — System Design
x: If strict correctness is needed, use WAIT for replica ACK (adds latency) or move to MemoryDB / a CP store — but call the trade-off out explicitly. Q. How do you keep global limits from becoming a hot key? A. Shard the global counter across N sub-keys ( rl:global:{0..N-1} ), route randomly, and check the aggregate — or push global throttling up to the API Gateway / WAF layer where it doesn't touch Redis at all. Never let all traffic pin one shard. Q. What's the worst-case blast radius if this component fails? A. Depends on the failure policy. Fail-open: rate limits are temporarily lifted, product stays up, abuse is possible.

The middleware looks up the policy by route and calls the appropriate Lua script. Operators change limits without redeploying code. Q. Bottlenecks? A. (1) Redis network round-trip — mitigate with connection pooling and colocated Redis (same VPC/AZ). (2) Hot keys — shard global counters.

You know their name — "Priya at Sunrise Towers" — but not their exact flat number. The postal system has to figure that out for you.

t: Request Flow — Browser → DNS → ISP → Cloudflare → WAF → LB → App
x: When you type example.com in your browser, the same thing happens under the hood. The name example.com is friendly for humans , but computers on the internet only talk to each other using numbers, like 203.0.113.42 . So the first job is to look up the number for the name — like flipping open a phonebook. That's what DNS does. Your computer asks its neighbour ("your ISP" — the company that gives you internet) if it knows the number. If not, the ISP asks the internet's master directory , which walks up the tree: "who owns .com ? Who owns example.com inside .com ?" Bit by bit it finds the answer. Now here's a twist. The number your computer gets back doesn't lead to your friend's flat directly.

t: Request Flow — Browser → DNS → ISP → Cloudflare → WAF → LB → App
x: It leads to a front desk — a huge one, run by a company like Cloudflare , with copies sitting in every major city in the world. That front desk does three things before your letter goes any further. First, it looks in a drawer of common replies — if someone else just asked for the same page (say, the homepage), it hands over the copy immediately without disturbing the office at the back. That's called a cache . Second, it reads your letter for anything suspicious — a burglar disguised as a customer, a stack of forged requests — and throws those away. That's the firewall (WAF).

t: Request Flow — Browser → DNS → ISP → Cloudflare → WAF → LB → App
x: Third, if the letter is real and not cached, it forwards it to the real office at the back — hidden behind a locked door only the front desk knows about. The real office isn't one person either. It's a team of clerks , and a supervisor at the door decides which clerk takes each letter based on how busy they are. That supervisor is the load balancer . The clerk that finally handles your letter is the application . When they write the reply, it goes back the same way — clerk → supervisor → front desk → your computer.

Domain, subdomain, and DNS delegation A fully-qualified name like app.example.com. reads right-to-left . The trailing dot is the root zone . Then comes com — the TLD, whose zone is operated by Verisign. Then example — a domain registered to your company. Finally app — a subdomain, which can either live in the same zone as example.com or be delegated to a different set of name servers via NS records.

x: Delegation is how a startup can run its marketing site on Vercel ( example.com ) while pointing api.example.com at AWS Route 53 — the two subtrees literally sit in different infrastructure. x: The ISP recursive resolver Your ISP (Airtel, Comcast, or a public one like Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1 ) runs a recursive resolver . It doesn't own any records — it walks the tree on your behalf and caches everything it sees. From a cold cache, it makes three UDP queries: to a root server (Anycast, ~10–30 ms), to a .com TLD server (Anycast, ~20 ms), and to Cloudflare's authoritative NS (~20 ms), totalling ~50–100 ms. On a warm resolver, the answer is served from cache in under 5 ms. This is the single biggest reason DNS feels instant most of the time.

x: The resolver also enforces DNSSEC validation if configured — it walks the signature chain from the root's KSK down to the record's RRSIG and returns SERVFAIL on any tampering. 3. Cloudflare authoritative DNS + Anycast When your domain is on Cloudflare, its authoritative name servers respond to the recursive resolver — but not with the origin IP . For any record marked "proxied" (the orange cloud in the dashboard), Cloudflare returns an Anycast IP it owns. Anycast means the same IP is announced via BGP from every Cloudflare PoP (330+ cities as of 2024). The internet's routing fabric naturally sends the client packet to the nearest one.

t: Request Flow — Browser → DNS → ISP → Cloudflare → WAF → LB → App
x: This gives Cloudflare three superpowers at once: it hides the origin IP (attackers can't target AWS directly), it puts a caching/security layer within ~10 ms of every internet user on earth, and it absorbs DDoS at the edge — a 388 Tbps combined capacity, larger than any single origin could survive. 4. TLS termination at the edge The browser opens a TCP handshake to the Anycast IP, then negotiates TLS. In TLS 1.3 the handshake is 1 RTT (or 0-RTT with a Pre-Shared Key). The client sends a Server Name Indication (SNI) extension — server_name = app.example.com — which lets Cloudflare's edge (a single IP hosting thousands of domains) pick the right certificate.

t: Request Flow — Browser → DNS → ISP → Cloudflare → WAF → LB → App
x: Cloudflare then either serves the response entirely from cache or opens a second TLS connection to the origin ALB. That origin-side connection uses the customer's own cert on the ALB, giving genuine end-to-end encryption. Encrypted Client Hello (ECH) is the newer version that also encrypts the SNI so an on-path observer can't even see which site you're visiting. 5. WAF and bot management The WAF sits inline with the TLS-terminated request stream. Cloudflare's WAF ships with the OWASP Core Rule Set (SQLi, XSS, RCE, path traversal, LFI) plus its own Managed Ruleset tuned from patterns Cloudflare sees across ~20% of all internet traffic.

x: Rules fire on request headers, URI, body, and JA3/JA4 TLS fingerprints for bot detection. Rate-limiting (per IP, per session, per header) rejects abusive clients before they cost origin CPU. Anything the WAF blocks never reaches your VPC — this is the primary cost-saver at scale. 6. CDN caching decisions For every request Cloudflare hits your origin for, the response is potentially cached at the edge. The cache key defaults to (host, scheme, path, query) and can be customised. Static assets (images, JS bundles) hit almost 100%. x: If your authoritative NS goes down (Dyn 2016, AWS us-east-1 Route 53 2019), no client can find your site — even if the origin is perfectly healthy. Mitigation: use two DNS providers in secondary mode. Long TTLs kill failover. A 3600 s TTL on an A record means it takes an hour for the internet to notice a new IP. Use 60 s for anything that can move. Cloudflare origin exposure — if your origin IP leaks (misconfigured DNS record, cert transparency logs, email headers), attackers bypass the CDN entirely. Fix: restrict the origin security group to accept traffic only from Cloudflare's published IP ranges.

Why is example.com often an A record but www.example.com a CNAME? A. A CNAME can't sit at the zone apex because DNS forbids a CNAME to coexist with the required SOA/NS records. So the apex needs a real A/AAAA — or a vendor-specific ALIAS/ANAME record that the DNS provider resolves internally. Q. What's Anycast vs Unicast? A. Unicast is one IP → one server. Anycast is one IP announced by many servers via BGP; internet routing picks the topologically nearest one.

t: Request Flow — Browser → DNS → ISP → Cloudflare → WAF → LB → App
x: It's how Cloudflare has 388 Tbps of edge capacity behind a handful of IPs, and how the DNS root servers scale. Q. Where does TLS actually terminate? A. Twice, usually. Once at Cloudflare (client → edge) so the WAF and cache can read the request. A second, separate TLS connection from Cloudflare to the origin ALB, using the customer's ACM cert. That's why "end-to-end encryption" here doesn't mean "no one in the middle sees plaintext" — it means every hop is encrypted, but Cloudflare deliberately sees plaintext to do its job. Q. How does the ALB pick a pod? A. Listener rules match host/path/header conditions in priority order. The winning rule points at a target group.

t: Request Flow — Browser → DNS → ISP → Cloudflare → WAF → LB → App
x: Within the target group, the algorithm is round-robin by default or "least outstanding requests"; unhealthy targets are removed via health checks. If sticky sessions are needed, an ALB-generated cookie pins subsequent requests to the same target. Q. ALB or NLB — when do I pick which? A. ALB for HTTP/HTTPS/gRPC — anything where you want to route on path/headers or terminate TLS. NLB for TCP/UDP, extreme RPS, or when you need a static IP the client can whitelist. Many real deployments put an NLB in front of the ALB just to get the static IP. Q. What happens on a total Cloudflare outage? A. Your users hit an error.

A downstream database slows down and starts returning 500s.

t: Protecting a Backend from Retry Storms — System Design
x: Every one of the 40 client fleets calling that API has retry logic — "if it fails, try 3 times." Suddenly the API is receiving 15,000 requests per second — three times normal — and the database it depends on is now getting hammered with retries from every layer above. Latency climbs, more requests fail, more retries pile on, and within a minute the entire service is unreachable. That is a retry storm : retries becoming the cause of the outage, not the cure. This failure mode has taken down real companies. It is the reason AWS S3 had a partial outage in 2017 , why Google engineered adaptive throttling into every one of their RPC clients, and why Netflix wrote Hystrix in 2011.

t: Protecting a Backend from Retry Storms — System Design
x: Every serious backend — Stripe, Shopify, AWS SDKs, gRPC, Envoy, Istio, .NET's Polly, Java's Resilience4j — ships built-in retry + circuit breaker + backoff protection today. Interviewers ask this because it separates people who have shipped production services (they will name five specific defenses) from people who have only written code that works on the happy path. The playbook has five layers, and a strong answer walks through them in order: rate limiting at the edge, circuit breakers at every remote call, exponential backoff with jitter in every retry loop, concurrent-request caps per client and per dependency, and load shedding when the process itself gets overloaded.

t: Protecting a Backend from Retry Storms — System Design
x: Each of those alone helps; layered, they turn a cascading outage into a graceful brownout. 🧑‍🎓 In laymen terms Why a slow website becomes a dead website Imagine a busy coffee shop. Normally 20 people order per hour and the two baristas keep up. One morning the espresso machine gets sluggish, and orders start taking twice as long. Some customers get impatient, walk out, and come right back in to re-order — thinking maybe the barista forgot them. Now there are 40 people in line. Seeing the huge line, more people re-order. Soon there are 80 people yelling their order at two baristas. The machine wasn't badly broken — but now nobody is getting coffee, and the whole shop is jammed.

t: Protecting a Backend from Retry Storms — System Design
x: That is what happens to a website when it gets a little slow. Every phone app, every browser, has a "try again if it fails" button — usually automatic, invisible to you. When the site becomes slow, thousands of phones start clicking that invisible button on their own, and the extra traffic pushes the site from "slow" to "dead." The very tool designed to make you patient — automatic retries — is what kills the site. This is called a retry storm . To protect the coffee shop we do a few simple things.

t: Protecting a Backend from Retry Storms — System Design
x: First, a bouncer at the door who counts customers per minute and asks people to wait outside — that's the "rate limiter." Second, when the espresso machine really is broken, we flip the "closed" sign for a few minutes so people stop pushing on the door instead of standing there frustrated — that's the "circuit breaker." Third, when a customer's order is delayed, we ask them to wait a little before re-asking , and each time to wait a little longer, with slightly different times for each person so they don't all storm the counter at once — that's "exponential backoff with jitter." Fourth, we cap how many drinks any one Uber Eats courier can pick up at a time so a single big order doesn't hog

t: Protecting a Backend from Retry Storms — System Design
x: both baristas — that's "concurrency limiting." Fifth, when the shop is truly full, we stop taking new orders for muffins and only serve coffee — that's "load shedding," dropping the least important work first. This isn't hypothetical. Every time you tap a button in Uber, WhatsApp, or Instagram and it feels a bit sluggish but doesn't fully crash, that's these five defenses quietly kicking in behind the scenes. Without them, one small slowdown on one server would take out the whole app — like it used to, in the early days of the web.

x: 📋 Requirements & scale What "good enough" looks like Retry-storm protection is not a product with users — it's a set of policies you bake into every service and client library. So instead of QPS estimates, an interviewer wants defensible numbers on defaults : what timeout, what retry count, what concurrency cap, what shed threshold. Nail these and you sound like someone who has tuned real systems. Functional requirements Every remote call has a timeout shorter than the caller's timeout. Every retry uses exponential backoff with jitter — never a fixed sleep. Every dependency is guarded by a circuit breaker with closed / open / half-open states.

t: Protecting a Backend from Retry Storms — System Design
x: Every service and every client has a concurrent-request cap . The service sheds low-priority load before it collapses, and returns 429 / 503 with a Retry-After header so clients back off correctly. Retries are only at the layer immediately above the failure — never at every layer in the call stack (that's what causes the storm). Without protection each failed request triggers 3 retries (default SDK behavior), so: Additional traffic = 10,000 × 0.20 × 3 = +6,000 rps of retries → 60% traffic increase in seconds. Add one more layer (client → gateway → service → DB, each retrying 3×) and the amplification is 3³ = 27× — a headline outage. With Google SRE's 10% retry budget , additional traffic is capped at 1,000 rps — a 10% bump, survivable. 🏗️ High-level architecture Where each defense lives in the request path Protection is a layered stack , not a single component.

x: The request enters through the edge (CDN / API Gateway), then a rate limiter, then the service — which itself has an admission controller, a bulkhead (semaphore) around every dependency, a circuit breaker per dependency, and a retry loop with backoff+jitter. If the service still becomes overloaded, load shedding kicks in and drops the least-important work. Each layer has one job, and the layers compose so failures never cascade upward.
