x: It covers process architecture , concurrency model (MVCC vs lock-based with optional row versioning), storage engine (heap + PK-clustered vs heap + optional CLUSTER), write-ahead logging (WAL vs T-log), replication and HA (streaming/logical vs Always On availability groups), partitioning , extensibility , licensing/cost , and ecosystem fit . Then it gives you a decision rubric with worked examples so you can pick fast in an interview. 🧑‍🎓 In plain English The story, told without any jargon Both SQL Server and PostgreSQL are filing cabinets for your business data .

t: SQL Server vs PostgreSQL — Architecture Comparison
x: Both keep every drawer neat, both can hand out receipts saying "your change is saved for good" (that's ACID), and both let you ask questions like "who spent the most money last month?" in the same language (SQL). If you only cared about the front door, they'd feel identical. The real difference is how they handle two people reaching for the same folder at the same time . SQL Server, by default, does what feels intuitive: it locks the folder — you wait until the other person finishes. Simple, predictable, but if the other person is slow, you sit around doing nothing. PostgreSQL does something clever: it photocopies the folder for you.

t: SQL Server vs PostgreSQL — Architecture Comparison
x: You each work on your own copy at the same time, and the system figures out how to merge (or reject) the changes at the end. That trick is called MVCC , and it is the single biggest architectural difference between the two products. The second difference is who owns them. SQL Server is a Microsoft product — you buy it, you're tied to Microsoft's licensing, and everything works beautifully if you already live in Windows/.NET/Azure. PostgreSQL is a free, open-source community project — no vendor, no licence fee, and it runs equally well on Linux, Docker, AWS, Google Cloud, your laptop, or a Raspberry Pi.

Concurrency: MVCC vs locking (with row-versioning opt-in) The single largest architectural difference.

t: SQL Server vs PostgreSQL — Architecture Comparison
x: PostgreSQL uses MVCC everywhere : every UPDATE creates a new tuple version rather than mutating in place; readers see the version visible to their transaction's snapshot; writers never block readers, readers never block writers. This gives Postgres exceptional read throughput under concurrent writes — at the cost of bloat (dead tuples pile up until autovacuum cleans them). SQL Server started life pessimistic and lock-based : readers hold shared locks that block writers and vice versa.

x: Since SQL Server 2005 you can opt-in to Read Committed Snapshot Isolation (RCSI) or Snapshot Isolation , which use row versioning stored in tempdb ; SQL Server 2022 added Optimized Locking (TID + LAQ) to reduce lock memory. Even so, most SQL Server deployments still run with the pessimistic default and lean on indexes to avoid escalation. This is why "converting a legacy SQL Server app to Postgres" is not a purely mechanical port — the isolation semantics can differ subtly. 2. Storage: heap + clustered index vs heap + optional cluster SQL Server stores data in 8 KB pages inside .mdf / .ndf files.

t: SQL Server vs PostgreSQL — Architecture Comparison
x: Every table has either a heap or a clustered index — and by default, the primary key IS the clustered index, so the table is physically sorted by PK. This makes range queries on PK fast but makes inserts anywhere except the tail slow, and it means every non-clustered index carries the PK as its row locator. PostgreSQL stores every table as a plain heap (unordered by default); the PK is just another B-tree index pointing into the heap. Ordering by insertion is preserved unless you explicitly CLUSTER . This gives Postgres more predictable insert performance and simpler mental model, at the cost of losing the "clustered scan" trick. 3.

t: SQL Server vs PostgreSQL — Architecture Comparison
x: Write-ahead log: T-log vs WAL Both engines use write-ahead logging (durability, crash recovery, replication all depend on it). SQL Server's transaction log ( .ldf ) and Postgres's WAL segments ( pg_wal/ ) serve the same purpose — flush the log before the data page . The differences are operational: SQL Server has a single per-database log file, backup modes ( SIMPLE , FULL , BULK_LOGGED ), and log-shipping/replication features tied to log backups. Postgres has fixed-size 16 MB WAL segments that stream continuously to replicas; recovery is naturally continuous (PITR to any second). Both support synchronous replication — commit blocks until the replica has ACKed the log record. 4.

Automatic failover uses Windows Server Failover Cluster (WSFC) as the quorum layer. Read-only routing at the listener lets you offload reads. Also available: log shipping (simple, granular), transactional replication (per-table CDC), Failover Cluster Instance (shared-storage HA). PostgreSQL gives you two flavours: physical streaming replication (byte-for-byte WAL shipped to hot standbys) and logical replication (row-level events, cross-version, subset of tables).

System Design · Interview Prep Stripe's Zero-Downtime Data Migration How Stripe moves hundreds of millions of live records — and reshapes the schema underneath them — without a single minute of downtime and zero data inconsistency. 🎯 Scenario 🧑‍🎓 Laymen 📋 Requirements 🏗️ Architecture 🎬 Animation 🔍 Deep-dive 🧮 DSA ☁️ AWS 💻 C# code ⚖️ Trade-offs 🗣️ Cheat sheet ❓ FAQ 📚 Sources 🎯 Real-world scenario What we're building & where it's used Stripe processes payments for millions of businesses — DigitalOcean, Squarespace, Shopify merchants, Amazon, Uber Eats — and its Subscriptions table alone holds hundreds of millions of live records.

In its early days, Stripe stored subscription data as an array field inside the Customer record . That worked at a few hundred customers. It stopped working at scale: every subscription change had to rewrite the whole Customer document, and the design collapsed once customers wanted multiple subscriptions. The obvious fix — pull subscriptions into their own dedicated table — is trivial on paper and terrifying in practice. The old field is referenced from thousands of lines of code across many services . The system serves live traffic 24/7 for businesses that make real revenue every second the API is up.

And running a bulk migration sequentially would take, in Stripe's own math, over three years for 100M records at one second each. This is the "engine change while the plane is flying" problem, and every large system hits it — Facebook, Shopify, GitHub, LinkedIn, Uber. The playbook Stripe wrote for it is now the industry-standard four-phase online migration : dual-write, backfill, migrate reads with a shadow-compare, then remove the old field. It's a classic staff/senior interview question because every candidate has to migrate a schema someday, and doing it without downtime — or a Sunday-morning outage post-mortem — is what separates senior engineers from principal ones.

🧑‍🎓 In laymen terms Explain it like I've never written code Imagine you run a massive filing cabinet business . Every customer has a folder, and inside that folder — jammed into the same page — you scribble down their monthly subscriptions. It worked when you had 200 customers. Now you have hundreds of millions , some with dozens of subscriptions each, and every time someone changes one, your clerk has to grab the whole folder, rewrite the whole page, and file it back. Everything is slow. Everything is fragile. You decide subscriptions deserve their own filing cabinet . Great idea — but here's the catch: your business never closes.

Customers are signing up, cancelling, and paying right now, this second . You cannot say "we'll be back Monday." You cannot lose a single record. And you have thousands of clerks in different departments who all know the old system by heart. So you move in four calm phases, and this is the whole trick: 1) Write to both places. From today, whenever a clerk updates a subscription, they write it in both the old folder and the new cabinet. New data is safe from day one. 2) Copy the old stuff over. At night, a huge team of movers scans a snapshot of every folder (not the live ones — a photocopy, so you don't slow the business down) and copies each subscription into the new cabinet.

When they're done, they run the scan again to confirm nothing was missed. 3) Switch reading, but check yourself. Now, whenever someone looks up a subscription, you read from the new cabinet — but you also secretly peek at the old folder and compare. If the two ever disagree, an alarm rings. Only when the alarms stay silent for weeks do you trust the new cabinet fully. 4) Throw out the old page. Finally, stop writing to the old folder, delete the scribbled subscription page, and the migration is done. Every big company you use — WhatsApp, Instagram, Uber, Netflix, your bank — has done this dance many times. Nobody noticed. That's the whole point.

📋 Requirements & scale Requirements and back-of-the-envelope math Functional requirements Move a live entity ( Subscriptions ) from being nested inside a parent record to its own dedicated table with its own schema. All existing code paths — thousands of call sites across many services — must keep working through the transition. New writes go to the new store from day one; old data must be reconciled without blocking traffic. Every read must return the correct value at every moment of the migration; there is no "wrong for 10 minutes" tolerance. Non-functional requirements Zero downtime. No maintenance windows.

Stripe's API SLA is 99.999%+ — every second of outage is real merchant money lost. Zero data inconsistency. Any divergence between old and new must be detected in seconds, not days. Bounded blast radius per change. Rollback must be possible at every phase. Incremental rollout. Ramp writes and reads by percentage, monitor, escalate. Back-of-the-envelope Dimension Number Why it matters Objects to migrate ~100M–500M subscriptions Stripe cites "hundreds of millions"; sizing anchor for the whole plan. Sequential time (1 s/obj) ~3.2 years for 100M Motivates parallel/offline processing. MapReduce parallelism 1,000–10,000 mappers 100M objects at 10k parallelism × 100 ms each ≈ 17 min pass.

Backfill throttle ~5–10% of prod QPS budget Enough to finish in days, not weeks; small enough not to page oncall. Dual-write overhead +1 write per mutation Roughly doubles the write path; ramp gradually while watching p99. Scientist mismatch budget < 0.001% after warmup Below that, cut reads over. Above it, keep debugging. Rollout duration Weeks to months per entity Not a sprint — a sustained, monitored campaign. 🏗️ High-level architecture How the four phases fit together The end-to-end pattern is a four-phase incremental rollout .

The system is never in a "transitional half-state" — at every moment one store is authoritative for reads, both stores are being written, and a shadow-compare is running to detect drift. The migration only progresses when the previous phase has been silent for long enough to trust. 1 Dual write New table exists; every write goes to both. Old store still authoritative for reads. 2 Backfill Copy the tail of old records into the new table using offline MapReduce over a DB snapshot. 3 Shadow reads Read from new, compare vs old with GitHub Scientist. When drift ≈ 0, cut reads over. 4 Cleanup Stop writing to old field, lazily delete stragglers, drop the old column.

Watch a write go to just the old store, then to both, then a backfill sweep, then a Scientist read comparison catching a mismatch, then the final cutover. ▶ Play Step → ← Back ↺ Reset Ready Press ▶ Play to start 🔍 Component deep-dive Phase 1 — Dual writing The first move is additive, not disruptive . Create the new Subscriptions table. Add a dual-write code path in the data-access layer so every mutation on a subscription writes to both stores.

Guard it behind a feature flag with a percentage rollout — Stripe ramps to 100% while watching p99 latency, error rate, and cache-hit rates on the primary DB. Existing objects that get touched during this phase are lazily copied on write, so hot data heals itself. The old field remains the source of truth for reads. Key invariants: writes are ordered (old first, then new — or use an outbox pattern to avoid partial failures); dual-write failures are logged and retried; the code path is small enough (a few hundred lines) to review in one PR. Phase 2 — Backfill via offline MapReduce Running the backfill against production would double the write load and page oncall.

Stripe instead used Hadoop snapshots — a nightly copy of the production DB into their data warehouse — and wrote MapReduce jobs using Scalding , Twitter's Scala DSL over Cascading. A "simple job in 10 lines of code" enumerates every subscription ID that exists in the old field, then a parallel multi-threaded migrator copies each into the new table via the same API path as a dual write. After the sweep, they re-run the Scalding job to confirm the delta is empty. This "scan → migrate → re-scan to zero" pattern is the safety net. Phase 3 — Shadow reads and Scientist Cutting reads over is the scariest phase — a bug here shows up as wrong data returned to real customers.

Stripe uses GitHub Scientist , a library that runs two code paths in production for the same request, returning the control's result to the caller while asynchronously executing the candidate and publishing a mismatch record when the two disagree. In practice this means every read from the old store is shadowed by a read from the new; the returned value is still from the old (so no user-facing risk), but the difference feeds a dashboard. Only when the mismatch rate stays effectively zero for days — after ignoring known-benign differences like ordering — does Stripe flip the primary read to the new store.

Even then, dual-writes and shadow reads on the old store are kept live for a while so rollback is a one-flag flip. Phase 4 — Cleanup and hard errors The last phase drops the deprecated field. Stripe's technique is aggressive: replace the old accessor with a hard error so any straggler code path that still touches it explodes in staging or canary before it can silently regress. The subscriptions array on Customer becomes Opus::Error.hard("Accessing subscriptions array on customer") . A final Scalding job lazily deletes any remaining data, and the column can eventually be dropped. Why it works The whole design is a staircase of small, reversible steps .

At every phase, one side is authoritative, the other is being validated. There is never a moment where the system depends on both being correct simultaneously. Every phase has a clear go/no-go metric — dual-write error rate, backfill completeness, Scientist mismatch rate — and rollback is always a feature-flag flip away. 🧮 The DSA behind it Data structures & algorithms Zero-downtime migration looks like ops, but under the hood it's a stack of classical CS primitives — parallel scans, set differences, distributed consensus (implicitly, through feature flags and consistent hashing), and probabilistic sketches for verification.

The core algorithms MapReduce over a snapshot — the backfill is a distributed map (parse each old record → emit the flattened row) with no reduce; Scalding compiles it down to Hadoop tasks. Complexity: O(N/P) wall time on P mappers. Set difference for completeness — after the sweep, compute {old_ids} − {new_ids} . If empty, we're done; otherwise re-migrate the delta. Two big-set diff via sort-merge is O(N log N) per store on the snapshot. Shadow compare (Scientist) — deep-equality of two candidate values, with configurable normalization for known-benign ordering / whitespace / rounding differences. Runs on every read; overhead is bounded by enabled? sampling.

Reservoir sampling / percentage rollout — feature flags use a hash of the object ID modulo 100 to decide "does this request take the new path?" — a deterministic sampler that ramps cleanly from 0% → 100% and gives idempotent per-object routing. Idempotent writes — dual writes must be safe to retry. Stripe uses idempotency keys (originally exposed in their public API) so the same write hitting both stores twice does not double-insert. Bloom / count-min sketches (optional) — for very large datasets, a Bloom filter of "already migrated IDs" fits in RAM and avoids re-processing during checkpointed sweeps.

Transactional outbox pattern — an alternative to raw dual-write; the app writes to one DB with an outbox row in the same transaction, and a relay tails that outbox and writes to the new store. Guarantees at-least-once delivery even on partial failures. n Mapping the design to AWS Stripe's own stack uses Ruby, MongoDB, Hadoop, and Kafka — but every piece of the pattern has a clean AWS counterpart, which is what interviewers usually want to hear. Migration component AWS service Why Old store (source) RDS PostgreSQL / DynamoDB Whatever the current primary is — the migration pattern is store-agnostic. New store (target) DynamoDB / RDS / Aurora The pattern works for any schema/store change, including cross-engine (RDS → Dynamo). Dual-write orchestrator Lambda + application code App code writes to both stores; feature flags gate the percentage. Feature flags AWS AppConfig or LaunchDarkly Percent rollout with instant kill switch, without redeploy.

Snapshot for backfill DMS + S3 · DynamoDB export to S3 Consistent point-in-time copy without hitting the live DB. Backfill compute AWS Glue · EMR (Spark) · Athena Distributed scan/transform over the S3 snapshot — the modern Scalding equivalent. Change data capture DynamoDB Streams · DMS CDC · Kinesis Streams post-snapshot mutations to the new store to close the gap. Observability CloudWatch · X-Ray · Managed Grafana Dashboards for mismatch rate, backfill progress, dual-write error rate. Rollback control plane AppConfig flag flip · IAM policy Every phase is one flag away from being undone. Concretely: use DMS with ongoing replication to seed the target and keep it warm ; run Glue Spark against a nightly S3 export for the heavy sweep; use DynamoDB Streams into Lambda to catch anything mutated after the export; drive dual-writes from application code guarded by AppConfig ; emit a mismatch CloudWatch metric from every shadow read and alarm on any non-zero value; and gate the read cutover on that alarm being silent for a full week.

💻 C# implementation Below is the shape of the pattern in C# — a repository wrapper that owns dual-write, shadow-read, and the Scientist-style compare. The exact percentages and stores are pluggable; the invariants are what matter. // SubscriptionRepository — a dual-write, shadow-read facade over old + new stores. // Feature flags drive the phase: dual-write %, read source, shadow-compare on/off.

public sealed class SubscriptionRepository { private readonly ISubscriptionStore _old; // Customers.subscriptions[] private readonly ISubscriptionStore _new; // dedicated Subscriptions table private readonly IFeatureFlags _flags; private readonly IMetrics _metrics; private readonly ILogger < SubscriptionRepository > _log; public SubscriptionRepository ( ISubscriptionStore oldStore, ISubscriptionStore newStore, IFeatureFlags flags, IMetrics metrics, ILogger < SubscriptionRepository > log) { _old = oldStore; _new = newStore; _flags = flags; _metrics = metrics; _log = log; } // ---------- WRITE PATH ---------- public async Task < Subscription > SaveAsync ( Subscription s, CancellationToken ct)

{ // Phase 1: always write to old; dual-write to new for X% of rollout. var saved = await _old. UpsertAsync (s, ct); if (_flags. IsEnabled ( "dual_write.subscriptions" , s.Id)) { try { await _new. UpsertAsync (saved, ct); } catch ( Exception ex) { _metrics. Increment ( "migration.dual_write.new.error" ); _log. LogError (ex, "dual-write to new store failed for {Id}" , s.Id); // swallow: old store is still authoritative in phase 1 } } return saved; } // ---------- READ PATH — Scientist-style shadow compare ---------- public async Task < Subscription? > GetAsync ( string id, CancellationToken ct) { bool readFromNew = _flags.

IsEnabled ( "read.subscriptions.from_new" , id); bool shadowCompare = _flags. IsEnabled ( "shadow.subscriptions" , id); // Choose "control" (returned to caller) and "candidate" (validated silently). var primary = readFromNew ? _new : _old; var secondary = readFromNew ? _old : _new; var primaryTask = primary. GetAsync (id, ct); if (!shadowCompare) return await primaryTask; // Run both, catch candidate exceptions, publish mismatches — never affect the caller. var secondaryTask = SafeGet (secondary, id, ct); await Task . WhenAll (primaryTask, secondaryTask); var p = primaryTask.Result; var s = secondaryTask.Result; if (! Equivalent (p, s)) { _metrics.

Increment ( "migration.shadow.mismatch" ); _log. LogWarning ( "mismatch id={Id} primary={P} secondary={S}" , id, p, s); } return p; } private async Task < Subscription? > SafeGet ( ISubscriptionStore store, string id, CancellationToken ct) { try { return await store. GetAsync (id, ct); } catch ( Exception ex) { _metrics. Increment ( "migration.shadow.error" ); _log. LogWarning (ex, "shadow read failed" ); return null ; } } // Normalize before compare — ordering, timestamps, whitespace, etc.

private static bool Equivalent ( Subscription? a, Subscription? b) { if (a is null && b is null ) return true ; if (a is null || b is null ) return false ; return a.Id == b.Id && a.CustomerId == b.CustomerId && a.Status == b.Status && a.PlanId == b.PlanId && a.PeriodEnd == b.PeriodEnd; } } // The backfill worker — idempotent, parallel, resumable. public sealed class BackfillWorker { public async Task RunAsync ( IAsyncEnumerable < string > snapshotIds, int parallelism, CancellationToken ct) { await Parallel . ForEachAsync (snapshotIds, new ParallelOptions { MaxDegreeOfParallelism = parallelism, CancellationToken = ct }, async (id, token) => { var record = await _oldStore.

GetAsync (id, token); if (record is null ) return ; // Idempotency: upsert by primary key so re-runs are safe. await _newStore. UpsertAsync (record, token); _metrics. Increment ( "migration.backfill.copied" ); }); } } The pattern generalizes: swap Ruby for C#, MongoDB for RDS, Hadoop for Glue — the shape is identical. Idempotent upserts, feature-flag ramps, shadow reads with a metric, and a bounded rollback path. ⚖️ Trade-offs, bottlenecks & likely follow-ups Where this pattern hurts Dual-write doubles the write path. If the primary store was already at 80% CPU, dual-writing sends it over.

Mitigation: ramp slowly, throttle backfill during business hours, run the sweep off a snapshot not the live DB. Alternative: the transactional outbox pattern — write only once (to the outbox) inside the primary transaction and let a relay do the second write async. See Transactional Outbox . Ordering across two stores is hard. If the new-store write succeeds but the old fails, you have a phantom row. Guardrails: idempotency keys, outbox to guarantee at-least-once, and a periodic reconciler that finds phantoms. Deep-equality is fragile. Two stores rarely produce byte-identical results — timestamps have different precision, JSON key ordering differs, floats round differently.

You'll spend real time writing the Equivalent() function and ignoring known-benign differences. Scientist supports this via ignore / compare blocks. Feature-flag explosion. A big migration accumulates dozens of flags: dual-write, shadow-read, cutover, backfill-scope. Own the lifecycle — every flag has an owner and a deletion date, or your codebase will drown in ifs. The final 0.001% is the hardest. Getting Scientist mismatches to zero takes weeks. The last mismatches are almost always real bugs in the new code path or race conditions between the two writes — that's exactly why the shadow phase exists.

Likely interview follow-ups Why not just take a maintenance window? For a payment API the outage cost is real merchant revenue and SLA credits. Even a 30-min window at Stripe's scale would strand thousands of live checkouts. And you can't "just do it faster" — sequential migration of 100M rows is measured in years. What if the backfill runs during dual-writes and overwrites a fresh value with an old one? Use compare-and-swap or last-write-wins with a version/timestamp column. Backfill writes only if new.updated_at < source.updated_at , so a live dual-write that hit the new store first is never clobbered. How do you handle deletes during the migration? Tombstones.

Deletes are dual-written just like inserts. Backfill of a snapshot must reconcile against a tombstone log so it doesn't "resurrect" already-deleted rows. How do you roll back if you're already in phase 3 and something goes wrong? Flip the read.from_new flag back to false . Because you kept dual-writing to the old store, its state is still fresh; the shadow-read alarm goes silent immediately. That's why you never remove the safety net early. Would you use CDC (Change Data Capture) instead? CDC (DynamoDB Streams, Debezium, DMS CDC) is a fine implementation of the "outbox tail" — it eliminates dual-write in application code by streaming DB changes into the new store.

The four-phase strategy stays; the mechanism changes. How is this different from a schema migration inside one DB? Same pattern, smaller blast radius. Add the new column, backfill it, cut reads over, drop the old. Tools like gh-ost / pt-online-schema-change for MySQL implement this at the storage layer. The Stripe pattern generalizes to cross-store and cross-schema. What's the analog to Scientist in a .NET / Java shop? There's no library as popular; teams roll their own. Practically it's ~50 lines: run both code paths inside a Task.WhenAll , catch candidate exceptions, deep-compare, publish a metric. That's the C# snippet above.

🗣️ Interview cheat sheet The 30-second pitch: "Stripe migrates hundreds of millions of live records with a four-phase online strategy: dual-write to both stores, backfill the tail from a Hadoop snapshot via Scalding MapReduce, cut reads over using GitHub Scientist for shadow-compare, then remove the old field. Every phase is feature-flag gated, monitored on a mismatch metric, and rollback is one flag flip away. That's the industry-standard playbook for zero-downtime schema changes." Numbers to quote: ~100M–500M subscriptions; sequential 1 s/obj = 3+ years; MapReduce parallelism = 1k–10k workers; mismatch budget < 0.001% before cutover.

Five talking points that win the round: The four phases , in order: dual-write → backfill → shadow-read → cleanup. Offline MapReduce over a snapshot — never hammer prod for backfill. Scientist / shadow reads: caller sees old, we compare new silently, alarm on drift. Every phase is feature-flag gated for percentage rollout and instant rollback. Kill the old field with a hard error so nothing sneaks a call back in. Words to say: "idempotent upsert", "outbox pattern", "shadow compare", "mismatch metric", "one-flag rollback", "CDC-driven variant". Trade-offs to volunteer: dual-write doubles load; deep-equality is fragile; feature-flag hygiene matters; the last 0.001% is real bugs.

x: You care about two things: (1) nobody peeks inside and (2) you're actually writing to your bank, not a scammer pretending to be them . Here's the trick real banks use. Your bank has a big ID card signed by a trusted authority — think of it like a passport office everyone in the world already trusts (Apple, Google, Microsoft all pre-installed a list of them on your phone). When you first knock on the bank's door, they show you the ID card. Your phone looks at the signature, walks up the chain — "this card was signed by GlobalTrust, and my phone trusts GlobalTrust, so I trust the bank" — and then quietly agrees on a secret handshake with the bank that no eavesdropper on the sidewalk can hear.

t: TLS Handshake Across Hops — System Design
x: Everything you send after that is scrambled with that secret. That's HTTPS . That agreement is called the TLS handshake . Now the twist. In real life, your letter doesn't go straight to the bank. It stops at a chain of post offices : first the neighborhood mailbox (the CDN — a fast local drop-off near you), then the sorting facility (the firewall that inspects for suspicious mail), then the regional depot (the load balancer that spreads mail across many bank branches), and only then the actual bank clerk (the application server).

t: TLS Handshake Across Hops — System Design
x: Each stop needs to make a choice: "do I open the envelope, read the address, and re-seal it before passing it on? Or do I forward the sealed envelope as-is?" Most big websites choose the "open and re-seal" approach at each stop, because otherwise the sorting facility can't sort — it doesn't know which branch the letter is for without reading the address. That's called TLS termination . Every re-sealing stop needs its own ID card (its own certificate), and it needs to trust the ID card of the next stop. When two neighboring stops both show ID to each other, that's called mTLS — mutual — like two secret agents flashing badges before speaking. Concrete example. You tap "pay" in the Amazon app.

t: TLS Handshake Across Hops — System Design
x: Your phone talks to a CloudFront server 30 km away (that's stop 1, and it shows you an amazon.com certificate). CloudFront decrypts your request, checks it, then opens a fresh sealed envelope to an Amazon load balancer inside AWS. The load balancer decrypts again, picks a healthy checkout server, and sends a third sealed envelope to that server. Three separate handshakes, three separate certificates, three chances for something to go wrong — and the padlock icon in your browser only sees the first one. The whole reason engineers design this so carefully is that the padlock on your screen is only proving the first hop . The rest is on the platform team.

Because RSA key exchange encrypts the pre-master secret with the server's long-term public key, so anyone who later steals that private key can decrypt all past traffic . ECDHE uses ephemeral keys — the private half is destroyed after the handshake — giving forward secrecy . TLS 1.3 removes RSA key exchange entirely for exactly this reason. Why AEAD-only ciphers? Because CBC + MAC-then-encrypt suffered a decade of attacks (Lucky Thirteen, BEAST, POODLE). AEADs combine encryption + integrity in one primitive with a formal security proof.

The CDN worker inspects the SNI in the ClientHello, looks up the tenant's cert bundle in a shared cache (typically keyed by hostname → SNI dictionary), and serves the right leaf. Because SNI is cleartext, an eavesdropper can still see which domain you're visiting even though the URL path is encrypted — ECH (Encrypted Client Hello) fixes this by wrapping the inner ClientHello in an outer hello encrypted to the CDN's HPKE key. Isn't mTLS operationally painful — cert distribution, rotation, revocation? Yes, unless you delegate it. That's what SPIFFE/SPIRE and service meshes exist to solve.

Distributed Systems · Interview Prep Two-Phase & Three-Phase Commit How independent nodes agree to commit one atomic transaction — the classic distributed-commit protocols, their blocking flaw, and what replaced them. 🎯 The problem 🧑‍🎓 Laymen 📋 Goals 🏗️ 2PC protocol 🔍 Failure modes 🧮 3PC & Saga ☁️ AWS mapping 💻 C# code ⚖️ Follow-ups 🗣️ Cheat sheet ❓ FAQ 📚 Sources 🎯 Real-world scenario The atomic-commit problem across machines Imagine transferring $100 from an account in the Payments database to a balance in the Ledger database — two separate systems on two separate machines. You need all-or-nothing : either both the debit and the credit happen, or neither does.

If the debit commits and the credit is lost, money vanishes. On a single database an ACID transaction handles this trivially, but the moment the data spans multiple independent nodes there is no shared transaction log to lean on. This is the distributed atomic commit problem, and Two-Phase Commit (2PC) is its textbook solution. You'll meet 2PC anywhere multiple resource managers must commit together: the XA transaction standard used by Java/JEE app servers and message brokers, distributed SQL engines, and older microservice designs that spanned several databases in one request.

Interviewers ask about it because it is the cleanest way to test whether you understand coordination under failure — and because its famous blocking weakness motivates everything that came after (Paxos, Raft, and the Saga pattern). 🧑‍🎓 In laymen terms The friends who want to swap concert seats — but only if everyone agrees You and five friends are at a concert, but you all got seated in random spots . You want to swap so you can sit together. The catch — a swap only works if every single one of the five is willing to move, at the same time. If even one person refuses, everybody stays put.

So one of you becomes the "organiser." The organiser walks around the row and asks each friend, one by one, " Are you ready to move if I tell you to? " Each friend thinks about it — packs up their popcorn, folds their jacket, and says either "yes, ready" or "no, my knee hurts, I'm not moving." The organiser writes down every answer on a piece of paper. This is phase one. Once everyone has said "yes," the organiser walks around a second time and says " OK, move now. " Everyone gets up together, swaps seats, and it's done. If even one person had said no, the organiser would instead say "abort, sit back down" — and everyone unpacks their popcorn again. This is phase two.

That is basically how banks, airlines, and old-style databases used to make sure two computer systems don't get out of sync when they need to change something together. Here is the ugly part. Suppose after everyone said "yes," the organiser goes to the bathroom and never comes back. Now the five friends are stuck. They've all promised they will move — they can't sit down, they can't get more popcorn, they can't even leave — because the organiser might return any moment with the "move now" signal. They are frozen , waiting. That is the famous blocking problem: one bad moment for the organiser, and the whole row is paralysed.

This is why modern apps like WhatsApp or Uber avoid this dance — they use a gentler pattern called a Saga, where each step can be undone later, so nobody has to freeze and wait. 📋 What atomic commit must guarantee Requirements of a distributed-commit protocol Property Meaning Agreement All participants that decide, decide the same outcome (all commit or all abort). No split decisions. Validity If any participant votes No, the outcome is abort. If all vote Yes and no failures, the outcome is commit. Stability / Durability Once a node commits or aborts, that decision is final and survives crashes (written to a stable log). Termination Non-faulty nodes eventually reach a decision.

This is the one 2PC fails to guarantee — hence its blocking problem. The roles: one coordinator (the transaction manager) drives the decision; multiple participants (also called cohorts or resource managers) each own a slice of the data and vote. Both sides write to a durable log so they can recover their state after a crash. 🏗️ The 2PC protocol Two phases: vote, then decide Phase 1 is prepare/voting : the coordinator asks everyone "can you commit?" Each participant does all the work up to the commit point — acquires locks, writes undo/redo log records — and replies Yes (I'm ready and I promise I can commit) or No .

Crucially, a Yes vote is a binding promise: the participant must now be able to commit even if it crashes and restarts, so it forces its prepare record to stable storage first. Phase 2 is commit/completion : if all voted Yes, the coordinator writes a commit record and broadcasts COMMIT ; if anyone voted No (or timed out), it broadcasts ABORT . Participants act, release their locks, and acknowledge. phase 1: prepare + vote phase 2: commit broadcast Prepare: coordinator logs BEGIN , sends CanCommit? to all participants. Vote: each participant does the work, force-writes a prepared record, replies Yes/No. After Yes it holds locks and waits — it is now in doubt .

Decide: coordinator force-writes the global decision (commit iff all Yes). This write is the point of no return. Broadcast & ack: coordinator sends the decision; participants apply it, release locks, and acknowledge. Coordinator completes once all acks arrive. 🔍 Failure modes — where 2PC hurts The blocking problem (the answer they're fishing for): Its greatest disadvantage is that 2PC is a blocking protocol. After a participant votes Yes it is "in doubt" — it holds its locks and cannot unilaterally decide . If the coordinator crashes after collecting votes but before broadcasting the decision, the in-doubt participants must block indefinitely , holding locks, until the coordinator recovers.

There is no safe timeout: the participant can't abort (maybe others already committed) and can't commit (maybe others aborted). Why a participant can't just guess Suppose P2 voted Yes, then loses contact with both the coordinator and its peers. It cannot ask "did we commit?" If it assumes commit and the real decision was abort, it diverges; if it assumes abort and the decision was commit, it diverges the other way. Safety forces it to wait. This is precisely the tension the CAP theorem predicts: 2PC chooses Consistency over Availability — it would rather freeze than risk divergence, making it a CP protocol.

Other costs Latency & disk: multiple forced log flushes to stable storage and two network round-trips per commit. Locks held across the round-trip hurt throughput and create contention/deadlock risk. Coordinator is a single point of failure unless it is itself replicated (which is what real systems do — replicate the coordinator via Paxos/Raft). Optimizations — presumed abort , presumed commit , tree/dynamic 2PC — cut messages and logging but never remove blocking.

🧮 3PC and the modern alternatives Three-Phase Commit and what actually replaced 2PC Three-Phase Commit (3PC) attacks the blocking flaw by inserting a pre-commit phase between voting and committing, and by giving every state a timeout. The extra phase guarantees that before anyone commits, everyone knows the decision will be commit . So if the coordinator dies, a surviving participant can look at its own state and safely time out toward the right outcome: if it reached pre-commit, it commits; if not, it aborts. This makes 3PC non-blocking under a single fail-stop failure.

2PC: [Prepare/Vote] ────────────────▶ [Commit] │ ▲ └── coordinator dies here → IN-DOUBT, BLOCKS ✗ 3PC: [Prepare/Vote] ─▶ [Pre-Commit] ─▶ [Commit] │ ▲ └ everyone knows outcome → timeout is SAFE ✓ The catch — and the reason 3PC is a textbook curiosity rather than a workhorse — is that it assumes synchronous timing and fail-stop crashes. Under network partitions , 3PC can still produce inconsistent decisions: two sides can time out toward different outcomes. It also adds a whole extra round-trip, worsening latency. Real systems therefore skipped 3PC and went to consensus .

Approach Blocking? Handles partitions? Used in practice 2PC Yes (coordinator failure) Chooses to block (CP) XA transactions, distributed SQL 3PC No (fail-stop only) No — can diverge under partition Rare; mostly academic Consensus (Paxos/Raft) No (majority quorum) Yes — minority stalls, majority proceeds etcd, ZooKeeper, Spanner, CockroachDB Saga pattern No Yes (eventual, no locks) Microservices, long-lived business txns The two winners you must name Consensus-backed commit: instead of one fragile coordinator, replicate the commit decision through Raft/Paxos so a majority agreeing is the decision — the coordinator can fail and a new one takes over from the replicated log.

Google Spanner and CockroachDB run 2PC on top of Paxos/Raft groups, getting atomic commit without the single-coordinator block. See the consensus page . Saga pattern: for microservices, avoid distributed locks entirely. Break the transaction into a sequence of local commits, each with a compensating action to undo it. If step 3 fails, run the compensations for steps 2 and 1 (refund, restock). You trade atomic isolation for availability and eventual consistency — the AP-style answer to the same problem. ☁️ AWS mapping How atomic commit shows up on AWS Modern AWS architectures generally avoid classic cross-service 2PC and lean on single-partition transactions, idempotency, or the Saga pattern.

Need AWS service / pattern Why Atomic multi-item write in one store DynamoDB TransactWriteItems ACID across items in a region without you running 2PC — the service coordinates internally. Saga orchestration AWS Step Functions Model each step + compensating step as a state machine; built-in retries and catch/rollback branches. Saga choreography EventBridge / SQS / SNS Services emit events; each reacts and emits the next, with compensation events on failure. Reliable "commit the DB write AND publish the event" Transactional Outbox + DynamoDB Streams / CDC Write business row and outbox row in one local transaction; a relay publishes the event — dodges dual-write 2PC.

Exactly-once effect Idempotency keys (DynamoDB conditional writes) Make retries safe so you don't need distributed locking. The interview-grade takeaway: in a cloud microservices world you almost never run true 2PC across services — you use Step Functions Sagas plus the Outbox pattern and idempotency to get correctness without the blocking coordinator. 💻 C# implementation — a 2PC coordinator This models the coordinator driving prepare → decide, and shows exactly where a Yes vote makes a participant "in doubt." Note the durable log writes at the decision point — that record is what lets recovery finish the transaction after a crash.

For microservices, prefer a Saga library (e.g. MassTransit sagas, or AWS Step Functions) over rolling your own coordinator. ⚖️ Trade-offs, bottlenecks & likely follow-ups "What is the single biggest problem with 2PC?" It blocks. If the coordinator fails after participants vote Yes, they're stuck holding locks in an in-doubt state until it recovers — it can't guarantee termination. That's the answer to lead with.

"Does 3PC fully fix it?" Only under synchronous timing and fail-stop crashes. Under network partitions 3PC can still make inconsistent decisions, and it costs an extra round-trip. That's why production systems use consensus (Raft/Paxos) instead. "How do real databases get atomic commit without blocking?" They replicate the coordinator/decision through consensus. Spanner and CockroachDB run 2PC over Paxos/Raft groups, so any single coordinator failure is recovered from the replicated log by a new leader — no permanent block. "When would you use a Saga instead?" Across microservices/services with separate databases, where holding distributed locks is unacceptable.

Sagas do local commits with compensating transactions and accept eventual consistency — trading isolation for availability. "Is 2PC consistent or available (CAP)?" Consistent — it's a CP protocol. It sacrifices availability by blocking rather than risk two participants diverging. 🗣️ Interview cheat sheet 30-second pitch: "Two-Phase Commit gives atomic all-or-nothing commit across nodes. Phase 1 the coordinator asks everyone to prepare and vote; a Yes is a durable promise. Phase 2 it commits iff everyone voted Yes. The fatal flaw is blocking: if the coordinator dies after the votes, prepared participants are in-doubt and freeze holding locks.

Three-Phase Commit adds a pre-commit phase to become non-blocking, but breaks under partitions — so real systems use consensus like Raft, or the Saga pattern for microservices." Two phases: Prepare/Vote → Commit/Complete. Yes vote = binding, durable promise. Blocking problem: coordinator crash after votes ⇒ in-doubt participants block, holding locks. No safe timeout. 2PC is CP: prefers consistency, sacrifices availability. 3PC = +pre-commit phase ⇒ non-blocking under fail-stop, but unsafe under partitions. Modern answer: consensus-backed commit (Spanner/CockroachDB on Paxos/Raft) or Sagas (compensating transactions) for microservices.

AWS: Step Functions Sagas + transactional Outbox + idempotency, not cross-service 2PC. ❓ FAQ — your follow-up questions Questions asked about this topic No follow-up questions yet — ask one about this topic and it'll be logged here with a compact answer. 📚 Sources Two-phase commit protocol — Wikipedia Three-phase commit protocol — Wikipedia Saga pattern — microservices.io (Chris Richardson) Google Spanner — 2PC over Paxos, TrueTime Bernstein, Hadzilacos & Goodman — "Concurrency Control and Recovery in Database Systems" (atomic commit). System Design · Interview Prep Design Uber (Ride-Sharing) Millions of moving drivers, millions of waiting riders, and a match in under a second — the classic real-time, geospatial, event-driven system design. 🎯 Scenario 🧑‍🎓 Laymen 📋 Requirements 🏗️ Architecture 🎬 Animation 🔍 Deep-dive 🧮 DSA ☁️ AWS 💻 C# code ⚖️ Trade-offs 🗣️ Cheat sheet ❓ FAQ 📚 Sources 🎯 Real-world scenario What we're building & where it's used You're building the guts of a ride-sharing platform : a rider opens the app, sees the nearest cars moving on the map in real time, taps Request , and within a second a driver is offered the trip.

Behind that one tap is a continuous firehose of GPS pings from millions of moving vehicles, a geospatial index that answers "who is within 2 km of this lat/lng right now?" thousands of times per second, and a matching engine that reserves exactly one driver per rider even when three riders reach for the same car in the same 200 ms window. This is the canonical real-time marketplace problem, solved in production by Uber, Lyft, Ola, Didi, Grab, Bolt, Careem , and — with variations — by DoorDash, Uber Eats, Instacart, Amazon Flex .

It shows up in interviews because it forces you to reason about write-heavy geo-indexing , consistent hashing over stateful services , persistent bidirectional connections , event streaming (Kafka) , and partial-failure recovery — all inside a single, tangible product everyone has used. Real-world grounding: Uber's own dispatch stack introduced this pattern ( Supply / Demand / DISCO ), built on Ringpop (consistent hashing + SWIM gossip), Google S2 for the live dispatch grid, and H3 (Uber's own hexagonal grid) for supply-and-demand analytics that drive surge pricing .

🧑‍🎓 In laymen terms (for a beginner) Explain it like I have never opened a code editor You're standing on a corner, tired, and you want a car to come pick you up. You open an app, it shows you tiny cars moving around on a map, you tap a button, and a minute later a car pulls up. Simple to feel — enormously tricky to build. Let's walk through it like a story. Every driver's phone is like a tiny lighthouse , blinking its exact position out to a big control room every four seconds . Multiply that by millions of drivers around the world and you get a river of blinks pouring in — millions per second, day and night.

Now the trick: when you tap Request , the app has to find the drivers near you , not sift through every driver on Earth. So the world is chopped up into a huge grid of small tiles — think of the city like a giant honeycomb where each hexagon is about half a kilometer wide. Every driver "lives" in one tile at any moment. When you ask for a ride, the system just looks in your tile and a few neighboring tiles. That turns "search five million drivers" into "look inside a dozen tiles" — the difference between checking every house in a city and just checking your street.

Once a few candidates are found, another service asks: Which one gets to me fastest by road? (Not "shortest as the crow flies" — real streets, one-ways, traffic.) It picks the winner and offers the ride. The tricky part here is that only one driver can get your ride — even if two riders tap at the same instant for the same car, the system has to say "yes" to exactly one and "sorry, try again" to the other. Think of a single bakery ticket: whoever grabs it first, gets the loaf. And the last bit — surge pricing . At 8pm on New Year's Eve in a downtown block, riders vastly outnumber drivers.

The system watches, per hexagon, how many people are asking versus how many cars are free, and if the ratio is bad it nudges the price up. Higher price pulls more drivers into the area, and prices settle back down. It's not greed; it's a thermostat for supply and demand, tuned every few seconds per tile. Products that work this way: Uber, Lyft, Ola, DoorDash, Instacart . Same shape, different cargo — sometimes it's you, sometimes it's a burrito. 📋 Requirements & scale Requirements and back-of-the-envelope math Functional Drivers broadcast their location continuously; the system tracks who is available , on-trip , or offline .

Riders can request a ride from a lat/lng; the system returns the best-matched nearby driver within ~1 second . A driver can be matched to at most one active rider — no double-booking. Both apps maintain a live picture: rider sees the ETA and car moving; driver sees turn-by-turn. Surge pricing is computed per geographic cell in near real time. Payments, ratings, notifications, and trip history are stored durably. Non-functional Latency: match < 1 s p99; location update ingest < 100 ms p99. Availability: five 9s on the match path — a downed matching engine strands entire cities. Consistency: per-driver assignment must be strongly consistent (linearizable CAS).

The geo index itself can be eventually consistent — a driver's location being 4 s stale is fine. Scale: tens of millions of DAUs; millions of active drivers globally. The first justifies Kafka + in-memory sharding; the second is why you don't need to store the live index in a database at all — you can rebuild it in one ping cycle. 🏗️ High-level architecture How the pieces fit together Think of the platform as three planes riding on top of a Kafka firehose .

The ingest plane (green) takes the driver-location tsunami and routes each ping to the shard that owns that geographic cell. The match plane (blue) takes a rider request, queries the live geo index for nearby drivers, ranks them by road-network ETA, and atomically reserves the winner. The marketplace plane (amber) consumes the same location stream to run surge pricing and demand prediction, feeding the price back to the rider at request time. Two protocol choices matter. Drivers push locations over a persistent WebSocket / bidirectional gRPC channel — much cheaper than an HTTPS handshake per ping, and it lets the server push back a match offer instantly.

Riders open the same kind of channel while watching cars. Everything else (payments, history) is boring stateless HTTP. Ingesting a million pings per second Every driver's phone opens a persistent WebSocket (or bidirectional gRPC stream) to the API gateway when it goes online. Roughly every four seconds the app pushes a compact protobuf frame containing driver_id , lat , lng , bearing , speed , and a monotonic seq .

Using a persistent channel rather than fresh HTTPS per ping is a huge win : no TLS handshake per update, half-duplex is free, and the same socket carries offer pushes back to the driver. The gateway does not write to a database. It publishes to Kafka on a topic like location.driver.updates , partitioned by driver_id — that keeps a single driver's updates ordered on one partition. From here two consumers fan out: the Location Service updates the live geo index, and downstream analytics consumers feed surge, ETA training, fraud detection, and long-term storage. 2. The live geospatial index (Location Service) The Location Service is a stateful, sharded, in-memory fleet.

Each node owns a set of geographic cells; the world is chopped by Google S2 (Uber's dispatch grid at level 12, ~3–6 km²) or H3 hexagons at a comparable resolution. The cell_id is the sharding key, and shards are placed on a consistent hash ring managed by Ringpop with the SWIM gossip protocol for membership. Within a shard, two co-located maps live in memory: cell → List<Driver> and driver_id → Location . Updates within the same cell are O(1) — just mutate the driver's lat/lng. A cell crossing costs three coordinated writes: remove from the old cell's list, add to the new cell's list, update the driver → cell pointer.

If the destination cell lives on a different shard, the update is rerouted via the ring. Nothing is written to disk on the hot path. The index is a throwaway: if a shard dies, the next four seconds of driver pings will fully repopulate it. Location durability lives in Kafka's retained log; the shard is just a fast projection. 3. Finding nearby drivers (the query side) To find drivers near a rider, the Matching service converts the rider's lat/lng to a cell ID and asks: give me all drivers in this cell and its k-ring neighbors . In H3 that's kRing(cell, 1) — the center hex plus the six surrounding hexes.

Why the ring? Because a driver 20 m from the rider could easily be sitting on the other side of a cell boundary; a single-cell lookup would miss them. Cell size is chosen so that k=1 covers the intended match radius (typically 1–2 km). The candidate set (dozens, not millions) is then filtered — must be available , must have the right vehicle class, must not be on-trip — and passed to the ETA/routing service to compute a road-network arrival time using OSRM (Dijkstra with contraction hierarchies precomputed nightly). The winner is the driver with the smallest ETA. 4.

The atomic reservation (the interesting part) Now the subtle bit: at any instant, three riders may all be reaching for the same driver. The system must reserve the driver for exactly one rider — this is the one place we need linearizability . Uber's DISCO does a compare-and-swap on the driver's status field: UPDATE drivers SET status='reserved', reserved_by='rider-42', reserved_at=now() WHERE driver_id='D7' AND status='available'; Whichever transaction executes first sees 1 row affected and wins. The others see zero and iterate to the next candidate. This is coordinated per driver_id , so total contention is tiny — a hot key would need multiple riders reaching for one specific car.

The rest of the system remains eventually consistent. 5. Surge pricing (the marketplace loop) A stream job (Flink or Spark Streaming) consumes the location firehose plus a parallel ride.requests topic, bucketing both by H3 cell at ~1 km resolution over a rolling 1–5 minute window . For each cell it computes a simple ratio: open requests ÷ available drivers . When that ratio crosses thresholds, a surge_multiplier for that cell is written to a low-latency store (Redis) keyed by H3 cell. When a rider requests a ride, the matching service reads the surge multiplier for the rider's cell and applies it to the fare estimate.

The higher price signals both directions: riders may defer, and drivers in nearby cells are notified — many will migrate toward the surge tile, closing the gap in minutes. The whole loop is fully event-driven : no user asked for a price update; the stream job is always running. 6. Hot cells & the boundary problem Downtown at 5pm can hold thousands of drivers in one cell — an obvious hotspot. Two mitigations: (a) adaptive resolution — use finer cells in dense zones so no cell is overloaded; and (b) sub-shard splitting — split a hot cell into C#0..C#3 keyed by hash(driver_id) , so writes distribute and reads fan out four ways in parallel.

Uber's engineering blog notes that hard-coded cell size (level 12) is a known limitation of their earlier S2-based design. 7. Failure & datacenter failover Because the live index is throwaway, a shard crash is nearly free — the ring rebalances, in-flight requests retry, drivers repopulate the new owner in a single ping cycle. For full datacenter failover , Uber uses a clever trick: DISCO periodically sends the driver's phone an encrypted state digest of any in-progress trip. If the primary DC dies and the secondary DC has no trip state, the driver's next ping uploads the digest back , reconstructing state without cross-DC replication of hot trip data.

🧮 The DSA behind it Data structures & algorithms Almost every classic geospatial data structure appears somewhere in a ride-sharing stack. Interviewers love to see you name them and pick one with reasons. Component Structure / Algorithm Why chosen Complexity Live geo index (dispatch) Hierarchical grid cells — S2 (int64 cell IDs) or H3 (hex cells) Cell ID is a natural shard key; fixed-cost lookup; ring queries via bit ops. Uber uses S2 in dispatch, H3 in analytics. Insert / lookup: O(1) ; k-ring: O(k²) cells Analytics / surge H3 hexagons , 16 resolutions, 122 base cells Uniform neighbor distance (unlike squares, which have 2). Perfect for supply/demand smoothing.

Same as above Alternative index Geohash (base-32 string encoding) Simple, portable, prefix-friendly for range scans. Downside: rectangular cells vary in size by latitude, and 8 vs 6 neighbors. Insert / lookup: O(1) ; adjacency: O(8) Alternative index Quadtree — dynamic recursive subdivision Great when driver density is very uneven (splits hot regions automatically). Trickier to shard across machines than fixed grids. Insert / lookup: O(log n) ; range query: O(√n + k) for balanced trees Consistent hashing (Ringpop) Hash ring with virtual nodes + SWIM gossip Minimizes reshuffle when a shard joins/leaves; gossip converges in O(log N) .

Lookup: O(log N) with sorted-set impl Road-network ETA Dijkstra / A* / Contraction Hierarchies (OSRM) Real streets have turn costs, one-ways, traffic — cannot use haversine. Contraction hierarchies precompute shortcuts to answer queries in ms. Query: O(k · log n) with contraction hierarchies Matching contention CAS / linearizable UPDATE on driver_id Single-key linearizability — cheap, correct, no distributed locks. Amortized O(1) Surge windowing Tumbling / sliding windows over Kafka stream Compute supply/demand ratios per H3 cell per minute; standard Flink pattern.

O(events / window) Trip state Finite state machine (requested → matched → en_route → started → completed) Clarity, invariants, idempotent transitions. O(1) per transition Why H3 (hexagons) and not squares? Hexagons have a single neighbor distance : every one of a hex's six neighbors sits the same distance from its center. Squares have two neighbor distances (edge-shared vs. diagonally-shared), and triangles have three. This matters when you're computing gradients — like "how does surge fall off from the hot cell to its neighbors?" — because a uniform metric means fewer coefficients and much simpler math.

H3 also uses 16 resolutions where each level's cells are ~1/7 the area of their parent, and cell IDs pack into a 64-bit int for cheap hashing and set membership. Why not just a B-tree on (lat, lng)? Because a 2-D range query lat BETWEEN a AND b AND lng BETWEEN c AND d on a B-tree is a bad fit — the B-tree is 1-D. You either scan a wide range or maintain two indexes and intersect. Grid cells collapse 2-D locality into a 1-D key, and that key doubles as a shard partition. ☁️ AWS implementation Mapping the design to AWS If we were rebuilding this on AWS today, here's how each box maps.

Uber's own stack pre-dates most managed services and is largely home-grown (Ringpop, Schemaless, in-house Kafka), but AWS has direct equivalents. Component AWS service Why Persistent driver / rider connections AWS API Gateway (WebSocket) or ALB + ECS/EKS gRPC Managed WS terminates millions of connections; gRPC on ALB when you need bidi streaming and protobuf. Location firehose Amazon MSK (managed Kafka) or Kinesis Data Streams MSK gives Kafka semantics with partition-by- driver_id . Kinesis is simpler if you're all-in on AWS.

Location / matching services ECS Fargate or EKS Stateful shards need a container platform with per-pod DNS; combine with an ALB per shard set or service discovery via Cloud Map. Consistent-hash sharding Roll your own (Ringpop-style) on top of ECS No managed equivalent — this is the hard part. DynamoDB partitioning doesn't help because the state lives in RAM. Hot state (surge multipliers, session) ElastiCache for Redis (cluster mode) Sub-ms reads for surge lookups on the request path. Trip / user / payment records DynamoDB + Aurora DynamoDB for high-cardinality writes (trips, ratings); Aurora for financial ledgers.

Analytics stream processing Kinesis Data Analytics (Flink) or MSK + self-managed Flink on EKS Windowed aggregations by H3 cell for surge. Raw GPS trail archive S3 (Kinesis Firehose → Parquet) Cheap, queryable via Athena; source for ML training. Push notifications SNS / SQS / APNS & FCM Fan out driver offers, receipts, marketing. Maps & routing Amazon Location Service or self-hosted OSRM on EC2 Location Service gives geocoding + routing; large fleets typically self-host OSRM for cost. CDN & edge auth CloudFront + Cognito Static app bundles, driver auth flows. Multi-region failover Route 53 + Global Accelerator Health-check-driven cutover.

Deployment picture: two regions active–active, drivers pin to their nearest via Route 53 latency-based routing. Location Service pods run in each region, backed by an in-region MSK cluster. Trip state writes go to a regional DynamoDB with global tables replicating summary records. Surge lives in ElastiCache regionally — surge is inherently local, so no cross-region replication is needed. The nightly graph build for routing runs on EMR and publishes CH-compressed graphs to S3 for OSRM pods to load. 💻 C# implementation The core of the system is the geospatial shard plus the atomic reservation.

Below is an interview-ready reference: an in-memory geo index keyed by cell, a k-ring nearby-driver query, and a CAS-style reservation. In production you'd back the geo maps with ConcurrentDictionary and per-cell locks; the reservation would be a single-partition Cassandra or DynamoDB conditional update. // GeoIndexShard.cs — one shard owns a set of H3 cells and keeps drivers in memory. // The real system uses the H3 library; here we abstract cell resolution behind ICellIndex.

about this code: Out-of-order pings are dropped via ts comparison. Kafka partitions by driver_id already give per-driver ordering, but retries and DC failover can rewind — the timestamp check protects us. Cell crossings are the only moderately expensive path — same-cell updates are just a field mutation. TryReserve is CAS in a loop , mirroring what Cassandra's LWT or DynamoDB's ConditionExpression would give you across nodes. In production this call goes to the durable store, not the in-memory shard. ICellIndex is abstracted so you can plug in H3, S2, or geohash. Uber's own OSS H3 has a .NET binding; S2 does too.

Alternative languages/tools: Uber's own dispatch was Node.js (fits async I/O well); many peers now use Go for the geo shards (better GC for sustained high-throughput). C# / .NET is a perfectly reasonable choice on modern kestrel + ASP.NET Core. ⚖️ Trade-offs, bottlenecks & likely follow-ups Bottlenecks and mitigations Hot cells. Downtown is a spatial hot key: one cell with 20K drivers dominates a shard. Mitigate with (a) adaptive resolution — finer cells in dense zones; (b) sub-shard splitting — hash driver_id into cell#0..#3 and scatter-gather queries; (c) shed the oldest queued pings first when a shard's inbox backs up. Ingest write amplification.

Every driver writes every 4 s regardless of whether they moved. Compress: skip pings if displacement < ε and heading unchanged. Batch pings client-side into a single 4-second frame with sub-second sub-samples. Some fleets drop from 4 s → 2 s only when a trip is active. Cross-cell coordination. A driver near the boundary flips cells often. Add hysteresis: don't reassign until the driver is > ε deep into the new cell. ETA is the slowest step. Road-network Dijkstra on a big graph is the highest-latency piece per match. Contraction hierarchies + memoized ETAs per (origin cell, destination cell) at coarse resolution take it from 100 ms to a few ms. Consistency choices Geo index: eventual.

A stale location by 4 seconds means we might offer a driver who is 30 m off — the driver either accepts or the system re-matches. Cheap error. Driver status: linearizable per key. Double-booking is a product bug we cannot ship. CAS on a single key gives strong consistency where we need it without a global transaction. Trip state: sequential per trip. Trip transitions (requested → matched → started → ended) are single-key state machines, easy to keep consistent. Failure modes Shard death: Ringpop rebalances; the fresh owner rebuilds its slice of the index from the next ping cycle. Match requests in flight retry idempotently.

Kafka outage: The gateway falls back to a smaller regional store or short-lived in-memory buffer; on recovery, the backlog drains. Surge freezes at its last value. Network partition (rider ↔ driver): WebSocket reconnects with an exponential backoff carrying the trip ID; the server treats the trip as authoritative until a timeout. DC failover: The encrypted state-digest trick puts a lightweight backup of trip state on the driver's phone — the ultimate distributed backup medium. Likely interviewer follow-ups How would you handle a stalled/crashed driver phone? Timestamp each ping.

If a driver's last ping is older than N intervals (say 20 s), mark Offline , remove from the cell's candidate set, and stop offering. When a fresh ping arrives, re-add. Why not just put every driver in Redis with GEOADD? Redis geo commands work for small fleets but are single-node bottlenecks at Uber scale — GEOSEARCH on millions of points is slow and Redis doesn't shard by geo naturally. In-memory sharded services with a consistent hash ring scale linearly; Redis geo is fine for a startup, not for a global fleet. Quadtree vs. geohash vs. H3 vs.

S2 — how do you pick? Fixed grids (H3, S2, geohash) shard trivially by cell ID and give O(1) lookups; use them when driver density is roughly uniform or when you can adapt resolution. Quadtrees adapt to skew automatically — great for extreme non-uniformity — but are harder to shard and rebalance. Uber picked S2 for dispatch (fixed level 12 cells) and H3 for analytics (hexagons for uniform gradients / surge). How does surge feed back into behavior? The multiplier is displayed to the rider (deterrent) and pushed to nearby drivers via notification ("busy area — 1.8×"). Over ~2–5 minutes drivers migrate in, the ratio normalizes, and surge decays.

It's a slow control loop over Kafka events, not a synchronous negotiation. Why not a single global geo database? Because at 1–2 M writes/sec no single-master database keeps up cheaply, and geo locality lets us shard perfectly by cell — same-city queries hit the same shard, cross-region traffic is naturally zero. Splitting is free. How do you keep matches fair across drivers? DISCO can factor idle time and recent trip volume when ranking within a candidate set — not purely nearest-ETA. There's also a per-driver rate limiter on how many offers they can decline before de-prioritization. 🗣️ Interview cheat sheet 30-second pitch: "Uber is a real-time marketplace.

Drivers stream GPS pings every 4 s over persistent WebSockets into a Kafka firehose — about 1–2 million writes per second at scale. The pings feed an in-memory geospatial index sharded by H3 or S2 cell IDs on a consistent hash ring. When a rider requests a ride, the matching service does a k-ring lookup in the rider's cell, ranks candidates by road-network ETA via OSRM, and reserves the winner with a linearizable CAS on driver status. A parallel stream job aggregates supply and demand per H3 cell every minute for surge pricing.

The whole hot path is throwaway state — nothing is persisted on the location-update path — so shards die cheaply and drivers repopulate them in one ping cycle." The five numbers to volunteer: 5M active drivers · GPS every 4 s · ~1.25 M writes/s · ~500 MB in-memory index · sub-second match latency. The five talking points that win: (1) H3 hexagons over squares for uniform neighbor distance; (2) k-ring to handle boundary drivers; (3) OSRM/CH for road-network ETA (not haversine); (4) atomic CAS on driver_id for reservation; (5) throwaway in-memory shards backed by Kafka. Where consistency lives: eventual for locations, linearizable per-key for status — say this out loud.

Surge is a control loop: supply/demand ratio per cell → multiplier → decays as drivers migrate. Not a bidding auction. Datacenter failover trick: encrypted state digest on the driver's phone reconstructs trip state — impress the interviewer with this one. ❓ FAQ — your follow-up questions Questions asked about this topic No follow-up questions yet — ask one about this topic and it'll be logged here with a compact answer.

System Design · Interview Prep 🔗 URL Shortener Turn a long, ugly link into a tiny one like bit.ly/3xY9aZ — and serve the redirect in milliseconds, billions of times a day. 🎯 Scenario 🧑‍🎓 Laymen 📋 Requirements 🏗️ Architecture 🔍 Deep-dive 🧮 DSA ☁️ AWS 💻 C# code ⚖️ Trade-offs 🗣️ Cheat sheet ❓ FAQ 📚 Sources 🎯 Real-world scenario What we're building & where it's used A URL shortener is a service that takes a long URL — say a 200-character product link with tracking parameters — and returns a compact alias such as https://bit.ly/3xY9aZ . When anyone visits the short link, the service looks up the original URL and issues an HTTP redirect so the browser lands on the real page.

It sounds trivial, but it's a favourite interview question precisely because it hides almost every distributed-systems concept behind a one-sentence problem statement: unique ID generation, read-heavy caching, horizontal sharding, the consistency-vs-availability trade-off, and global low-latency delivery. You use one every day. Bit.ly and TinyURL are the classic public shorteners; t.co is Twitter/X's internal shortener that wraps every link in a tweet; lnkd.in (LinkedIn), fb.me (Facebook), youtu.be (YouTube), and g.co (Google) are first-party shorteners.

Companies build them for very practical reasons: Shareability — short links fit in SMS, tweets, QR codes, and printed ads where character count or pixels matter. Analytics & attribution — every click can be logged, so marketers see geography, device, referrer, and campaign performance in real time. Link management — the destination behind a short code can be changed later, links can expire, and malicious destinations can be revoked centrally. Safety & branding — wrapping outbound links (like t.co) lets a platform scan for spam/malware and present a branded domain.

Say this in the interview: "It's a read-heavy, write-light key-value lookup at global scale where the hard parts are generating collision-free short keys and serving redirects in single-digit milliseconds." 🧑‍🎓 In laymen terms The tiny sticker with a code, and the giant address book You've probably tried to text a friend a link to a product on Amazon and watched a horrifying 250-character monster tumble into the chat — full of question marks, equals signs, and random numbers. Nobody wants to type or share that. What you really want is something like bit.ly/xyz — six letters, easy to say out loud, fits on a business card. That's the whole job of a URL shortener. Think of it like this.

Imagine you're organising a wedding and you print out little sticker codes to hand to guests — "Table 7", "Table 14". Each sticker is short and cheap, but the code by itself doesn't tell you anything. It only makes sense because there's a huge printed address book at the entrance saying "Table 7 → Aunt Sarah's family in the red van, seated left of the DJ." The sticker is the short link; the address book is the shortener's database. When someone shows up with a sticker, the greeter flips to that entry and points them to the real destination. You use these every day.

When you click a link in a tweet, that t.co/abc you glimpsed is a sticker Twitter attached — it looks it up in its address book and quietly redirects you to the real article. Bit.ly, TinyURL, LinkedIn's lnkd.in , YouTube's youtu.be — all doing the same trick. The reason companies bother: short links fit in text messages, look tidy on posters, print nicely on receipts, and — bonus — the sticker can be counted every time someone touches it, so marketers can see which poster actually worked. The hard part? Making sure no two stickers ever collide , and answering "which sticker is this?" in the blink of an eye when a billion people are asking at once.

That's what all the clever machinery underneath is quietly solving. 📋 Requirements & scale Requirements and back-of-the-envelope math Always split requirements into functional (what it does) and non-functional (how well it must do it). Interviewers grade you on volunteering the non-functional ones and the capacity math without being asked. Functional requirements Given a long URL, return a unique short URL. Given a short URL, redirect (HTTP 301/302) to the original long URL. Optional: custom aliases (vanity links), link expiration (TTL), and per-link click analytics. Non-functional requirements High availability — if the redirect path is down, every link everywhere breaks. Target 99.9%+.

Low latency — redirects must feel instant (< ~10 ms server-side, single-digit ms from cache/edge). Scalable & read-heavy — reads dominate writes by ~100:1. Short codes must be unpredictable-ish and unique — no collisions, hard to enumerate. Capacity estimation (the numbers to quote) Assume 100 million new URLs per month with a 100:1 read:write ratio — a common interview setup.

The math falls out from there: Metric Estimate How you derive it New URLs (writes) 100M / month given assumption Write QPS ~40 writes/sec 100M ÷ (30 × 24 × 3600 ≈ 2.5M sec) Read QPS ~4,000 reads/sec 40 × 100 (read:write ratio) Storage / record ~500 bytes short code + long URL + metadata + timestamps Storage / year ~600 GB/yr (~3 TB over 5 yr) 1.2B records/yr × 500 B Read bandwidth ~2 MB/sec 4,000 reads/sec × 500 B Cache memory (hot 20%) ~35 GB/day cache the 20% of links driving 80% of reads Key length 7 chars (Base62) 62⁷ ≈ 3.5 trillion combinations The punchline to say out loud: "Storage is small and writes are trivial — only ~40/sec.

The system is utterly dominated by reads, so my design is really a distributed cache in front of a key-value store , optimised for redirect latency." Note: the canonical system-design-primer pastebin variant uses smaller numbers (~4 writes/sec, ~40 reads/sec, 360M links over 3 years); the shape is identical — pick a scale and stay consistent. 🏗️ High-level architecture How the pieces fit together There are two distinct paths and you should draw them separately.

The write path (create a short link) is rare and can afford a little work: a request hits the load balancer, lands on a stateless write service, which obtains a unique ID, Base62-encodes it into a 7-char code, and persists the code → long URL mapping in the database. The read path (resolve & redirect) is the hot path and must be brutally fast: the request hits a CDN/edge, then the load balancer, then a stateless read service that checks Redis cache first and only falls through to the database on a miss, returning a 301/302 redirect. Click events are emitted asynchronously to a queue so analytics never slow the redirect.

Synchronous request path Async (fire-and-forget) analytics Cache Walk the interviewer through the redirect: client requests /3xY9aZ → edge/LB routes to a read service → Redis lookup → on hit, return 301 immediately; on miss, read the DB, populate the cache, then redirect → fire a click event onto the queue and return. That's the whole hot path, and it's why latency stays in single-digit milliseconds. 🔍 Component deep-dive 1. Short-code generation (the heart of the design) This is what the interviewer is really testing.

There are three credible strategies, and you should name the trade-offs: Hash + truncate (MD5/SHA → Base62, take 7 chars): hash the long URL (plus a salt like timestamp), Base62-encode, and keep the first 7 characters. Simple and stateless, but can collide , so you must check the DB and retry on collision, and identical URLs naturally map to the same code. Counter + Base62 (recommended): keep a globally unique, monotonically increasing 64-bit counter; Base62-encode the number to get the code. Zero collisions by construction and O(1) generation.

The challenge becomes distributing the counter — solved with a Key Generation Service (KGS) that hands out ranges/tickets to each app server, or a Snowflake-style ID (timestamp + machine-id + sequence). Pre-generated keys (KGS): a separate service generates random unique 7-char keys in advance, stores them, and hands them to write servers in batches. Generation is moved off the critical path entirely. Most strong answers settle on counter-based Base62 via a KGS or Snowflake because it eliminates the collision-check round-trip and keeps writes O(1). 2.

Caching strategy Because reads dominate, an in-memory cache (Redis/Memcached) sits in front of the DB using a cache-aside (lazy loading) pattern with an LRU eviction policy — the 20% of links that are "hot" (a viral campaign, a pinned tweet) serve the bulk of traffic from memory. Mappings are immutable once created, so cache invalidation is a non-issue except for deletions/expiry; you can cache aggressively with long TTLs. 3. Datastore & partitioning The access pattern is a pure key lookup ( code → long URL ), so a NoSQL key-value store (DynamoDB, Cassandra) is the natural fit — it scales horizontally and gives single-digit-ms reads.

Partition/shard by the short code (hash-based sharding) so reads and writes spread evenly across nodes; range-based sharding risks hot partitions. A relational DB works at smaller scale with the short code as the primary key. 4. Redirect type: 301 vs 302 A subtle point that impresses: 301 (permanent) lets browsers cache the redirect, cutting load — but then you lose per-click analytics because repeat visits never hit your server. 302 (temporary) forces every click through your service, preserving analytics at the cost of more traffic. Analytics-driven products (bit.ly) lean 302. 5.

Analytics & rate limiting Click events are pushed to a queue (Kafka/SQS) and aggregated offline so the redirect never waits on analytics writes. A rate limiter on the create endpoint (by API key/IP) prevents abuse and key-space exhaustion. 🧮 The DSA behind it Data structures & algorithms Behind the buzzwords, a URL shortener runs on a few classic data-structures-and-algorithms ideas: Base62 encoding — convert a 64-bit integer ID into [0-9a-zA-Z] (62 symbols). It's just base conversion: repeatedly take n % 62 and n /= 62 . 7 digits give 62⁷ ≈ 3.5 trillion codes. Base62 (not Base64) avoids the URL-unsafe + and / characters.

Distributed counter / Snowflake ID — a 64-bit unique ID assembled from a timestamp, a machine/worker id, and a per-ms sequence counter, guaranteeing global uniqueness without coordination on every request. Hashing (MD5/SHA-256) — used by the hash-and-truncate strategy to map a long URL to a fixed-width, uniformly-distributed value before Base62. Hash table — the cache and the KV store are conceptually one giant hash map: O(1) average lookup from code to URL. Bloom filter — a probabilistic set used to answer "have we seen this short code / custom alias before?" in O(1) memory-cheap time, avoiding a DB round-trip on most negatives.
