⚖️ Trade-offs, bottlenecks & likely follow-ups Where it breaks under load: the redirect read path is the bottleneck, mitigated by caching and edge CDN. The unique-ID generator is the second risk — a single global counter is a single point of failure and a write hotspot, which is exactly why you distribute it (KGS ranges or Snowflake). Hot keys (one viral link) can overload a single cache node; mitigate with client-side caching, request coalescing, or replicating the hot entry. Consistency vs availability: a URL mapping is immutable after creation, so eventual consistency is fine — favour availability (AP) on the read path.

A brief replication lag just means a freshly created link might 404 for a few hundred ms; acceptable. Never sacrifice redirect availability for strong consistency. Q: How do you avoid two servers generating the same short code? A: Don't hash-and-hope. Use a globally unique 64-bit ID source — a KGS handing out non-overlapping ranges, or Snowflake (timestamp+machineId+sequence) — then Base62-encode it. Uniqueness is guaranteed by construction, so no collision check is needed. Q: 301 or 302 redirect? A: 302 if you want per-click analytics (every visit hits your server); 301 if you want to offload traffic by letting browsers cache the redirect, at the cost of losing repeat-click data.

Q: How do you handle custom/vanity aliases? A: Treat the alias as a chosen key; check existence (Bloom filter → DB) and reject duplicates. Keep custom and generated keys in the same namespace so they can't collide. Q: How do you expire or delete links? A: Store a TTL/expiry timestamp; lazily treat expired rows as 404 on read and sweep them with a background job (or DynamoDB native TTL). Evict from cache on delete. Q: How do you stop abuse and key-space exhaustion? A: Rate-limit the create endpoint per API key/IP (token bucket), require auth for bulk creation, and scan destinations for malware/spam.

🗣️ Interview cheat sheet 30-second pitch: "A URL shortener is a read-heavy, write-light key-value service. I generate a unique 64-bit ID per URL — via a distributed Key-Generation Service or Snowflake — Base62-encode it into a 7-character code, and store the code→URL mapping in a horizontally-sharded NoSQL store like DynamoDB. Reads go through Redis with cache-aside, fronted by a CDN, so redirects return a 301/302 in single-digit milliseconds. Click events fire async to a queue for analytics.

It's available (AP) over strongly consistent because mappings are immutable." Numbers to quote 100:1 read:write ratio → ~40 writes/sec, ~4,000 reads/sec (at 100M new URLs/month) 7 Base62 chars → 62⁷ ≈ 3.5 trillion unique codes ~500 bytes/record → ~600 GB/year storage Cache the hot 20% of links (serves ~80% of reads) 5 talking points that win the round Unique IDs by construction (KGS/Snowflake + Base62) — not hash-and-retry. Read path = cache + CDN ; the DB is almost a fallback. Shard by short code (hash partitioning) to avoid hot partitions. 301 vs 302 trade-off framed around analytics. AP over CP because mappings are immutable; async analytics off the hot path.

❓ FAQ — your follow-up questions Questions asked about this topic Why is horizontal scaling necessary here, not vertical scaling? Vertical = one bigger box; horizontal = more boxes sharing load. Horizontal wins because: (1) data outgrows one machine — ~600 GB/yr forever → multi-TB, past any single server's disk/RAM ceiling; sharding spreads it across N nodes. (2) availability — a single big box is a single point of failure, fatal when the whole job is "always up"; many nodes across AZs survive a node/AZ loss. (3) hard ceiling vs near-unlimited growth — the biggest instance is finite, but you meet 10× spikes by adding stateless read nodes.

(4) cost/elasticity — commodity nodes are cheaper per unit throughput and auto-scale out/in, vs paying for one peak-sized monster 24/7. (5) the design is already built for it — stateless services + hash-partitioned KV + cache/CDN, all of which add identical copies behind a load balancer. Balanced note: scale vertically first for simplicity, then out once you outgrow one node — but a global always-on service inevitably ends up horizontal.

asked 2026-06-26 It's read-heavy, so why choose NoSQL — and how is sharding chosen for NoSQL? NoSQL isn't picked because it's read-heavy (SQL reads fast too) — it's picked because the workload is a pure key lookup ( GET by short_code , no joins/scans/transactions), needs billions of rows with automatic horizontal scaling , and tolerates eventual consistency / favours availability (AP) since mappings are immutable. At small scale, PostgreSQL with short_code as PK is perfectly fine; NoSQL wins on scale + access-pattern fit, not because SQL "can't". Sharding: partition by hash of the short_code (DynamoDB internal hash; Cassandra Murmur3 on a consistent-hashing ring).

Hash — not range — because counter-based Base62 codes are sequential, so range sharding would dump all new/hot links on the last shard (hotspot); hashing scatters them uniformly. Reads stay single-shard (you know the exact code → route to one partition → O(1)). Consistent hashing means adding a node remaps only a few keys. Viral hot keys are absorbed by the cache/CDN, not by changing the shard key. asked 2026-06-26 📚 Sources System Design Primer — Design Pastebin.com / a URL shortener (donnemartin) — capacity estimation, Base62 + MD5 key generation, caching and storage model. System Design · Interview Prep Vertical Partitioning & Zero-Downtime Sharding Splitting one wide table into narrow ones by columns — using ZooKeeper as the routing map, MySQL binlog / Postgres WAL to keep them in sync, and live cutover so users never see a blip. 🎯 Scenario 🧑‍🎓 Laymen 📋 Requirements 🏗️ Architecture 🎬 Animation 🔍 Deep-dive 🧮 DSA ☁️ AWS 💻 C# code ⚖️ Trade-offs 🗣️ Cheat sheet ❓ FAQ 📚 Sources 🎯 Real-world scenario The problem: one table is doing too much Every fast-growing product hits the same wall.

Your users table started with a handful of columns — id, email, password hash — and, three years later, it has 47 columns, some of them 4-KB blobs, and it's the hottest table in the database. Every login reads it, every profile view reads it, every settings page reads it. The table is too wide : rarely-used columns bloat the buffer pool, cold JSON payloads share a page with the hot ones, and a lock on any user row for any reason blocks unrelated queries. Vertical partitioning is the surgical answer. Instead of splitting rows (that's horizontal sharding), you split columns — the wide table becomes several narrow tables that share the same primary key. The hot columns land in user_core .

Profile bio and avatar go to user_profile . Preferences, notification settings, feature flags — the cold, rarely-touched fields — move to user_preferences . The hot path only reads user_core ; the entire hot working set now fits in RAM, and locks on cold data no longer block auth. This is exactly the pattern YouTube's Vitess team formalised as a first-class workflow ( MoveTables ), which is how they carved up MySQL for YouTube, Slack, and Square. Pinterest , Facebook , and Uber all describe similar moves in their engineering blogs — usually to isolate a hot subsystem from a slower one.

The interview question is: how do you actually pull it off without downtime, without data loss, and without a big-bang deploy where hundreds of engineers have to change code at the same time? The answer is a coordinated dance between ZooKeeper (for the routing map) , MySQL binlog / Postgres WAL replication (to backfill and keep the shards in sync), and reactive re-routing driven by ZooKeeper watches so the application layer picks up the new topology automatically. 🧑‍🎓 In laymen terms Splitting one enormous filing cabinet into three specialised ones Imagine one giant filing cabinet in the office that holds a folder for every customer.

Each folder has grown huge over the years — a name and phone number at the top, then a chunky biography, a photo, a wish-list, notification preferences, historical purchases, feature-flag experiments the marketing team keeps adding, and so on. Every time anyone pulls a folder out, they lug the whole thing over — even if they only wanted the phone number. The office manager decides to split each folder into three thinner folders , all with the same customer number stapled on top. The first folder — Core — holds only the name, email, and password. The second — Profile — holds the bio and photo. The third — Preferences — holds the notification settings and marketing preferences.

The Core folders are the ones staff grab a hundred times a day, so they stay in a small locked drawer near the front desk. Profile and Preferences live in less-hot cabinets in the back room. Suddenly, the front-desk drawer is small enough that any folder can be found in seconds. Here's the tricky part: doing this without closing the office. There's already a live queue of customers at the desk. You can't just say "we'll be back tomorrow." So the team does it in stages. First, they set up the three new cabinets, empty. Then a helper copies existing folders into the new cabinets, one customer at a time, in the background — while the front desk keeps working with the old cabinet.

Every time a customer updates their address at the front desk, a "little scribe" writes the same update to the new cabinets too, so they stay in sync. Once the copy is complete and the scribe confirms both sets match perfectly, the office manager updates the noticeboard — a wall-mounted map that tells every staff member which cabinet holds which type of folder — and everyone switches to reading from the new cabinets. Nobody was turned away. The switchover took a second. The noticeboard is called ZooKeeper. The little scribe is called binary-log replication .

And the reason it doesn't lose any change is that the scribe reads the office's own daily log of updates — every write is recorded before it happens, so the scribe just replays those log entries into the new cabinet. Concrete example. LinkedIn ran their profile system this way for years — hot login data on one MySQL shard, resume & work history on another, feed activity on a third. When you log in, you hit the fast one. When you view your resume, a second call goes to the slow one. Because the noticeboard says exactly where each type of data lives, the application code doesn't need to know the actual server addresses — it asks the noticeboard, gets an answer, and reads.

📋 Requirements & scale Functional & non-functional Functional Split a wide table into ≥2 narrower tables by column group, preserving the primary key. Perform the migration online — reads and writes continue throughout. Route each query to the correct shard based on which columns it needs. Keep source and target in strict sync during backfill and steady-state. Allow reversible cutover — if something goes wrong, flip back to the old table with zero data loss. Support cross-shard reads (joins) and, where necessary, transactions across shards.

running Back-of-the-envelope A billion-row users table with 47 columns totalling 4 KB average per row = 4 TB . If the hot path only needs 5 columns totalling ~200 bytes, then after vertical partitioning the hot table is 200 GB — small enough to hold entirely in RAM on a decent MySQL box. That single number — 4 TB → 200 GB — is the reason vertical partitioning is one of the highest-leverage database optimisations in existence.

🏗️ High-level architecture The migration architecture, top-down Three moving parts do the heavy lifting: (1) a routing proxy (Vitess VTGate, Pinterest PinDB, or your own thin layer) that reads a routing map from ZooKeeper and translates each query into requests against the right physical shards; (2) a replication worker (Vitess VReplication, Debezium, or a hand-rolled reader) that tails the source database's binlog (MySQL) or WAL (Postgres) and applies each change to the new tables; and (3) ZooKeeper itself , which holds the routing map and pushes updates via watches the instant the operator flips the cutover.

Three colour flows: the blue query path is what the app sees — one SQL statement fans out to whichever shards hold the columns it selected. The amber replication path is asynchronous — the worker tails the source binlog and writes to the new tables continuously. The green watch push is instant — the moment the operator changes the routing map, every proxy re-reads and re-routes without a restart. 🎬 Animation Live migration: backfill → dual-write → cutover Watch a wide users table split into user_core , user_profile , and user_preferences with zero downtime. What vertical partitioning actually is (and isn't) Vertical partitioning splits columns . Horizontal partitioning (sharding) splits rows . Given the classic problem — a wide users table with 47 columns — vertical splitting decomposes it into narrow tables that share the same primary key: Before: users(id, email, pwd_hash, status, display_name, bio, avatar_url, phone, country, locale, timezone, notification_email, notification_sms, notification_push, marketing_optout, feature_flag_1..N, last_login_at, ...) — 4 KB average row width.

After: user_core(id, email, pwd_hash, status) — ~120 bytes/row. Every auth request reads this table. user_profile(id, display_name, bio, avatar_url, phone, country, locale, timezone) — ~1 KB/row. Read on profile view. user_preferences(id, notification_email, notification_sms, notification_push, marketing_optout, feature_flags jsonb) — ~2 KB/row. Read on settings page only. The critical property: every row in every child table shares the same user_id , so the original table can always be reconstructed via a three-way join. This 1:1 relationship is what distinguishes vertical partitioning from normalisation — you're not eliminating redundancy, you're isolating by access pattern . 2.

Vertical vs horizontal — when to reach for each Symptom Right tool Too many rows (billions) on one node; disk full Horizontal (sharding by user_id / hash) Table is too wide; cold columns bloat memory Vertical (split by column group) Hot subsystem (auth) blocked by cold subsystem (analytics events) Vertical, then move cold table to its own server Read QPS higher than one primary can serve Read replicas first, then horizontal Locks on unrelated fields hurt throughput Vertical Uneven skew — one user has 90% of rows in a related table Horizontal with hash-based routing They compose. Vitess routinely does vertical first, then horizontal on the tables that stay hot.

YouTube's original migration path: monolithic MySQL → vertically split into ~30 keyspaces (users, videos, comments, ads) → horizontally shard the hottest 5-6 of those keyspaces to hundreds of shards each. 3. ZooKeeper's job — the routing map The routing map is the single source of truth for "given a query for column X of table T, which physical DB holds it?" It lives in ZooKeeper as a small JSON blob under a well-known path, e.g.: /vitess/topology/keyspaces/users/routing { "users.user_core": { "physical": "shard-users-old", "state": "serving" }, "users.user_profile": { "physical": "shard-users-new1", "state": "serving" }, "users.user_preferences": { "physical": "shard-users-new2", "state":

"serving" }, "users": { "view_of": ["user_core","user_profile","user_preferences"] } } Every VTGate (or your query proxy) sets a persistent watch on this znode. When the operator flips the map, ZooKeeper pushes the update to every proxy in under a second — the proxies re-read and start routing to the new physical destination immediately, without a restart. See the full ZooKeeper mechanics on this page . Why ZooKeeper and not just a config file? Because a config file doesn't push updates. You'd have to poll or restart.

And a config server that isn't strongly consistent might tell one proxy the new map and another the old map, causing writes to hit different physical DBs — a split-brain scenario that corrupts data. ZooKeeper's ZAB guarantees every proxy sees the same map at any point in wall-clock time, or gets an error. 4. Binlog / WAL replication — the "little scribe" MySQL's binlog (binary log) and Postgres's WAL (write-ahead log) both record every write in strict order, before it's committed to the data files. This log is the foundation of every replication tool.

Vitess's VReplication — the workflow originally built at YouTube — attaches to the binlog stream identified by a global transaction ID ( GTID ) and processes each event in order. The migration runs in three canonical phases: Copy phase. The worker takes a consistent snapshot of the source (using MySQL's --single-transaction or Postgres logical replication slot) and streams rows into the target tables via a SELECT column_subset FROM users . Because it's a projection, only the columns you're moving actually get copied. This phase handles a billion rows in hours, not weeks, and can be interrupted and resumed at the same GTID. Replicate phase.

Once the copy is done, the worker seamlessly transitions to tailing the binlog from the GTID at which the copy started . Every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on the source is projected and applied to the targets. Steady-state lag is milliseconds on a healthy system. Verification (VDiff). The worker takes fresh consistent snapshots of both sides and compares them row-by-row for the moved columns. Any drift is replayed. Only after VDiff reports 100% match do you cut over. 5. The cutover — SwitchTraffic in stages Cutover is not a big bang. Vitess splits it into reads first, then writes , with a reversible checkpoint in between: SwitchReads.

Update the routing map in ZooKeeper so read queries for the moved columns now go to the new tables. Writes still go to the old wide table; the replication worker still keeps the new tables current. If anything looks wrong (latency spike, error rate), the operator flips the map back and it's as if nothing happened. Freeze & drain. Wait for the binlog tail to reach zero lag — the new tables are 100% caught up. SwitchWrites. Briefly pause writes on the moved columns (~100 ms), wait for any in-flight replication to complete, update the routing map to send writes to the new tables. Because the pause is bounded by the wait for the last GTID to apply, it's imperceptible at the client.

Vitess journals the binlog position of the cutover event so the reverse-replication stream (new → old) knows exactly where to start, giving you a working reverse replication in case rollback is needed. Drop the old columns. After a confidence window (hours or days), the columns are dropped from the source. This step is not urgent — the migration is already logically complete. 6. Handling reads & joins after the split Queries that used to be a single table scan now become fan-out queries. The proxy is responsible for splitting a query like SELECT id, email, bio FROM users WHERE id = ? into two lookups — one against user_core , one against user_profile — and merging the results by user_id .

For hot-path queries that only need core columns, the proxy sends a single query to a single shard — the whole point of the exercise. For legacy code that still writes SELECT * FROM users , most proxies (including Vitess VTGate) expose a logical view that transparently joins the underlying tables. This lets you migrate the schema without simultaneously migrating every client — the client cutover can be an independent, gradual effort. 7. Transactions across the split If all vertical partitions live on the same MySQL/Postgres instance , a standard local transaction covers all of them — no distributed transaction needed.

This is the easy and common case; vertical partitioning does not require separate physical machines. The benefit even on one machine is smaller pages, better cache locality, and reduced lock contention. If you move a partition to a different server for capacity reasons, cross-partition writes need either two-phase commit (correct but slow — Vitess supports 2PC with reasonable latency) or the outbox pattern (eventual consistency, no distributed transaction). In practice, most vertical splits keep all partitions on one host or one MySQL group so 2PC never comes up.

Register the source in the ZK topology. Kick off MoveTables with the column projection defining the vertical split. Monitor lag via VReplication metrics; when VDiff reports zero drift, run SwitchReads then SwitchWrites . Leave reverse replication armed for a week before dropping the old columns. Total wall-clock for a 1 TB migration: 4–8 hours copy phase, then arbitrary hold at zero lag, then seconds for cutover. 💻 C# implementation — the routing proxy Here's the core of the query proxy — the piece that reads the routing map from ZooKeeper and dispatches each SQL statement to the right underlying connection.

In production this is Vitess VTGate written in Go; below is an idiomatic C# port showing the two important patterns: routing-map-driven dispatch and reactive re-load on ZK watch . // Reactive routing proxy — reads the routing map from ZooKeeper, watches for // updates, and dispatches each SQL statement to the correct physical shard. using System.Text.Json; using org.apache.zookeeper; public class RoutingMap { // logical_table.column_group → physical_dsn public Dictionary < string , string > Routes { get ; set ; } = new (); } public class VerticalRouter : Watcher { private readonly ZooKeeper _zk; private const string ROUTING_PATH = "/vitess/topology/keyspaces/users/routing" ; private volatil

e RoutingMap _map = new (); public VerticalRouter ( ZooKeeper zk) { _zk = zk; } public async Task StartAsync () { // Read the map AND arm the watch atomically. var res = await _zk.getDataAsync(ROUTING_PATH, watcher: this ); _map = JsonSerializer .Deserialize< RoutingMap >(res.Data)!; } // Fires on any change to the routing znode — including operator SwitchTraffic.

public override async Task process ( WatchedEvent ev) { if (ev.get_Type() == Event .EventType.NodeDataChanged && ev.getPath() == ROUTING_PATH) { var res = await _zk.getDataAsync(ROUTING_PATH, watcher: this ); _map = JsonSerializer .Deserialize< RoutingMap >(res.Data)!; // Sub-second: every query from this point onward uses the new map. } } // Given a query plan (which columns from which logical table) return // the set of physical connections to fan out to.

public List < string > Route ( string logicalTable, HashSet < string > columns) { var shards = new HashSet < string >(); foreach ( var col in columns) { var key = $"{ logicalTable }.{ ColumnGroupFor(col) }" ; if (_map.Routes.TryGetValue(key, out var dsn)) shards.Add(dsn); } return shards.ToList(); } // A simple column → group mapping. In production this is part of the schema config.

private static string ColumnGroupFor ( string column) => column switch { "id" or "email" or "pwd_hash" or "status" => "user_core" , "display_name" or "bio" or "avatar_url" => "user_profile" , "notification_email" or "feature_flags" => "user_preferences" , _ => "user_core" }; } // Executing a query — fan out, gather, merge on primary key. public async Task < List < UserRow >> SelectUsers ( VerticalRouter router, HashSet < string > columns, long [] userIds) { var shards = router. Route ( "users" , columns); var perShard = await Task .WhenAll(shards.Select(dsn => QueryShard (dsn, columns, userIds))); // Merge results keyed by user_id — each shard returned a subset of columns.

var merged = new Dictionary < long , UserRow >(); foreach ( var partial in perShard) foreach ( var row in partial) { if (!merged.TryGetValue(row.Id, out var agg)) merged[row.Id] = agg = new UserRow { Id = row.Id }; agg.Merge(row); // copy over columns present in this partial } return merged.Values.ToList(); } Two things this snippet gets right: (a) the routing map is reloaded inside the watch callback and the watch is re-armed — same pattern as the ZooKeeper watches page. Miss this and you get exactly one update and then silently stop reacting.

(b) The query merge happens on the primary key in the proxy layer — no cross-shard SQL join, just parallel single-shard reads followed by in-memory zip-by-PK. This keeps every physical DB doing single-table lookups, which is the whole reason vertical partitioning is fast in the first place. ⚖️ Trade-offs, bottlenecks & likely follow-ups Where it actually breaks Cross-shard joins. If a query needs 10 columns spread across all three tables, you're doing three shard reads + merge on every request. For hot paths, either duplicate a small hot column across shards or redesign the split so the hot path only ever hits one shard. Foreign key constraints.

Traditional FK constraints don't cross physical shards. You lose that referential integrity at the DB layer and have to enforce it in application code (delete-cascades become application-level cleanup jobs). Backfill throttling. A naïve copy-phase can max out the source disk IO and hurt production. Every serious tool (Vitess, DMS, gh-ost) throttles based on replica lag. Replication lag during binary migrations. If you're doing dual-write from the app instead of binlog-based replication, a partial failure between the two writes leaves the shards drifted — you must catch and reconcile.

Binlog replication doesn't have this failure mode because the binlog write itself is transactional with the data write. Consistency during cutover Between SwitchReads and SwitchWrites, reads come from the new table but writes still land in the old and get replicated over. If replication lags by even 100 ms, a read-your-writes flow (user updates bio, immediately reloads profile) can show stale data. The mitigation is either (a) wait for zero lag before cutover, (b) route "read-your-writes" traffic to the old side until SwitchWrites completes, or (c) enforce read-after-write via a session cookie routed to primary — the same techniques you'd use with normal read replicas.

See Consistency Models . Interviewer follow-ups (with crisp answers) Q. When would you pick vertical over horizontal? A. When the pain is row width , heterogeneous access patterns , or subsystem isolation — not row count. If your users table is huge because there are two billion users, that's horizontal. If it's huge because each user has 50 KB of columns most of which are rarely read, that's vertical. Very often the answer is "vertical first, then horizontal on the resulting hot table." Q. Why use binlog replication instead of dual-write from the application? A.

Binlog replication is transactionally consistent — the log is written atomically with the row commit, so there's no window where the app crashes between writes and the shards diverge. Dual-write requires distributed-transaction discipline (2PC or a compensating-action outbox) that most application code doesn't get right. The binlog is already there ; use it. Q. Why ZooKeeper for the routing map — why not put it in Redis or a config service? A. Because during cutover, every proxy must see the same map at the same wall-clock instant. ZooKeeper's ZAB guarantees a single system image with sub-second watch propagation.

Redis with keyspace notifications is best-effort and won't survive Redis restarts; a plain config service isn't strongly consistent. For a cutover that mustn't cause split writes, you want a coordinator with real consensus. Q. How does Vitess achieve zero-downtime cutover exactly? A. Three moves: reads flip first (readable from new tables, writes still on old, reverse replication armed); wait for replication lag to hit zero; then a brief coordinated pause on writes for the split columns while the last binlog events apply, then the routing map is flipped for writes. The write pause is bounded by the wait for the final GTID to catch up, usually under 100 ms.

VReplication also journals the cutover position so reverse replication can start exactly there. Q. What's a good acceptance test for the migration before flipping? A. VDiff: a full row-by-row comparison of source and target using consistent snapshots. Ideally run it end-to-end at least once with zero mismatches, then re-run it in "streaming" mode during the confidence window. Also verify: replication lag is stable near zero for a sustained period, and no application errors under load with the new routing. Q. How do you roll back if something goes wrong after SwitchWrites? A.

Because reverse replication was armed at the SwitchWrites moment, the old wide table has been receiving every new-side write via replication. To roll back, you simply update the routing map back to the old table — the old table is already caught up. This is the entire reason Vitess journals the cutover binlog position. 🗣️ Interview cheat sheet 30-second pitch: "Vertical partitioning splits a wide table into narrow tables by column group, sharing the same primary key, so hot columns get their own small fast table and cold columns get their own.

To do it online, you use a routing proxy like VTGate that reads its map from ZooKeeper , a replication worker like VReplication that tails the source database's binlog to backfill and keep the new tables in sync, and a two-stage cutover: SwitchReads flips reads to the new tables while writes still go to the old and continue to replicate, then SwitchWrites briefly pauses, waits for zero lag, and flips writes — with reverse replication armed for rollback. ZooKeeper watches propagate the routing-map change to every proxy in under a second, so nobody needs a restart.

This is the same pattern YouTube built into Vitess and Pinterest, LinkedIn, and Uber use in various forms." Numbers to quote Hot table footprint after split: 5–20% of original . Replication lag steady-state: < 1 s p99 . Cutover write pause: < 100 ms , bounded by "wait for last GTID." Routing-map propagation: < 1 s via ZK watch. Backfill throughput: 10k–100k rows/sec per stream. Rollback time: < 1 minute — just flip the routing map back. 5 talking points that win the round Say "column-group projection, same primary key" — that's the crisp definition. Describe the three replication phases: copy, replicate, verify. Interviewers listen for VDiff.

Split the cutover into SwitchReads and SwitchWrites — the reversible checkpoint is the win. Name ZooKeeper watches as the mechanism that avoids proxy restarts. Reverse replication is armed at cutover — that's what makes rollback safe, not a database backup. ❓ FAQ — your follow-up questions Questions asked about this topic No follow-up questions yet — ask one about this topic and it'll be logged here with a compact answer.

x: Understanding how a packet enters your VPC, gets checked by half a dozen controls, hits your workload, and gets a response back is the single most probed topic in AWS Solutions Architect / SysOps / DevOps interviews, and a foundational conversation in any principal-level cloud infrastructure loop. Consider what happens when a customer opens your React app: a browser request travels from the public internet, through an Internet Gateway , gets steered by a route table , is filtered by the NACL on the subnet, then by the Security Group on the target's Elastic Network Interface (ENI), and finally reaches your EC2 instance / ALB / Lambda ENI.

Segment that space into subnets, each pinned to one Availability Zone. Route traffic between subnets, to the internet, to other VPCs, to on-prem, and to AWS services — using route tables. Reach AWS services privately without going over the internet (Gateway & Interface endpoints). Log flows for audit and forensics (VPC Flow Logs).

x: Internet Gateway (IGW) The IGW is a horizontally scaled, redundant, no-bandwidth-cap logical component you attach to a VPC. Only one IGW may be attached per VPC. It exists so packets can enter and leave the VPC over IPv4/IPv6. For IPv4 it also performs 1:1 NAT : an instance's private IP (say 10.0.1.42 ) is invisible on the internet; when its packet leaves via the IGW, the source is rewritten to the associated public/Elastic IP, and inbound the destination is rewritten back to the private IP before delivery. Without a route in the subnet's route table pointing to the IGW, a subnet is private — regardless of whether an instance has a public IP.

x: Cost: the IGW itself is free; you pay for data transfer. 2. Route table Every subnet is associated with exactly one route table (implicitly the VPC's main table, or explicitly a custom one). A route table is an ordered list of (destination CIDR → target) rules; the most-specific match wins . The local route 10.0.0.0/16 → local is created automatically and cannot be deleted. Typical entries: 0.0.0.0/0 → igw-xxx (public subnet), 0.0.0.0/0 → nat-xxx (private subnet), pl-6fa54006 (S3 prefix list) → vpce-xxx (Gateway Endpoint), 10.1.0.0/16 → pcx-yyy (VPC peering), 0.0.0.0/0 → tgw-zzz (Transit Gateway).

x: Route tables are the only way traffic finds its next hop — SGs and NACLs come after the routing decision, not before. 3. Network ACL (NACL) — subnet-level, stateless A NACL sits at the boundary of a subnet. Every subnet must have one; if you don't associate a custom NACL, you get the default one (which allows all). NACLs are stateless : inbound rules govern packets entering the subnet, outbound rules govern packets leaving, and the two are evaluated independently. Rules are numbered 1–32766 and evaluated in ascending order — first match wins . Each rule can allow or deny — unlike SGs, NACLs can express explicit denies.

x: Because they're stateless, if you allow inbound HTTPS on port 443, you also have to allow outbound on the client's ephemeral port range (Linux typically 32768–60999, Windows 49152–65535; AWS docs use 1024–65535 as the safe superset) or your replies get dropped. This is the #1 gotcha interviewers probe: "why does traffic work through the SG but fail at the NACL?" 4. Elastic Network Interface (ENI) An ENI is a virtual NIC — a private IP, MAC address, and a set of attached Security Groups. Every EC2 instance, Lambda-in-VPC, ALB target, RDS instance, and VPC endpoint has one or more ENIs. This is where Security Groups actually attach; SGs are not attached to instances, they're attached to ENIs.

x: 5. Security Group (SG) — ENI-level, stateful, allow-only An SG is a virtual firewall wrapped around an ENI. Its rules are allow-only (no deny — the absence of a matching allow is the deny) and stateful : if a packet is allowed inbound, the entire flow (including the reverse direction) is tracked and the response is automatically permitted regardless of outbound rules, and vice versa. Rules can be scoped by CIDR, another SG's id (a powerful abstraction — "allow from anything wearing this SG"), or a prefix list. A single ENI can have up to 5 SGs by default (16 by quota increase), and rules across all SGs are OR'd — one allow anywhere is enough.

NAT Gateway (or NAT instance) A NAT Gateway sits in a public subnet with an Elastic IP. Private subnets route 0.0.0.0/0 to it. It performs port-address translation : outbound packets from many private IPs are rewritten to a single Elastic IP with unique source ports (up to 55 000 concurrent connections per unique destination). It's a managed service — 5 Gbps baseline, bursting to 100 Gbps, no OS to patch.

System Design · Interview Prep Web Crawler How Google, Bing, and the Internet Archive discover, download, and de-duplicate 10 billion pages — politely, in under a week, without getting sued or trapped. 🎯 Scenario 🧑‍🎓 Laymen 📋 Requirements 🏗️ Architecture 🎬 Animation 🔍 Deep-dive 🧮 DSA ☁️ AWS 💻 C# code ⚖️ Trade-offs 🗣️ Cheat sheet ❓ FAQ 📚 Sources 🎯 Real-world scenario What we're building & where it's used A web crawler — sometimes called a spider or a bot — is the piece of software that walks the web, downloads pages, extracts the links inside them, and then walks those links too, recursively.

Every big search engine has one: Google runs Googlebot , Microsoft runs Bingbot , and the Internet Archive runs the open-source Heritrix . Beyond search, crawlers power price-comparison sites, SEO auditors, LLM pre-training pipelines (Common Crawl is the internet's biggest public crawl), and enterprise site-search over your own intranet. Interviewers love this problem because it's a Rorschach test for distributed-systems intuition.

It sounds like a homework assignment ("just download HTML and parse the links"), but at real scale it exposes every hard problem in the field: queue design, deduplication at the URL and content level, rate limiting and politeness, DNS bottlenecks, fault tolerance under partial failure, crawl-trap detection, ordering under a fixed bandwidth budget, and freshness re-crawl scheduling. A senior candidate should be able to talk through crawling 10 billion pages in under 5 days and defend every number.

The reference bar in real interviews — set by Meta/Uber/Airbnb-style loops — is: (1) fetch scale, (2) URL frontier queueing, (3) politeness and robots.txt , (4) content dedup, (5) crawler-trap defense, (6) freshness re-crawling. Miss any of those six and it's a hire-fail on this round. Get all six, plus the freshness/priority follow-up, and you've cleared staff-level bar. 🧑‍🎓 In laymen terms Explaining it to someone who's never heard of Googlebot Imagine you want to make a giant phone book of the entire internet . Not a hand-picked "best websites" list — every page anyone has ever put online.

How would you even start? You'd start with a handful of well-known websites (say, Wikipedia and BBC) and write down their addresses. Call these your starter list . Now you'd visit the first address, print out the page, and — importantly — write down every link on that page. Then you'd visit each of those links and do the same thing again. And again. This tireless address-collecting robot is what engineers call a crawler . Now, here's where it stops being simple. There are billions of pages on the internet , and most of them keep changing. If one robot did this alone, it would take decades.

So you hire thousands of robots — like a small army of postmen — and give each one a slice of the address list. But now new problems appear. First: don't be rude. If a hundred of your robots all knock on Wikipedia's door at the same second, Wikipedia crashes. So the robots have to be polite — one visit per second per website, and they always read the "please don't come in here" sign every website posts (this is a real file called robots.txt ). Second: don't waste time. The same page can appear at ten different addresses ( example.com vs www.example.com vs example.com/index.html ). You need a giant checklist so you don't crawl the same page twice. Third: watch for traps.

Some pages generate infinite links (imagine a calendar with "next month" buttons going forward forever). Robots can get stuck there. The tiny example. Your seed URL is bbc.com . Robot A downloads it, sees links to bbc.com/news and bbc.com/sport , and drops those into a shared to-do list. Robot B picks up bbc.com/news , downloads it, finds more links, adds those to the list. Multiply by ten thousand robots. In four days, you've made your phone book. Then you have to start over, because the internet has already changed. Think of it as: an army of postmen delivering thank-you cards to every address they've ever heard of, then writing down the addresses on the mailboxes they pass, forever.

📋 Requirements & scale Requirements and back-of-the-envelope math Functional requirements (what it does) Take a set of seed URLs and crawl reachable pages, following links to a bounded depth. Store the raw HTML and extracted text for each page. Deduplicate at both URL level (same address twice) and content level (near-duplicate pages). Support re-crawling on a schedule so the index stays fresh. Non-functional requirements (how well) Politeness: respect robots.txt and never hit one domain faster than ~1 req/sec. Scale: crawl 10 10 pages in ≤ 5 days. Fault tolerance: crash of any worker must not lose URLs or double-write content.

Extensibility: parser must be swappable — HTML today, JavaScript-rendered pages tomorrow. ead time Mercator paper — caching is mandatory Two numbers to volunteer in the interview: ~23 k pages/sec is the throughput bar, and ~5 PB gzipped is the storage bar. Everything else is a consequence. 🏗️ High-level architecture How the pieces fit together A production crawler is a pipeline of stateless workers connected by durable queues, plus a set of shared metadata stores. The stages don't share memory — they hand work off through Kafka/SQS so any one worker can crash and its message is redelivered.

The pipeline: seed URLs are pushed into the URL Frontier ; Fetcher workers pull URLs, honor robots.txt and per-domain rate limits, download HTML, and store it in blob storage; a Parser stage extracts text and outbound links; extracted URLs are normalized, deduplicated, and filtered , then pushed back into the frontier; a Scheduler occasionally re-injects known URLs for freshness. The Metadata DB tracks per-URL state (queued/fetched/failed), per-page content hash, and per-domain robots.txt policy plus last-fetched timestamps.

Three things to note about this diagram in an interview: (1) the pipeline is looped — parsed URLs re-enter the frontier, which is what makes it a crawler and not a scraper. (2) The Metadata DB and Blob store are the only stateful things ; every worker is stateless and horizontally scalable. (3) The DNS resolver has its own dashed line because it's the single stealthiest bottleneck in the whole system — the Mercator paper measured it at up to 70% of per-thread time.

🎬 Animation Watch one page crawl, then a duplicate get rejected This animation walks a single URL through the pipeline — seed → frontier → fetcher (with robots.txt check) → parser → dedup → newly discovered URLs back into the frontier. Then it shows a duplicate content page get rejected by the SimHash filter. ▶ Play Step → ← Back ↺ Reset Ready Press ▶ Play to start 🔍 Component deep-dive 1) URL Frontier — the priority queue of the internet The frontier is where every design decision comes to a head.

It has three simultaneous jobs: (a) hold billions of pending URLs durably (so a worker crash doesn't lose them), (b) enforce per-domain politeness (never let two workers hit bbc.com at the same second), and (c) enforce a priority order so important pages are crawled first. The classic Mercator design uses two queues: a front queue for priority (high-PageRank pages first) and a back queue for politeness (one queue per host, so a fetcher's next URL is guaranteed to be on a different host from the last one). In practice today, teams use Kafka partitioned by domain or SQS with per-domain FIFO groups as the durable substrate, plus a Redis-backed rate limiter in front of the fetcher.

2) Fetcher — the network-bound heart Each fetcher is an async HTTP client that pulls a URL from the frontier, does a per-domain rate check, resolves DNS (from cache), reads the cached robots.txt , downloads with a size cap ( HTTP HEAD first for large-file probing), and stores the raw response in S3. The two things that matter here: concurrency model (Rust/Go/C# async on ~10 k in-flight connections per box; not thread-per-request) and DNS caching . Mercator observed DNS lookups eating up to 70% of per-thread time; every real crawler runs an in-process resolver with a per-domain TTL and rotates across multiple upstream DNS providers (Google 8.8.8.8, Cloudflare 1.1.1.1, own recursive resolver).

3) robots.txt and politeness — don't be the reason your IP gets banned The robots exclusion protocol is a plaintext file at /robots.txt that says which paths a bot may fetch. Politeness has two layers: (a) parse and respect Disallow plus Crawl-delay , cached in the Metadata DB with a 24-hour TTL; (b) enforce a per-domain rate limit using a Redis SETNX lock or a token-bucket keyed by host — even in the absence of a Crawl-delay directive, 1 req/sec is the sensible default. Skip either and (in order of severity) you get IP-banned, blacklisted by CDNs, or sued. 4) Parser + URL normalization The parser extracts text (for the search index), and every <a href> , <link> , and <iframe> URL.

Then it normalizes each URL — lowercasing host, resolving ./ and ../ , stripping fragments, sorting query params, adding a trailing slash for empty paths. Without normalization, example.com/a?x=1&y=2 and Example.com/a?y=2&x=1 would look like different URLs and both get crawled. 5) Dedup — URL-seen vs content-seen Two orthogonal dedup layers: URL-seen (have I ever queued this address?) and content-seen (have I already downloaded this content , even at a different address?). URL-seen is a giant Bloom filter (or a Metadata DB primary-key check) — cheap, small, wrong 0.1% of the time. Content-seen at exact-match level is a SHA-256 of the response body .

Content-seen at near-duplicate level uses SimHash or MinHash — you compute a 64-bit fingerprint and consider two pages duplicate if their Hamming distance is ≤ 3. Near-dup detection is essential: mirror sites, print-friendly copies, and syndicated news articles otherwise get indexed dozens of times. 6) Crawler traps — depth-bounded BFS Some URLs are infinite — a calendar with "next month" buttons, a session-ID-generating URL, an infinite-scroll paginator. The defense is a hop depth counter stored per URL: depth 0 = seed, and every followed link increments. Cap at 15–20 hops and the trap dies.

A second-line defense: reject URLs with pathological query-string cardinality on a per-domain basis (if example.com?sid= keeps generating new URLs, blacklist the parameter). 7) Fault tolerance — the message contract The pattern is at-least-once with idempotent writes : queue messages carry URL IDs, not raw HTML . If a fetcher dies mid-download, the message's visibility timeout expires and another worker picks it up. The blob store write is keyed by URL ID, so a duplicate delivery just overwrites the same S3 object. After N retries a URL goes to a dead-letter queue for human inspection. 8) Freshness & the re-crawl scheduler The first crawl builds the index; the re-crawl maintains it.

Simple strategy: re-inject each URL into the frontier at an interval proportional to its change frequency (news sites daily, static docs monthly). Better: Cho & Garcia-Molina showed the uniform policy beats the proportional one for average freshness — treat all pages equally rather than trying to be clever, and deprioritize extremely volatile pages. Priority buckets ("news / product / blog / rest") are the practical middle ground. 🧮 The DSA behind it Data structures & algorithms that make it work 1) Bloom filter for URL-seen A bit-array of size m and k hash functions. Inserting a URL sets k bits; checking asks "are all k bits set?" — if any is 0 the URL is definitely new .

For 10 B URLs at 1% false-positive rate, m ≈ 12 GB (fits in one big Redis or partitioned across a few). The 1% FP means we miss a few new URLs; we never re-crawl a duplicate falsely. 2) SimHash / MinHash for near-dup SimHash produces a 64-bit fingerprint of a document's shingle set; two fingerprints with Hamming distance ≤ 3 are near-duplicates. Lookup is done with permutation tables — you keep a few sorted copies of the 64-bit fingerprints with different bit permutations, then a candidate match is a range query on each table. O(1)ish per document at a few tens of MB per million.

3) Priority queue for frontier front A binary heap keyed by priority score (PageRank estimate + freshness deficit). At 23 k pops/sec across 10 B entries, this is partitioned per domain and per priority bucket — Kafka topics with bucketed partitions do this in practice. 4) Trie / suffix automaton for URL filters To reject URLs by hostname pattern or path prefix (e.g. crawl only *.wikipedia.org ), a Trie over reversed hostnames answers "is this in-scope?" in O( k ) where k is the hostname length.

5) Consistent hashing for domain-partitioning Which fetcher handles which domain? Consistent hashing on host(url) gives each fetcher a stable slice; adding/removing a fetcher moves only K/N domains, and per-host rate limits stay coherent because one fetcher owns each host. A second ECS service parser-svc reads that, extracts text + links, hashes and SimHashes the content, checks the URL Bloom filter and content-hash index in Redis/DynamoDB, and pushes new URLs back onto the frontier queue. A separate scheduler Lambda re-enqueues URLs based on last-crawl-time. If you can explain that in five sentences on the whiteboard, the AWS section is done. 💻 C# implementation — the fetcher core The most interviewable part is the fetch loop : it hides the politeness gate, DNS caching, size cap, and normalize/dedup pipeline in idiomatic C#.

Below is a self-contained sketch — production code adds retries, DLQ push, and per-domain Redis locks, but this is what you should be able to sketch on a whiteboard. using System; using System.Collections.Concurrent; using System.Net.Http; using System.Security.Cryptography; using System.Text; using System.Threading; using System.Threading.Tasks; // 1) A URL work item on the frontier queue — just the ID + normalized URL. public sealed record CrawlJob ( string UrlId, Uri Url, int Depth); // 2) Ports the fetcher depends on — kept as interfaces so tests can fake them.

Real crawlers are typically written in Go (Colly), Rust (custom async on Tokio + reqwest), Java (Nutch, Heritrix, StormCrawler), or Python (Scrapy). C#'s HttpClient is a first-class async fit for this workload — the only thing you'd swap in production is HttpClient for something like YARP 's HttpMessageInvoker to bypass the connection-pool ceilings. ⚖️ Trade-offs, bottlenecks & likely follow-ups The bottlenecks in order of pain (1) DNS. Uncached, DNS is up to 70% of your fetcher's clock. Fix: in-process cache with TTL + multiple upstream resolvers + Route 53 Resolver. (2) Politeness.

The per-domain 1-req/sec limit means a slow domain can't be sped up — throughput scales only if the crawl is spread across many domains . If your seed set is 90% Reddit, you'll be idle waiting for the rate limit. (3) Bandwidth. At 23 k pages/sec × 2 MB = ~370 Gbps. This is why fetcher hosts are network-optimized instances, not compute-optimized. (4) Storage & dedup lookup. 12 GB Bloom filter, 5 PB S3 — cheap and easy. The lookup latency (~1 ms Redis, ~5 ms DynamoDB) is what caps QPS per parser worker. (5) Crawler traps. A single misconfigured site can produce millions of unique URLs per hour and eat your frontier. Depth cap + per-domain URL budget.

Common interviewer follow-ups (with crisp answers) "How do you keep the crawler polite?" Two layers: (1) fetch and cache robots.txt per host with a 24h TTL, respect Disallow and Crawl-delay . (2) A per-host token bucket in Redis (SETNX + TTL) enforces a hard 1 req/sec floor across the whole fleet. Add jitter to avoid synchronized retry storms. "How do you deduplicate?" Two orthogonal checks. URL-level: a global Bloom filter for "have I ever queued this URL?" — 12 GB for 10 B URLs at 1% FPR. Content-level: SHA-256 for exact match, SimHash (Hamming ≤ 3) for near-dup — catches mirror sites, print-versions, syndicated articles.

"How do you avoid crawler traps?" A hop-depth counter on each URL (0 at seed, +1 on follow), capped at ~20. Plus a per-domain URL budget: if example.com is generating >100 k unique URLs an hour, blacklist the query parameter that's exploding. "How do you scale to 10 B pages in 5 days?" Roughly 23 k pages/sec. On c6in.32xlarge (200 Gbps NIC, ~3.7 k pages/sec sustained at 30% network utilization), ~8 hosts saturate the target. Parser and storage scale independently — Lambda for parsing, S3 for HTML. "How do you handle JavaScript-rendered pages?" A separate "heavy fetcher" fleet running headless Chromium (Playwright/Puppeteer).

It's ~50× more expensive per page — you route only URLs flagged as JS-heavy (either via a per-site heuristic or from a first-pass fetch that detects <noscript> boilerplate). "How do you re-crawl for freshness?" A scheduler re-injects URLs at intervals per priority bucket — news daily, product docs weekly, static content monthly. Cho & Garcia-Molina showed a uniform revisit policy beats a proportional one for average freshness; deprioritize extremely volatile pages. "What if a fetcher crashes mid-download?" Messages carry only URL IDs; SQS visibility timeout returns the message to the queue if not ack'd. The blob write is keyed by URL ID, so a redelivery is idempotent.

After N failed retries, the URL goes to a DLQ for human inspection. "How do you prioritize which URLs to fetch first?" A front-queue priority score — usually a mix of PageRank estimate, freshness deficit, and manual boosts (news, homepages). Mercator's classic design uses a front-queue selector (priority) that feeds a back-queue-per-host (politeness). "How do you keep the crawl from being blocked?" Rotate outbound IP pools, respect robots.txt and Crawl-delay , identify honestly via User-Agent, back off on 429/503, and monitor per-host block rates in real time. Malicious crawler spoofing is what gets you blacklisted.

🗣️ Interview cheat sheet 30-second pitch: "It's a pipelined, stateless fleet of workers behind a durable URL frontier. Fetchers pull URLs, honor robots.txt and per-host rate limits, download HTML, and store to S3. Parsers extract text and links, deduplicate by URL Bloom filter and by content SimHash, and push new URLs back to the frontier. Metadata DB tracks per-URL state.

To hit 10 B pages in 5 days we need ~23 k pages/sec on ~8 network-optimized instances, and the sneakiest bottleneck is DNS — which we cache aggressively and load-balance across multiple providers." Numbers to quote: 23 k pps target, 2 MB avg page, ~5 PB gzipped, ~12 GB URL Bloom filter, 1 req/sec/host politeness floor, hop-depth 20 for trap defense. The six components: frontier, fetcher, DNS resolver, parser, dedup (URL + content), storage. Always show them as pipeline stages, never as one process. The three sneaky bottlenecks: DNS (70% of thread time uncached), politeness ceiling, crawler traps.

The two dedup layers: URL Bloom filter (cheap, false-positive-tolerant) and content SimHash (catches near-duplicates a hash can't). The mental model: stateless workers + durable queues + idempotent writes = crash-safe. Everything stateful (Bloom filter, dedup index, blob store) is externalized. ❓ FAQ — your follow-up questions Questions asked about this topic No follow-up questions yet — ask one about this topic and it'll be logged here with a compact answer.

System Design · Interview Prep Webhooks & AWS EventBridge Two ways to move an event from "something just happened over here" to "now do X over there" — one is an open-web HTTP contract, the other is a managed AWS event bus. Same shape, different blast radius. 🎯 Scenario 🧑‍🎓 Laymen 📋 Requirements 🏗️ Architecture 🎬 Animation 🔍 Deep-dive 🆚 Combined view 🧮 DSA ☁️ AWS 💻 C# code ⚖️ Trade-offs 🗣️ Cheat sheet ❓ FAQ 📚 Sources 🎯 Real-world scenario What we're building & where it's used Every non-trivial modern product has to solve the same problem: something happened in system A, and system B needs to react to it . A customer's card charged in Stripe → your dashboard updates.

A build finished in GitHub Actions → Slack pings the channel. An order status changed in your warehouse → 3 downstream systems (billing, notifications, analytics) all need to know within seconds. Polling APIs every few seconds is wasteful, slow, and doesn't scale, so we need push-based, event-driven plumbing. Two dominant designs solve this. A webhook is the open-web version: the producer signs an HTTPS POST and fires it at a public URL you control — used by Stripe, GitHub, Shopify, Twilio, Slack, PayPal, HubSpot, SendGrid, and virtually every SaaS API.

AWS EventBridge is the same idea implemented as a managed service inside AWS : a serverless event bus where producers PutEvents , rules pattern-match on JSON, and matched events fan out to up to 5 targets per rule (Lambda, SQS, Step Functions, another AWS account, or even a webhook via API Destinations). Same conceptual shape — event → route → deliver → retry — but one is public-HTTP and the other is AWS IAM-secured. Interviewers love this pair because it forces you to talk about at-least-once delivery, signing, idempotency, retries with backoff, dead-letter queues, ordering guarantees and the classic dual-write problem.

If you can compare the two crisply, you demonstrate you understand event-driven architecture in general, not just one vendor's implementation. 🧑‍🎓 In laymen terms The whole thing, explained without any tech words Imagine you order a pizza online. You could stand at the window every 30 seconds and shout "Is it here yet? Is it here yet?" — that's what a computer program does when it "polls" a website. Annoying, wasteful, and if the pizza shows up a second after you last checked, you don't know for a whole 30 seconds. A better idea is that the delivery driver rings your doorbell when the pizza actually arrives. That doorbell ring is a webhook.

A webhook is just a "please ring my doorbell when X happens" arrangement between two companies. When you shop online, the shop tells the payment company (say, Stripe): "here's my doorbell address — myshop.com/paid — please ring it the instant a customer's card goes through." Then the shop can put you on their thank-you page and email your receipt immediately. Nobody had to keep asking.

This is how Uber knows the driver arrived, how WhatsApp shows your friend's typing dots, how Slack pops up a notification the moment someone messages you, and how GitHub tells your build system "hey, someone just pushed code." Now imagine you're a huge apartment building with hundreds of tenants — the pizza guy, the mailman, the plumber, the neighbour returning a bowl — all wanting to ring different apartments. You'd get chaos if every visitor had to know every apartment number. Instead, the building has a front desk . Every visitor drops off their delivery there, tells the receptionist what it is, and the receptionist looks at a little book and forwards it to the right tenants.

That front desk is what AWS EventBridge is inside Amazon's cloud — a smart receptionist for events. One thing happens, and it can automatically be forwarded to 5 different tenants at once, without the sender needing to know any of them. The hard parts, in plain words: sometimes the doorbell rings and you're in the shower — the visitor keeps ringing back until you answer, which means you might hear the same news twice ("your pizza's here" x3), so you have to remember what you already knew. Sometimes the pizza arrives before the drink even though they left the shop in the opposite order — things arrive out of order .

And someone could pretend to be the pizza guy, so you need a secret handshake to know it's really them. That's basically every hard problem in this whole page, in three sentences. A tiny example to walk through: you buy a $12 book. Your card gets charged. Stripe fires a "payment succeeded for order #A47" doorbell at the bookshop's server. The bookshop confirms the handshake, writes "order A47 = paid" in its notebook, then sends you the confirmation email. If the doorbell rings twice for the same order (Stripe wasn't sure the first ring got through), the shop looks at its notebook, sees "A47 already paid", and quietly ignores the duplicate. That's the whole thing.

📋 Requirements & scale Requirements and back-of-the-envelope math Functional requirements Producer emits an event when something interesting happens (state change, transaction, external trigger). Router matches events to zero or more interested consumers using a pattern/filter (event type, source, JSON body attributes). Delivery pushes the event to consumer(s) with retries on failure. Authenticity — consumer must verify the event really came from the producer (HMAC signature, or IAM). Observability — the sender can see delivery attempts, status, and manually replay failed ones. Non-functional requirements At-least-once delivery — never drop an event, even if the consumer is briefly down.

Consumer must handle duplicates. Low delivery latency — sub-second p50 in-region for EventBridge; a few seconds for public webhooks. Durable retry with backoff — exponential, capped, then dead-letter. Security — signed payloads, HTTPS-only, replay-attack protection. Fan-out — one event → N consumers without the producer knowing them. e timeout ~1–10s (Stripe: "quickly", most providers 3–10s) Target-specific (Lambda 15 min, HTTP endpoint 5s) Retry window Stripe: 3 days (exponential); GitHub: 8h; Shopify: 48h Default 24 hours , up to 185 attempts , exponential backoff Manual replay Stripe: 15d via dashboard, 30d via CLI Archive + Replay — configurable retention (days to indefinite) Fan-out 1 event → 1 endpoint (register endpoint per consumer, max 16 endpoints/account in Stripe) 1 event → up to 5 targets per rule , and up to 300 rules/bus = 1500-way fan-out Ordering Not guaranteed Not guaranteed (use FIFO SQS target if needed) Delivery guarantee At-least-once At-least-once A useful mental anchor: at 10,000 events/sec × 250

bytes each = 2.5 MB/sec ingress, ~9 GB/hour. If you fan out to 5 targets each, that's 50,000 downstream invocations/sec — enough to fill 100 concurrent Lambdas at 500/sec each. In webhook land, the same 10 k/sec producer would need 10,000 consumer servers if each takes 1 second per POST — which is why the golden rule is "consumer returns 200 in < 200 ms, enqueues, processes async." 🏗️ High-level architecture How the pieces fit together Both systems share a five-stage pipeline: Emit → Enrich/Sign → Route → Deliver → Confirm/Retry . The stages are almost identical; the difference is who runs which stage and how it authenticates.

Webhook flow (open-web) The producer's application writes the event to its own outbox table in the same DB transaction as the state change (this defeats the dual-write bug). A relay worker polls that outbox (or reads a CDC stream), looks up the subscribers registered for that event type, serialises a JSON body, computes HMAC-SHA256(body, endpoint_secret) , and fires an HTTPS POST at the consumer's URL. The consumer verifies the signature, drops the payload onto its own internal queue, and returns 200 OK in under a second. If it doesn't respond in time or returns 5xx, the relay schedules an exponential-backoff retry (t+1min, t+5min, t+30min, ..., up to hours or days).

After the final failure the event goes to a dead-letter store and is surfaced in a "failed deliveries" UI where an operator can replay. EventBridge flow (AWS-internal) An AWS service (or your own app calling PutEvents ) drops an event onto an event bus . EventBridge evaluates the JSON event pattern on every rule attached to that bus; a rule may match on source , detail-type , and content filters inside detail (prefix, suffix, numeric ranges, existence, IP-CIDR, wildcards).

Every matching rule fans the event out to up to 5 targets — Lambda, SQS, SNS, Step Functions, Kinesis, another event bus (cross-account/cross-region), or an API Destination (a signed HTTPS webhook, so EventBridge itself can play producer). Failed target invocations are retried for up to 24 h with exponential backoff (up to 185 attempts), then routed to a per-target SQS dead-letter queue with a rich error envelope (rule ARN, error code, exhausted-retry reason).

Webhook flow (public HTTPS + HMAC) EventBridge flow (in-AWS + IAM) Retry / DLQ path Look at the two lanes side by side and notice the shape is identical: producer → durable buffer → pattern match / lookup → deliver → confirm or retry to DLQ . Webhooks bolt each of those stages together with your own outbox, your own relay, your own signing, your own retry scheduler; EventBridge just gives you all of them managed with a single PutEvents call. 🎬 Animation Watch the core mechanic run, step by step This animation walks one event through both systems in parallel: the top lane is a Stripe-style webhook and the bottom lane is EventBridge.

You'll see the moment they behave identically (fan-out, retry) and the moment they diverge (signing vs IAM). ▶ Play Step → ← Back ↺ Reset Ready Press ▶ Play to start 🔍 Component deep-dive 1. Event envelope Both systems standardise on a JSON envelope with three parts: metadata (id, timestamp, type), source (who emitted it), and detail/data (the domain payload). EventBridge names them exactly: id , time , source , detail-type , detail . Stripe uses id , created , type , data.object . GitHub uses X-GitHub-Event + body. The event id is load-bearing : it's what consumers use to deduplicate replays. 2.

Durable buffer & the dual-write problem Neither system lets you skip the "the event must survive if the producer crashes" step. Webhook producers solve this with the transactional outbox pattern — write the domain change and the "to-be-delivered event" row in one DB transaction, then a separate relay worker drains the outbox and fires the HTTP POST. EventBridge takes the durability off your plate: once PutEvents returns 200, AWS owns the event's fate. Under the hood the bus is backed by replicated storage per partition (unpublished internal detail, but the API contract is "if you got 200, it's durable").

This is the single biggest operational win of EventBridge over rolling your own webhooks. 3. Routing / matching Webhook systems typically use a simple subscriptions table : (event_type, endpoint_url, secret) . When an event fires, look up matching rows, POST to each. EventBridge uses richer content-based filtering : a rule contains a JSON event pattern that can match by exact value, prefix, suffix, wildcard, numeric range, IP CIDR, existence — all evaluated in-memory against the event's JSON. Pattern size is capped at 2048 chars; you can have 300 rules per bus with up to 30 of them containing wildcards. 4.

Signing & authentication Webhooks live on the open internet, so the consumer must prove the caller is the real producer. The universal answer is HMAC-SHA256 over the raw body plus a timestamp , using a shared secret per endpoint. Stripe puts it in Stripe-Signature: t=<unix>,v1=<hex> . The consumer recomputes and compares in constant time. The timestamp defends against replay — reject if |now − t| > 5 min . EventBridge doesn't need any of this inside AWS: the producer's identity is authenticated by IAM SigV4 signing of the PutEvents call, and each target grants EventBridge permission via a resource policy.

When EventBridge fires outbound to an API Destination it becomes the webhook producer and does the signing itself (via Connections with Basic / OAuth / API Key / Bearer credentials stored in Secrets Manager). 5. Retries, backoff, DLQ Both systems retry on 5xx / timeouts and eventually give up. Stripe retries for 3 days on live mode with exponential backoff. EventBridge retries for 24 hours by default, with exponential backoff up to 185 attempts ; you can set MaximumEventAgeInSeconds (60–86400) and MaximumRetryAttempts (0–185) per target.

When retries are exhausted (or on non-retryable errors like NO_PERMISSIONS , NO_RESOURCE ) the event is routed to the target's SQS DLQ with RULE_ARN , ERROR_CODE , EXHAUSTED_RETRY_CONDITION , and RETRY_ATTEMPTS in message attributes. Replay is a manual operation from the DLQ, or from EventBridge's built-in Archive + Replay (store all matching events for N days, then StartReplay to re-fire them at a rule). 6. Idempotency at the consumer Because delivery is at-least-once, every consumer MUST be idempotent.

The pattern is: on receipt, look up the event id in a seen-events store (Redis SET with TTL, or a DynamoDB item with the id as PK), and if it's already there, return 200 without re-processing. This is the number-one interview trap — candidates who forget this get grilled on "what happens if the same event is delivered twice while your first invocation is mid-flight?" The answer is: dedupe by event id, and use conditional writes so the second delivery loses the race. 7. Ordering Neither system guarantees ordering. Stripe explicitly says events may arrive out of order (e.g. invoice.paid can arrive before invoice.created ).

EventBridge has the same contract; if you need ordering, use an SQS FIFO queue as your target and derive a group id from a business key (customer id, order id). Alternatively, embed a monotonically-increasing sequence number in your payload and let the consumer discard stale events by comparing against the last-seen sequence for that entity. 🆚 Combined view — same architecture, different chassis The reason to talk about both in one page is that they solve the exact same problem, just in different environments. If you understand the shape, you can pick the right chassis for the job.

The most powerful production setups combine both — EventBridge routes events internally, and one of the targets is an API Destination that lets EventBridge itself fire the webhook out to customers, with Connections handling the auth.

That way you get the managed durability and pattern-matching of EventBridge plus the "reach the outside world" of webhooks in one pipeline. Webhook mental model "I own both the producer and the delivery mechanism. I'm going to POST HTTPS with a signed body across the internet, retry when it fails, and give the customer a portal to see failed deliveries." EventBridge mental model "I emit an event to a bus and let AWS route it. I don't know or care which team's Lambda picks it up. New consumers just add a rule — I never change my code." 🧮 The DSA behind it Data structures & algorithms Under the covers, this is a very DSA-heavy space.

The interviewer often probes: "how does EventBridge match 300 rules against every event without becoming O(n) slow?" Here are the key ones. paths + predicate tree ~O(rules × pattern depth), amortised sub-linear via prefix sharing Matches each event against all rules cheaply by grouping shared prefixes Signature verification HMAC-SHA256 + constant-time compare O(body size) Prevents timing-attack leaks of the secret Rate limiting outbound Token bucket per endpoint O(1) Don't DDOS a slow consumer during a spike Ordering (when needed) Per-partition sequence number + LWW compare O(1) Discard stale events on the consumer Circuit breaker on failing endpoint Sliding-window failure counter O(1) Stop hammering a dead consumer; save retry budget The most interesting one is rule matching .

Naively evaluating 300 patterns × 5 fields each on every one of 10 000 events/sec is 15 million comparisons/sec — do-able but wasteful. EventBridge (and open-source alternatives like AWS's own Ruler library) uses a tokenised prefix trie where common prefixes (e.g. source = "aws.s3" ) are evaluated once and shared across all rules that mention them. That reduces the expected work from O(rules × depth) to closer to O(depth) plus the number of rules that actually matched. ☁️ AWS implementation Mapping the design to AWS Two deployments — one where you build a webhook system, one where you use EventBridge — and one recommended hybrid.

e three snippets are the whole spine: verify the sender, publish reliably, dedupe on receipt . Every real production system layers monitoring, poison-message handling and business logic on top, but the load-bearing correctness is right here. ⚖️ Trade-offs, bottlenecks & likely follow-ups Trade-offs Push vs pull. Push (webhook/EventBridge) gives near-real-time delivery and eliminates polling waste, but forces every consumer to run a public endpoint or a listener. Pull (polling APIs, Kafka consumer groups) is simpler for the consumer but wastes cycles when nothing is happening.

Rule of thumb: use push when events are irregular and time-sensitive; use pull when they're continuous and the consumer sets its own pace. At-least-once vs exactly-once. Both webhooks and EventBridge are at-least-once — no exceptions. The industry has largely accepted that exactly-once delivery is a lie; instead you get exactly-once processing by making the consumer idempotent. Idempotency-by-id is the only correct answer. Ordering vs throughput. Guaranteeing ordering across a stream requires either a single partition (bottleneck) or per-key partitioning (SQS FIFO groups, Kinesis shard keys). Neither system does this by default because most workloads don't need it.

Push to customers: DIY webhook infra vs API Destinations. Rolling your own gives you full control (custom auth schemes, custom retry policies, custom UI). But it's a huge amount of undifferentiated heavy lifting — a whole product's worth of features. API Destinations get you 80% of it for cents per million events. Bottlenecks & failure modes Slow consumer — one tenant's endpoint takes 30 s to respond, retries pile up, connection pool exhausts. Fix: per-endpoint circuit breaker + rate limit; drop to DLQ fast when latency is bad. Thundering herd on outage recovery — a consumer recovers and gets 24 h of retries in one minute. Fix: jittered backoff + concurrency cap per endpoint.

Schema drift — you add a field, an old consumer breaks. Fix: additive-only changes, versioned event types, Schema Registry. Signature secret leak — rotate immediately, support dual secrets during rotation, keep a rotation cadence. Poison message — a payload that crashes every consumer. Fix: retry cap + DLQ + alarm; process from DLQ manually. EventBridge PutEvents throttling — 10 k/sec cap in us-east-1 (raiseable). Batch entries in one call (up to 10 entries × 256 KB = 2.56 MB per call), or shard across buses. Duplicate at boundary — the consumer processes the event, dies before returning 200; producer retries. Fix: idempotency guard at the top of the handler, before the side effect.

Likely interviewer follow-ups (with crisp answers) Why not just use SNS? SNS is a pub/sub topic with a simpler filter language and no rules-with-multiple-targets abstraction, no archive/replay, no schema registry, and no API destinations. EventBridge is a superset for event-driven use cases. SNS wins on raw throughput and price for simple broadcast; EventBridge wins on routing complexity, observability, and cross-account/cross-region. Why is HMAC signing better than a shared bearer token? A bearer token proves possession but says nothing about the payload — if it leaks, everything is compromised, and a MITM can tamper with the body.

HMAC over the body means an attacker who steals the header can't reuse it for a different payload, and rotating the secret invalidates all replays. How do you handle a consumer that's been down for a day? EventBridge retries up to 24 h with exponential backoff; after that the events land in the target's SQS DLQ with error metadata. When the consumer recovers, drain the DLQ into it (via a Lambda pointed at the DLQ). For longer outages, use Archive + Replay — you can replay any event received in the last N days by time range and pattern. Ordering matters for my domain — what do I do? Send events to an SQS FIFO queue as the target, with MessageGroupId derived from a business key (e.g.

order id). FIFO groups guarantee ordering within a group and parallelism across groups. Alternatively, embed a sequence number and drop stale events on the consumer. How do you prevent replay attacks on a webhook? Sign the timestamp along with the body, and reject anything more than ~5 minutes old on the consumer side. Also dedupe by event id in a store with a TTL longer than your retry window. How would you send webhooks to 100 000 different customer endpoints? Central EventBridge bus in your account; one rule with an API Destination target per customer, or one shared API Destination and a Lambda that looks up the right endpoint. Store per-customer secrets in Secrets Manager (Connections).

This scales because EventBridge handles the durability, retries, and DLQs — you just wire config. What if the same event triggers two rules — do I get duplicate delivery? Yes, that's fan-out: two rules × their targets. You either accept it (each consumer is idempotent) or restructure your patterns so rules are mutually exclusive. 🗣️ Interview cheat sheet 30-second pitch: "Webhooks and EventBridge solve the same problem — push an event from producer to consumer with retries and idempotency — but at different altitudes. Webhooks are the open-web version: HTTPS POST, HMAC signature, you own the outbox, relay, and DLQ.

EventBridge is a managed AWS event bus with content-based JSON pattern routing, up to 5 targets per rule, 300 rules per bus, 10 k events/sec, 24-hour retries with exponential backoff, and built-in DLQs and replay via archives. Both are at-least-once so consumers must dedupe by event id. The killer combo is EventBridge internally + API Destinations to fire webhooks to external customers — you get managed durability plus external reach." Numbers to quote EventBridge PutEvents : up to 10 000/sec per region, event size 256 KB . Fan-out: 5 targets/rule × 300 rules/bus . Retries: default 24 h max age , up to 185 attempts , exponential backoff.

Stripe retries: 3 days with exponential backoff on live mode. Consumer must return 2xx within seconds — enqueue and process async. Idempotency dedupe TTL should be ≥ retry window (so ≥ 24 h for EventBridge, ≥ 3 d for Stripe). Replay-attack tolerance: 5 minutes . Five talking points that win the round At-least-once forces idempotency — event id + conditional put + TTL. Say it out loud. Signing goes over the body + timestamp , not just the body — protects against replay. Dual-write problem — solve it with the transactional outbox (or let EventBridge own durability via PutEvents ). Fan-out is a rule-per-consumer pattern; consumers add rules, producer never changes.

DLQ + replay is not optional — it's how you keep a spike from turning into permanent data loss. ❓ FAQ — your follow-up questions Questions asked about this topic No follow-up questions yet — ask one about this topic and it'll be logged here with a compact answer. 📚 Sources Amazon EventBridge — What is EventBridge?
