System Design · Interview Prep WhatsApp / Chat System A planet-scale, low-latency, end-to-end encrypted messenger — 2 billion users, 100 billion messages a day, delivered in under a second whether you're online, offline, or on four devices at once. 🎯 Scenario 🧑‍🎓 Laymen 📋 Requirements 🏗️ Architecture 🎬 Animation 🔍 Deep-dive 🧮 DSA ☁️ AWS 💻 C# code ⚖️ Trade-offs 🗣️ Cheat sheet ❓ FAQ 📚 Sources 🎯 Real-world scenario What we're building & where it's used We're designing a real-time messaging system — the class of product that powers WhatsApp, Facebook Messenger, iMessage, Telegram, Signal, Slack, Discord, WeChat and Microsoft Teams .

A user opens the app, types a message, and it appears on the other person's phone in well under a second — even though the two devices might be on different continents, on different networks, and one of them might have been offline for the last three hours. Under the hood the system must maintain hundreds of millions of persistent connections , route messages to whichever server owns the receiver's socket, buffer anything the receiver hasn't picked up yet, and deliver every message exactly once, in order, with strong delivery and read receipts .

This scenario is the archetypal stateful system-design interview: unlike a URL shortener where every request is a one-shot HTTP call, a chat backend has to hold long-lived connections and coordinate fan-out across devices. Interviewers use it to probe how you reason about WebSockets, service discovery, message queues, event-driven fan-out, distributed key-value storage, presence detection, and multi-device synchronization — and how you defend the trade-offs when they push back. 🧑‍🎓 In laymen terms The whole thing, without any jargon You type "hey, are you free tonight?" and tap send. A second later your friend's phone buzzes. That short second is what we're designing.

It sounds trivial — but two billion people are doing this at the same time, from every country, on flaky trains and packed metros, and the app promises the message will always arrive, in the right order, even if their phone was off when you sent it. Picture a giant international post office. When you sign in to WhatsApp, the app quietly walks over to one specific clerk's window and says "I'm here — anything for me?" and then stays at the window with the phone line open . That's the trick: instead of you calling every few minutes to ask "got any mail?" , you leave a permanent line running so the clerk can just shout your name the instant a letter drops on the counter.

This permanent line is called a WebSocket , and it's what makes chat feel instant instead of laggy. When your friend Priya sends you a message, her app hands it to her clerk. Her clerk stamps it with a number so ordering never gets scrambled, writes a copy into a giant filing cabinet (in case something breaks), and then figures out which clerk you're currently talking to — using a big directory that says "Sonu is at window 47B." Your clerk shouts down your open line, your app buzzes, and up pops the message. What if your phone was off when Priya sent it? Easy — the message just waits in the filing cabinet , and the moment you sign back in, the system replays everything you missed, in order.

This is why WhatsApp never says "you missed 3 messages, sorry" — it will always catch you up. The little grey ticks you see are the story of that journey: one tick means the server got it, two ticks mean your friend's phone got it, two blue ticks mean their eyes actually looked at it. Each tick is a tiny confirmation message travelling the other way. And when you use WhatsApp Web at the same time as your phone, the same trick keeps both screens in sync — every device gets a copy through its own line. The hard part isn't one message — it's a hundred billion messages a day . No single post office could hold that.

So there are thousands of clerks in dozens of buildings around the world, all talking to each other over super-fast internal pipes, and a smart directory that tells your app which building to walk into. That's the design. 📋 Requirements & scale Requirements and back-of-the-envelope math Functional requirements 1-on-1 messaging with delivery + read receipts (single grey tick → double grey tick → double blue tick). Group messaging (WhatsApp caps at 1024 members per group; WeChat caps at 500). Presence (online/last-seen). Offline delivery — messages sent while you were offline arrive as soon as you reconnect, in order. Media messages (images/video) stored separately in blob storage.

Multi-device — same account on phone + web + desktop, kept in sync. End-to-end encryption — the server can never read message content. Non-functional requirements Low latency : p99 send-to-deliver < 500 ms for online users. Extreme availability : multi-region active-active, 99.99% uptime. Durability : never lose a message that the server has acknowledged. Ordering : monotonic ordering within a conversation (not globally). Consistency : read-your-writes and monotonic reads within a device. Back-of-the-envelope estimates Metric Estimate How we got it Daily active users (DAU) ~2 billion Public WhatsApp figure. Messages/day ~100 billion 50 msgs/user/day × 2B users.

Messages/sec (avg) ~1.2 M/s 100B ÷ 86,400 s. Peak QPS (send + fan-out) ~3–5 M/s ~3× average during peak hours. Avg message size ~100 bytes Text-dominated, ~20 words. Storage/day (text) ~10 TB/day 100 B × 100B msgs. Storage/year (text) ~3.6 PB/year 10 TB × 365. Bandwidth (steady) ~1 Gb/s 10 TB/day / 86 400 s ≈ 116 MB/s. The two anchor facts to memorise: ~100 B messages/day and ~1 M WebSocket connections per server . Everything else derives from those. 🏗️ High-level architecture How the pieces fit together The system splits into three planes. Stateless services (auth, signup, profile, friend list, media upload) sit behind a normal load balancer — any node can serve any request. Stateful chat services hold long-lived WebSocket connections; each client is pinned to exactly one chat server, so we need a service-discovery layer (typically Apache ZooKeeper ) to tell a signing-in client which chat server to connect to.

Finally, storage is split: user profiles and group metadata live in a relational DB (MySQL), messages live in a horizontally sharded key-value store (Cassandra / HBase / DynamoDB), and media blobs live in an object store (S3) fronted by a CDN. When Priya sends a message to Sonu, the request travels: Priya's phone → her chat server → ID generator (Snowflake) → message KV store → message sync queue (Kafka) → Sonu's chat server → Sonu's phone . If Sonu is offline, the last hop is replaced with a push notification via APNs/FCM; the message stays in the KV store until Sonu reconnects and pulls anything above his last-synced message ID.

Read receipts flow the same way in reverse, encoded as tiny control messages on the same WebSocket. 🎬 Animation Watch a message travel — send, ack, deliver, read, sync Priya sends "hey" to Sonu. Sonu has two devices online (phone + web). WebSocket connection — how messages reach online users Every online user opens a WebSocket (WSS on port 443) to a specific chat server.

Unlike HTTP request/response, a WebSocket is bidirectional and persistent — the server can push a new message the millisecond it arrives without the client polling. Behind the scenes the server pins userId → (server, socket_fd) in an in-memory table (backed by Redis across the fleet) so that any other server can look up "where is Sonu right now?" in O(1). This is the piece a lot of candidates get wrong: chat is stateful — a load balancer alone doesn't help, because you need to route the packet to the exact server that owns the recipient's socket.

Why WebSocket and not HTTP long-polling? Three reasons interviewers want to hear: (1) real bidirectional push, no polling waste; (2) one connection per device instead of one HTTP request per message — massively lower CPU and memory; (3) the server can immediately detect a graceful close, so presence flips cleanly. The trade-off: WebSockets are stateful , so autoscaling is harder — you can't just add a box and route half the traffic to it. 2. Offline handling — Kafka + durable KV Before a message is acked to the sender, the chat server writes it to Kafka (a FIFO log) and to a replicated key-value store (Cassandra / HBase / DynamoDB). Only then does it send the single grey tick back.

This is the write-then-ack pattern — the message is durable before we promise anything. If the recipient is offline, we simply skip the WebSocket push; the message sits in the KV store keyed by (recipient_id, message_id) where message_id is a time-sortable Snowflake ID. When the recipient reconnects, its device sends "give me everything > cur_max_message_id" — a bounded, ordered replay. WhatsApp historically used Mnesia (an Erlang-native distributed DB) for pending-message storage, which is why they can run so few servers per user — but modern designs use Cassandra or DynamoDB with a similar shape. 3.

Guaranteed delivery — at-least-once + idempotent client-ack Real messengers are at-least-once with client-side dedup , not exactly-once. The flow: the sender generates a client-side UUID ( client_msg_id ) and retries the send until it gets a server-ack. The server generates a durable Snowflake ID and stores the mapping client_msg_id → server_msg_id . If the sender ever retries the same client_msg_id , the server returns the existing server_msg_id instead of creating a duplicate. On the receiver side, the client also tracks the highest server ID it has stored and drops duplicates by ID. This gives you effectively exactly-once without needing distributed 2PC. 4.

Read receipts — three-state ACK chain Every message has three delivery states, each triggering a tiny control packet the other way: Server-ack (✓ single grey tick) — chat server has durably stored the message. Delivery-ack (✓✓ double grey tick) — receiver's device has received it over its WebSocket. Read-ack (✓✓ blue) — the receiver actually opened the chat and rendered the message. These acks are just small JSON envelopes on the same WebSocket: {type: "ack", state: "read", server_msg_id: 87342...} . The sender's client renders them into the little ticks you see under each bubble. 5.

Multi-device sync — per-device identity + client fan-out The 2021 WhatsApp multi-device rewrite (see the Meta engineering post in Sources) is worth memorising because it flips a common assumption. Instead of the phone being the single source of truth that mirrors to companions, each device (phone, web, desktop, Portal) has its own identity key . When Priya sends a message to Sonu, her client encrypts and transmits N times — once per device in Sonu's device list, using pairwise Signal Protocol sessions. This is called client-fanout . The server never sees plaintext; it just routes N ciphertexts.

For app state (contact names, archived chats, starred), the server holds an end-to-end encrypted snapshot each device can pull. For sync ordering, every device tracks cur_max_message_id . On reconnect it asks "give me everything > my max" and gets back an ordered stream. Because Snowflake IDs are monotonic within a partition, this is trivially O(log N) with a range query. 6. Presence — heartbeats, not disconnect events Naïvely you'd say "flip user to offline when the WebSocket closes." That fails in practice — mobile users drop and reconnect constantly (tunnels, metros, switching Wi-Fi ↔ 4G). A single close-event would make Priya's app flicker "online / last seen 3s ago" every 30 seconds.

Instead, clients send a heartbeat every 5 seconds , and presence flips offline only after ~30 seconds of no heartbeat . Presence changes fan out via pub/sub (Redis channels or Kafka) to only the friends who currently have that user's chat open — not to everyone. 7. Group messaging — server fan-out vs client fan-out Two approaches: (a) server fan-out — the sender ships one ciphertext to the server, the server duplicates it into N recipient inboxes; (b) client fan-out — the sender's client ships N ciphertexts, one per recipient. WhatsApp uses (b) for E2E encryption reasons (server can't hold decryption keys).

For large groups (1024 members) this uses the Signal Sender Key optimisation: the sender encrypts the message once with a symmetric group key and only sends that group key pairwise to each member — a huge reduction. Facebook Messenger and Discord historically used server fan-out because they don't do E2E by default. 8. Storage schema Two tables in a Cassandra-style KV store: -- 1-on-1 messages (partitioned by chat_id, ordered by message_id) CREATE TABLE messages ( chat_id uuid, -- deterministic hash(min(a,b), max(a,b)) message_id bigint, -- Snowflake, time-sortable sender_id uuid, content blob, -- ciphertext sent_at timestamp, PRIMARY KEY ((chat_id), message_id) ) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (

message_id DESC); -- Per-user inbox (used for offline replay) CREATE TABLE inbox ( user_id uuid, message_id bigint, chat_id uuid, PRIMARY KEY ((user_id), message_id) ) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (message_id DESC); The messages table is the source of truth. The inbox table is a per-user projection that makes "pending offline messages for user X" a single partition read. Both are shardable by their partition key. 🧮 The DSA behind it Data structures & algorithms A chat backend isn't fancy algorithms — it's the right data structure at each layer.

Observability CloudWatch + X-Ray + OpenTelemetry Trace a message across services; alert on p99 latency and delivery-lag. Deployment shape: multi-region active-active . Each region owns a slice of users (assigned by phone-number country code hashed into a region). Cross-region messages travel over a Kafka MirrorMaker link to the destination region, then out to the recipient's chat server. DynamoDB Global Tables replicate the message store between regions asynchronously for disaster recovery, but the write path is region-local for latency.

ble ( route:{userId} ) is the entire trick — any server can push to any user in one Redis lookup; (2) the send handler acks after durable persist, not on socket accept — that's what makes the single grey tick meaningful; (3) the Redis pub/sub channel-per-server means a message crosses at most one hop between chat servers; (4) heartbeat + TTL on the Redis key handles graceful and non-graceful disconnects uniformly. ⚖️ Trade-offs, bottlenecks & likely follow-ups The scaling bottlenecks The WebSocket layer is always the first bottleneck. Each connection burns ~30–50 KB of kernel + user memory, plus a file descriptor.

On a well-tuned Linux box you can push ~1–2M concurrent sockets, WhatsApp reportedly ran up to ~10M with heavy kernel tuning on Erlang. Above that you're just adding boxes. The routing table (Redis) is the second bottleneck — it takes a hit on every message; you shard it by hash(userId) % N . The message store is the third: at 1M writes/sec you must partition by chat_id , not by user or by time. Consistency trade-off We chose availability over strong consistency (AP in CAP terms). If a partition happens between regions, sending still works — messages queue locally and reconcile when the link heals.

The cost is that a message can very briefly land out of order if it crossed a region right at partition — the Snowflake ID lets clients reorder on receive, so users never see it. Delivery-guarantee trade-off We do at-least-once + client-side idempotency, not exactly-once. Building true exactly-once would require distributed 2PC on every message — too slow. The dedup key ( client_msg_id ) makes retries invisible in practice. Follow-ups you should expect What happens if a chat server crashes with 1M connected users? All those TCP connections drop. Clients detect the RST and immediately reconnect through the load balancer, which routes them (via ZooKeeper/Cloud Map) to a healthy server.

On reconnect, each client asks the KV store for messages above its cur_max_message_id . Nothing is lost because the message was durable before we acked it. How do you scale groups to 1000+ members without server fan-out costing 1000× storage? Two techniques. (1) Client fan-out with Signal Sender Keys: sender encrypts once with a group key, sends N tiny key envelopes but only one ciphertext. (2) Server stores one copy of the ciphertext in a "channel" partition and uses per-user pointers rather than duplicating. How is ordering preserved when two people type at the same time? Ordering is only guaranteed within a conversation .

Both messages get Snowflake IDs; the client sorts by ID before rendering. Because Snowflake embeds a millisecond timestamp, ties are extremely rare and broken deterministically by machine ID. How does WhatsApp Web stay in sync with your phone? Post-2021 architecture: each device has its own identity key and its own WebSocket to the server. Every message is client-fanout'd to every device in the recipient's device list. On new-device link, the primary device transfers an E2E-encrypted history bundle. App state (mutes, archives) sits on the server as an E2E-encrypted blob each device can pull.

How do you handle a user with 100,000 friends going online? You don't broadcast presence to all of them. Presence pub/sub only fires for the subset of friends who currently have that user's chat open — a much smaller set. For the rest, presence is fetched on demand when they next open the chat. How does end-to-end encryption survive multi-device without exposing keys server-side? The server holds identity public keys , one per device, and never sees a private key. The Signal Protocol's Double Ratchet establishes a pairwise session between every (sender-device, receiver-device) pair. The server just routes ciphertexts.

🗣️ Interview cheat sheet 30-second pitch: "I'd build it as three planes — stateless APIs behind ALB, stateful chat servers holding WebSockets, and durable storage in DynamoDB + S3. A Redis routing table maps userId → chat_server so any node can push to any user in one hop. Sends are written to Kafka + DynamoDB before we ack, giving durable at-least-once delivery with client-side dedup on client_msg_id . Offline users get catch-up via a range scan on their inbox partition. Read receipts are just typed control frames on the same socket.

Multi-device works via per-device identity keys and client-fanout, so E2E encryption stays intact." Write-then-ack — durable persist before returning ✓; that's how the single grey tick becomes a promise. Snowflake IDs — monotonic, time-sortable, decentralised — enable "everything above my last ID" replay.

Client fan-out for multi-device — per-device identity keys keep E2E encryption intact across web/phone/desktop. System Design · Interview Prep Design YouTube 500 hours uploaded every minute, a billion hours watched every day — an upload/transcode/CDN/recommendation pipeline that has to feel instant on any device, on any network, anywhere on Earth. 🎯 Scenario 🧑‍🎓 Laymen 📋 Requirements 🏗️ Architecture 🎬 Animation 🔍 Deep-dive 🧮 DSA ☁️ AWS 💻 C# code ⚖️ Trade-offs 🗣️ Cheat sheet ❓ FAQ 📚 Sources 🎯 Real-world scenario What we're building & where it's used We're designing a global user-generated video platform : a creator uploads a large file once, and viewers on every device and every network watch a version that looks great and starts instantly.

This is the archetype for YouTube , and closely related to TikTok , Instagram Reels , Vimeo , Netflix (though Netflix is a curated library, not user uploads), Twitch (live streaming variant), and Facebook Watch . The interview version usually asks for on-demand video only — live streaming is a follow-up. Companies build this because video is the dominant medium of the internet and every large platform eventually needs a media pipeline: a social product wants shortform, an e-commerce site wants product videos, a corporate LMS wants training content.

The design touches every heavyweight concept in a distributed systems curriculum: large blob storage , asynchronous processing at massive fan-out , CDN and edge caching , adaptive bitrate streaming , and ranked recommendation at billion-item scale . That's why it's a favorite interview question — a good answer proves you can reason about the entire stack, not just one layer. 🧑‍🎓 In laymen terms Explained without any tech words The everyday problem. Imagine you shoot a 15-minute video on your phone — a birthday, a cooking tutorial, whatever.

You want to share it, and you want any random person on any device to be able to watch it without waiting, without buffering, and without it looking blurry on their new TV or eating up their mobile data. That is genuinely hard, and it's what YouTube quietly does for you. The story of one video. When you press "Upload," your phone doesn't try to send the whole video in one go — it slices it into small pieces, like tearing a long letter into pages, and sends each page separately. If your connection drops halfway, only the missing pages get re-sent, not the whole thing.

Once all the pages arrive at YouTube's building, an army of "converter workers" takes your original video and makes many copies of it — a small blurry one for old phones, a medium one for laptops, a big sharp one for TVs, all at the same time. Each copy is then chopped into tiny 4- to 6-second clips and stored in a giant warehouse of hard drives spread across many cities. Where things live. When someone in Tokyo taps play, YouTube doesn't fetch your video from a warehouse in California — that would be slow. Instead, YouTube keeps copies of popular videos in mini-warehouses close to viewers , kind of like how supermarkets keep the popular snacks up front and the odd stuff in a back room.

Those little clips arrive one after another, so playback starts in a second or two even if the whole video is an hour long. The hard part. The tricky bit is that hundreds of millions of people press play every hour , and each person is on a different network, a different device, and speaks a different language. YouTube also has to guess which video you'll enjoy next — otherwise you'd close the app after the first video. So on top of the storage and delivery, there's a giant "recommendation kitchen" running in the background, tasting billions of viewing patterns to serve you a personalized playlist.

The magic is that almost none of this happens while you wait — the heavy work was done long before you tapped play. 📋 Requirements & scale Requirements and back-of-the-envelope math Functional requirements Upload a video (large file, resumable, chunked). Transcode the source into multiple resolutions (144p → 4K) and codecs (H.264, VP9, AV1) for adaptive playback. Stream to any device with adaptive bitrate (HLS/DASH) so quality follows the network. Search by title, tags, channel. Recommend a personalized "up next" list and homepage feed. Social : likes, comments, subscriptions, views.

Non-functional requirements Availability > strong consistency — a stale view count is fine; a broken play button is not. Low startup latency : playback should begin in < 2 seconds worldwide. Durability of the master copy: ~11 nines. Losing an uploaded video is catastrophic for creators. Global reach : viewers on every continent, on cellular to fiber. Read-heavy : watches vastly outnumber uploads (roughly 100 : 1 ). Back-of-the-envelope (YouTube-scale) Metric Estimate How we got there DAU ~1 B daily active users Public figure; ~2 B monthly. The two dominant costs are storage (durable master + many renditions) and egress bandwidth (billions of hours streamed). That's why the entire design orients around doing the heavy work once, offline , and serving the results from cache close to the viewer . 🏗️ High-level architecture How the pieces fit together The whole system splits cleanly into two flows that meet only at the metadata database.

The upload/ingest flow is offline and heavy — it moves bytes into durable object storage, generates renditions and thumbnails, extracts metadata, and publishes the video as "ready." The read/watch flow is online and light — the player fetches a manifest, then pulls small segments from the CDN and adapts quality as bandwidth changes. Recommendations run alongside , feeding two-stage ranked lists into the homepage and up-next slots. Synchronous request flow Asynchronous processing Two subtle points that separate a good answer from a great one: the master copy in the raw object store is precious — everything else can be regenerated from it, and durability requirements are highest here.

And the CDN is not a single layer — there's an edge PoP close to the viewer, a regional mid-tier that fills cold edges without hammering origin, and only then origin storage. This tiering keeps origin egress bandwidth manageable even at YouTube scale. 🎬 Animation Watch the core mechanic run, step by step This animation walks through the two flows that make a video watchable: upload → transcode fan-out → store , then viewer → CDN edge → adaptive segments . Upload flow — resumable, chunked, direct-to-blob The client asks the upload service for a signed pre-authorized URL (S3 pre-signed URL or the equivalent) and then uploads directly to object storage , bypassing the application server. Uploads use the tus.io resumable protocol (or S3 multipart): the file is split into ~5–10 MB parts, each part is uploaded independently, and if the connection dies only the missing parts are retried. When all parts land, the client calls completeUpload and the server assembles them into a single object.

Two crucial properties: (a) the application tier never becomes a bandwidth bottleneck, and (b) resumability turns "phone died in a tunnel" from a fatal error into a five-second retry. On completion, the service writes a videos row with status=UPLOADED and enqueues a transcode job — the API returns 200 immediately , and everything downstream is asynchronous. 2.

Transcoding — the biggest asynchronous fan-out in the stack A single source has to become many outputs : multiple resolutions (144p, 240p, 360p, 480p, 720p, 1080p, 1440p, 2160p) × multiple codecs (H.264 for compatibility, VP9 and AV1 for bandwidth savings on modern devices) × segmented into 4–6-second chunks × plus a thumbnail sheet, captions, and content-ID fingerprint. To make this tractable at 500 hours-uploaded-per-minute, transcoding is chunk-parallelized : the source is split into scene-cut boundaries or fixed intervals, each interval is transcoded on a different worker (MapReduce-style), then reassembled.

YouTube built a custom silicon accelerator called the VCU (Video Coding Unit) that gave them 20-33× the compute efficiency of CPU transcoding — proof of how much this workload dominates infrastructure. In an interview, describe it as "a Kafka topic per resolution, workers pull chunks, and a reducer stitches segments and writes the manifest." 3. Streaming — HLS/DASH adaptive bitrate Every stored video is not one file — it is a manifest (M3U8 for HLS, MPD for DASH) plus many 4–6-second segments , one segment per (resolution, codec) combination. When the player opens a video, it downloads the manifest first (a few KB), then requests segments one at a time.

The player measures its own bandwidth and buffer level and switches quality between segments — so a viewer whose Wi-Fi drops from strong to weak sees the next segment come down in 480p instead of stalling. This is why segments are short: shorter segments mean faster quality adaptation, at the cost of more manifest overhead. YouTube typically uses ~5-second segments as the sweet spot. 4. Storage tiers — cheap-and-cold, fast-and-hot Videos are stored in three logical tiers. The master original lives in a durable, replicated blob store (S3 Standard / GCS) — this is the source of truth from which any lost rendition can be regenerated.

The renditions and segments live in the same blob store but are the objects actually served. Cold videos — anything not watched in, say, 90 days — are migrated to a cheaper storage class (S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval or similar) with slightly higher retrieval cost. Metadata (title, uploader, view count, likes) lives in a sharded relational store (Vitess on MySQL for YouTube itself); high-volume denormalized reads (comments, subscription feeds) sit in a wide-column store like Bigtable/Cassandra. 5. CDN strategy — three tiers to keep origin quiet The CDN is the only reason this design is affordable .

It has three tiers: the edge PoP is the closest to the user (Google Global Cache lives in ISP networks and inside universities; CloudFront lives in ~600 PoPs globally); the regional mid-tier aggregates edge misses so origin sees only unique content; and the origin is the blob store of last resort. Hot content is promoted into the CDN by popularity — a video that starts trending is pulled up from origin into the edge on its first miss. A cold long-tail video may never be cached, and that's fine: for a video watched twice a month, cache miss cost is trivial.

Interviewers love hearing you say "we don't cache the long tail because the working-set is Zipf-distributed — 90% of watches are on 10% of videos." 6. Recommendations — two-stage funnel The recommendation problem is "from ~1 billion videos, pick 10 for this user right now." You cannot rank a billion candidates per request — the classic solution, publicly described in the 2016 paper "Deep Neural Networks for YouTube Recommendations" , is a two-stage architecture . Stage 1 — candidate generation — takes user embeddings and does approximate nearest-neighbor lookup over item embeddings to return a few hundred candidates in milliseconds.

Stage 2 — ranking — takes those hundreds of candidates plus rich features (watch time, freshness, session context, user demographics) and applies a deep model to produce a final ordered list. Real-time signals (this session's watches) feed both stages so the feed adapts as you scroll. Training data comes from the analytics pipeline: every play, pause, and skip is logged to Kafka , processed by Spark, and lands in BigQuery for offline model training. 7. View counting & social — write-behind, eventually consistent View counts do not go through a synchronous DB write.

Every play emits an event to Kafka , a stream job aggregates counts per window, and the count DB is updated in batches — a viewer refreshing the page might see the counter go from 1,203 to 1,847 in one jump. This is deliberate: strong consistency on a global counter would require distributed locking, which is impossible at YouTube throughput. The same pattern applies to likes and watch history — write to a durable log first, materialize the aggregate later . 🧮 The DSA behind it Data structures & algorithms YouTube looks like it's "all infrastructure," but under every subsystem is a specific algorithm doing the heavy lifting. Naming them in an interview signals depth.

Component Structure / algorithm Why chosen & complexity Video ID generation Snowflake-style 64-bit IDs Time-sortable, globally unique without coordination. O(1) per ID. Upload chunk assembly Content-addressable hashing (SHA-256 per part) Detect corruption & dedupe re-uploads. O(n) over bytes; parallelizable. Transcode fan-out MapReduce / DAG of chunks Split source at scene cuts, transcode chunks in parallel, reduce (stitch). Wall-clock shrinks from O(video length) to O(chunk length). Segment lookup on watch Hash-partitioned key-value on (videoId, resolution, segmentIndex) O(1) get from blob store; CDN caches by URL.

Adaptive bitrate selection Rate-based EWMA on client bandwidth + PID-style buffer controller Smooths quality switches; O(1) per segment on the client. Search index Inverted index + TF-IDF / BM25 (Elasticsearch/Lucene) O(k + log N) per term over posting lists. Candidate generation (recs) Approximate nearest neighbor over embeddings (HNSW, ScaNN) Sub-linear (~O(log N)) over a billion items vs O(N) brute force. Ranking (recs) Deep neural net over hundreds of features O(F × depth × candidates); candidates capped at a few hundred, so bounded. Trending / view aggregation Count-min sketch, HyperLogLog for unique viewers Sub-linear memory, approximate but tight bounds; O(1) update.

Hot content in CDN LRU-K / LFU with admission (TinyLFU) Keeps hot working-set (Zipf head) in edge cache. O(1) amortized. Duplicate / Content-ID detection Perceptual hashing + Bloom filter pre-filter Bloom rules out obvious non-matches in O(1); full pHash comparison only on candidates. The one to remember: MapReduce for transcoding . It's the reason a 3-hour 4K upload doesn't take 3 hours to become watchable — chunks encode in parallel and the reducer stitches them. ☁️ AWS implementation Mapping the design to AWS YouTube itself runs on Google's infrastructure (GCS, Bigtable, Spanner, Borg, custom VCU silicon, Google Global Cache).

If we build the same design on AWS , the mapping is remarkably direct — the primitives all have close cousins. Component AWS service Why Client edge / DNS Route 53 + CloudFront Anycast DNS + global CDN with ~600 PoPs and shield tier for origin protection. Upload service API Gateway + Lambda (for pre-signed URL) → direct S3 multipart upload Client uploads bytes directly to S3, bypassing app tier; API only mints URLs. Raw / master blob storage S3 Standard (with S3 Intelligent-Tiering) 11 nines durability; cross-region replication for DR. Cold archive S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval Long-tail videos rarely watched — ~⅕ the storage cost of Standard.

Transcode queue SQS (or MSK/Kinesis for higher throughput) Decouples upload from transcode; per-resolution queue for prioritization. Transcoder workers AWS Elemental MediaConvert (managed) or ECS/EKS with FFmpeg + g5 GPU nodes MediaConvert is the fastest interview answer; DIY on ECS/EKS if you need custom codecs or VCU-like acceleration. Renditions & segments S3 (same bucket, prefix /renditions/{videoId}/{res}/ ) Serves as CDN origin. Content packaging MediaPackage (for HLS/DASH manifests) Also does DRM (Widevine/FairPlay/PlayReady) and just-in-time packaging. CDN CloudFront (with regional edge caches / Origin Shield) Three tiers: edge PoP → regional edge cache → S3.

Origin Shield collapses cache-fill traffic. Metadata DB Aurora MySQL (sharded) or DynamoDB with GSIs Videos, channels, uploaders, subscriptions. Aurora if you need joins; DynamoDB for pure item lookups. Wide-column (comments, watch history) DynamoDB or Amazon Keyspaces (Cassandra) Write-heavy, denormalized reads by partition key. Search Amazon OpenSearch Inverted index over title, description, tags, transcripts. Cache ElastiCache Redis (with DAX for DynamoDB) Manifest metadata, hot video info, session state. Event stream (views, likes) Kinesis Data Streams or MSK Millions of events/sec, replay-able for reprocessing.

Analytics / training data Kinesis Firehose → S3 → EMR (Spark) → Redshift / Athena Feeds the recommender's training pipeline. Recommendations (candidate gen) SageMaker + OpenSearch k-NN or Amazon MemoryDB for Redis (vector search) ANN over user/item embeddings; sub-linear lookup at billion-item scale. Recommendations (ranking) SageMaker real-time endpoint (deep model) Ranks candidates with rich features; low-latency p99. Live streaming (extension) MediaLive + MediaPackage + CloudFront RTMP/SRT ingest, HLS/DASH out. Deployment story : services run on EKS across three Availability Zones per region, with active-active multi-region for user-facing APIs.

S3 uses Cross-Region Replication so a whole region can go down without losing the master copy. CloudFront's global anycast means viewers in Tokyo, São Paulo, and Frankfurt all get their nearest edge automatically. The recommender's online serving lives in every region behind an ALB; the offline training is a single global pipeline that publishes updated embeddings and model weights on a daily cadence. 💻 C# implementation Two representative pieces of the design in C#: (1) the upload service returning a pre-signed S3 URL and publishing a transcode job, and (2) a transcoder worker that pulls a job, launches FFmpeg for one rendition, and writes segments back to S3.

Both are deliberately compact — the point in an interview is to show you can code the seam between service tiers, not to write a full media server. In production, chunked parallel transcoding would split the source further (say, one worker per 30-second scene) and a reducer would stitch segments — this is where the MapReduce framing shines. For AWS-first answers, replace the FFmpeg worker entirely with Elemental MediaConvert — same conceptual pipeline, but managed.

⚖️ Trade-offs, bottlenecks & likely follow-ups Where it can break The three real bottlenecks are egress bandwidth cost , transcoder throughput during viral upload bursts , and metadata DB hot shards (e.g., a global superstar channel writing a video that every user queries). Egress is handled by aggressive CDN caching and by tiered edge → regional → origin fill; transcoder bursts absorb into the queue and workers autoscale; hot shards are handled by caching the item view (Redis) and by write-behind counters . A subtle failure mode: a coding bug that produces a corrupted rendition — you never want to lose the master, so renditions are re-derivable and can be blown away and regenerated .

Consistency vs availability Everything user-facing chooses availability . View counts, likes, subscriber counts are all eventually consistent — a viewer refreshing may see the count jump. Payment/monetization data (revenue share, ad billing) is the exception and lives in a separate strongly-consistent system with 2PC/Saga semantics. In an interview, name that split explicitly: "read paths are AP; the money path is CP." Likely follow-up questions (with crisp answers) How do you keep viral videos from melting origin? Origin Shield / regional mid-tier collapses cache-fill traffic to one request per region per edge miss.

Plus request coalescing : if 10 000 edges miss simultaneously, only one goes to origin. Why 4–6-second HLS segments? Why not 2s or 10s? Shorter segments = faster ABR adaptation and lower live latency but more manifest overhead and more HTTP requests. Longer = fewer requests, better cache hit ratio, but slow to react to bandwidth changes. 4–6s is the industry-standard sweet spot. How do you handle "fresh upload not yet transcoded, viewers hitting play"? Show a "processing" state until the first watchable rendition (typically 360p) is ready — this is why 360p is transcoded first. Once ready, unlock playback and continue transcoding higher resolutions in the background.

How does the recommender avoid stale results after a viral event? Real-time signals feed both stages: recent watches are added to the user's session vector and to a real-time popularity index. Candidate ANN over embeddings uses the fresh session embedding; ranking uses live features. Full model retraining is daily; feature freshness is minutes. Why not gRPC everywhere instead of HTTP for streaming? Video segments are big and cacheable — HTTP is a first-class citizen of every CDN, browser, and mobile player, and HTTP/2 already multiplexes. gRPC gives you nothing on the segment path and would kill CDN-ability.

Use gRPC on the control plane (upload service ↔ metadata) and HTTP on the data plane. How would you extend this to live streaming? RTMP/SRT ingest, real-time transcode to LL-HLS or CMAF chunked-transfer, edge CDN with same three-tier fill. End-to-end latency ~2–5s (versus 15–30s classic HLS). YouTube Live uses this pattern. How do you prevent unauthorized downloads / DRM? Encrypt segments (AES-128 in CMAF) with per-user session keys handed out through DRM licensing (Widevine / FairPlay / PlayReady). Pre-signed segment URLs with short TTLs prevent link-sharing. 🗣️ Interview cheat sheet "YouTube is fundamentally a write-once, read-a-billion-times problem.

The uploader hits a chunked, resumable upload that lands the master file in blob storage. That triggers an asynchronous, MapReduce-style transcode into 6–8 resolutions × 2–3 codecs × 4-second HLS segments. Viewers hit a three-tier CDN — edge PoP, regional cache, origin — and the player switches quality between segments as bandwidth changes. Metadata lives in sharded MySQL; comments in a wide-column store; views ride a Kafka pipeline into an aggregate. Recommendations are a two-stage funnel : ANN over embeddings picks a few hundred candidates from a billion, then a deep ranker scores them.

Choose availability over consistency everywhere except billing." Numbers to quote 500 hours uploaded/minute (public YouTube figure). ~1 B DAU, ~5 B views/day , read:write ratio ~100:1. ~2 PB/day raw upload growth , ~1 EB/year with renditions. 4–6 second HLS/DASH segments . <2 s startup latency target; 11 nines durability on the master. Five talking points that win the round " The client uploads bytes directly to S3 via a pre-signed URL — my app never becomes the bandwidth bottleneck." " Transcoding is MapReduce : split at scene cuts, transcode chunks in parallel, reduce back into segments + a manifest." " Three-tier CDN — edge PoP, regional, origin — because a single-tier CDN can't survive

a viral event; regional collapses fill traffic." " Player-side adaptive bitrate using the same manifest — the server has one job, the player has all the intelligence." " Recs are a two-stage funnel : ANN over embeddings for recall (billions → hundreds), deep ranker for precision (hundreds → 10)." ❓ FAQ — your follow-up questions Questions asked about this topic No follow-up questions yet — ask one about this topic and it'll be logged here with a compact answer.

t: ZooKeeper & the Watch Mechanism — System Design
x: What makes it an interview darling is the watch mechanism — a pull-then-push model that lets a client register interest in a "znode" (ZooKeeper's word for a node in its tree) and receive a single asynchronous callback the instant that znode is created, deleted, or modified. This one primitive, layered on top of ZooKeeper's ZAB consensus, is what makes elegant, reactive designs for service discovery , dynamic configuration , leader election , and distributed locks possible.

t: ZooKeeper & the Watch Mechanism — System Design
x: Understanding it well signals that a candidate can reason about push-vs-pull, session lifecycle, thundering-herd, and the gap between "eventually notified" and "strictly ordered." 🧑‍🎓 In laymen terms The office noticeboard that texts you when it changes Imagine a big company with fifty offices in different cities, all working on the same project. Every office needs to know: who is the current CEO? which supplier are we using this week? which fifteen offices are actually open today? If each office had to phone every other office each morning to find out, work would grind to a halt. Instead, the company puts up one central noticeboard in a special coordination room.

t: ZooKeeper & the Watch Mechanism — System Design
x: It's not a big board — just a tree of little slots. One slot says "current CEO". Another slot says "today's supplier". A folder called /open-offices holds one small note per office that's open today. Every morning, each open office puts a sticky note in that folder with its name on it — and that sticky note is magical : if the office closes or loses connection, its note falls off automatically. This is how everyone can see, at a glance, exactly which offices are alive right now. Now here's the clever bit. Any office can walk up to a slot and say "tell me the moment this changes." The coordination room writes that request on a little side-list.

t: ZooKeeper & the Watch Mechanism — System Design
x: When the slot changes — someone updates the CEO, or a new sticky note falls off — the coordination room sends a text message to that office . The office doesn't have to keep walking back to check. This is called a watch . Because the coordination room is so important, it's not a single room — it's three or five identical rooms in different buildings, all keeping the same board in sync. If the main one catches fire, the others take over in under a second. But they'll never disagree with each other, because before any note goes on the board, a majority of the rooms have to sign off on the change.

t: ZooKeeper & the Watch Mechanism — System Design
x: Why is this hard? Because texts can get delayed, offices can go offline, and if two offices both try to claim "I'm the new CEO" at the same time, the system has to pick exactly one. It has to feel instant — under a second — and it has to be correct , even if half the coordination rooms are broken. Concrete example. Kafka (the giant messaging system used by LinkedIn, Uber, and Netflix) used ZooKeeper for a decade. Every Kafka broker on startup wrote an ephemeral sticky note under /brokers/ids/ .

t: ZooKeeper & the Watch Mechanism — System Design
x: When a broker crashed, its note vanished, ZooKeeper sent a watch notification to the Kafka "controller," and the controller reassigned that broker's work to healthy brokers — all in about 300 milliseconds. No polling. No wasted heartbeats. Just: state changed → you get a text → you react . 📋 Requirements & scale What ZooKeeper has to do — and how much Functional Store small hierarchical key-value data (znodes) with strong consistency across the ensemble. Notify interested clients the moment a znode is created, deleted, or its data changes — the watch primitive. Elect a leader among a set of contenders using ephemeral+sequential znodes.

The bottleneck shows up when you push write rates past ~50k/s, when watch churn from ephemeral node flapping causes storms, or when total znode count crosses ~1M (RAM footprint + snapshot size). 🏗️ High-level architecture An ensemble, a filesystem, and a watchlist per client ZooKeeper runs as an ensemble of 3, 5, or 7 servers. One is the leader , elected via a fast leader-election protocol at start-up. All writes flow through the leader; all reads can be served by any follower.

t: ZooKeeper & the Watch Mechanism — System Design
x: The state is a rooted tree of znodes — think of it as a tiny, in-memory, replicated Linux filesystem where each file also has a version, an ACL, and can host watches . Two flows dominate. Writes (amber) are always forwarded to the leader, which broadcasts a ZAB proposal, waits for a majority to ack the disk fsync, and commits — that's why write latency has a floor of one disk sync + one majority round-trip. Watch notifications (green dashed) flow back from the follower a client is connected to, in strict order relative to the client's other events. Reads are served straight from the follower's in-memory replica, which is why ZooKeeper scales reads by adding followers .

The znode — a "file that's also a directory" The ZooKeeper data model is a rooted tree of znodes .

t: ZooKeeper & the Watch Mechanism — System Design
x: Each znode has a name , up to ~1 MB of opaque byte-data , an ACL, a stat structure with version numbers and timestamps, and zero or more child znodes. Every path is absolute: /kafka/brokers/ids/1 . There are three important flavours: persistent Persistent znode — the default; lives until explicitly deleted. Used for durable config: /config/cache-ttl . ephemeral Ephemeral znode — tied to the session that created it. When that session times out or the client crashes, ZooKeeper deletes it automatically . This is the trick behind service discovery — the znode itself is the liveness signal.

t: ZooKeeper & the Watch Mechanism — System Design
x: sequential Sequential suffix — when creating a znode, you can ask for a monotonically-increasing 10-digit counter to be appended by the server. So create("/lock/-", EPH+SEQ) yields /lock/-0000000001 , then -0000000002 , and so on. Combined with ephemeral, this is the entire basis of ZooKeeper's classic leader-election recipe. 2. Watches — the pull-then-push notification primitive All three read operations — getData , getChildren , and exists — accept a boolean flag that says "also set a watch." Setting a watch is essentially free: it's a small entry recorded on the follower the client is talking to.

t: ZooKeeper & the Watch Mechanism — System Design
x: When the target znode changes, the follower fires exactly one event to the client and forgets about the watch. The client must re-read to re-arm if it wants to keep watching. This "one-shot" semantics is what keeps ZooKeeper's memory bounded even under a fleet of thousands of clients. There are three logical watch types , and mutations fire them selectively: Mutation Fires on target znode Fires on parent create data watch (from exists ) child watch (from getChildren ) setData data watch (from getData / exists ) — delete data watch + child watch child watch Watches carry two guarantees that make reactive designs correct: (1) the client sees the watch event before it can see the new data — so

t: ZooKeeper & the Watch Mechanism — System Design
x: if your callback re-reads, it's guaranteed to see the state that fired the event; and (2) watch order matches the global update order for that client. That's what lets you build a state machine driven by a stream of events without racing. Persistent / recursive watches (ZooKeeper 3.6+) — set with addWatch() — are the newer option: they don't clear after firing, and can recursively cover an entire subtree. They're perfect for a configuration bus : point one recursive watch at /config and get every child change as long as your session is alive. 3. Session lifecycle — the heartbeat that keeps ephemerals alive A ZooKeeper session is a stateful connection between a client and the ensemble.

t: ZooKeeper & the Watch Mechanism — System Design
x: The client sends heartbeats (technically "pings") every third of a session timeout by default. If the ensemble stops hearing pings for the full session timeout, the leader expires the session and deletes all ephemeral znodes it owned — and fires all corresponding watches. This is the "sticky note falls off automatically" magic. Session IDs are opaque 64-bit values; on TCP failure the client can transparently reconnect to a different server as long as it presents the same session ID before the timeout, keeping the ephemeral state alive.

t: ZooKeeper & the Watch Mechanism — System Design
x: This is why proper session-timeout tuning is the #1 source of production incidents on ZooKeeper — too low and you flap, too high and you don't notice dead brokers fast enough. 4. ZAB — the consensus protocol under the hood ZooKeeper's writes go through ZAB — ZooKeeper Atomic Broadcast . It's Paxos-adjacent, purpose-built for the "one leader, ordered log of transactions" pattern. Every transaction gets a globally unique 64-bit zxid where the high 32 bits are the "epoch" (bumped on every leader election) and the low 32 bits are the counter within that epoch.

t: ZooKeeper & the Watch Mechanism — System Design
x: When a client writes, the leader (a) picks the next zxid, (b) sends a PROPOSE to every follower, (c) waits for ACKs from a quorum (majority), (d) sends COMMIT. Every follower fsyncs the proposal to its transaction log before ack'ing. That double disk sync is why writes cost a few milliseconds even on LAN — and why running the transaction log on a dedicated SSD is the classic ZooKeeper performance tune. When the leader dies, followers run a fast leader election (documented at < 200 ms), the new leader gathers highest-zxid state from the quorum, and the ensemble resumes.

t: ZooKeeper & the Watch Mechanism — System Design
x: Because of ZAB's ordering, every follower sees every commit in the same order , which is the mathematical foundation of the "single system image" guarantee. 5. The four canonical use-cases you'll be asked about Service discovery. Each instance creates an ephemeral child under /services/<name>/ . Consumers getChildren with a watch. Instance crashes ⇒ session expires ⇒ znode auto-deleted ⇒ child watch fires ⇒ consumer re-reads ⇒ dead instance dropped from routing. Latency from crash to reaction: session-timeout + ~1 network hop. Leader election. Each contender creates /election/n- with ephemeral+sequential. Everyone lists the children; whoever holds the lowest number is the leader.

t: ZooKeeper & the Watch Mechanism — System Design
x: Every non-leader watches only the znode immediately above theirs — this avoids the thundering herd where all N contenders wake up when the leader dies. When the current leader crashes, only one node's watch fires, that node checks if it's now the lowest, and if so becomes leader. Distributed lock. Same recipe as leader election — the "leader" is the lock holder. Release is deleting your znode. Fair-queued because the sequential suffix orders contenders in creation order. Reactive configuration. Store config as data on /config/<key> . Every app instance does getData with a watch on startup. On NodeDataChanged , re-read (which delivers the new bytes and re-arms the watch).

x: Config rollout from operator write to entire fleet updated: sub-second. 6. The mapping / reactive-update pattern explicitly Your question was specifically about "watches for mapping and reactive updates." Here's the canonical pattern: model the mapping as a znode subtree — say /routes/{tenantId} = "backendPool-3" — and let each edge process hold a persistent recursive watch (3.6+) on /routes . Any operator change (add tenant, move tenant to a different pool) is a single setData . ZooKeeper pushes the event to every watching edge in sub-second, and the edges re-read only the changed subtree to update their local routing map. No poll loop, no config reload restart, no external message bus.

x: If 10,000 clients all watch /services/order-api and one flap creates+deletes children repeatedly, the follower delivers 10,000 events per flap. Mitigation: partition the tree, use persistent recursive watches sparingly, and rate-limit flapping instances at the client layer. Session timeout tuning. Too low and a GC pause on the client causes false failover; too high and dead instances linger in your routing table. The sweet spot is usually 10-30 seconds. Log disk fsync latency. Sharing the transaction-log disk with anything else is the classic cause of degraded ZK. Always dedicate an SSD. Large znodes.

x: ZK is a coordination store, not a data store; bytes over ~a few KB slow snapshotting and replication. Split-brain. Impossible on paper (majority quorum), but wildly asymmetric AZ partitions have caused real outages. Deploy across ≥3 AZs. Consistency vs. availability ZooKeeper picks C over A in CAP terms. If the ensemble loses quorum (e.g., 2 of 3 nodes down), it stops accepting writes and even reads become stale by definition — the safe behavior. This makes it correct-first, and is why every operational playbook says "size your ensemble to survive the number of failures you actually plan for." See the CAP theorem page for the fuller reasoning. Interviewer follow-ups (with crisp answers) Q.

x: What exactly is an ephemeral znode? A. A znode whose lifetime is tied to the ZooKeeper session that created it. When the session ends — whether by clean close or timeout — the ensemble automatically deletes the znode and fires any watches on it. That's what makes ZooKeeper's service-discovery elegant: presence itself becomes a first-class primitive. Q. Watches are one-shot — how do you not miss changes? A. You re-arm the watch in the same call that reads the new data ( getData(path, watch=true) ).

t: ZooKeeper & the Watch Mechanism — System Design
x: ZooKeeper guarantees the watch event arrives before the client can observe the new state, and events are ordered globally per client, so if you always re-read on the event and re-set the watch, you can't miss an eventual state — you might collapse rapid consecutive changes into one, but that's usually fine because you're reading the current state each time anyway. If you truly need every change, use ZK 3.6+ persistent watches or move to a real event log (Kafka). Q. How does leader election work with sequential ephemeral znodes? A. Every contender creates /election/n- as EPHEMERAL_SEQUENTIAL , resulting in -0000000001 , -0000000002 , and so on. All read getChildren .

t: ZooKeeper & the Watch Mechanism — System Design
x: Whoever holds the lowest-numbered znode is leader. Non-leaders each set an exists watch on only the znode immediately below theirs — not on the whole list — so a leader crash wakes up exactly one node, avoiding a thundering herd. That node checks if it's now the lowest, and if so becomes leader. Q. Why odd ensemble sizes (3, 5, 7)? A. A 4-node ensemble tolerates only 1 failure (needs 3 for majority), same as a 3-node ensemble. But 4 nodes are more expensive and have more failure modes than 3 (twice the chance of any one being down). So even sizes are strictly worse than the odd size below them. Q. What replaced ZooKeeper for modern Kafka? A.

x: KRaft mode — Kafka's own built-in Raft implementation. It embeds a metadata quorum into the Kafka controller itself, eliminating the ZK dependency, reducing operational surface, and letting Kafka scale metadata to millions of partitions. Introduced in KIP-500, GA in Kafka 3.3, and default for new clusters from Kafka 3.5+. Q. Why not just use Redis for service discovery? A. Redis has no built-in "notify when this key changes" primitive that's session-safe (keyspace notifications are best-effort, fire-and-forget, and don't survive Redis restarts). Redis also isn't strongly consistent across replicas by default.

If you must rebuild/scan an array using O(1) extra space, two indices do it in one pass. Two flavours — know which one each problem wants: ① slow / fast (read–write) — both start at the left and move the same direction.

fast = read cursor that visits every element; slow = write cursor marking where the next kept element goes. When fast finds a keeper, copy it to slow and bump slow . At the end slow = new length. → remove / dedupe in place. ② opposite ends — one pointer at each end moving toward each other (or filling from the back). → merge / pair-sum on sorted data. #88 Merge Sorted Array Easy 🔑 Signals two sorted arrays · merge in place into nums1's spare tail opposite ends · from the back 💡 Bite Pointer i at end of nums1's data, j at end of nums2, write cursor k at the very end; copy the larger tail into k and step backwards.

⏱ O(m+n) time · O(1) space ⚠ Trick Fill back-to-front so you never overwrite unmerged nums1 values; leftover nums2 still gets copied. #27 Remove Element Easy 🔑 Signals remove all val in place · order may change · return new length slow / fast 💡 Bite fast reads every element; when it's a keeper ( ≠ val ) write it at slow and advance slow . slow ends as the new length. ⏱ O(n) time · O(1) space #26 Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array Easy 🔑 Signals sorted · keep each unique once, in place slow / fast 💡 Bite fast scans; write to slow only when nums[fast] != nums[slow-1] (differs from the last kept value), so duplicates are skipped.

⏱ O(n) time · O(1) space ⚠ Trick "Sorted" is what lets you compare only against the previous kept element instead of a whole set. #80 Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array II Medium 🔑 Signals sorted · keep each value at most twice, in place slow / fast + look-back 💡 Bite Write nums[fast] to slow only if slow < 2 or it differs from nums[slow-2] — peek 2 back. Generalises to "keep at most k" via slow-k . ⏱ O(n) time · O(1) space ⚠ Trick Compare against nums[slow-2] (the position), not a running count — works only because it's sorted. Greedy Trigger words: maximum / minimum , can you reach , "best so far" — and a locally-best choice is provably globally best.

The move: sweep once, keep a single running "best" (min price, farthest reach, running tank…) and make the obvious greedy choice at each step. Never look back, never store the whole history — that's what keeps it O(1) space. #121 Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock Easy 🔑 Signals one transaction · maximise profit track min-so-far 💡 Bite Sweep once keeping the cheapest price seen on the left; at each day candidate profit = price − minSoFar , keep the max.

⏱ O(n) time · O(1) space #122 Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock II Medium 🔑 Signals unlimited transactions · maximise profit sum the rises 💡 Bite Add every positive day-to-day delta price[i]−price[i-1] — catching every upward step equals the best multi-trade profit. ⏱ O(n) time · O(1) space #55 Jump Game Medium 🔑 Signals can you reach the last index? · jump lengths track farthest reach 💡 Bite Sweep keeping maxReach ; if an index is beyond maxReach you're stuck → false, else extend reach with i + nums[i] .

⏱ O(n) time · O(1) space #45 Jump Game II Medium 🔑 Signals minimum jumps to reach the end greedy BFS by levels 💡 Bite Each jump is a "level"; track current level's end and the farthest reachable. When i == currentEnd , jumps++ and set currentEnd = farthest . ⏱ O(n) time · O(1) space ⚠ Trick It's implicit BFS — the level boundary is what counts a jump. #134 Gas Station Medium 🔑 Signals circular route · find the unique start that completes the loop running tank + reset start 💡 Bite If total gas ≥ total cost a start exists; track running tank, and whenever it dips below 0 reset start to the next station and zero the tank.

⏱ O(n) time · O(1) space ⚠ Trick A failing segment can't contain the answer, so the station right after a deficit is the only candidate. Prefix / Suffix Product Trigger words: except self / "all elements but this one", or " no division " — each answer needs an aggregate of everything before and after an index. The move: two sweeps. Pass 1 (L→R) stores the running product of everything to the left ; pass 2 (R→L) multiplies in the running product of everything to the right . Left × Right = "all except me".

#238 Product of Array Except Self Medium 🔑 Signals product of all except self · no division · O(n) required prefix × suffix 💡 Bite Pass 1 L→R fills each slot with the product of everything to its left; pass 2 R→L multiplies in everything to its right (held in one scalar). ⏱ O(n) time · O(1) extra space (output reused) ⚠ Trick Division is banned because a single 0 breaks total/nums[i] ; prefix/suffix handles zeros for free. Boyer-Moore Voting Trigger words: more than n/2 times (strict majority) and a demand for O(1) space (no hashmap). The move: keep one candidate + a count . Matching element → count++, different → count−−, count hits 0 → adopt the current element as the new candidate.

The true majority can never be fully cancelled, so it survives. #169 Majority Element Easy 🔑 Signals element appearing more than n/2 times · want O(1) space vote & cancel 💡 Bite One candidate + count: same ++ , different −− , adopt new candidate when count==0 — majority outlasts all cancellations. ⏱ O(n) time · O(1) space ⚠ Trick Only valid because a strict majority is guaranteed; a HashMap count is the easy O(n)-space fallback. Array In-Place Tricks Trigger words: transform the array in place, O(1) space — reach for reversal tricks, cyclic replacement, or index-as-hash.

#189 Rotate Array Medium 🔑 Signals rotate right by k · in place, O(1) space triple reversal 💡 Bite Reverse the whole array → reverse first k → reverse the rest. Each element lands in its rotated spot. ⏱ O(n) time · O(1) space ⚠ Trick Do k %= n first; reversal avoids the GCD bookkeeping of cyclic swaps. Sorting / Counting Trigger words: an order statistic or a threshold over a distribution (k-th, "at least h with ≥ h") — sort then scan, or bucket-count in O(n).

#274 H-Index Medium 🔑 Signals largest h with ≥ h items ≥ h · answer bounded by n counting sort 💡 Bite Bucket citations (clamp > n into bucket n), scan high→low accumulating a running count; first index where running count ≥ index is the answer. ⏱ O(n) time · O(n) space — or O(n log n)/O(1) with sort+scan ⚠ Trick Clamp citations above n — they can't push h beyond n anyway. Design / Hashing Trigger words: an API needing O(1) insert + delete + random — pair a hash map (value → index) with a backing array. The move: the array gives O(1) random pick + O(1) append; the map gives O(1) locate.

To delete in O(1) without leaving a hole, swap the target with the last element, pop the last, and fix the moved element's index in the map . #380 Insert Delete GetRandom O(1) Medium 🔑 Signals insert + delete + getRandom all O(1) array + hashmap(val→idx) 💡 Bite Array for random/append, map for lookup; delete = swap target with last element, pop, and update the moved element's index in the map. ⏱ O(1) average per op · O(n) space ⚠ Trick The swap-with-last on delete is the whole point — and don't forget to repoint the moved element in the map. x: 🤖 What is an agent? 🧩 Chain of Thought 🔁 ReAct 🧑‍⚖️ HITL 🪞 Reflexion 🗺️ Plan-and-Execute 🌳 Tree of Thoughts 🧮 Self-Consistency 🛠️ Tool Use 📚 RAG 🚦 Router / Handoff 👥 Multi-Agent ⚖️ Compare 🗣️ Cheat sheet 🎯 The setup What actually makes a program "an agent"? An agent is an LLM wrapped in a loop that (1) can decide what to do next, (2) can call tools to affect the outside world, and (3) can observe the result and adjust. Take away the loop and you just have "call the model once." Take away tools and you have a chatbot. Take away the ability to observe results and you have a script that hallucinates its outputs.

t: Agent Design Patterns — AI Study Hub
x: Every pattern below is a recipe for that loop: what the LLM should be thinking about at each step (reasoning), who is allowed to act (the model, a human, another agent), how many paths are explored (one, N, a tree), and where the knowledge comes from (weights, retrieval, or a delegated specialist). Mental model. Pick a pattern the same way you pick a data structure: first understand the shape of the problem (deterministic vs open-ended, one-shot vs multi-step, cheap vs high-stakes), then pick the pattern whose trade-offs match. Composing patterns is normal — a production agent is usually ReAct + RAG + HITL + a Router, not one pattern in isolation.

x: 🧑‍🎓 The whole page in one paragraph An agent is a very literal assistant with a small toolbelt Picture a new intern who is brilliant at reading and writing but has never worked in your office. To make them useful, you have to teach them a few habits: Think out loud before answering hard questions — that's Chain of Thought . Try, look at what happened, try again instead of guessing in one shot — that's ReAct . Ask a grown-up before doing anything scary (sending money, deleting files) — that's Human-in-the-Loop . Grade your own work and redo the bad parts — that's Reflexion . Write a plan first, then follow it — that's Plan-and-Execute .

Give them a phone and a calculator — that's Tool Use / Function Calling . Let them look things up in the company wiki — that's RAG . Have a receptionist decide which specialist to call — that's a Router / Handoff . A whole team of interns coordinating — that's Multi-Agent . The rest of this page is those bullets, one section each, with a diagram of the loop, the trade-offs, and when to reach for it. 🧩 Foundational reasoning technique Chain of Thought (CoT) — how it works Origin: Wei et al.

t: Agent Design Patterns — AI Study Hub
x: (Google, 2022), Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models . On GSM8K math, adding six words — "Let's think step by step" — lifted PaLM-540B from ~18% to ~57% accuracy. That single result kicked off the entire modern reasoning-agent field. The core idea in one line Instead of asking the model to jump to the answer, ask it to write down the intermediate steps , one by one, and only then commit to the final answer. Because LLMs generate token-by-token, every step it writes becomes context for the next step — so the reasoning literally happens on the page. Layman: If I asked you "what's 23 × 47?" out loud, you'd probably fumble.

t: Agent Design Patterns — AI Study Hub
x: If I said "show your work," you'd write 23 × 47 = 23 × 40 + 23 × 7 = 920 + 161 = 1081 . CoT is the exact same trick — the model gets more right when it's allowed to write intermediate work, because each written step becomes an anchor for the next one. Two flavors Flavor What you write When to use Zero-shot CoT Just append "Let's think step by step." to the question. Quick, no examples handy, model is big enough (>60B). Few-shot CoT Give 2–8 example (question, reasoning, answer) triples before the real question. Higher accuracy, more control over the reasoning format, works on smaller models too.

t: Agent Design Patterns — AI Study Hub
x: Under the hood — why writing helps An LLM predicts the next token by attending to every previous token . When the model writes "step 1: I need to find the total revenue first," those tokens are now available as context for step 2. Without CoT, all the intermediate computation has to happen inside the fixed number of transformer layers between "read prompt" and "emit answer" — and there just aren't enough layers to do multi-step arithmetic in one forward pass. CoT turns depth (number of transformer layers) into width (number of output tokens), and the model has plenty of the latter.

Another leaves at 4:00 pm from the same station going 75 mph in the same direction. When does the second catch up? assistant: 6:00 pm. ← usually wrong // ✅ CHAIN OF THOUGHT (right most of the time) user: Same question. Step 3: Time to close 45 miles at 15 mph = 45 / 15 = 3 hours. Step 4: 4:00 pm + 3 h = 7:00 pm .

The paper that turned CoT from "think in a straight line" into "think, do, observe, think again." The core idea Loop through three token types: Thought (reasoning), Action (call a tool), Observation (what the tool returned). Repeat until the model emits a "Final Answer." The Thought steps are CoT. The Action steps make it an agent. Layman: Imagine solving a mystery. You think about a suspect, ask them a question, hear their answer, then think again about the next suspect based on what you just learned.

x: ReAct is Sherlock Holmes for LLMs — reason, act, observe, repeat. User question → Thought → Action(tool) → Observation → Thought → … → Final Answer Example trace — "Who is older, the CEO of OpenAI or the CEO of Anthropic?" Thought: I need the birth years of Sam Altman and Dario Amodei. Action: web_search("Sam Altman date of birth") Obs: "April 22, 1985" Thought: Altman = 1985. Now the other one. Action: web_search("Dario Amodei date of birth") Obs: "1983" Thought: Amodei is 1983, Altman 1985. 1983 < 1985 → Amodei is older. Final: Dario Amodei is older than Sam Altman. ✅ Why ReAct wins Reasoning grounds the action (" why am I calling this tool?").

Every mainstream agent framework — LangChain agents, AutoGen, CrewAI, LangGraph — implements ReAct under the hood. When someone says "an LLM agent," they usually mean ReAct. 🧑‍⚖️ Safety pattern Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) The core idea The agent runs autonomously up to a boundary .

x: A planner (usually a bigger, slower model) reads the goal and produces a full task list up front. An executor (often a cheaper, faster model) picks each task off the list and runs it — usually with a mini ReAct loop of its own. The planner can be called again mid-run to re-plan if the world changed. Layman: Imagine planning a wedding versus reacting to whatever the caterer just texted. Plan-and-Execute is the wedding planner writing the whole timeline on Monday, then the assistants ticking boxes Tuesday through Saturday. ReAct alone is more like "figure out lunch when it's noon" — fine for short trips, bad for weddings.

Focus: executor sees only "task 4 of 12" instead of the whole conversation, so it doesn't lose the plot. Auditability: the plan is a document — you can inspect and edit it before running. Modern flavors: LLMCompiler (Kim et al. 2023) has the planner emit a DAG so independent tasks run in parallel. ReWOO (Xu et al. 2023) has the planner emit tasks with placeholders that get filled in as tools return — cutting tool-call round-trips. 🌳 Search-based reasoning Tree of Thoughts (ToT) Origin: Yao et al.

The core idea Chain-of-Thought is a path — one linear sequence of reasoning steps. Tree-of-Thoughts is search — at each step, the agent generates multiple candidate next steps , scores them (with the same or a different LLM as evaluator), keeps the promising ones, prunes the rest, and expands the best. It's classic BFS/DFS with the LLM as both the successor function and the heuristic. Layman: Chess.

Problem → Generate k next-steps → Score each → Keep top-m → Expand each → Repeat ✅ When ToT is worth the cost Puzzles with a clear "is this branch dead" signal (Sudoku, 24, crosswords). Planning under constraints with pruning heuristics available. When ~10× more compute is acceptable for >3× accuracy. ⚠️ Skip ToT when No good scoring function — you can't tell branches apart.

If seven of them say 1,081 — even though each of them took a slightly different route to get there — you're much more sure the answer is 1,081. x: Temperature is the chef's mood. At low temperature the chef always picks the "safest" ingredient — same note gets almost the same dish every time. At high temperature the chef gets creative and mixes ingredients that could work — you get variety, sometimes brilliance, sometimes nonsense. Neither is right or wrong; it's a knob for the kind of kitchen you want. Non-determinism is the queue. Even if two people slip identical notes through, the exact tables around them change the way the chef batches orders, and the tiny arithmetic differences (adding numbers in a different order gives slightly different results on a GPU) can push the chef to grab a slightly different first ingredient.

Structured Output is handing the chef a fixed plate ("serve exactly on this bento box, no extra bowls") so the waiter downstream knows where the rice goes.

t: Prompt LLMs Reliably — AI System Design (Session 1)
x: Every current transformer-based LLM (Claude, GPT, Gemini, Llama, Mistral, DeepSeek) does the same eight things. Tokenize. The input string is split by a BPE/tiktoken/SentencePiece vocabulary into integer token IDs. "Hello, world!" → typically 3–5 tokens depending on the vocab. Every provider has a different tokenizer; costs are billed per token. Embed. Each token ID is looked up in an embedding matrix, producing a d_model -dimensional vector (e.g. 4096 for Llama-3-8B, 12288 for GPT-4 class). Positional information is added. Prefill (parallel). The whole prompt is pushed through N transformer layers in parallel . This is compute-bound (matmul-heavy) — it's the fastest per-token phase.

t: Prompt LLMs Reliably — AI System Design (Session 1)
x: The KV-cache for each layer is built and saved. Prefill dominates time-to-first-token . Attention scoring. Each layer runs multi-head self-attention: for every position, compute query·key T , softmax, weighted-sum with values. The KV-cache lets subsequent decode steps skip re-computing keys/values for earlier tokens. LM head. The final hidden state of the last position is multiplied by the un-embedding matrix (usually tied to the embedding matrix) to produce a logit vector of size vocab_size (~100k–200k). Sample.

t: Prompt LLMs Reliably — AI System Design (Session 1)
x: Logits are scaled by 1/temperature , passed through softmax to get a probability distribution, optionally truncated by top-k / top-p / repetition penalty, then a single token is drawn. This is where non-determinism enters. Decode (autoregressive loop). The sampled token is appended, its embedding is pushed through the layers, KV-cache is extended by one position, LM head runs again — and repeat. Decode is memory-bandwidth-bound (each step reads the whole KV-cache); it dominates inter-token latency . Stop. A stop token ( <|end_of_text|> , </s> ), a max-tokens cap, or a stop sequence provided by the caller ends the loop. The token stream is de-tokenized and returned.

x: KV-cache is why streaming feels instant. Without it, each decode step would re-attend to the whole context — O(n²) per step. With it, each step is O(n) memory read + O(1) new attention scores. On a 128k-context model with a 100k-token prompt, the KV-cache is often 20–60 GB — which is why memory bandwidth is the decode-time bottleneck. Prefill vs decode economics. Prefill: batch-friendly, compute-bound, ~5-10× tokens/s per H100. Decode: hard to batch across users because each has a different sequence, memory-bound, ~30-100 tokens/s per user. Continuous batching (vLLM's PagedAttention, TensorRT-LLM in-flight batching) tries to blur the line.

x: 🎲 Why LLM output is non-deterministic (even at temperature = 0) Every engineer building on LLMs eventually runs the same experiment: same prompt, same model, same seed, same temperature = 0 — and gets two different outputs. There are five independent causes, and only one of them is the sampler. 1. Batch composition Providers batch your request with other users' requests to amortise GPU cost. The batch dimension changes the shape of every matmul, which changes the order in which floating-point additions happen, which — because floating-point addition is not associative — produces slightly different logits. A 1e-7 difference near a near-tie logit can flip which token wins argmax .

t: Prompt LLMs Reliably — AI System Design (Session 1)
x: You never control the batch you land in. 2. GPU kernel non-associativity CUDA reduction kernels (used inside every attention softmax and layernorm) sum many values in parallel using tree reductions. The exact tree the runtime picks depends on tensor shapes, stream schedule, and even the fill of the SMs at that instant. (a + b) + c ≠ a + (b + c) at float precision. Two identical inputs on the same GPU can trace different reduction orders and produce different bits. 3. Mixture-of-Experts routing Modern MoE models (Mixtral, DeepSeek-V3, GPT-4-class routing, Grok) route each token to a small subset of "expert" FFN blocks. The router is a small gate network — but with load-balancing constraints.

x: If a token is on the boundary between experts and the batch tips the load slightly, the router picks a different expert. Different expert = different weights = different logits. 4. Speculative decoding & system-level optimizations Some backends run a small "draft" model that proposes several tokens ahead, then a large model verifies. If the draft loses in one place it doesn't lose in another, the accepted path can differ. Similarly, prefix caching, dynamic quantization (INT8/FP8), and even NVLink topology can influence which numerical path a request takes. 5. Sampler (the small one) Even at T=0 , ties in argmax are broken by an implementation-specific rule (first index, random, seeded).

The idea: instead of asking the model for the answer, ask it to show its working . On GSM8K arithmetic word problems, PaLM-540B with 8-shot CoT hit 56.9% — up from 17.9% direct-answer, a +39 point jump . The lift only appears above a critical model scale (~60B parameters in the original paper); below that, CoT can actively hurt. Without CoT (direct) Q: Roger has 5 tennis balls. The answer is 11. Same model → ~57% on GSM8K. The reasoning trace changes the distribution. How it works. The model is a next-token predictor. If the next token has to be a final answer, it must "guess" all intermediate arithmetic in one step. If the next tokens can be reasoning, each step conditions on the ones before it — the model does one small inference at a time, which is what it was trained to do well. Zero-shot vs few-shot CoT. Self-Consistency (Wang et al., 2022) The follow-up: since CoT is a sampling process, why trust one sample? Sample N reasoning paths at T > 0 , then majority-vote the final answer . On GSM8K with PaLM-540B, CoT alone was 56.9%; CoT + Self-Consistency @ N=40 was 74.4% — a further +17.5 points. Why it works. Wrong reasoning paths tend to fail in different ways; correct reasoning tends to converge. Voting kills the tail.
